<a id="st1-bhargava-parametrization-of-quartic-rings"></a>

### 1.20 Bhargava: pairs of ternary quadratic forms parametrize quartic rings with cubic resolvents

There is a canonical bijection between GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits on W(Z) = (Sym^2 Z^3 tensor Z^2)* and isomorphism classes of pairs (Q, R) with Q a quartic ring and R a cubic resolvent ring of Q; it sends (A, B) to (Q(A,B), R(A,B)) and a pair (Q, R) to the pair of ternary quadratic forms representing the resolvent map phi : Q/Z -> R/Z in bases. It preserves discriminants: Disc(A, B) = Disc(Q) = Disc(R). In based form: every pair (A, B) is the resolvent pair of a based quartic ring and cubic resolvent, unique up to isomorphisms preserving the chosen quotient bases modulo scalar translates, and changing the bases realizes exactly the GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbit.

**Hypotheses.** Base Z (the same proof works over Z_p and F_p with the appendix's definition).; Cubic resolvents in the sense of quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent; degenerate pairs included.; A cubic resolvent includes its quadratic map and orientation. Keeping only the isomorphism classes of the two underlying rings can identify different resolvent data. Based uniqueness refers to bases of Q/Z and C/Z; arbitrary lifts can differ by scalars, and exact equality of lifted bases requires normality.

**Dependencies.** [The quartic ring Q(A,B) and cubic resolvent ring R(A,B) of a pair](#st1-quartic-ring-of-a-pair) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-of-a-pair`); [Quartic rings and their cubic resolvent rings](#st1-quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent`); [Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form](#st1-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); [Delone-Faddeev: GL2(R)-classes of binary cubic forms parametrize cubic rings](#st1-delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Theorem 1, printed p. 1330. The theorem. [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Proposition 13, printed p. 1345. Discriminant preservation.

**Proof route.**

1. (A,B) |-> (Q(A,B), R(A,B)) is a based cubic resolvent (quartic-ring-of-a-pair).
2. Conversely, for a based cubic resolvent the identity (12) determines the structure constants of the normal basis as in (21)-(23), so Q is Q(A,B) (HCL III Proposition 10), and (34) determines R as R(A,B) by Delone-Faddeev (Proposition 11; in the degenerate case by the appendix's definition).
3. The two constructions are mutually inverse on based objects; changing bases of Q/Z and R/Z by (g_3, g_2) acts on (A,B) by the action of pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms, so isomorphism classes correspond to orbits.
4. Discriminants: quartic-ring-of-a-pair.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Z^4 corresponds to the orbit of a pair of conics through four points of P^2(Q) in general position, with R = Z^3.
- The trivial ring Z + Z x_1 + Z x_2 + Z x_3 (all products 0) corresponds to the pairs spanning a space of dimension <= 1.

**Interface qualification.** The suggested file states existence and uniqueness up to scalar translates of lifted basis vectors. It omits the former orbit iff based-existence assertion: that assertion forgot the resolvent map and orientation, so it was too strong. The full orbit bijection requires bundled resolvent data and compatible isomorphisms as specified in the statement.

<a id="st1-existence-and-number-of-cubic-resolvents"></a>

### 1.21 Every quartic ring has a cubic resolvent; primitive (in particular maximal) quartic rings have exactly one

(a) Every quartic ring Q has at least one cubic resolvent ring. (b) The number of cubic resolvent rings of Q (with Q fixed: isomorphisms of resolvent data must induce the identity on Q) depends only on the content n = ct(Q) and equals sigma(n) = sum_{d | n} d, the number of index-n sublattices of Z^2. (c) In particular a primitive quartic ring (content 1), hence every maximal quartic ring and every ring of integers of a quartic field, has a unique cubic resolvent ring up to isomorphism, namely the cubic invariant ring R_inv(Q). (d) Two pairs give the same quartic ring iff they are related by GL3(Z) x GL2^{+-1}(Q).

**Hypotheses.** Q nontrivial for (b)-(d) (the trivial ring has infinite content).; Maximal quartic rings of nonzero discriminant are Gorenstein and have content 1.; The count sigma(n) retains the fixed quartic ring Q. Quotienting also by Aut(Q), as in the unbased GL3 x GL2 orbit classification, can identify these resolvent structures and changes the count.

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava: pairs of ternary quadratic forms parametrize quartic rings with cubic resolvents](#st1-bhargava-parametrization-of-quartic-rings) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/bhargava-parametrization-of-quartic-rings`); [The quartic ring Q(A,B) and cubic resolvent ring R(A,B) of a pair](#st1-quartic-ring-of-a-pair) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-of-a-pair`); [Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form](#st1-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); [Cubic rings, their discriminant, and maximality at a prime](#st1-cubic-ring) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-ring`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Corollaries 4-5, printed p. 1333. Parts (a)-(c). [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Lemma 17, printed p. 1349. The counting lemma. [P/odorney-small-rank-2016](#source-p-odorney-small-rank-2016), Corollary 8.5 and Example 8.10. Explicit distinction between resolvents over the fixed ring and orbits under its automorphisms; for Z + 2 Z⁴ the counts are three and one respectively.

**Proof route.**

1. The structure constants of a normal basis of Q determine the fifteen lambda^{ij}_{kl} by (21), and associativity gives the Pluecker syzygies (27) (HCL III Section 3.8).
2. Lemma 16: fifteen constants satisfying (27), not all zero, are the lambda-invariants of a unique SL2(C)-orbit, which contains an integral point when the constants are integers (elementary divisors).
3. With a fixed normal basis of Q, the fifteen lambda-invariants are fixed. Their nonzero gcd n specifies an orientation of the pencil. The relevant SL2(Z)-orbits, not full GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits, correspond to index-n sublattices in the maximal integral pencil lattice, with the induced orientation. Hermite normal form counts these as Σ_(d|n) d. Arbitrarily oriented bases would produce both lambda and −lambda, so the orientation is retained throughout.
4. Apply the based parametrization and then forget the chosen basis of the fixed ring Q, transporting it by the identity of Q. This counts resolvent structures over Q without quotienting by its automorphisms. The gcd of lambda is ct(Q) by (21)–(23).
5. Maximal rings: a ring Z + nQ' with n > 1 is not maximal (contained in Q'), so maximal rings are primitive.

**Acceptance checks.**

- A maximal quartic order has exactly one resolvent.
- Z + 2 Z^4 (content 2) has sigma(2) = 3 cubic resolvents.

<a id="st1-maximality-of-quartic-rings-at-p"></a>

### 1.22 Maximality of Q(A,B) at p in terms of the lambda-invariants

If a quartic ring Q is not maximal at p, there is a Z-basis <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> of Q such that Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z alpha_2 + Z alpha_3, or Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z(alpha_2/p) + Z alpha_3, or Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z(alpha_2/p) + Z(alpha_3/p) is a ring. For Q = Q(A, B) these read, after a GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-change of the pair: (i) lambda^{11}_{22}, lambda^{11}_{23}, lambda^{11}_{33}, lambda^{12}_{13} = 0 mod p and lambda^{11}_{12}, lambda^{11}_{13} = 0 mod p^2; (ii) lambda^{11}_{13}, lambda^{11}_{23}, lambda^{12}_{13}, lambda^{12}_{23}, lambda^{13}_{22}, lambda^{22}_{23} = 0 mod p and lambda^{11}_{12}, lambda^{11}_{22}, lambda^{12}_{22} = 0 mod p^2; (iii) all lambda = 0 mod p. Q(A, B) is maximal at p iff (A, B) is in the set U_p of pairs for which none of (i)-(iii) can be achieved; the U_p are defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; quartic rings of nonzero discriminant for the geometric reading of (i), (ii) (double intersection points, double lines) in HCL III Section 4.2.

**Dependencies.** [The quartic ring Q(A,B) and cubic resolvent ring R(A,B) of a pair](#st1-quartic-ring-of-a-pair) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-of-a-pair`); [Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form](#st1-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); [Cubic rings, their discriminant, and maximality at a prime](#st1-cubic-ring) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-ring`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Lemma 22, printed p. 1356. The lemma. [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Section 4.2, printed p. 1357. The lambda conditions.

**Proof route.**

1. Choose a finite p-primary overring Q′ and let m ≥ 1 be minimal with p^m Q′ contained in Q. Then S = Q + p^(m−1)Q′ is a proper overring and pS is contained in Q (expand products to see that S is a ring). Since 1 is primitive in these finite Z-algebras, Smith normal form on Q/Z inside S/Z gives a basis containing 1 and the three displayed possibilities. This direct construction replaces the incomplete exponent-reduction iteration in the printed proof of HCL III Lemma 22.
2. Translate the three shapes into congruences on the lambda through the explicit c^k_ij (quartic-ring-of-a-pair).
3. Conversely each of (i)-(iii) exhibits the overring, so Q(A,B) is not maximal.
4. When normalizing a Smith basis after the overring has been chosen, closure of the divided basis implies that each scalar translation of alpha_i used to impose the normal-basis convention is divisible by p^{e_i}. Thus the translation preserves the scaled overring lattice; arbitrary integral translations would not suffice.

**Acceptance checks.**

- A pair with p | all coefficients gives a nonmaximal Q (case (iii)).
- Pairs with Disc(A,B) not divisible by p^2 give Q maximal at p.

<a id="st1-splitting-types-of-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms"></a>

### 1.23 Splitting symbols of pairs and the structure of Q(A,B)/p

For a pair (A, B) over Z (or Z_p, F_p) whose conics A = 0, B = 0 meet in four points of P^2 over F_p-bar counted with multiplicity, let ((A,B), p) = (f_1^{e_1} f_2^{e_2} ...) record the residue degrees and multiplicities of the intersection points. Then (A,B) is in T_p(sigma) iff Q(A,B)/(p) = F_{p^{f_1}}[t_1]/(t_1^{e_1}) + ..., except for sigma = (1^4), where Q(A,B)/p may also be F_2[x,y]/(x^2, xy + y^2), F_p[x,y]/(x^2, y^2) or F_p[x,y]/(xy, x^2 + n y^2). In particular Disc(A,B) is nonzero mod p iff the conics meet in four distinct points iff Q(A,B)/p is etale over F_p; for maximal Q(A,B), ((A,B), p) is the splitting type of p.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; the two conics have no common component, so their intersection is zero-dimensional of length four. This allows discriminant-zero and nonreduced intersections; it does not require four distinct geometric points.

**Dependencies.** [The quartic ring Q(A,B) and cubic resolvent ring R(A,B) of a pair](#st1-quartic-ring-of-a-pair) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-of-a-pair`); [Nonzero discriminant corresponds to etale cubic algebras](#st1-nondegenerate-forms-and-etale-cubic-algebras) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/nondegenerate-forms-and-etale-cubic-algebras`); `mathlib:Algebra.Etale`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl3-2004](#source-p-bhargava-hcl3-2004), Section 4.1, (36)-(37), printed p. 1353. The statement.

**Proof route.**

1. The ring Q(A,B)/p depends only on the GL3(F_p) x GL2(F_p)-orbit of (A,B) mod p (base change of quartic-ring-of-a-pair).
2. Write the multiplication table at one representative of each of the eleven orbit types (HCL III Section 4.1, 'direct calculation').
3. Nonzero discriminant mod p: four distinct intersection points, and Disc(Q/p) = Disc(A,B) mod p is nonzero, so Q/p is etale.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Four F_p-rational points in general position give F_p^4.
- A double line in the pencil gives one of the non-reduced types (over-ramified cases).

<a id="st1-quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms"></a>

### 1.24 Quadruples of quinary alternating 2-forms and the GL4 x SL5 action

For a commutative ring R, V(R) = R^4 tensor wedge^2 R^5 is the module of quadruples A = (A_1, ..., A_4) of alternating 5 x 5 matrices over R (recorded by their entries above the diagonal). The group GL4(R) x SL5(R) acts by (g_4, g_5) . A = (sum_s (g_4)_{rs} g_5 A_s g_5^T)_r. The 4 x 4 sub-Pfaffian map Q(X) = (Q_1(X), ..., Q_5(X)), Q_i(X) = (-1)^{i-1} Pf(X with row and column i deleted), is a quadratic covariant: X Q(X) = 0 for every alternating X, and Q(cX) = c^2 Q(X). The SL5-invariants {ijklm} = Q(A_i, A_j)^T A_k Q(A_l, A_m) (Q(.,.) the symmetric bilinear form with Q(X,X) = 2Q(X)) determine the multiplication table of the quintic ring R(A); the fundamental relative invariant is the degree-40 discriminant Disc(A), with Disc((g_4,g_5) . A) = det(g_4)^10 Disc(A). Thus it is invariant under GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), but is generally only a relative invariant over other base rings. The same matrix formula extends to GL4(R) x GL5(R), with relative discriminant weight det(g_4)^10 det(g_5)^16. Over Z this has the same orbits as GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), since replacing a determinant-minus-one g_5 by −g_5 leaves its congruence action unchanged. Over a field the full rational orbit for minimality uses this extended group.

**Hypotheses.** The discriminant is not written out as a polynomial (degree 40); it is characterized in HCL IV Section 3 and equals Disc R(A).; The displayed GL4 x SL5 action can have a nontrivial kernel away from Z: (zeta^(-2) I_4, zeta I_5) acts trivially whenever zeta^5 = 1. Do not identify its stabilizers or rational orbits with those of the effective quotient without accounting for this kernel and descent.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup`; `mathlib:Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl4-2008](#source-p-bhargava-hcl4-2008), Theorem 1 and Section 4, printed pp. 54 and 66. The sub-Pfaffian covariant. [P/bhargava-hcl4-2008](#source-p-bhargava-hcl4-2008), (18), printed p. 67. The brackets.

**API.**

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple` (structure): Quadruples of alternating 5 x 5 matrices by upper-triangular entries.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.toMatrix` (projection): The r-th alternating matrix.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.ofMatrices` (constructor): The quadruple with given matrices (upper triangle).
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.instMulAction` (instance): The GL4 x SL5 action.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.subPfaffian` (data): The signed 4 x 4 sub-Pfaffians.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.toMatrix_transpose` (characterisation): Each matrix is alternating: A_r^T = -A_r.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.subPfaffian_smul_scalar` (relation): Q(cX) = c^2 Q(X).
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.mulVec_subPfaffian` (relation): X Q(X) = 0.

**Checks.**

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.test_toMatrix_diag` (degenerate): The diagonal entries of toMatrix are 0.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.test_ofMatrices_toMatrix` (characterisation): ofMatrices (toMatrix A) = A.
- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.test_subPfaffian_standard` (computation): For the alternating matrix with x_12 = x_34 = 1 (0-indexed (1,2), (3,4)) the sub-Pfaffian vector is (1, 0, 0, 0, 0).

**Proof route.**

1. Define the entries, the matrices, the action and the sub-Pfaffians explicitly; the action axioms are matrix identities.
2. X Q(X) = 0: the Pfaffian expansion of the 6 x 6 alternating matrix with a repeated row (checked by expansion; verified symbolically for the sign convention (-1)^{i-1}).
3. The invariants P^+ and P^- of HCL IV (11)-(14) and the brackets {ijklm} (18) are polynomial SL5-invariants of degree 5.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For the matrix with x_12 = x_34 = 1 (0-indexed entries (1,2), (3,4)) the sub-Pfaffian vector is (1, 0, 0, 0, 0).
- The diagonal of each A_r is zero.

### 1.25 Bhargava: quadruples of quinary alternating forms parametrize quintic rings with sextic resolvents

(a) There is a canonical bijection between GL4(Z) x SL5(Z)-orbits on V(Z) = Z^4 tensor wedge^2 Z^5 and isomorphism classes of pairs (R, S) with R a quintic ring and S a sextic resolvent ring of R (HCL IV Theorems 1 and 8; for nondegenerate pairs Disc(A) = Disc(R) = (1/16) Disc(S)^{1/3}); the sextic resolvent is defined by HCL IV Definitions 10-11 (a sextic ring S with a Z-linear map phi : R/Z -> wedge^2(S/Z) such that R(phi) = R and S(phi) = S). (b) Every quintic ring is R(A) for some A, so every quintic ring has a sextic resolvent (Theorem 17, Corollary 18). (c) If R is maximal, A is unique up to GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), so a maximal quintic ring has a unique sextic resolvent (Theorem 17, Corollary 19). (d) The classical resolvent map of Cayley is 4 times the sub-Pfaffian covariant (Theorem 9).

**Hypotheses.** The multiplication tables of R(A) (HCL IV Section 4, (16)-(25)) and S(A) (Section 6) are part of the statement; they are specified by the source and not re-derived here.

**Dependencies.** [Quadruples of quinary alternating 2-forms and the GL4 x SL5 action](#st1-quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms`); [Cubic rings, their discriminant, and maximality at a prime](#st1-cubic-ring) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-ring`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl4-2008](#source-p-bhargava-hcl4-2008), Theorem 1, printed p. 54. Part (a). [P/bhargava-hcl4-2008](#source-p-bhargava-hcl4-2008), Theorem 2 and Corollary 3, printed p. 55. Parts (b)-(c).

**Proof route.**

1. From A, Lemma 4 expresses the determinants built from conjugates through the invariants P^+, P^- and the brackets {ijklm}, which determines the normalized structure constants of R(A) (Section 4) and of S(A) (Section 6).
2. The fundamental map g : wedge^2 S~ -> R~ realizes the inverse (Sections 5 and 7), giving Theorem 8 for nondegenerate elements; the appendix-style Definitions 10-11 extend it to all elements (Section 9).
3. Existence and uniqueness for maximal rings: the invariant theory of Section 10 (Theorem 12 and Lemmas 13-16) constructs an integral A with prescribed structure constants and shows uniqueness when R is maximal (minimal integral model), giving Theorem 17 and Corollaries 18-19.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Z^5 corresponds to the quadruple whose sub-Pfaffians vanish at five points of P^3 in general position.
- A maximal quintic ring has exactly one sextic resolvent.

**Interface qualification.** Statement-level node: the proof steps summarize HCL IV Sections 3-11, which are not decomposed into lemma nodes here (see the coverage remaining list). The suggested Lean file omits the statement because it needs the multiplication tables of R(A) and S(A).

<a id="st1-maximality-of-quintic-rings-at-p"></a>

### 1.26 Maximality of R(A) at p is a congruence condition U_p on quadruples

For A in V(Z), R(A) is maximal iff A is in U_p for every prime p, where U_p is the union of the seventeen sets U_p(sigma) of elements of splitting type sigma whose ring is maximal at p (defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2); R(A) is maximal exactly when A is a minimal integral model (smallest nonzero absolute discriminant in its GL4(Q) x GL5(Q)-orbit meeting V(Z)).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; nondegenerate A.; Minimality is in the full GL4(Q) x GL5(Q) orbit and orders by absolute discriminant. Restricting to GL4(Q) x SL5(Q) only allows discriminants to scale by tenth powers and can miss an overring of index p.

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava: quadruples of quinary alternating forms parametrize quintic rings with sextic resolvents](#st1-bhargava-parametrization-of-quintic-rings) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/bhargava-parametrization-of-quintic-rings`); [Quadruples of quinary alternating 2-forms and the GL4 x SL5 action](#st1-quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms`); [Cubic rings, their discriminant, and maximality at a prime](#st1-cubic-ring) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-ring`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-hcl4-2008](#source-p-bhargava-hcl4-2008), Theorem 21, printed p. 92. The statement (the density belongs to ST.3).

**Proof route.**

1. For a proper finite p-primary overring R′, choose m ≥ 1 minimal with p^m R′ contained in R. Then S = R + p^(m−1)R′ is a proper overring with pS contained in R. Smith normal form on R/Z inside S/Z gives four shapes, of indices p,p²,p³,p⁴, dividing a nonempty subset of the four nonconstant basis vectors by p. Ring closure is detected by structure-constant congruences modulo p². Use the polynomial multiplication table and normalize determinant units before lifting elementary basis changes from Z/p²Z to Z. Section 12 supplies the splitting-type decomposition; it does not state the erroneous three-shape index-p assertion.
2. Theorem 12 and Lemma 16 (minimal integral models) give maximality iff minimality.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Elements with p^2 not dividing Disc(A) are in U_p.

**Interface qualification.** Statement-level node, as for the parametrization; not stated in the suggested Lean file.

<a id="st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms"></a>

### 1.27 The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers

Let R be a commutative ring and V(R) the binary quartic forms over R (ST.0), with the twisted action gamma * f = (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma) of GL2(R) (ST.0), on which the centre acts trivially. It therefore induces an action of PGL2(R) = GL2(R)/centre (Mathlib's Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup). The invariants I and J are PGL2(R)-invariant, so the orbit space PGL2(R)\V(R) maps to R x R; its fibre over (I, J) is the set of orbits of forms with invariants I, J. The stabilizer of f is Stab_{PGL2(R)}(f). Over Z (and any ring whose units have square 1) the PGL2-orbits are the orbits of GL2 under plain substitution.

**Hypotheses.** The twist exponent is -2, so that I and J are invariant (ST.0 records the untwisted weights (det gamma)^4, (det gamma)^6).; PGL2 is the quotient by the full centre (scalar matrices), not PSL2.

**Dependencies.** [Binary quartic forms, the GL₂ action by linear substitution and the twisted PGL₂ action](#st0-binary-quartic-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-form`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`); [Relative invariance: I(γ·f) = (det γ)⁴I(f) and J(γ·f) = (det γ)⁶J(f)](#st0-relative-invariance-of-i-and-j) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/relative-invariance-of-i-and-j`); `mathlib:Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup`; `mathlib:Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup.mk_surjective`; `mathlib:Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.center_eq_range_scalar`; `mathlib:MulAction.stabilizer`; `mathlib:MulAction.orbitRel`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 2.6, (32), printed p. 16. The action and its descent to PGL2. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 2.6, printed p. 16. Integral orbits.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.instPGLAction` (instance): The PGL2(R)-action induced by the twisted action.
- `BinaryQuartic.pgl_smul_mk` (simp): mk gamma . f = twistedSMul gamma f.
- `BinaryQuartic.invI_pgl_smul` (relation): I is PGL2-invariant.
- `BinaryQuartic.invJ_pgl_smul` (relation): J is PGL2-invariant.
- `BinaryQuartic.PGLOrbit` (data): The orbit space PGL2(R)\V(R).
- `BinaryQuartic.PGLOrbit.invariants` (projection): The invariants (I, J) of an orbit.
- `BinaryQuartic.pgl_orbits_eq_gl_orbits_int` (compatibility): Over Z, PGL2-orbits are GL2(Z)-orbits under plain substitution.

**Checks.**

- `BinaryQuartic.test_pgl_scalar_trivial` (degenerate): The class of a scalar matrix acts trivially.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_pgl_diag` (computation): diag(2, 1) sends (a,b,c,d,e) to (4a, 2b, c, d/2, e/4).
- `BinaryQuartic.test_neg_not_equivalent` (non-example): x^3 y - y^4 is not PGL2(Q)-equivalent to its negative (J changes sign), although both have the same I.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the action through a set-theoretic section of GL2(R) -> PGL2(R); well-definedness is ST.0's twistedSMul_scalar (scalars act trivially); the action axioms follow from twistedSMul_mul.
2. Invariance of I and J: the twisted action multiplies I by (det gamma)^4 (det gamma)^{-4} (ST.0 relative invariance).
3. Over Z: det gamma = +-1 so the twist is trivial and the orbits agree with those of the plain action.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Scalars act trivially.
- diag(2, 1) in PGL2(Q) sends (a, b, c, d, e) to (4a, 2b, c, d/2, e/4).
- x^3 y - y^4 (J = 27) and its negative (J = -27) lie in different orbits.

**Consumers.** ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e — orbits of soluble forms with given invariants parametrize E(K)/2E(K); ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion — the stabilizer is identified with E(K)[2]; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp — orbits of PGL2(Z) on V_Z are counted with weights 1/#Stab; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three — Selmer elements are counted as PGL2(Q)-classes of integral forms

<a id="st1-soluble-binary-quartic-forms"></a>

### 1.28 Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms

A binary quartic form f over a field K is K-soluble if z^2 = f(x, y) has a solution with x, y, z in K and (x, y) != (0, 0). Over a number field K, f is (everywhere) locally soluble if f is K_v-soluble for every completion K_v: at every finite place (Mathlib's adicCompletion at each height-one prime of O_K) and at every infinite place (Mathlib's InfinitePlace.Completion). Over Q this means R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every prime p; an integral form is locally soluble if its rational form is. The rational-linear-factor locus consists of forms with a zero in P^1(Q); this is only part of the polynomial-reducible locus, which also includes products of two quadratic factors. Ordinary irreducible forms have a != 0 and f(X, 1) irreducible over Q. Solubility is invariant under PGL2(K), stable under field extension, and holds whenever f has a zero in P^1(K) or its leading coefficient is a square.

**Hypotheses.** (x, y) != (0, 0) is required; z may be 0.; When char K ≠ 2, for forms of nonzero discriminant, K-solubility is equivalent to the genus-one curve z^2 = f(x, y) having a K-point, but the definition does not refer to curves.

**Dependencies.** [Binary quartic forms, the GL₂ action by linear substitution and the twisted PGL₂ action](#st0-binary-quartic-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-form`); `mathlib:IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.adicCompletion`; `mathlib:NumberField.InfinitePlace.Completion`; `mathlib:NumberField.InfinitePlace`; `mathlib:Padic`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 3.1, printed p. 23. K-solubility. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 3.1, printed p. 23. Local solubility over Q.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.IsSoluble` (data): K-solubility.
- `BinaryQuartic.IsEverywhereLocallySoluble` (data): Solubility over every completion of a number field.
- `BinaryQuartic.IsLocallySolubleQ` (data): A rational form: R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for all p.
- `BinaryQuartic.IsLocallySoluble` (data): An integral form is locally soluble: its rational form is IsLocallySolubleQ.
- `BinaryQuartic.HasRationalLinearFactor` (data): An integral form has a zero in P¹(Q), the rational-linear-factor locus corresponding to the identity Selmer class. It is not the whole polynomial-reducible locus.
- `BinaryQuartic.IsIrreducibleOverQ` (data): An integral form is irreducible over Q (a != 0 and f(X,1) irreducible).
- `BinaryQuartic.isLocallySoluble_iff` (characterisation): An integral form is locally soluble iff it is R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every prime p.
- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_pgl_smul` (relation): Solubility is PGL2(K)-invariant.
- `BinaryQuartic.IsSoluble.map` (functoriality): Solubility is preserved by field homomorphisms.
- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_of_eval_eq_zero` (constructor): A zero in P^1(K) gives solubility.
- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_of_isSquare_a` (constructor): A square leading coefficient gives solubility.
- `BinaryQuartic.isLocallySolubleQ_iff` (characterisation): Unfolding of local solubility over Q.

**Checks.**

- `BinaryQuartic.test_negative_definite_insoluble` (non-example): -x^4 - y^4 is not R-soluble.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_linear_factor_soluble` (computation): x^3 y + y^4 is Q-soluble (zero at (1, 0)).
- `BinaryQuartic.test_locally_not_globally` (non-example): 2x^4 - 34y^4 (Lind-Reichardt) is locally soluble over Q but not Q-soluble.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_hasRationalLinearFactor` (computation): x^3 y + y^4 has the rational linear factor y and is locally soluble.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_reducible_without_linear_factor` (non-example): (x²+y²)(x²+2y²) = x⁴+3x²y²+2y⁴ is reducible over Q but has no rational projective zero.

**Proof route.**

1. PGL2-invariance: if f(x,y) = z², then its twisted transform has the solution ((x,y) gamma inverse, z/(det gamma)). The inverse transformation proves the converse.
2. Base change: a solution over K maps to one over L.
3. Zeros of f give solutions with z = 0; f(1, 0) = a a square gives (1, 0, sqrt a).

**Acceptance checks.**

- -x^4 - y^4 is not R-soluble.
- x^3 y + y^4 is Q-soluble.
- Lind's quartic 2x^4 - 34y^4 is locally soluble over Q but not Q-soluble.

### 1.29 The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic

For g = (a, b, c, d, e), the quartic covariant is g_4 = (3b^2 - 8ac) X^4 + 4(bc - 6ad) X^3 Y + 2(2c^2 - 24ae - 3bd) X^2 Y^2 + 4(cd - 6be) X Y^3 + (3d^2 - 8ce) Y^4 (= -(1/3) times the Hessian determinant of g where 3 is invertible), and the sextic covariant is g_6 = (b^3 + 8a^2 d - 4abc) X^6 + 2(16a^2 e + 2abd - 4ac^2 + b^2 c) X^5 Y + 5(8abe + b^2 d - 4acd) X^4 Y^2 + 20(b^2 e - ad^2) X^3 Y^3 - 5(8ade + bd^2 - 4bce) X^2 Y^4 - 2(16ae^2 + 2bde - 4c^2 e + cd^2) X Y^5 - (d^3 + 8be^2 - 4cde) Y^6. Under the twisted action they transform as g_4(gamma * g) = gamma * g_4(g) (weight -2 twist, like g) and g_6(gamma * g)(x,y) = (det gamma)^{-3} g_6(g)((x,y) gamma).

**Hypotheses.** Cremona-Fisher normalization; the seminvariants are p = 3b^2 - 8ac = g_4(1,0), r = b^3 + 8a^2 d - 4abc = g_6(1,0).

**Dependencies.** [Binary quartic forms, the GL₂ action by linear substitution and the twisted PGL₂ action](#st0-binary-quartic-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-form`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Section 1, printed p. 2. The definitions.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.hessian` (data): The quartic covariant g_4.
- `BinaryQuartic.sexticCoeff` (data): The seven coefficients of g_6.
- `BinaryQuartic.sextic` (data): Evaluation of g_6.
- `BinaryQuartic.hessian_twistedSMul` (functoriality): g_4 is equivariant for the twisted action.
- `BinaryQuartic.sextic_twistedSMul` (functoriality): g_6 transforms with the factor (det gamma)^{-3}.
- `BinaryQuartic.hessian_eq_neg_third_hessianDet` (compatibility): g_4 = -(1/3)(F_xx F_yy - F_xy^2).

**Checks.**

- `BinaryQuartic.test_hessian_x3y` (computation): g_4(x^3 y) = 3x^4.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_sextic_x3y` (computation): g_6(x^3 y) = x^6.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_hessian_resultant` (characterisation): At the root (1, 1) of x^4 - y^4 the Hessian covariant is 48 != 0.

**Proof route.**

1. Define by the explicit coefficients.
2. Equivariance: Cremona-Fisher Lemma 5 (a proper equivalence (M, lambda) sends g_4 to lambda^2 g_4^M and g_6 to lambda^3 mu^3 g_6^M); a polynomial identity.
3. The Hessian relation: expand F_xx F_yy - F_xy^2.

**Acceptance checks.**

- g_4(x^3 y) = 3x^4 and g_6(x^3 y) = x^6.
- g_4(x^4 - y^4)(1, 1) = 48.

**Consumers.** ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic — G = (4 phi g + g_4)/3 and N(G) = g_6^2; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants — the syzygy relating g, g_4, g_6, I, J; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/bilinear-factor-criterion-for-proper-equivalence — the comparison form g_1 h_2 - g_2 h_1 uses the Hessians

### 1.30 The syzygy 27 g_6^2 = g_4^3 - 48 I g^2 g_4 - 64 J g^3

For every binary quartic g over a commutative ring, 27 g_6(x,y)^2 = g_4(x,y)^3 - 48 I(g) g(x,y)^2 g_4(x,y) - 64 J(g) g(x,y)^3.

**Hypotheses.** Polynomial identity in Z[a, b, c, d, e, x, y].

**Dependencies.** [The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic](#st1-covariants-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/covariants-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Section 1, printed p. 2. The identity.

1. Expand both sides (verified by computer algebra; Cremona-Fisher Section 1).

**Acceptance checks.**

- At (1, 0): 27 r^2 = p^3 - 48 I a^2 p - 64 J a^3 (the seminvariant syzygy).

### 1.31 The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}

Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. Let E_{I,J} : y^2 = x^3 - 27 I x - 27 J (a short Weierstrass curve, the Jacobian of z^2 = g(x,y)) and A_{I,J} = K[T]/(T^3 - 27 I T - 27 J), which is Tau Ceti's W.A for W = E_{I,J}; M_{I,J} = A^x/(A^x)^2 is W.M. For a binary quartic g with invariants I, J put phi = -T/3 (a root of X^3 - 3IX + J) and G(x, y) = (4 phi g(x,y) + g_4(x,y))/3 in A_{I,J}. Then N(G(x, y)) = g_6(x, y)^2; G(x, y) is a unit iff g_6(x, y) != 0; and the class z(g) = [G(x, y)] in M_{I,J} does not depend on the choice of (x, y) with g_6(x, y) != 0 (such a point exists when K is not F_5). z commutes with base change along field homomorphisms (the restriction of square classes, Tau Ceti's localRes).

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3; #K != 5 for the existence of a point with g_6 != 0 (P^1(F_5) has 6 points and g_6 has degree 6).; The curve is E_{I,J} : y^2 = x^3 - 27 I x - 27 J, isomorphic to Bhargava-Shankar's y^2 = x^3 - (I/3) x - J/27 by (x, y) |-> (x/9, y/27).

**Dependencies.** [The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic](#st1-covariants-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/covariants-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The syzygy 27 g_6^2 = g_4^3 - 48 I g^2 g_4 - 64 J g^3](#st1-syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`); `mathlib:AdjoinRoot`; `mathlib:powMonoidHom`; `mathlib:Algebra.norm`; `mathlib:AdjoinRoot.map`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.A`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.M`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.localRes`

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Section 2, Lemma 1, Proposition 2, printed pp. 2-3. The construction and its well-definedness. [P/fisher-cassels-tate-2022](#source-p-fisher-cassels-tate-2022), Section 2, printed pp. 2-3. The same invariant, and its role as the group law on the Selmer group.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.curveIJ` (data): The curve y^2 = x^3 - 27 I x - 27 J.
- `BinaryQuartic.etaleAlgebra` (data): Abbreviation of the imported (curveIJ I J).toAffine.A, the cubic étale algebra.
- `BinaryQuartic.squareClasses` (data): Abbreviation of the imported (curveIJ I J).toAffine.M, the square classes of units in the cubic algebra.
- `BinaryQuartic.curvePoly` (data): The cubic T^3 - 27 I T - 27 J.
- `BinaryQuartic.restrictSquareClasses` (functoriality): The native localRes for the Algebra induced by the field map, transported along curveIJ_map; no copied descent quotient.
- `BinaryQuartic.irrationalCovariant` (data): G(x, y) = (4 phi g(x,y) + g_4(x,y))/3 with phi = -T/3.
- `BinaryQuartic.cubicInvariant` (constructor): z(g), the class of G at an admissible point.
- `BinaryQuartic.cubicInvariant_eq_mk` (characterisation): z(g) is the class of G(x,y) for every admissible (x,y).
- `BinaryQuartic.isUnit_irrationalCovariant` (characterisation): G(x,y) is a unit when g_6(x,y) != 0.
- `BinaryQuartic.norm_irrationalCovariant` (relation): N(G(x,y)) = g_6(x,y)^2.
- `BinaryQuartic.exists_sextic_ne_zero` (other): An admissible point exists when #K != 5 and Delta != 0.
- `BinaryQuartic.cubicInvariant_map` (functoriality): z commutes with restriction along field homomorphisms.

**Checks.**

- `BinaryQuartic.test_cubicInvariant_x3y` (degenerate): z(x^3 y - x y^3) = 1 in M_{3,0}.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_irrationalCovariant_leading` (computation): G(1, 0) = ((3b^2 - 8ac)/3) - (4a/9) T.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_norm_square` (characterisation): N(G(1,2)) = g_6(1,2)^2 for x^4 - y^4 (I = -12, J = 0).

**Proof route.**

1. N(G) = g_6^2: the norm of a linear element u + v phi is u^3 - 3 I u v^2 - J v^3; substituting and using the syzygy gives g_6^2 (checked symbolically: Res(3G, X^3 - 3IX + J) = 27 g_6^2).
2. Independence: Cremona-Fisher Lemma 1, G(x_1, y_1) G(x_2, y_2) = F(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)^2 with F in A[x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2] explicit; hence the classes at two admissible points agree.
3. Existence of an admissible point for #K != 5: g_6 has at most 6 zeros in P^1(K) (it is nonzero when the discriminant is nonzero: Res(g, g_6) = Delta^3/3^9 up to the normalization).
4. Base change: the formula is polynomial in the coefficients.

**Acceptance checks.**

- At (1, 0), G = (4 a phi + 3b^2 - 8ac)/3.

### 1.32 z(g) is constant on PGL2(K)-orbits

If g has invariants I, J and gamma is in PGL2(K), then z(gamma * g) = z(g).

**Hypotheses.** Same hypotheses as the construction of z.

**Dependencies.** [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic](#st1-covariants-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/covariants-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers](#st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Proposition 6, printed p. 5. The statement; proper equivalence is the PGL2(K)-equivalence of the twisted action.

**Proof route.**

1. G(gamma * g)(x, y) = (det gamma)^{-2} G(g)((x, y) gamma) by the equivariance of g and g_4 (Cremona-Fisher Lemma 5); (det gamma)^{-2} is a square, and (x,y) gamma is admissible for g when (x, y) is admissible for gamma * g (equivariance of g_6).

**Acceptance checks.**

- A diagonal substitution rescales G by a square.

<a id="st1-linear-factor-forms"></a>

### 1.33 Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit

Let g have invariants I, J with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. (a) z(g) = 1 if and only if g has a linear factor over K (a zero in P^1(K)). (b) Every such g is PGL2(K)-equivalent to the normal form q_0 = (1/27) Y (27 X^3 - 9 I X Y^2 - J Y^3) = X^3 Y - (I/3) X Y^3 - (J/27) Y^4; hence the forms with a linear factor and invariants I, J form one orbit.

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2,3, and #K ≠ 5 for the chosen admissible-evaluation construction of z.

**Dependencies.** [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The syzygy 27 g_6^2 = g_4^3 - 48 I g^2 g_4 - 64 J g^3](#st1-syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants`); [The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers](#st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Proposition 7, printed p. 5. Part (b). [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Proposition 8, printed p. 6. Part (a).

**Proof route.**

1. (a, linear factor implies z = 1) At a zero (x, y) of g, g_4(x, y) != 0 and g_6(x,y) != 0 (resultants Delta^2/3^2, Delta^3/3^9), and the syzygy gives G(x, y) = g_4(x,y)/3 = (3 g_6/g_4)^2, a square (Cremona-Fisher Lemma 3).
2. (a, z = 1 implies linear factor) If a = 0 the factor Y already gives the conclusion; otherwise, with r = g_6(1, 0) != 0 after a proper change, z = G(1,0) has characteristic polynomial Z^3 - pZ^2 + qZ - r^2; if z = z_1^2 then h(Z^2) = -h_1(Z) h_1(-Z) and -(u + b)/(4a) is a root of g (Cremona-Fisher Proposition 8).
3. (b) Move the linear factor to Y, translate X to kill c, and rescale with (M, lambda) of determinant 1 (Cremona-Fisher Proposition 7).

**Acceptance checks.**

- x^3 y - x y^3 has z = 1 and is the normal form with I = 3, J = 0.

<a id="st1-auxiliary-quartic-root-from-equal-cubic-invariants"></a>

### 1.34 Equal cubic invariants give a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2

Let g_1, g_2 have the same invariants I, J, with seminvariants a_i = g_i(1,0), p_i = g_{i,4}(1,0), r_i = g_{i,6}(1, 0), and suppose r_1, r_2 != 0. If z(g_1) = z(g_2), then the binary quartic p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 (h_2 the Hessian covariant of g_2) has a zero in P^1(K).

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3.

**Dependencies.** [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic](#st1-covariants-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/covariants-of-a-binary-quartic`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Lemma 9, printed p. 6. The lemma, with g~ = (1/a) g(X + b, -4a).

**Proof route.**

1. Put z_i = (4 a_i phi + p_i)/3; h(X) = N(X - z_1^{-1} z_2) = X^3 - pX^2 + qX - r^2 with p = s_1/(3 r_1)^2, q = s_2/(3r_1)^2, r = r_2/r_1.
2. z(g_1) = z(g_2) gives w with w^2 = z_1^{-1} z_2 and N(w) = r; comparing coefficients in h(X^2) = -h_0(X) h_0(-X) with h_0 = N(X - w) = X^3 - uX^2 + vX - r gives (u^2 - p)^2 - 8ru - 4q = 0, i.e. 3 r_1 u is a root of g~(X) = X^4 - 2 s_1 X^2 - 216 r_1^2 r_2 X + s_1^2 - 36 r_1^2 s_2.
3. g~(X) = (1/a) g(X + b, -4a) for g = p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 with coefficients (a, b, ...) when a != 0 (computer algebra), so g has a zero; if a = 0 then (1, 0) is a zero.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For g_1 = g_2 the comparison form p g - a h vanishes at a point of P^1(K).

<a id="st1-linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence"></a>

### 1.35 A zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 gives a PGL2(K)-equivalence

Let g_1, g_2 have the same invariants with r_1 = g_{1,6}(1, 0) != 0. If p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 has a zero in P^1(K), then g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent.

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3.

**Dependencies.** [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); [The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic](#st1-covariants-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/covariants-of-a-binary-quartic`); [The syzygy 27 g_6^2 = g_4^3 - 48 I g^2 g_4 - 64 J g^3](#st1-syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/syzygy-of-binary-quartic-covariants`); [The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers](#st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Lemma 10 and proof, printed pp. 6-7. The lemma.

**Proof route.**

1. Move the zero to (1, 0) by a proper change of g_2: p_1 a_2 = a_1 p_2.
2. If a_1 = 0 then p_1 != 0, so a_2 = 0 and both forms have a linear factor: equivalent by linear-factor-forms.
3. Otherwise a_1 ≠ 0. Also a_2 ≠ 0, since a_2 = p_2 = 0 would force b_2 = 0 and make g_2 singular. Put t = a_2/a_1, so p_2 = t p_1, without dividing by p_1 (which may be zero). The seminvariant syzygy gives r_2² = t³ r_1². Since t and r_1 are nonzero, r_2 is nonzero and t = (r_2/(t r_1))². A proper diagonal change makes a_2 = a_1, p_2 = p_1 and r_2 = r_1; a shift makes b_2 = b_1. Then p,r,I recover c,d,e successively because a_1,2,3 are invertible, so g_2 = g_1.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For g_1 = g_2 the identity equivalence is found.

<a id="st1-cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit"></a>

### 1.36 Cremona-Fisher: the cubic invariant determines the PGL2(K)-orbit

Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3, K != F_5, and g_1, g_2 binary quartics with the same invariants I, J, 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. Then z(g_1) = z(g_2) if and only if g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent.

**Hypotheses.** Includes the cases I = 0 or J = 0, where equivalence by GL2 x GL1 with the same invariants need not be proper; the theorem is about PGL2(K) (proper) equivalence.

**Dependencies.** [z(g) is constant on PGL2(K)-orbits](#st1-cubic-invariant-is-an-orbit-invariant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-is-an-orbit-invariant`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); [Equal cubic invariants give a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2](#st1-auxiliary-quartic-root-from-equal-cubic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/auxiliary-quartic-root-from-equal-cubic-invariants`); [A zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 gives a PGL2(K)-equivalence](#st1-linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Theorem 11, printed p. 7. The theorem.

**Proof route.**

1. <=: cubic-invariant-is-an-orbit-invariant.
2. =>: if z = 1 both have linear factors (linear-factor-forms). Otherwise neither has a linear factor; after proper changes r_1, r_2 != 0; auxiliary-quartic-root-from-equal-cubic-invariants gives a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2, and linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence concludes.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The proper transformation diag(2,1) sends x⁴−y⁴ to 4x⁴−y⁴/4. Both have I = −12, J = 0 and a rational linear factor, hence cubic invariant 1.
- When J ≠ 0, g and −g have different pairs (I,J), so their cubic invariants live in different specified cubic algebras and are not compared by this theorem.

<a id="st1-quartic-of-a-point"></a>

### 1.37 The binary quartic q(P) attached to a point of E_{I,J}

For P in E_{I,J}(K) define q(O) = X^3 Y - (I/3) X Y^3 - (J/27) Y^4 (the linear-factor normal form) and, for P = (xi, eta), q(P) = X^4 - (xi/6) X^2 Y^2 - (eta/27) X Y^3 + ((36 I - xi^2)/432) Y^4. Then q(P) has invariants I and J, is K-soluble (its leading coefficient is 1, or it has the linear factor Y), and q(-P) is PGL2(K)-equivalent to q(P). In Bhargava-Shankar's normalization y^2 = x^3 - (I/3) x - J/27 the same quartic is (1/4) X^4 - (3/2) xi' X^2 Y^2 + 2 eta' X Y^3 + (I/3 - (3/4) xi'^2) Y^4 with (xi', eta') = (xi/9, eta/27), up to PGL2(K).

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3.

**Dependencies.** [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st1-soluble-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/soluble-binary-quartic-forms`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`); `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point`

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Section 6, printed p. 10. The construction. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.2, printed p. 23. Bhargava-Shankar's normalization of the same map.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.quarticOfPoint` (constructor): P |-> q(P).
- `BinaryQuartic.invI_quarticOfPoint` (relation): I(q(P)) = I.
- `BinaryQuartic.invJ_quarticOfPoint` (relation): J(q(P)) = J.
- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_quarticOfPoint` (relation): q(P) is K-soluble.
- `BinaryQuartic.quarticOfPoint_neg` (relation): q(-P) is PGL2(K)-equivalent to q(P).
- `BinaryQuartic.linearFactorForm` (data): The normal form X^3 Y - (I/3) X Y^3 - (J/27) Y^4 = q(O).

**Checks.**

- `BinaryQuartic.test_quarticOfPoint_zero` (degenerate): q(O)(1, 0) = 0.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_quarticOfPoint_invariants` (computation): On y^2 = x^3 - 27x, q((0,0)) = X^4 + Y^4/12, with I = 1, J = 0.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_quarticOfPoint_leading_square` (characterisation): The leading coefficient of q(P) at an affine point is 1.

**Proof route.**

1. Invariants: direct computation using eta^2 = xi^3 - 27 I xi - 27 J (checked symbolically, also for the Bhargava-Shankar formula).
2. Solubility: (1, 0, 1) is a solution for affine P; q(O) vanishes at (1, 0).
3. q(-P): the substitution Y -> -Y (determinant -1, trivial twist) changes the sign of the eta-term.
4. The Bhargava–Shankar representative is exactly the twisted transform of the Cremona–Fisher representative by diag(−1/2,1); substitute (xi′,eta′) = (xi/9,eta/27).

**Acceptance checks.**

- q(O) vanishes at (1, 0).
- On y^2 = x^3 - 27x the 2-torsion point (0, 0) gives X^4 + Y^4/12.
- The leading coefficient of q(P) at an affine point is 1.

**Consumers.** ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e — the forward map of the bijection; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point — z(q(P)) = mu(P); ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three — the PGL2(Q_p)-classes of soluble forms are counted by #E(Q_p)/2E(Q_p)

### 1.38 z(q(P)) is the image of P under the x - T map

For P in E_{I,J}(K), z(q(P)) = mu(P) in M_{I,J}, where mu is Tau Ceti's descent map WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μ: for P = (xi, eta) with eta != 0 it is the class of xi - T; at a 2-torsion point (xi, 0) it is the class of the corrected representative xi - T + (T^2 + xi T + xi^2 - 27 I) (Tau Ceti's fCofactor); and mu(O) = 1.

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3; the identification phi = -T/3 of the resolvent root.; #K ≠ 5 for the chosen construction of z by an admissible evaluation. The F_5 orbit parametrization is handled separately without invoking this construction.

**Dependencies.** [The binary quartic q(P) attached to a point of E_{I,J}](#st1-quartic-of-a-point) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-of-a-point`); [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μ`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μX_of_eval_f_ne_zero`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μX_of_eval_f_eq_zero`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Proof of Theorem 13(1), printed pp. 10-11. The computation. [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Section 6, printed p. 10. The Cassels map, which is Tau Ceti's mu with T = -3 phi.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.cubicInvariant_quarticOfPoint_eq_mu` (compatibility): Under char≠2,3, #K≠5 and ellipticity, z(q(P)) equals native WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μ at every point, including infinity and rational two-torsion.

**Proof route.**

1. For eta != 0: G(1, 0) = (4 phi + p)/3 with p = g_4(1,0) = 3.0 - 8.1.(-xi/6) = 4 xi/3, so G(1,0) = (4/9)(xi + 3 phi) = (2/3)^2 (xi - T) (Cremona-Fisher Theorem 13(1); g_6(1, 0) = 8(-eta/27) != 0).
2. For eta = 0 (so g_6(1, 0) = 0) evaluate G at another admissible point; the resulting class agrees with the corrected representative (the conjugate of G at the vanishing coordinate is replaced by the product of the other two, Cremona-Fisher Section 2 remarks), matching Tau Ceti's μX_of_eval_f_eq_zero.
3. mu(O) = 1 and q(O) has a linear factor, so z = 1 (linear-factor-forms).

**Acceptance checks.**

- On y^2 = x^3 - 43x + 42 (roots 1, 6, -7), P = (-3, 12) gives square classes (-1, -1, 1) componentwise for both z(q(P)) and xi - e_i (checked numerically).

### 1.39 Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics

Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. The map P |-> PGL2(K) . q(P) induces a bijection between E_{I,J}(K)/2E_{I,J}(K) and the set of PGL2(K)-orbits of K-soluble binary quartic forms with invariants I and J; the identity class corresponds to the orbit of forms with a linear factor over K. When #K ≠ 5, equivalently, z restricted to soluble orbits is a bijection onto the image of Tau Ceti's mu, and z o q = mu.

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3; for K = F_5 (excluded from the construction of z) the statement is verified by exhaustive computation.

**Dependencies.** [The binary quartic q(P) attached to a point of E_{I,J}](#st1-quartic-of-a-point) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-of-a-point`); [z(q(P)) is the image of P under the x - T map](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point`); [Cremona-Fisher: the cubic invariant determines the PGL2(K)-orbit](#st1-cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); [Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st1-soluble-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/soluble-binary-quartic-forms`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.ker_μ_eq`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μ`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.2, printed p. 23. The theorem. [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Theorem 13, printed p. 10. The proof route.

**Proof route.**

1. Well-defined and injective: z(q(P)) = mu(P) (cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point), z is injective on orbits (cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit) and ker mu = 2E(K) (Tau Ceti ker_μ_eq); so q(P) ~ q(Q) iff mu(P) = mu(Q) iff P - Q in 2E(K).
2. Surjective onto soluble orbits: a soluble g with a zero is in the linear-factor orbit = q(O); otherwise a proper change gives leading coefficient 1 and b = 0, and then (xi, eta) = (-6c, -27d) lies on E_{I,J} and q(xi, eta) = g (Cremona-Fisher Theorem 13(2), using the formulas for I, J).
3. Identity: q(O) is the linear-factor form (linear-factor-forms).
4. K = F_5: finitely many forms, points and matrices; check directly.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Over R: #E(R)/2E(R) = #E(R)[2]/2, which is 1 if Delta < 0 and 2 if Delta > 0; so there are that many PGL2(R)-orbits of R-soluble forms with given invariants.
- Over F_p (p >= 5): #E(F_p)/2E(F_p) = #E(F_p)[2], and every nondegenerate quartic over F_p is soluble.

<a id="st1-bilinear-factor-criterion-for-proper-equivalence"></a>

### 1.40 Cremona-Fisher: proper equivalences correspond to bilinear factors

Let g_1, g_2 be binary quartics with the same invariants and Hessians h_1, h_2, and F_{g_1,g_2}(X_1, Y_1, X_2, Y_2) = g_1(X_1,Y_1) h_2(X_2,Y_2) - g_2(X_2,Y_2) h_1(X_1,Y_1). Then g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent iff F has a K-rational bilinear factor (X_1 Y_1) A (X_2 Y_2)^T with A in GL2(K); the factor with matrix A gives the equivalence M = A^T (0 1; -1 0). Moreover F_{g,g} = -3 (X_1 Y_2 - Y_1 X_2) R(X_1X_2, X_1Y_2 + X_2Y_1, Y_1Y_2) with R a ternary cubic form that is, up to a nonzero constant, the norm from L = K[phi] of an L-linear form; hence over K-bar, F_{g,g} has exactly three further bilinear factors, one for each root phi_i of X^3 - 3IX + J, and such a factor is K-rational iff phi_i is in K.

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2,3, and the common discriminant is nonzero. The proof using a preliminary sextic-nonzero evaluation assumes #K ≠ 5; the field F_5 case is checked separately by finite enumeration.

**Dependencies.** [The Hessian and sextic covariants of a binary quartic](#st1-covariants-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/covariants-of-a-binary-quartic`); [A zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 gives a PGL2(K)-equivalence](#st1-linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence`); [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Theorem 12, printed p. 9. The criterion. [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Remark 1 after Theorem 12, printed p. 9. The count used for stabilizers.

**Proof route.**

1. If g_2 = det(M)^{-2} g_1^M then F_{g_1,g_2} = det(M)^{-2} F_{g_1,g_1}(X_1, Y_1, (X_2,Y_2)M), and F_{g_1,g_1} has the factor X_1 Y_2 - Y_1 X_2.
2. Conversely a bilinear factor, specialized at (X_1, Y_1) = (1, 0) (after making r_1 != 0), gives a zero of p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2, and linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence applies.
3. The factorization of F_{g,g} and of R as a norm from L = K[phi] (Cremona-Fisher Section 6, identities (1)-(2), verified by computer algebra) identifies the nontrivial bilinear factors with the conjugates of an L-linear factor.
4. For K = F_5, enumerate nonsingular forms with each invariant pair and invertible bilinear matrices modulo scalars, checking divisibility of the comparison polynomial and the corresponding transformation. This bypasses the preliminary-evaluation argument, which can fail on P¹(F_5).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For g = X^4 - Y^4 the proper self-equivalences over Q(i) are 4 in number.

<a id="st1-stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion"></a>

### 1.41 Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E(K)[2]

Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and f a binary quartic over K with invariants I, J and 4I^3 - J^2 != 0 (not necessarily K-soluble). Then Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E_{I,J}(K)[2]. It is an elementary abelian 2-group of order 1 + #{roots of X^3 - 3IX + J in K}; over R it has order 4 if Delta(f) > 0 and 2 if Delta(f) < 0 (never 1).

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3; the discriminant is nonzero.

**Dependencies.** [Cremona-Fisher: proper equivalences correspond to bilinear factors](#st1-bilinear-factor-criterion-for-proper-equivalence) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/bilinear-factor-criterion-for-proper-equivalence`); [The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers](#st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.card_ker_nsmul_two`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.2, second paragraph, printed p. 23. The theorem. [P/bhargava-ho-coregular-2013](#source-p-bhargava-ho-coregular-2013), Remark 4.3, printed p. 26. The geometric statement (for PGL(V) x 2G_m); the PGL2 part is E[2].

**Proof route.**

1. Order: stabilizer elements are the proper self-equivalences; by bilinear-factor-criterion-for-proper-equivalence they correspond to the K-rational bilinear factors of F_{f,f}: the trivial one and one for each K-rational root of the resolvent.
2. Exponent 2: a self-equivalence is given by M = (-alpha_2 alpha_1; -alpha_3 alpha_2) (Cremona-Fisher Section 6), of trace 0, so M^2 = -det(M) I is scalar.
3. E(K)[2]: its order is 1 + #{roots of x^3 - 27Ix - 27J in K} (Tau Ceti card_ker_nsmul_two), and the roots correspond to those of X^3 - 3IX + J under T = -3 phi. Elementary abelian 2-groups of equal order 1, 2 or 4 are isomorphic.
4. Over R: the resolvent has three real roots iff its discriminant 27 Delta is positive.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Over R: order 4 if Delta > 0, 2 if Delta < 0; these give Bhargava-Shankar's GL2(R)-stabilizer orders 8 and 4 (Lemma 2.2) and n_0 = 4, n_1 = 2, n_{2+-} = 4.
- x^4 - y^4 over Q: resolvent X^3 + 36X has one rational root (0), so the stabilizer has order 2.

<a id="st1-image-of-the-cubic-invariant"></a>

### 1.42 Which square classes are cubic invariants: linear representatives and the conic

Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 with #K != 5, I, J with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0, and m in A_{I,J}^x with square norm. Then the following are equivalent: (a) [m] = z(g) for a binary quartic g with invariants I, J; (b) m is represented by a unit linear in T (m w^2 = u + v phi for a unit w); (c) the ternary quadratic form Q_m(t) = coefficient of T^2 in m (t_0 + t_1 T + t_2 T^2)^2 (reduced modulo T^3 - 27IT - 27J) has a nontrivial zero. Q_m is regular: its Gram determinant is exactly -N(m) in the displayed power basis. If v != 0 and N(u + v phi) = r^2, Simon's quartic (1/(12 v))(X^4 - 6u X^2 Y^2 + 8r X Y^3 + (12 I v^2 - 3 u^2) Y^4) has invariants I, J and cubic invariant (u + v phi)/(9 v^2).

**Hypotheses.** char K not 2, 3, #K != 5.

**Dependencies.** [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); `mathlib:Polynomial.modByMonic`; `mathlib:QuadraticMap.Anisotropic`; `mathlib:QuadraticMap.not_anisotropic_iff_exists`

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Theorem 13(3) and proof, printed pp. 10-11. (a) <=> (b) and Simon's quartic. [P/cremona-fisher-oneil-simon-stoll-2008](#source-p-cremona-fisher-oneil-simon-stoll-2008), Introduction, printed p. 5. The conic as the obstruction for n = 2.

**Proof route.**

1. (a) => (b): z(g) is represented by G(x, y), which is linear in phi.
2. (b) => (a): if v = 0 the norm condition makes m a square, take the linear-factor form; otherwise Simon's quartic works (invariants and z checked symbolically; Cremona-Fisher Theorem 13(3)).
3. (b) <=> (c): a unit w satisfies m w² linear iff its T²-coefficient vanishes. Given a nontrivial zero, the regular conic has a K-point and hence is isomorphic to P¹_K. It has more than six K-points since char K ≠ 2,3 and #K ≠ 5. Over an algebraic closure the nonunits lie on three projective lines, each meeting the smooth conic in at most two points. Thus a K-point outside their union supplies a unit w.
4. Regularity: det Q_m = -N(m) for a depressed cubic (checked symbolically).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For m = 1 the conic has the zero t = (1, 0, 0).
- For I = 3, J = 0 and m = u + v phi linear, Simon's quartic has invariants (3, 0).

<a id="st1-locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group"></a>

### 1.43 Locally soluble quartics and Tau Ceti's 2-Selmer group (Bhargava-Shankar Proposition 3.3)

Let K be a number field and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. The cubic invariant z induces a bijection between the PGL2(K)-orbits of everywhere locally soluble binary quartic forms over K with invariants I, J and Tau Ceti's 2-Selmer group selmerGroup_2 of E_{I,J} (relative to O_K and the family of completions at the infinite places); the orbit of forms with a linear factor goes to 1. Equivalently (coefficient form): z is injective on these orbits, and a square class m of square norm is the cubic invariant of a locally soluble global form iff for every place v the restriction of m is the cubic invariant of a K_v-soluble form with invariants I, J.

**Hypotheses.** K a number field; Tau Ceti's selmerGroup_2 is defined by the norm condition and the local conditions localRes m in range(mu over K_v) at all finite places and at the infinite completions.; At complex places every form is soluble and the local condition is automatic.

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e`); [Cremona-Fisher: the cubic invariant determines the PGL2(K)-orbit](#st1-cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit`); [Which square classes are cubic invariants: linear representatives and the conic](#st1-image-of-the-cubic-invariant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/image-of-the-cubic-invariant`); [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st1-soluble-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/soluble-binary-quartic-forms`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.selmerGroup₂`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.mem_selmerGroup₂_iff`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.localRes_comp_μ`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.localCondition`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.normM`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.range_μ_le_ker_normM`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii; tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/GlobalQuadraticForms#layer-5-hasseminkowski-isotropy

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proposition 3.3, printed p. 23. The statement over Q. [P/fisher-cassels-tate-2022](#source-p-fisher-cassels-tate-2022), Lemma 2.1, printed p. 2. The number-field statement. [P/cremona-fisher-oneil-simon-stoll-2008](#source-p-cremona-fisher-oneil-simon-stoll-2008), Introduction, printed pp. 4-5. The local-global step, which for n = 2 is the conic.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.mem_selmerGroup₂_iff` (characterisation): A class m in native W.M lies in W.selmerGroup₂ (O_K) (archimedean completions) iff it is the cubic invariant of an everywhere locally soluble quartic with invariants I,J.

**Proof route.**

1. Into the Selmer group: for locally soluble g, z(g) has square norm, and at each place v, localRes z(g) = z_v(g) (cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic, base change) is in z_v(soluble orbits) = range(mu_v) (binary-quartic-parametrization-of-E-mod-2E over K_v, Tau Ceti localRes_comp_μ); this is membership in selmerGroup_2 (Tau Ceti mem_selmerGroup₂_iff).
2. Injective: cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit (K is infinite).
3. Surjective: for m in selmerGroup_2, at each place m_v = mu_v(P_v) = z_v(q(P_v)) is represented by a linear unit, so the conic Q_m is isotropic over every K_v (image-of-the-cubic-invariant over K_v); it is regular, so by Hasse-Minkowski for ternary forms (GlobalQuadraticForms Layer 5) it is isotropic over K; hence m = z(g) for some g with invariants I, J (image-of-the-cubic-invariant over K). Then z_v(g) = m_v = z_v(q(P_v)), so g is PGL2(K_v)-equivalent to the soluble q(P_v) (injectivity over K_v): g is locally soluble.
4. Identity: linear-factor-forms.

- Lind's quartic 2x^4 - 34y^4 (I = -816, J = 0) is locally soluble with no rational point: its cubic invariant lies in selmerGroup_2 of y^2 = x^3 + 22032 x but not in the image of mu.

<a id="st1-primitive-vectors-extend-to-special-linear-matrices"></a>

### 1.44 A primitive vector over a PID is a column of a matrix in SL3

Let O be a principal ideal domain and v in O^3 with coordinates generating the unit ideal (a primitive vector). Then for every j there is M in SL3(O) whose j-th column is v; in particular SL3(O) acts transitively on P^2(Frac O) (on primitive vectors up to units).

**Hypotheses.** O a PID (Z, Z_p, Z_(p)).

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'`; `mathlib:IsCoprime.exists_SL2_col`; `mathlib:Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup`

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Lemma 3.13, printed pp. 14-15. The lemma used in the projection argument.

**Proof route.**

1. O^3/Ov is finitely generated and torsion-free (v primitive), hence free of rank 2 over the PID (Mathlib Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'); so v extends to a basis of O^3.
2. First permute the extended basis so that v is its j-th column. Its determinant is a unit u; multiply a different column by u^{-1}. This preserves the chosen column and makes the determinant 1, including the sign of the permutation.

**Acceptance checks.**

- v = (1290, -383, 1000) (the point 2(3,5) of y^2 = x^3 - 2 in projective coordinates) is a column of a matrix in SL3(Z).

<a id="st1-ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants"></a>

### 1.45 Ternary cubic forms and their invariants c_4, c_6

A ternary cubic over a commutative ring R is U = a x^3 + b y^3 + c z^3 + a_2 x^2 y + a_3 x^2 z + b_1 x y^2 + b_3 y^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c_2 y z^2 + m x y z. Its invariants c_4(U) (25 terms, degree 4) and c_6(U) (103 terms, degree 6) are the integer polynomials in the coefficients determined by Fisher's normalization H(lambda U + mu H) = 3(c_4 lambda^2 mu + 2 c_6 lambda mu^2 + c_4^2 mu^3) U + (lambda^3 - 3 c_4 lambda mu^2 - 2 c_6 mu^3) H, where H(U) = -(1/2) det(Hessian of U); c_4 = -216 abcm + 144 abc_1c_2 + ... + m^4 and c_6 = 5832 a^2b^2c^2 - 3888 a^2 b b_3 c c_2 + ... - m^6. For the Weierstrass cubic y^2 z - x^3 - A x z^2 - B z^3 they are c_4 = -48A and c_6 = -864B, the usual invariants of y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B; and c_4^3 - c_6^2 = 1728 Delta. Substitution: (U o M)(x, y, z) = U(M^T (x, y, z)).

**Hypotheses.** The polynomials are written out explicitly (derived from the Hessian identity and checked on the Weierstrass family); their leading terms agree with Fisher's printed partial expansions.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Matrix.det`

**Sources.** [P/fisher-invariants-2008](#source-p-fisher-invariants-2008), Section 7.2, printed p. 27. The definition and normalization. [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Lemma 3.11, printed pp. 13-14. The Weierstrass values.

**API.**

- `TernaryCubicForm` (structure): Ternary cubics by ten coefficients (Fisher's coordinates).
- `TernaryCubicForm.eval` (data): Evaluation.
- `TernaryCubicForm.c4` (data): The invariant c_4.
- `TernaryCubicForm.c6` (data): The invariant c_6.
- `TernaryCubicForm.comp` (functoriality): The cubic U(M^T (x,y,z)).
- `TernaryCubicForm.eval_comp` (simp): Evaluation of the substituted cubic.
- `TernaryCubicForm.weierstrass` (example): The Weierstrass cubic y^2 z - x^3 - A x z^2 - B z^3.
- `TernaryCubicForm.c4_weierstrass` (example): c_4 = -48 A.
- `TernaryCubicForm.c6_weierstrass` (example): c_6 = -864 B.
- `TernaryCubicForm.c4_cube_sub_c6_sq` (relation): c_4^3 - c_6^2 is divisible by 1728 (defines Delta).

**Checks.**

- `TernaryCubicForm.test_c4_fermat` (computation): c_4(x^3 + y^3 + z^3) = 0.
- `TernaryCubicForm.test_c6_fermat` (computation): c_6(x^3 + y^3 + z^3) = 5832.
- `TernaryCubicForm.test_c4_weierstrass_value` (non-example): c_4(y^2 z - x^3 + x z^2) = 48, not -48: the sign of Fisher's normalization is pinned.

**Proof route.**

1. Compute H(U), the first and second directional derivatives of H at U in the direction H(U), and read off c_4, c_6 from the lambda^2 mu and lambda mu^2 coefficients (exact polynomial division by the coefficient a; checked symbolically).
2. Evaluate on the Weierstrass cubic.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Fermat cubic x^3 + y^3 + z^3: c_4 = 0, c_6 = 5832.
- y^2 z = x^3 - x z^2: c_4 = 48.

**Consumers.** ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/projection-of-a-plane-cubic-from-a-rational-point — I and J of the projected quartic are c_4 and 2 c_6; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics — SL3-invariance transports the Weierstrass invariants to the moved cubic; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5 — ternary cubics parametrize 3-Selmer elements (Bhargava-Shankar, Ternary cubic forms having bounded invariants), a source-scoped higher-moment input

### 1.46 c_4 and c_6 are SL3-invariants of weights 4 and 6

For a ternary cubic U and a 3 x 3 matrix M over a commutative ring, c_4(U o M) = det(M)^4 c_4(U) and c_6(U o M) = det(M)^6 c_6(U).

**Hypotheses.** Polynomial identities in the coefficients of U and the entries of M.

**Dependencies.** [Ternary cubic forms and their invariants c_4, c_6](#st1-ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Theorem 2.8(i), printed p. 6. The statement.

**Proof route.**

1. Both sides are polynomials; the identities are multiplicative in M, so it suffices to check them for elementary transvections and diagonal matrices over Q (these generate GL3(Q), which is Zariski dense), and they then hold over every commutative ring (Cremona-Fisher-Stoll Theorem 2.8(i); Fisher, Section 4).

**Acceptance checks.**

- c_4 of the Weierstrass cubic moved by any M in SL3(Z) is still -48A.

<a id="st1-projection-of-a-plane-cubic-from-a-rational-point"></a>

### 1.47 Projection of a plane cubic from the point (0:1:0): the binary quartic f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3

Let U be a ternary cubic with b = 0, i.e. with (0:1:0) on U = 0, written U = f_1(x,z) y^2 - f_2(x,z) y - f_3(x,z) with f_1 = b_1 x + b_3 z, f_2 = -(a_2 x^2 + m x z + c_2 z^2), f_3 = -(a x^3 + a_3 x^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c z^3). Its projection quartic is the binary quartic F_U = f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3 in (x, z) (the discriminant in y of U along the line through (0:1:0) with slope (x : z)). If U is integral then F_U is integral, and I(F_U) = c_4(U), J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U). For the Weierstrass cubic of y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B, F = 4(x^3 z + A x z^3 + B z^4), with invariants (-48A, -1728B) = (2^4 I, 2^6 J) for I = -3A, J = -27B.

**Hypotheses.** U(0,1,0) = b = 0.; The generalized quartic y^2 + f_2 y = f_1 f_3 of Cremona-Fisher-Stoll (3.4) becomes F_U after completing the square (times 4), which is how integrality at 2 is kept.

**Dependencies.** [Ternary cubic forms and their invariants c_4, c_6](#st1-ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants`); [Binary quartic forms, the GL₂ action by linear substitution and the twisted PGL₂ action](#st0-binary-quartic-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-form`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`)

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Lemma 3.14, printed p. 15. The projection correspondence between (3.5) and (3.4). [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Proof of Lemma 3.10(i), printed p. 16. The projection argument.

**API.**

- `TernaryCubicForm.projectionQuartic` (constructor): F_U = f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3 as a binary quartic.
- `TernaryCubicForm.invI_projectionQuartic` (relation): I(F_U) = c_4(U) when b = 0.
- `TernaryCubicForm.invJ_projectionQuartic` (relation): J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U) when b = 0.
- `TernaryCubicForm.projectionQuartic_eval` (characterisation): F_U(x, z) = (a_2 x^2 + m x z + c_2 z^2)^2 - 4 (b_1 x + b_3 z)(a x^3 + a_3 x^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c z^3).

**Checks.**

- `TernaryCubicForm.test_projection_weierstrass_origin` (computation): For the Weierstrass cubic, F = (0, 4, 0, 4A, 4B).
- `TernaryCubicForm.test_projection_invariants_numeric` (computation): For A = -7, B = 10: I(F) = 336 and J(F) = -17280.
- `TernaryCubicForm.test_projection_integral` (compatibility): Projection commutes with the base change Z -> Q.

**Proof route.**

1. Lines through (0:1:0) are parametrized by (x:z). Their residual homogeneous quadratic has discriminant F_U. In characteristic different from 2, when f_1(x,z) ≠ 0 its two residual intersection points are rational (with multiplicity) iff F_U(x,z) is a square. The direction f_1(x,z)=0 requires the separate linear/tangent case; the polynomial construction and invariant identities impose neither restriction.
2. I(F_U) = c_4(U) and J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U) for b = 0: polynomial identities (checked symbolically; Cremona-Fisher-Stoll: 'a generic computation shows that the genus one models (3.4) and (3.5) have the same discriminant', here with c_4, c_6 themselves).

**Acceptance checks.**

- Weierstrass cubic: F = (0, 4, 0, 4A, 4B).
- A = -7, B = 10: I(F) = 336, J(F) = -17280.
- Integrality is compatible with base change to Q.
