### 1.48 The projected quartic from P has invariants (2^4 I, 2^6 J) and cubic invariant mu(P)

Let E : y² = x³ + Ax + B be nonsingular over a field K of characteristic different from 2 and 3 with #K ≠ 5. Let P=(xi,eta) in E(K) and M in SL3(K) whose middle row is lambda·(xi,eta,1), for some lambda in K× (equivalently Mᵀe_2 represents P). The projection quartic F of the row-substituted cubic U∘M has invariants I(F)=−48A, J(F)=−1728B and is PGL2(K)-equivalent to q(P′), where P′=(36xi,216eta) on E_{−48A,−1728B}. Consequently its cubic invariant is mu(P′), with the corrected representative at 2-torsion. For P=O the same construction has a rational linear factor and cubic invariant 1. The orbit statement itself also holds over F_5; only the evaluation construction of z excludes that field.

**Hypotheses.** char K ≠ 2,3 and 4A³+27B² ≠ 0; #K ≠ 5 when expressing the conclusion using z.; The middle row represents the projective point: a nonzero scalar multiple is allowed, as required for primitive integral coordinates.

**Dependencies.** [Projection of a plane cubic from the point (0:1:0): the binary quartic f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3](#st1-projection-of-a-plane-cubic-from-a-rational-point) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/projection-of-a-plane-cubic-from-a-rational-point`); [c_4 and c_6 are SL3-invariants of weights 4 and 6](#st1-invariance-of-ternary-cubic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/invariance-of-ternary-cubic-invariants`); [The cubic invariant z(g) in the square classes of the etale algebra of E_{I,J}](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-a-binary-quartic`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.μ`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Section 3.2, printed p. 13. The reduction to one representative per class, which the cubic invariant makes explicit for n = 2.

**Proof route.**

1. Invariants follow from det(M)=1, the ternary-cubic transformation laws, and I(projection U)=c_4(U), J(projection U)=2c_6(U).
2. For affine P take M_0 with rows (1,0,0), (xi,eta,1), (0,−1,0); det(M_0)=1. Substituting (X,Y,Z)=(x+xi·y,eta·y−z,y) and using eta²=xi³+Axi+B gives U∘M_0=−((3xi²+A)x+2eta·z)y²+(z²−3xi·x²)y−x³. Its projection is z⁴−6xi·x²z²−8eta·x³z−(3xi²+4A)x⁴, exactly q(P′)(z,x). The variable swap has determinant −1 and trivial determinant-square twist.
3. For any permitted M, L=M M_0^{-1} has middle row (0,lambda,0). Write its other rows as (a,b,c),(d,e,f). The induced change in (x,z) is Gamma=((a,c),(d,f)), and det(Gamma)=lambda^{-1}. Translation of y by bx+ez leaves the quadratic discriminant unchanged; scaling y by lambda multiplies it by lambda². Thus projection(U∘M)=Gamma twistedSMul projection(U∘M_0). This also proves independence of the primitive projective representative.
4. Apply z(q(P′))=mu(P′) and invariance of z under PGL2. This identity handles 2-torsion without evaluating a nonunit representative. For O, the original Weierstrass projection 4(x³z+Axz³+Bz⁴) has the factor z; the same block-matrix calculation proves the assertion for every M representing O.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For A = -43, B = 42 and P = (-3, 12) the square classes of z(F) and (xi - e_i) are both (-1, -1, 1).

<a id="st1-local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics"></a>

### 1.49 Every Q_p-soluble quartic with invariants (-48A, -1728B) has a Z_p-integral representative

Let p be a prime, A, B in Z_p with 4A^3 + 27B^2 != 0, and f a Q_p-soluble binary quartic over Q_p with I(f) = -48A and J(f) = -1728B. Then f is PGL2(Q_p)-equivalent to a binary quartic with coefficients in Z_p (with the same invariants).

**Hypotheses.** p arbitrary (including 2 and 3): the factor 4 in F = f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3 is what makes the argument uniform at 2.; This is the n = 2 case of the Cremona-Fisher-Stoll Minimisation Theorem (minimal level 0 for soluble models), in the normalization with invariants (2^4 I, 2^6 J).

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e`); [A primitive vector over a PID is a column of a matrix in SL3](#st1-primitive-vectors-extend-to-special-linear-matrices) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/primitive-vectors-extend-to-special-linear-matrices`); [The projected quartic from P has invariants (2^4 I, 2^6 J) and cubic invariant mu(P)](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-the-projected-quartic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-the-projected-quartic`); [Cremona-Fisher: the cubic invariant determines the PGL2(K)-orbit](#st1-cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit`); [Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st1-soluble-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/soluble-binary-quartic-forms`); `mathlib:PadicInt`

**Sources.** [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Theorem 3.4, printed p. 10. The general theorem whose n = 2 case this is. [P/cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010](#source-p-cremona-fisher-stoll-minimisation-2010), Theorem 3.8, printed p. 12. The form of the statement proved by projection.

**Proof route.**

1. By binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e over Q_p (for E_{-48A,-1728B}), f ~ q(P') for some P' = (36 xi, 216 eta), P = (xi, eta) in E_{A,B}(Q_p), or f has a linear factor (P = O).
2. Write P projectively as a primitive vector (X_0 : Y_0 : Z_0) in Z_p^3 and choose M in SL3(Z_p) with row 1 equal to it (primitive-vectors-extend-to-special-linear-matrices, applied to the transpose).
3. The Weierstrass cubic o M is integral with b = 0; its projection quartic F is integral with invariants (-48A, -1728B) and cubic invariant mu(P') (cubic-invariant-of-the-projected-quartic).
4. z(F) = z(q(P')) = z(f), so F ~ f by cubic-invariant-determines-the-orbit (Q_p is infinite).

**Acceptance checks.**

- y^2 = x^3 - 2 over Q_2: the class of 2(3, 5) = (129/100, -383/1000) is represented by an integral quartic with invariants (0, 3456).

<a id="st1-integrality-from-local-integrality"></a>

### 1.50 Local integral representatives at every prime give a global one

Let f be a binary quartic over Q such that for every prime p there is gamma_p in PGL2(Q_p) with gamma_p * f integral over Z_p. Then there is gamma in PGL2(Q) with gamma * f integral over Z.

**Hypotheses.** Twisted action; scalars act trivially, so lattices up to scaling suffice.

**Dependencies.** [The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers](#st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms`); `mathlib:Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'`; `mathlib:PadicInt`; `mathlib:Padic`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 3.1, printed p. 23. The global statement this lemma reduces to local ones (the local-global step is standard and not written in the source).

**Proof route.**

1. For almost all p, f is already Z_p-integral (finitely many denominators); take gamma_p = 1 there.
2. Lift each gamma_p to GL2(Q_p), using the identity at almost all p, and set Lambda_p=Z_p² gamma_p. Choose a positive integer D supported on the finite exceptional set such that D Z_p² ⊂ Lambda_p ⊂ D^{-1}Z_p² for all p. Set Lambda={v in D^{-1}Z² : v belongs to every Lambda_p}. It lies between D Z² and D^{-1}Z². The Chinese remainder theorem on these finite quotient lattices shows Lambda tensor Z_p = Lambda_p for each p; density at a single prime alone would not establish simultaneous compatibility.
3. Lambda is free (Z a PID): Lambda = Z^2 gamma for gamma in GL2(Q); then gamma_p = k_p gamma with k_p in GL2(Z_p).
4. gamma * f = k_p^{-1} * (gamma_p * f) is Z_p-integral for every p (GL2(Z_p) preserves V(Z_p)), hence integral.

**Acceptance checks.**

- If a rational local matrix gamma at the only bad prime p also belongs to GL2(Z_q) at every q ≠ p (equivalently gamma and gamma^{-1} have entries in Z[1/p]), it works globally. Rationality alone is insufficient: diag(1/3,1) is integral and invertible over Z_2, but sends x⁴+y⁴ to x⁴/9+9y⁴, introducing a denominator at 3.

<a id="st1-integral-representatives-of-locally-soluble-quartics"></a>

### 1.51 Bhargava-Shankar Lemma 3.4: locally soluble quartics with invariants divisible by (48, 1728) have integral representatives

Let f in V_Q be locally soluble with integral invariants I, J such that 2^4 . 3 | I and 2^6 . 3^3 | J (equivalently I = -48A, J = -1728B with A, B in Z) and 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. Then f is PGL2(Q)-equivalent to an integral binary quartic form.

**Hypotheses.** Only Q_p-solubility for every p is used (R-solubility is not needed for integrality).

**Dependencies.** [Every Q_p-soluble quartic with invariants (-48A, -1728B) has a Z_p-integral representative](#st1-local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics`); [Local integral representatives at every prime give a global one](#st1-integrality-from-local-integrality) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/integrality-from-local-integrality`); [Soluble and locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st1-soluble-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/soluble-binary-quartic-forms`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Lemma 3.4, printed p. 23. The lemma; the source defers the proof to Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer, replaced here by the projection argument.

**Proof route.**

1. Put A = -I/48, B = -J/1728 in Z.
2. For every p, f is Q_p-soluble, so local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics gives gamma_p.
3. integrality-from-local-integrality.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Every 2-Selmer element of y^2 = x^3 - 2 is represented by an integral quartic with invariants (0, 3456).

<a id="st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer"></a>

### 1.52 Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.5: 2-Selmer elements are PGL2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral quartics with invariants 2^4 I, 2^6 J

Let E = E_{A,B} : y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B with A, B in Z, 4A^3 + 27B^2 != 0, and I = I(E) = -3A, J = J(E) = -27B. Then the elements of the 2-Selmer group of E are in bijection with the PGL2(Q)-equivalence classes of locally soluble integral binary quartic forms with invariants 2^4 I = -48A and 2^6 J = -1728B. The bijection sends the class of g to z(g), an element of Tau Ceti's selmerGroup_2 of E_{2^4 I, 2^6 J} : y^2 = x^3 + 1296 A x + 46656 B, transported to E by the variable change x |-> 36x, y |-> 216y. The integral forms with a rational linear factor and these invariants form one PGL2(Q)-class, corresponding to the identity. Stabilizers: Stab_{PGL2(Q)}(g) is isomorphic to E(Q)[2] for every such g.

**Hypotheses.** A, B integers (the minimal-pair condition is not needed; it pins the curve within its isomorphism class, as in EllipticCurves Layer 8).; The rescaling by 2^4, 2^6 is forced: Lemma 3.4's divisibility hypotheses hold for (2^4 I, 2^6 J) and not in general for (I, J).; PGL2(Q)-classes of rational forms, each represented by integral forms; two integral forms in one class need not be GL2(Z)-equivalent (the weights m(f) of ST.4 count this).

**Dependencies.** [Locally soluble quartics and Tau Ceti's 2-Selmer group (Bhargava-Shankar Proposition 3.3)](#st1-locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group`); [Bhargava-Shankar Lemma 3.4: locally soluble quartics with invariants divisible by (48, 1728) have integral representatives](#st1-integral-representatives-of-locally-soluble-quartics) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/integral-representatives-of-locally-soluble-quartics`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E(K)[2]](#st1-stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion`); [Forms with a linear factor: trivial cubic invariant and a single orbit](#st1-linear-factor-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/linear-factor-forms`); [The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)](#st0-invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.selmerGroup₂`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii; tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/GlobalQuadraticForms#layer-5-hasseminkowski-isotropy

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.5, printed p. 23. The theorem. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.5, second paragraph, printed p. 23. The identity class.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group over Q to I' = 2^4 I, J' = 2^6 J: locally soluble orbits with these invariants correspond to selmerGroup_2 of E_{I',J'}, the linear-factor orbit to 1.
2. Each such orbit contains an integral form: integral-representatives-of-locally-soluble-quartics (I' = -48A, J' = -1728B).
3. Transport to E_{A,B}: E_{I',J'} is E_{A,B} rescaled by u = 1/6; the explicit Selmer group, mu and the local conditions are compatible with this variable change (request to EllipticCurves Layer 6).
4. Stabilizers: stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion, and E_{I',J'}(Q)[2] = E(Q)[2].

**Acceptance checks.**

- y^2 = x^3 - x (A = -1, B = 0): Sel_2 has order 4 = #E(Q)[2]; the classes are those of the integral quartics q(P') for the three 2-torsion points and the linear-factor class.
- Scaling check: the quartics with invariants (I, J) themselves (without 2^4, 2^6) need not have integral representatives.

### 1.53 Comparison of the quartic parametrization with the cohomological 2-Selmer group

For an elliptic curve E_{I,J} over a number field K, the composite of the bijection (locally soluble quartic classes) -> selmerGroup_2 (locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group) with the EllipticCurves Layer 7 identification of the explicit etale-algebra 2-Selmer group selmerGroup_2 with Sel_2(E/K) in H^1(K, E[2]) is a bijection onto Sel_2(E/K); it sends the class of q(P) to the Kummer image delta(P) and the linear-factor class to 0, so the classes of K-soluble quartics are exactly the image of E(K)/2E(K) in Sel_2 and the locally soluble classes without K-points map onto Sha(E/K)[2] \ {0} under Sel_2 -> Sha[2].

**Hypotheses.** Uses only the Layer 7 comparison milestone and exact sequence; no new cohomology is built here.

**Dependencies.** [Locally soluble quartics and Tau Ceti's 2-Selmer group (Bhargava-Shankar Proposition 3.3)](#st1-locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/locally-soluble-quartics-and-the-two-selmer-group`); [z(q(P)) is the image of P under the x - T map](#st1-cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point`); `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.selmerGroup₂`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4

**Sources.** [P/stoll-descent-2006](#source-p-stoll-descent-2006), Proposition 1.4 and the case n = 2, printed p. 10. The cohomological Selmer group realized by quartics. [P/cremona-fisher-quartics-2009](#source-p-cremona-fisher-quartics-2009), Remarks after Theorem 13, printed p. 11. The identification supplied by Layer 7.

**Proof route.**

1. Compose the two bijections; the image of E(K)/2E(K): z o q = mu (cubic-invariant-of-the-quartic-of-a-point) and Layer 7 matches mu with the Kummer map.
2. The exact sequence 0 -> E(K)/2E(K) -> Sel_2 -> Sha[2] -> 0 (Layer 7) gives the statement about Sha.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For 571a1 over Q: Sel_2 has order 4, E(Q)/2E(Q) is trivial, and the three nonzero classes (Fisher's g_1, g_2, g_3) map onto Sha[2] \ {0}.

### 1.54 The embedding phi of binary quartic forms into pairs of ternary quadratic forms and the map psi on orbits

Let A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2 (Gram matrix antidiag(1/2, -1, 1/2)) and, for f = (a, b, c, d, e) in V_Z, B_f = a x_1^2 + b x_1 x_2 + c x_2^2 + d x_2 x_3 + e x_3^2 (Gram matrix (a, b/2, 0; b/2, c, d/2; 0, d/2, e)). Then phi(f) = (A_1, B_f) in W_{Z,1} = {(A_1, B)} (Bhargava-Shankar (30)). phi is injective, its image is the set of (A_1, B) with B_13 = 0, and every F_{Z,1}-class of W_{Z,1} (F_{Z,1} the lower unitriangular matrices of GL2(Z), acting by (A_1, B) |-> (A_1, B + r A_1)) has a unique representative in the image. phi preserves discriminants, and 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) = x^3 + c x^2 y + (bd - 4ae) x y^2 + (a d^2 + b^2 e - 4ace) y^3 is the monic cubic resolvent of f (same I, J). With rho(gamma) = (det gamma)^{-1} (a^2, ab, b^2; 2ac, ad + bc, 2bd; c^2, cd, d^2) for gamma = (a b; c d), rho : GL2(Z) -> SO(A_1, Z) is a homomorphism and phi(gamma . f) = rho(gamma) . phi(f) modulo F_{Z,1}. The induced map psi : PGL2(Z)\V_Z -> (GL2(Z) x SL3(Z))\W_Z is the composite of the orbit bijection with forgetting the slice.

**Hypotheses.** rho is written in the coordinate order that makes phi equivariant for the action g . B = g B g^T; the matrix printed as (31) in Bhargava-Shankar has the coordinates in the reverse order (ArithmeticStatistics/E203).; The resolvent form is 4 Det(A x - B y); the 'Det(Ax - By)' printed on p. 16 has leading coefficient 1/4 (ArithmeticStatistics/E201).

**Dependencies.** [Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form](#st1-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); [The PGL2-action on binary quartic forms, orbits with given invariants, and stabilizers](#st1-pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms`); [Binary quartic forms, the GL₂ action by linear substitution and the twisted PGL₂ action](#st0-binary-quartic-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-form`); [The invariants I and J and the discriminant Δ of a binary quartic form](#st0-binary-quartic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-invariants`); [Δ(f) is Mathlib's polynomial discriminant of f(X, 1)](#st0-quartic-discriminant-is-the-polynomial-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/quartic-discriminant-is-the-polynomial-discriminant`); `mathlib:Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup`; `mathlib:Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.toGL`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), (30)-(31), printed p. 16. The embedding and the slice. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 2.6, printed p. 16. The normalized representatives. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 2.8, printed p. 21. The monic cubic resolvent with the factor 4.

**API.**

- `BinaryQuartic.veroneseForm` (data): A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2.
- `BinaryQuartic.embed` (constructor): phi(f) = (A_1, B_f).
- `BinaryQuartic.rho` (data): rho : GL2(Z) -> SL3(Z), in the coordinate order compatible with (30).
- `BinaryQuartic.slice` (data): W_{Z,1} = {(A, B) : A = A_1}.
- `BinaryQuartic.embed_injective` (characterisation): phi is injective.
- `BinaryQuartic.mem_range_embed_iff` (characterisation): The image of phi is {(A_1, B) : B_13 = 0}.
- `BinaryQuartic.exists_unique_normalized` (characterisation): Each F_{Z,1}-class of the slice meets the image of phi exactly once.
- `BinaryQuartic.disc_embed` (relation): Disc phi(f) = Disc f.
- `BinaryQuartic.resolventForm_embed` (simp): 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) = x^3 + c x^2 y + (bd - 4ae) x y^2 + (ad^2 + b^2 e - 4ace) y^3.
- `BinaryQuartic.rho_det` (relation): det rho(gamma) = 1.
- `BinaryQuartic.veroneseForm_comp_rho` (relation): rho(gamma) preserves A_1.
- `BinaryQuartic.embed_smul` (functoriality): phi(gamma . f) = rho(gamma) . phi(f) modulo F_{Z,1}.
- `BinaryQuartic.unipotentT` (example): The element (1 1; 0 1) of GL2(Z).

**Checks.**

- `BinaryQuartic.test_embed_x3y` (computation): The resolvent form of phi(x^3 y) is x^3.
- `BinaryQuartic.test_rho_T` (computation): rho(1 1; 0 1) = (1 1 1; 0 1 2; 0 0 1).
- `BinaryQuartic.test_rho_equivariance_T` (non-example): The x_1^2-coefficient of rho(T) . B_{y^4} equals that of B_{(x+y)^4} = B_{T . y^4}, namely 1; with the printed order of (31) it would be 0.

**Proof route.**

1. phi and the slice: explicit; the (1,3)-entry of B + r A_1 is B_13 + r/2 in half-integral units, so exactly one r makes it 0.
2. Discriminant and resolvent: expand 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) (checked symbolically); its I, J equal I(f), J(f) and its discriminant is disc(f).
3. rho is a homomorphism into SO(A_1): rho(gamma) A_1 rho(gamma)^T = A_1 and det rho(gamma) = 1 (polynomial identities).
4. Equivariance: rho(gamma) B_f rho(gamma)^T - B_{gamma . f} is a multiple of A_1, checked on the generators (1 1; 0 1), (0 1; 1 0), (1 0; 0 -1) of GL2(Z) and symbolically for general gamma.

**Acceptance checks.**

- phi(x^3 y) = (A_1, x_1 x_2) with resolvent x^3.
- rho(1 1; 0 1) = (1 1 1; 0 1 2; 0 0 1).
- The x_1^2-coefficient of rho(T) . B_{y^4} equals that of B_{(x+y)^4}, namely 1 (the printed order gives 0).

**Consumers.** ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/uniformity-estimate-for-infinitely-many-congruence-conditions — transport of Bhargava's uniformity estimate on W_Z (BS Theorem 2.19) to V_Z through psi, which needs the orbit bijection (orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding) and the fibre bound (fibres-of-the-embedding-are-uniformly-bounded); ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/eligible-invariant-pairs — the proof of Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 1.7 reads eligibility off the monic cubic resolvent 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y); ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-of-a-pair — Remark 2.15: the orbit of phi(f) corresponds to a quartic ring with a monogenized cubic resolvent (Wood)

<a id="st1-special-orthogonal-group-of-the-veronese-form"></a>

### 1.55 rho maps GL2(Z) onto SO(A_1, Z)

An element M of SL3(Z) preserves A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2 (M A_1 M^T = A_1) if and only if M = rho(gamma) for some gamma in GL2(Z); rho has kernel {+-1}, so it induces an isomorphism PGL2(Z) = SO(A_1, Z).

**Hypotheses.** The coordinate order of rho as in the embedding node.

**Dependencies.** [The embedding phi of binary quartic forms into pairs of ternary quadratic forms and the map psi on orbits](#st1-embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); `mathlib:Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Section 2.6, printed p. 16. The statement (the cited thesis is not used; the proof above replaces it). [P/wood-quartic-rings-2012](#source-p-wood-quartic-rings-2012), Lemma 3.2, printed p. 6. The same statement in Wood's coordinates.

**Proof route.**

1. Over a field K of characteristic not 2: M in SO(A_1)(K) preserves the conic A_1 = 0, parametrized by (s : t) |-> (s^2 : st : t^2); M restricted to the conic is (Q_1 : Q_2 : Q_3) with Q_2^2 = Q_1 Q_3 and Q_1, Q_3 coprime binary quadratics, so Q_1 = L_1^2, Q_3 = L_2^2, Q_2 = L_1 L_2 up to a scalar, and M agrees with rho(gamma) (gamma given by the linear forms L_1, L_2) on the conic, which spans P^2; hence M = lambda rho(gamma), and det = 1 with M A_1 M^T = A_1 forces lambda = 1.
2. Integrality: if rho(gamma) is integral with gamma = (a b; c d) scaled to be a primitive integral matrix, then ad - bc divides a^2, b^2, c^2, d^2, so every prime dividing ad - bc divides a, b, c, d; hence ad - bc = +-1 and gamma is in GL2(Z).
3. Kernel: rho(gamma) = 1 forces gamma scalar, and scalars in GL2(Z) are +-1.

**Acceptance checks.**

- rho(-1) = 1.
- rho(0 1; 1 0) reverses the coordinates up to sign and preserves A_1.

<a id="st1-orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding"></a>

### 1.56 Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.14: phi induces a bijection of PGL2(Z)-orbits with F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-orbits

The map phi induces a canonical bijection between PGL2(Z)-orbits on V_Z and F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1, Z)-orbits on W_{Z,1}. Equivalently: f and g are GL2(Z)-equivalent iff there are M in SL3(Z) preserving A_1 and r in Z with B_g = r A_1 + M B_f M^T.

**Hypotheses.** F_{Z,1} (acting on the pair) and SO(A_1, Z) (acting on the variables) commute.

**Dependencies.** [The embedding phi of binary quartic forms into pairs of ternary quadratic forms and the map psi on orbits](#st1-embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); [rho maps GL2(Z) onto SO(A_1, Z)](#st1-special-orthogonal-group-of-the-veronese-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/special-orthogonal-group-of-the-veronese-form`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 2.14, printed p. 16. The theorem.

**Proof route.**

1. phi induces a bijection V_Z -> F_{Z,1}\W_{Z,1} (embedding node).
2. This bijection intertwines gamma with rho(gamma) (embed_smul), and rho(GL2(Z)) = SO(A_1, Z) (special-orthogonal-group-of-the-veronese-form); so orbits correspond.

**Acceptance checks.**

- x^3 y and x^3 y + x y^3 are not equivalent, and neither are their images.

<a id="st1-fibres-of-the-embedding-are-uniformly-bounded"></a>

### 1.57 Bhargava-Shankar Proposition 2.16: the fibres of psi over nondegenerate classes are uniformly bounded

Let N be an upper bound for #{(x, y) in Z^2 : g(x, y) = 1} over all integral binary cubic forms g of nonzero discriminant (N = 12 by Delone and Evertse; N = 10 by Bennett). An element of (GL2(Z) x SL3(Z))\W_Z of nonzero discriminant has at most 2N preimages in PGL2(Z)\V_Z under psi.

**Hypotheses.** Nonzero discriminant.; The source states the bound 12 = N; its argument gives 2N (ArithmeticStatistics/E202). Any uniform bound suffices for Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.20 and the uniformity estimate.

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.14: phi induces a bijection of PGL2(Z)-orbits with F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-orbits](#st1-orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding`); [Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form](#st1-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); `DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.4`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proposition 2.16 and proof, printed p. 17. The statement. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Proposition 2.16, printed p. 17. The imported Thue-equation bound.

**Proof route.**

1. By orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding it suffices to bound the F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1, Z)-classes in W_{Z,1} inside a GL2(Z) x SL3(Z)-orbit w; fix (A_1, B_0) in w and let g = 4 Det(A_1 x - B_0 y) (monic).
2. An element (A_1, B) = (g_2, g_3) . (A_1, B_0) of the slice has first form p A_1 + q B_0 transformed to A_1, so 4 Det(p A_1 + q B_0) = 1, i.e. g(p, -q) = 1 for the first row (p, q) of g_2 (4 Det is multiplied by det(g_3)^2 = 1).
3. Two such elements with the same first row differ by g_2' g_2^{-1} = (1 0; r s) with s = +-1 and by an element of SO(A_1, Z): for s = 1 they are F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1, Z)-equivalent, for s = -1 they differ by (A_1, B) |-> (A_1, -B) (the forms f and -f).
4. Hence the number of classes is at most 2 #{(x, y) : g(x, y) = 1} <= 2N.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For f with J(f) != 0, f and -f are distinct classes in the same fibre (J(-f) = -J(f)).
- For the resolvent x^3 - x^2 y - 2 x y^2 + y^3 (disc 49, 9 solutions of g = 1, automorphism group of order 3) the fibre has at most 18 elements by this argument.

**Interface qualification.** The uniform bound on the number of solutions of cubic Thue equations is requested from DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.4.

<a id="st1-refinement-quartic-minors"></a>

### 1.58 Quartic coefficient minors

Write the coefficient rows of the parent pair of ternary integral quadratic forms in the order 11,12,13,22,23,33, using the integral polynomial coefficients, including cross terms without halving. Set λ(i,j)=a_i b_j−a_j b_i. The 15 entries with i<j give the oriented SL₂-invariant wedge of the two coefficient rows.

**Hypotheses.** Base Z; scalar extension to any commutative ring preserves the formulas.

**Dependencies.** [Pairs of ternary quadratic forms, the GL3 x GL2 action and the cubic resolvent form](#st1-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); `mathlib:Matrix.det`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl3](#source-s1-hcl3), §3.7, (20),(27), pp.1347–1348. The coefficient minors and their Plücker relations give the quartic multiplication invariants.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quarticMinors` (constructor): For a 2×6 integral coefficient matrix M, return λ(i,j)=M(0,i)M(1,j)−M(0,j)M(1,i).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quarticMinors_swap` (relation): Swapping i and j negates λ(i,j).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quarticMinors_plucker` (relation): For i<j<k<l, λ(i,k)λ(j,l)=λ(i,j)λ(k,l)+λ(i,l)λ(j,k).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quarticMinors_mul` (functoriality): For h a 2×2 integer matrix, quarticMinors(hM)=det(h)·quarticMinors(M). In particular determinant-one row operations preserve the fixed-label fibre.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.minors_standard` (computation): For rows (1,0,0,0,0,0) and (0,1,0,0,0,0), λ(0,1)=1.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.minors_row_swap` (non-example): Interchanging those two rows gives λ(0,1)=−1.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.minors_dependent` (degenerate): If the second row is an integer multiple of the first, all λ(i,j)=0.

**Proof route.**

1. Expand the two-by-two determinants. Row operations of determinant one preserve them; expanding four columns gives λ(i,k)λ(j,l)=λ(i,j)λ(k,l)+λ(i,l)λ(j,k). No symmetric-matrix denominators enter.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For rows (1,0,0,0,0,0) and (0,1,0,0,0,0), λ(0,1)=1.
- Interchanging those two rows gives λ(0,1)=−1.
- If the second row is an integer multiple of the first, all λ(i,j)=0.

**Consumers.** HCL III Lemmas16–17 and Corollary18, §§3.6–3.8, pp.1346–1350; integral-minor-fibres — The Plücker relation identifies the rational rank-two plane; row-change compatibility permits counting its integral lattices without changing the six labelled minors.

<a id="st1-refinement-integral-minor-fibres"></a>

### 1.59 Integral fibres of quartic minors

Every nonzero integral alternating 6×6 array satisfying the four-index Plücker equations is the minors array of an integral 2×6 matrix. If d>0 is the gcd of its entries, its fibre modulo SL₂(Z), with the six coefficients fixed, is in bijection with index-d sublattices of the saturated oriented rank-two coefficient lattice, and has Σ_{a|d}a elements. The zero array is excluded from this finite-count theorem. This is a based coefficient assertion, not a quotient by quartic-ring automorphisms.

**Hypotheses.** At least one prescribed minor is nonzero.; The six coefficient labels remain fixed; only the two rows change basis.

**Dependencies.** [Quartic coefficient minors](#st1-refinement-quartic-minors) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-quartic-minors`); `mathlib:Module.Basis`; `mathlib:Submodule.span`; `mathlib:Submodule.smithNormalForm`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl3](#source-s1-hcl3), Lemmas16–17 and their proofs, pp.1348–1349. The proof uses SL₂(Z) fibres. The displayed G_Z wording is interpreted through the fixed labelled lattice, consistently with the parent’s reviewed fixed-ring convention.

**Proof route.**

1. Choose a nonzero minor to reconstruct the rational rank-two plane and use the Plücker equations to check its remaining coordinates. Saturate its intersection with Z⁶. The primitive minors specify an oriented basis of this lattice; minors scaled by d specify oriented sublattices of index d. Hermite normal forms count them by the divisor sum.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For primitive minors the fibre is a single SL₂(Z)-orbit.
- For gcd 2 there are three oriented lattice classes.
- A zero minors array includes many dependent pairs; no finite divisor-sum formula is assigned to it.

<a id="st1-refinement-quintic-multiplication"></a>

### 1.60 Normalized quintic multiplication

For the parent integral alternating quadruple A, construct the commutative ring R(A) on Z⁵ with identity e₀ and the usual additive group. Normalize c¹₁₂=c²₁₂=c³₃₄=c⁴₃₄=0. The remaining nonconstant coefficients in e_i e_j are the unique solution of HCL IV (21), with permutation signs and bracket denominators cancelled as integral polynomials. Define c⁰_ij=Σ_{r=1}⁴(cʳ_jk cᵏ_ri−cʳ_ij cᵏ_rk), choosing k≠i; this is independent of that choice. The multiplication is associative at every A, including A=0.

**Hypotheses.** A has zero diagonal and opposite off-diagonal entries; characteristic two is handled by the integral polynomial specialization.

**Dependencies.** [Quadruples of quinary alternating 2-forms and the GL4 x SL5 action](#st1-quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms`); `mathlib:Matrix.det`; `mathlib:Algebra.trace`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl4](#source-s1-hcl4), §4, (16)–(22), pp.67–69. The normalized degree-five multiplication table extends over Z and to discriminant-zero quadruples.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quinticRing` (constructor): Return a commutative ring structure on the coordinate carrier Z⁵.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quinticRing_add` (compatibility): Its addition is componentwise and its identity is e₀.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quinticCoeff_scale` (relation): A↦tA scales each nonconstant normalized structure coefficient by t⁵, and each constant coefficient by t¹⁰.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quintic_zero` (degenerate): At A=0, e_i e_j=0 for all i,j>0, so R(0)=Z⊕Z⁴ with square-zero augmentation ideal.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quintic_one` (characterisation): For every A, e₀ e_i=e_i; using the all-ones vector as identity fails this test.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.quintic_sparse` (computation): Take A₁=E₁₂−E₂₁+E₃₄−E₄₃, A₂=E₄₅−E₅₄, A₃=E₁₂−E₂₁+E₃₅−E₅₃, A₄=0. The coefficient of e₄ in e₁e₃ is 1, by (19).

**Proof route.**

1. Use Q(X,Y)=Q(X+Y)−Q(X)−Q(Y) from the parent Pfaffian covariant. The bracket is Q(A_i,A_j)ᵀ A_k Q(A_l,A_m). Repeated indices give divisibility by two or four before specializing. Solve (21) with the four normalization constraints, then impose the constant-coefficient associativity equation. Prove the remaining identities as universal integral polynomial identities, first on the dense nondegenerate locus and then identically.

**Acceptance checks.**

- At A=0, e_i e_j=0 for all i,j>0, so R(0)=Z⊕Z⁴ with square-zero augmentation ideal.
- For every A, e₀ e_i=e_i; using the all-ones vector as identity fails this test.
- Take A₁=E₁₂−E₂₁+E₃₄−E₄₃, A₂=E₄₅−E₅₄, A₃=E₁₂−E₂₁+E₃₅−E₅₃, A₄=0. The coefficient of e₄ in e₁e₃ is 1, by (19).

**Consumers.** HCL IV Theorem8 p.80, Theorem12 pp.84–88 and Lemma16 pp.88–89; integral-quintic-realization — The integral associative multiplication table constructs the order before orbit descent; coefficient homogeneity clears rational denominators and the fixed additive structure keeps the based order normalized.

<a id="st1-refinement-sextic-multiplication"></a>

### 1.61 Normalized sextic multiplication

Construct S(A) on Z⁶ with the usual addition and identity e₀. Form the 4×4 determinants δ of the four coefficient rows of A. Use the cubic contractions D of (35), but only the integral combinations specified in (36): individual D expressions need not be integral. Normalize d¹₁₂=d²₁₂=d³₃₄=d⁴₃₄=d⁴₄₅=0 and recover constant terms from the associative equation (38), choosing k≠i. The resulting table is integral and associative for all A. Its discriminant is (16 Disc(R(A)))³.

**Hypotheses.** The identity and all six coordinates are retained.; No nonzero-discriminant assumption is made for the polynomial table.

**Dependencies.** [Normalized quintic multiplication](#st1-refinement-quintic-multiplication) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-quintic-multiplication`); `mathlib:Matrix.det`; `mathlib:Algebra.trace`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl4](#source-s1-hcl4), §6, (34)–(38), Lemma7, pp.77–79; (33), p.76. The sextic table is built from integral combinations, and carries the factor 16 in its discriminant.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.sexticRing` (constructor): Return the commutative ring structure on Z⁶ associated to A.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.sexticRing_add` (compatibility): The addition is componentwise and the identity is e₀.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.sextic_discriminant` (relation): Disc S(A)=4096(Disc R(A))³.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.sextic_zero` (degenerate): For A=0, all products e_i e_j with i,j>0 vanish.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.sextic_one` (characterisation): The identity is e₀, and e₀ e₅=e₅.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.sextic_factor16` (non-example): If Disc R(A)=1, Disc S(A)=4096, so S(A) cannot be the split ring Z⁶ of discriminant 1.

**Proof route.**

1. The δ determinants are degree four. Lemma7 identifies the degree-twelve integral combinations as multiplication indices on the nondegenerate resolvent lattice. Normalization fixes translation ambiguity. Extend the table identities and discriminant identity polynomially to the zero-discriminant locus.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For A=0, all products e_i e_j with i,j>0 vanish.
- The identity is e₀, and e₀ e₅=e₅.
- If Disc R(A)=1, Disc S(A)=4096, so S(A) cannot be the split ring Z⁶ of discriminant 1.

**Consumers.** HCL IV Theorem8 p.80 and Definition11 p.83; based-sextic-resolvent — The same tensor must construct a rank-six integral ring with the stated trace discriminant, including degenerate tensors; the factor16 normalization identifies the correct resolvent lattice.

<a id="st1-refinement-based-sextic-resolvent"></a>

### 1.62 Based sextic resolvent data

For based quintic and sextic rings R,S with scalar-first normalized bases, a resolvent map is a Z-linear φ:R/Z→∧²(S/Z). Its 40 coordinates form the parent quadruple A. Require that the normalized multiplication tables recovered from A equal the given tables of both R and S. Based changes use GL₄(Z)×SL₅(Z), after compatible orientations are chosen. This defines the all-discriminant resolvent data; an abstract sextic ring without φ does not suffice.

**Hypotheses.** Ranks 5 and 6 with primitive scalar vector in each chosen basis.; Bases and orientation convention are explicit.

**Dependencies.** [Normalized quintic multiplication](#st1-refinement-quintic-multiplication) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-quintic-multiplication`); [Normalized sextic multiplication](#st1-refinement-sextic-multiplication) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-sextic-multiplication`); `mathlib:exteriorPower.ιMulti`; `mathlib:exteriorPower.map`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl4](#source-s1-hcl4), Definitions10–11, §9, pp.82–83. The definition retains the map and both recovered ring tables, allowing degenerate rings.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.IsBasedSexticResolvent` (characterisation): For a coefficient quadruple A and normalized coordinate ring structures R,S, the condition is R=R(A) and S=S(A). This coordinate predicate represents φ through its coefficients.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.basedSexticResolvent_self` (constructor): The pair R(A),S(A), with map having coordinates A, is resolvent data.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.basedSexticResolvent_disc` (relation): Resolvent data satisfies Disc S=4096(Disc R)³.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.resolvent_zero` (degenerate): A=0 gives resolvent data between the two square-zero rings of ranks 5 and6.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.resolvent_recovers_both` (characterisation): Holding A fixed forces both given coordinate multiplications, not only the quintic one.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.resolvent_wrong_disc` (non-example): A sextic structure with discriminant different from 4096(Disc R(A))³ fails the resolvent condition.

**Proof route.**

1. Identify R/Z and S/Z with their free coordinate modules through the chosen bases. Use the native exterior-power wedge basis to read φ as 40 coefficients. Compare multiplication and identity, rather than requiring equality of carrier types. Independence of normalized lifts follows from the translation rules in §§4 and6.

**Acceptance checks.**

- A=0 gives resolvent data between the two square-zero rings of ranks 5 and6.
- Holding A fixed forces both given coordinate multiplications, not only the quintic one.
- A sextic structure with discriminant different from 4096(Disc R(A))³ fails the resolvent condition.

**Consumers.** HCL IV Theorem1 pp.54–55 and Theorem17 p.89; quintic-minimal-model — The orbit correspondence keeps the map and oriented bases along with both rings; this datum is needed to distinguish minimal integral representatives and their based resolvents.

<a id="st1-refinement-nondegenerate-resolvent-comparison"></a>

### 1.63 Comparison with the nondegenerate resolvent lattice

For Disc R≠0, compare the all-discriminant map definition with a rank-six lattice S in the M-fixed part of the rational S₅-closure, where M is the order-20 metacyclic subgroup. Require 1 primitive, Disc S=(16 Disc R)³, and integral image of the alternating trace-dual map g:∧²(ann(1)⊂S*)→ann(1)⊂R*. With compatible oriented bases, its coordinates recover R and S and the lattice is closed under multiplication. The image condition and discriminant condition are both necessary.

**Hypotheses.** Nonzero discriminant; the rational S₅-closure and its permutation labels are specified.

**Dependencies.** [Based sextic resolvent data](#st1-refinement-based-sextic-resolvent) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-based-sextic-resolvent`); `mathlib:Algebra.trace`; `mathlib:exteriorPower.map`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl4](#source-s1-hcl4), Definition5, Proposition6, §§5.3–7, pp.73–80. The trace-dual and determinant conditions identify the nondegenerate lattice with the polynomial construction.

**Proof route.**

1. The alternating trilinear determinant f of (23), divided by 16 Disc R, is integral exactly when its orientation-dual bilinear map g is integral. The trace-zero dual modules have ranks four and five. Formula (32) and compatible orientations recover the quintic table; Lemma7 recovers the sextic table and proves ring closure.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The sextic discriminant is a cube with the factor 16 present.
- The map targets the annihilator of 1 in the dual, not the quintic ring itself.

<a id="st1-refinement-integral-quintic-realization"></a>

### 1.64 Integral realization of quintic multiplication invariants

An integral set of normalized nonconstant quintic structure coefficients that occurs among the SL₅ invariants of a complex alternating quadruple has an integral quadruple with those same coefficients. Applied to quintic rings, this supplies the existence part imported from the parent correspondence.

**Hypotheses.** The integral coefficients belong to the complex invariant image; associativity alone must first be proved to imply this.

**Dependencies.** [Normalized quintic multiplication](#st1-refinement-quintic-multiplication) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-quintic-multiplication`); `mathlib:Module.Basis`

**Sources.** [S1/hcl4](#source-s1-hcl4), Theorem12 and Lemmas13–15, §§10–11, pp.83–88. The invariant-realization theorem supplies integral representatives, while the omitted rational case is not silently treated as proved.

**Proof route.**

1. Lemma13 produces coefficients multiplied by an integer through row/column scaling after finding a common isotropic pair. Lemma14 clears rational denominators up to a multiplier. Lemma15 lowers a positive multiplier at a prime through its two Pfaffian normal forms. Induction yields multiplier one. The source omits the nonétale rational classification used before Lemma14; record that proof obligation separately. In the common-isotropic-pair argument choose v in the left kernel of A₁ and intersect the kernels of vᵀA₂,vᵀA₃,vᵀA₄; three linear conditions leave dimension at least2 and include v.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The chosen integral realization preserves every normalized coefficient, not merely the discriminant.
- Scaling all four matrices by n alone gives n⁵ coefficients and does not prove Lemma13.

<a id="st1-refinement-quintic-minimal-model"></a>

### 1.65 Quintic maximal rings and minimal integral models

For a nondegenerate rational alternating quadruple, minimal absolute integral discriminant in its GL₄(Q)×GL₅(Q)-orbit corresponds to the maximal quintic order. For a fixed maximal quintic ring and fixed normalized quotient basis, its integral realizations form a single SL₅(Z)-orbit. This strengthens the parent’s unbased GL₄(Z)×SL₅(Z) uniqueness with the basis fixed.

**Hypotheses.** Nonzero discriminant; minimality uses the full GL₅ rational action, as specified by the reviewed parent.

**Dependencies.** [Normalized quintic multiplication](#st1-refinement-quintic-multiplication) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-quintic-multiplication`); [Integral realization of quintic multiplication invariants](#st1-refinement-integral-quintic-realization) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-integral-quintic-realization`); [Maximality of R(A) at p is a congruence condition U_p on quadruples](#st1-maximality-of-quintic-rings-at-p) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/maximality-of-quintic-rings-at-p`)

**Sources.** [S1/hcl4](#source-s1-hcl4), Lemma16, Theorem17 and Corollaries18–19, pp.88–89. Fixed-ring uniqueness follows by saturation of the Pfaffian lattice.

**Proof route.**

1. Use the 252 maximal minors of the five Pfaffian quadrics: divisibility at a prime either exhibits content or the alternative normal form yielding an overring with quotient (Z/pZ)³. Maximality excludes both. The quadrics then span the saturated integral lattice in their common rational plane, so the transition matrix is integral unimodular.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The parent maximality congruences, including primes2 and3, are retained.
- No uniqueness claim is made for arbitrary nonmaximal rings.

<a id="st1-refinement-monogenized-resolvent"></a>

### 1.66 Monogenized cubic resolvents

A monogenization of a cubic ring C is an element ω modulo Z·1 with a lift w such that 1,w,w² is a Z-basis. Two lifts differing by an integer define the same monogenization. For a quartic ring, retain the full parent cubic-resolvent map and orientation as well as this monogenization. Isomorphisms must preserve ω, rather than merely the underlying monogenic ring.

**Hypotheses.** C is free of rank3 over Z; no discriminant restriction.

**Dependencies.** [Quartic rings and their cubic resolvent rings](#st1-quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent`); `mathlib:Module.Basis`; `mathlib:Algebra.adjoin`; `mathlib:AdjoinRoot`; `mathlib:LinearIndependent`

**Sources.** [S1/wood](#source-s1-wood), Defining paragraph p.5, Proposition2.3 p.6 and Proposition4.1 p.7. A generator class modulo scalars is extra resolvent data.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.IsMonogenizing` (characterisation): For a cubic Z-algebra C and w∈C, 1,w,w² are Z-linearly independent and span C.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.monogenizing_translate` (relation): IsMonogenizing(w+k)=IsMonogenizing(w) for k∈Z.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.monogenizing_adjoin` (compatibility): A monogenizing w satisfies Z[w]=C.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.monogenizing_truncated` (computation): In Z[t]/(t³), t is monogenizing.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.monogenizing_translate_test` (compatibility): In Z[t]/(t³), t+1 is monogenizing and gives the same quotient generator class.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.monogenizing_square_fails` (non-example): In Z[t]/(t³), t² is not monogenizing: its square is zero and its power basis misses t.

**Proof route.**

1. Translate the lift and compare the three power-basis columns by a unipotent integer matrix. The same determinant-one calculation gives the subgroup N of changes fixing the first quotient basis vector.

**Acceptance checks.**

- In Z[t]/(t³), t is monogenizing.
- In Z[t]/(t³), t+1 is monogenizing and gives the same quotient generator class.
- In Z[t]/(t³), t² is not monogenizing: its square is zero and its power basis misses t.

**Consumers.** Wood Proposition2.3 p.6, Proposition4.1 p.7, Theorem1.1 p.1 and §5 pp.8–9; wood-ring-interpretation — The binary-quartic inverse needs a generator of the cubic resolvent modulo scalars, with translation and sign controlled; the adjoin characterization separates a true generator from a proper suborder.

<a id="st1-refinement-wood-ring-interpretation"></a>

### 1.67 Ring interpretation of the binary quartic embedding

The parent PGL₂(Z)-orbit embedding into pairs of ternary integral quadratic forms has the following ring interpretation: its image parametrizes quartic rings equipped with a monogenized cubic resolvent. For Wood’s ordinary GL₂(Z) action the determinant-square twist is trivial on integral unimodular matrices, and scalar −1 acts trivially on quartics. Thus Wood’s GL₂(Z)-orbit set is the parent PGL₂(Z)-orbit set. The generator, the cubic-resolvent map and the ring discriminant are preserved.

**Hypotheses.** Integral unimodular groups; this equivalence of action conventions is not asserted over arbitrary fields.

**Dependencies.** [Monogenized cubic resolvents](#st1-refinement-monogenized-resolvent) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-monogenized-resolvent`); [The embedding phi of binary quartic forms into pairs of ternary quadratic forms and the map psi on orbits](#st1-embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 2.14: phi induces a bijection of PGL2(Z)-orbits with F_{Z,1} x SO(A_1,Z)-orbits](#st1-orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/orbit-bijection-for-the-embedding`); `GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.2`

**Sources.** [S1/wood](#source-s1-wood), Theorems1.1,2.5,3.1; Lemma3.2; §5 proof, pp.1,6–8. This is the additive ring-theoretic interpretation of the existing embedding, including its inverse and marked generator.

**Proof route.**

1. In Wood’s coordinates A₀ has 4det A₀=−1. The associated cubic multiplication makes 1,w,w² a basis. Conversely monogenization gives a ternary quadratic form with 4det=−1; its integral equivalence to the Veronese form supplies the inverse. The stabilizer calculation in the parent turns equivalence of based pairs into GL₂ equivalence of quartics. Respect the parent corrected quartic multiplication and the minus sign in 4det(Ax−By).

**Acceptance checks.**

- Dropping the generator class loses information and changes the orbit problem.
- Wood’s A₀ and the parent Veronese A₁ are equivalent coordinate conventions, not equal matrices.

<a id="st1-refinement-symmetric-pencil"></a>

### 1.68 Symmetric pencils and their invariant binary forms

Let Wₙ(R) be pairs (A,B) of symmetric n×n matrices over a commutative ring. Define f_A,B(x,y)=(−1)^{n(n−1)/2}det(xA−yB), represented by coefficients f_i of x^{n−i}y^i. SLₙ acts by simultaneous congruence. For even n the scalar μ₂ acts trivially, giving a group-scheme action of SLₙ/μ₂. Its R-points generally exceed SLₙ(R)/μ₂(R). Over C the invariant ring of SLₙ is the polynomial ring in the n+1 determinant coefficients.

**Hypotheses.** No halving of off-diagonal entries: these are bilinear Gram matrices.; Arithmetic solubility later requires a field of characteristic not2 and nonzero discriminant.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Matrix.IsSymm`; `mathlib:Matrix.det`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), §2, (1)–(2), pp.6–7; BSWII §3.1, (1), pp.7–8. The signed determinant fixes both the integral lattice and the relevant group action.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencilInvariant` (data): For any two n×n matrices, return the n+1 coefficients of the signed determinant; restrict to symmetric matrices for Wₙ.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencilInvariant_congr` (functoriality): Replacing A,B by gAgᵀ,gBgᵀ multiplies every coefficient by det(g)².
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencilInvariant_scalar` (simp): For A=aIₙ and B=bIₙ the invariant is (−1)^{n(n−1)/2}(ax−by)ⁿ.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencil_n1` (computation): For n=1, the coefficient vector is (a,−b).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencil_n3_identity` (non-example): For n=3 and A=I₃,B=0, f=−x³; the sign is not positive.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencil_zero` (degenerate): For n≥1, A=B=0 gives the zero binary form.

**Proof route.**

1. Expand the determinant universally, checking homogeneity. Congruence multiplies the invariant by det(g)². The two scalar factors cancel for the μ₂ action. The invariant-ring theorem is used over C as in the source; an integral invariant-ring theorem is not inferred from it.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For n=1, the coefficient vector is (a,−b).
- For n=3 and A=I₃,B=0, f=−x³; the sign is not positive.
- For n≥1, A=B=0 gives the zero binary form.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorem16 p.7, Corollary19 p.8 and Theorem24 pp.14–16; integral-pencil-orbits and pencil-existence — The signed determinant labels the integral and rational orbit fibres; congruence and scalar characters track how a change of basis or model changes that fibre.

<a id="st1-refinement-binary-discriminant"></a>

### 1.69 Resultant and ring normalizations of the binary discriminant

Use the fixed-degree universal binary discriminant Δ_n of ST.0/binary-discriminant. For n≥2, identify it with the signed universal resultant quotient Res(F,F′)/a₀, where the universal divisibility is established before specializing a₀. At degree 3 it agrees with the parent binary-cubic discriminant, at degree 4 with ST.0’s quartic invariant discriminant. The later refinement-binary-form-order target supplies the trace-discriminant equality for its associated rank-n order, using this normalization. Leading-zero specializations use Δ_n, not the lower-degree affine discriminant. ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.binaryDiscriminant is the evaluation interface for the same ST.0 polynomial, not a second construction.

**Hypotheses.** The homogeneous degree n is fixed even when the dehomogenized polynomial drops degree.

**Dependencies.** [Fixed-degree binary discriminant](#st0-binary-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-discriminant`); [Symmetric pencils and their invariant binary forms](#st1-refinement-symmetric-pencil) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-symmetric-pencil`); [The discriminant of R(f) equals the discriminant of f](#st1-discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form`); [The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)](#st0-invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs`); `mathlib:Matrix.det`; `mathlib:MvPolynomial.eval₂`

**Sources.** [S1/wood](#source-s1-wood), §2.1, p.3; BGW §2, pp.6–7. The ring discriminant equality uses the fixed binary-form degree, not a degree-dropping univariate convention.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.binaryDiscriminant` (compatibility): Evaluate the universal discriminant supplied by ST.0 in the symmetric-pencil coefficient convention.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.binaryDiscriminant_map` (functoriality): Coefficient ring maps commute with Δₙ.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.binaryDiscriminant_scale` (relation): Δₙ(tf)=t^{2n−2}Δₙ(f).

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.discriminant_quadratic` (computation): For ax²+bxy+cy² the value is b²−4ac.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.discriminant_infinity` (non-example): For the cubic xy(x−y), with leading coefficient zero, Δ₃=1.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.discriminant_repeated` (degenerate): For n≥2, Δₙ(xⁿ)=0.

**Proof route.**

1. Compare the ST.0 discriminant polynomial with the signed universal resultant quotient over Z, establishing divisibility before evaluating the leading coefficient. Compare on a splitting algebra with f₀^{2n−2} times the squared product of root differences, then specialize the polynomial identity. The associated-order comparison is proved in refinement-binary-form-order after that order is constructed.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For ax²+bxy+cy² the value is b²−4ac.
- For the cubic xy(x−y), with leading coefficient zero, Δ₃=1.
- For n≥2, Δₙ(xⁿ)=0.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorem16 pp.6–7; BSW II Theorem3.5 p.11 and Theorem3.7 p.13; q-discriminant-divisibility — Nonzero discriminant supplies the étale algebra in the orbit dictionary. Integral specialization and the degree character are required for square divisibility, including forms with zero leading coefficient.

<a id="st1-refinement-common-isotropic"></a>

### 1.70 Common isotropic subspaces of a pencil

For a field K of characteristic not2, symmetric n×n matrices A,B and r≥0, define F_r(K) to be the set of dimension-r K-submodules U⊂Kⁿ on which both bilinear forms vanish identically. This coordinate definition includes degenerate pencils. If the invariant binary form has nonzero discriminant, for n=2g+1 and r=g it is the K-point set of a finite torsor scheme under the norm-one restriction of scalars of μ₂; the K-point set may be empty. Under the same nonzero-discriminant hypothesis, for n=2g+2 and r=g it is the K-point set of the smooth Fano variety F. The vector-space dimension is g and the projective-plane dimension is g−1.

**Hypotheses.** Use full bilinear restriction, not merely a test on coordinate basis vectors.; The finite-torsor and smooth-Fano assertions require Δ(f_{A,B})≠0; they do not apply to the zero pencil.

**Dependencies.** [Symmetric pencils and their invariant binary forms](#st1-refinement-symmetric-pencil) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-symmetric-pencil`); `mathlib:Submodule.span`; `mathlib:Module.finrank`; `mathlib:Matrix.toLin'`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), §4, pp.12–13, before Theorem23. The correct isotropic dimension is essential to the Fano and Jacobian identifications.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.commonIsotropic` (characterisation): Return the set of rank-r submodules with both bilinear restrictions zero.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.commonIsotropic_congr` (functoriality): Congruence by an invertible matrix transports common isotropic subspaces by the inverse transpose.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.commonIsotropic_zero` (simp): For the zero pencil the set consists of every dimension-r subspace.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.isotropic_zero_line` (degenerate): Every line in K³ is common isotropic for (0,0).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.isotropic_positive` (non-example): For (I₃,0) over R there is no common isotropic line.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.isotropic_block` (characterisation): If the first g×g blocks of both matrices vanish, the span of the first g coordinate vectors is common isotropic.

**Proof route.**

1. The native rational-point predicate is finite rank and ∀u,v∈U, uᵀAv=uᵀBv=0. On the nonzero-discriminant locus, use the regular-pencil geometric assertions of BGW §4. The Grassmannian/Fano and group-scheme carriers remain explicit supplier gaps; no geometric conclusion is inferred for a degenerate pencil.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Every line in K³ is common isotropic for (0,0).
- For (I₃,0) over R there is no common isotropic line.
- If the first g×g blocks of both matrices vanish, the span of the first g coordinate vectors is common isotropic.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorem23 pp.12–13, Theorem28 pp.18–19 and Theorem29 p.20; pencil-fano-torsor — The bilinear vanishing condition defines the Fano points used for solubility; dimension and congruence compatibility identify the correct g-dimensional vector planes in even degree.

<a id="st1-refinement-binary-form-order"></a>

### 1.71 Orders and distinguished ideals of a binary form

Let D be a Dedekind domain with fraction field K, n≥3, and f a binary n-ic form with f₀≠0 and Δ≠0. In L=K[t]/(f(t,1)), with θ the image of t, set ζ_i=Σ_{j=0}^{i−1}f_j θ^{i−j}. The D-lattice R_f=⟨1,ζ₁,…,ζ_{n−1}⟩ is a ring. For 0≤k≤n−1, I_f(k)=⟨1,θ,…,θᵏ,ζ_{k+1},…,ζ_{n−1}⟩ is an R_f-stable full lattice. Disc R_f=Δ(f), and f′(θ)^{-1}I_f(n−2) is its trace dual. L can be a product of fields; it is not assumed a domain.

**Hypotheses.** D is a Dedekind domain; char K≠2 for the consuming pencil theorem.; The quotient has degree n and is separable.

**Dependencies.** [Resultant and ring normalizations of the binary discriminant](#st1-refinement-binary-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-binary-discriminant`); `mathlib:Submodule.span`; `mathlib:Algebra.adjoin`; `mathlib:Algebra.trace`; `mathlib:AdjoinRoot.root`; `mathlib:IsFractionRing`; `mathlib:IsDedekindDomain`; `mathlib:LinearMap.mulLeft`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), §2, pp.6–7, before Theorem16. The order and special ideals provide the integral parametrization carrier.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formOrder` (constructor): The D-subalgebra generated by 1 and ζ_i; its underlying module equals their D-span under the hypotheses.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formIdeal` (data): Return the displayed D-span defining I_f(k).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formIdeal_traceDual` (compatibility): Under the trace pairing, the dual order is f′(θ)^{-1}I_f(n−2).
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formOrder_span` (compatibility): If θ satisfies f(θ,1)=0 and n≥3, the underlying D-module of formOrder is the D-span of 1,ζ₁,…,ζ_{n−1}. This identifies the subalgebra constructor with the displayed order lattice.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formIdeal_stable` (structure): For 0≤k≤n−1 and f(θ,1)=0, multiplication by each element of formOrder preserves formIdeal f θ k.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formOrder_monic` (compatibility): If f₀=1, R_f=D[θ].
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formIdeal_zero` (characterisation): I_f(0) is the D-module of R_f.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.formOrder_nonmonic` (non-example): For f=2x⁴−y⁴ over Z, R_f has basis 1,2θ,2θ²,2θ³ and does not contain θ, even though θ lies in its rational algebra.

**Proof route.**

1. Construct the lattices as native D-submodules of the quotient algebra. Check their multiplication on the displayed generators. The triangular change from power coordinates establishes full rank, the discriminant equality and the trace-dual formula. Treat general ideals as lattices in a finite étale algebra, not FractionalIdeal D L with an invalid field assumption.

**Acceptance checks.**

- If f₀=1, R_f=D[θ].
- I_f(0) is the D-module of R_f.
- For f=2x⁴−y⁴ over Z, R_f has basis 1,2θ,2θ²,2θ³ and does not contain θ, even though θ lies in its rational algebra.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorem16 p.7 and Proposition34 pp.26–28; integral-pencil-orbits and integral-soluble-pencils — The explicit order and fractional ideals encode nonmonic integral fibres. Their trace-dual identity turns ideal products into the two symmetric forms, and their generators implement the integral representative construction.

<a id="st1-refinement-oriented-ideal-triples"></a>

### 1.72 Oriented ideal data for integral pencils

For the preceding (D,K,L,f), an oriented orbit triple is (I,α,s), with I an R_f-stable full D-lattice in L, α∈L× and s∈K×, such that I²⊂αI_f(n−3), N(I)=sD and N(α)=s²f₀^{n−3}. Here N(I) is the determinant fractional D-lattice relative to the basis 1,ζ₁,…,ζ_{n−1}: span of determinants of coordinates of n vectors of I. Equivalence for SLₙ is (I,α,s)∼(cI,c²α,N(c)s). Retain s itself; replacing it with its principal ideal forgets orientation.

**Hypotheses.** n≥3; n=2 needs the negative-index ideal convention and is a recorded boundary refinement.; L is finite étale over K and I is full finite projective.

**Dependencies.** [Orders and distinguished ideals of a binary form](#st1-refinement-binary-form-order) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-binary-form-order`); `mathlib:Algebra.norm`; `mathlib:Module.Basis`; `mathlib:Submodule.span`; `mathlib:LinearMap.mulLeft`; `mathlib:Module.Finite`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Theorem16 and its construction, pp.7–8. Integral orbits keep both the ideal and its determinant orientation.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.idealNorm` (data): D-span of coordinate determinants relative to an explicit K-basis of L.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.IsOrbitTriple` (characterisation): Require n≥3, f(θ,1)=0 and compatibility of the chosen basis with 1,ζ₁,…,ζ_{n−1}, together with lattice stability, finite/full rank, product inclusion, norm-ideal equality and the scalar norm identity. The dictionary additionally uses the preceding nonzero-leading-coefficient and nonzero-discriminant hypotheses.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.orbitTriple_rescale` (relation): Multiplication by c∈L× sends the triple to cI,c²α,N(c)s and preserves its conditions.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.triple_monic` (computation): For a monic f, the triple (R_f,1,1) satisfies the conditions.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.triple_orientation` (non-example): Both s and −s satisfy the same norm and ideal constraints; their identification requires an explicit norm-minus-one square root, rather than equality of the principal ideals.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.triple_zero_lattice` (degenerate): The zero lattice fails the full-rank condition and cannot have norm ideal sD with s≠0.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.triple_degree_two` (non-example): For a rank-two algebra and a coefficient vector of degree2, IsOrbitTriple is false; the n≥3 condition rejects the negative-index boundary.

**Proof route.**

1. Use Submodule D L and the determinant line, with R_f stability expressed by multiplication. For free I, N(I)=sD chooses an oriented basis; over a Dedekind domain principal determinant gives freeness. Scalar multiplication changes the determinant by N(c), making the equivalence compatible with every constraint.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For a monic f, the triple (R_f,1,1) satisfies the conditions.
- Both s and −s satisfy the same norm and ideal constraints; their identification requires an explicit norm-minus-one square root, rather than equality of the principal ideals.
- The zero lattice fails the full-rank condition and cannot have norm ideal sD with s≠0.
- The natural-exponent interface rejects n=2, where I_f(−1) would be required; it must not replace that exponent by zero.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorems16–17 pp.6–8; integral-pencil-orbits — The product inclusion constructs the pencil, while the determinant ideal and retained scalar give its orientation and invariant. Rescaling records exactly which triples yield the same integral orbit.

<a id="st1-refinement-integral-pencil-orbits"></a>

### 1.73 Integral symmetric-pencil orbit classification

For n≥3, Theorem16 identifies SLₙ(D)-orbits with the oriented ideal triples above, preserving f. The stabilizer is the norm-one 2-torsion units of End_{R_f}(I)⊂L. For even n≥4, SLₙ/μ₂(D) uses the additional relation (I,α,s)∼(MI,tα,t^{n/2}s) where tD=M². The latter stabilizer contains End_{R_f}(I)×[2]_{N=1}/D×[2], but need not equal it; the Pic(D)[2] and unit-square extensions must be retained.

**Hypotheses.** f₀ and Δ(f) are nonzero; char K≠2.; The acting integral group is the group scheme’s D-points.

**Dependencies.** [Symmetric pencils and their invariant binary forms](#st1-refinement-symmetric-pencil) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-symmetric-pencil`); [Oriented ideal data for integral pencils](#st1-refinement-oriented-ideal-triples) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-oriented-ideal-triples`)

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Theorems16–17, Remark18, pp.7–8. The inverse construction and the extra quotient-group action determine integral orbit multiplicities.

**Proof route.**

1. Given a triple, extract the ζ_{n−1} and ζ_{n−2} coefficients of λμ/α on I_f(n−3); these define the two Gram matrices in a basis with determinant s. Conversely A^{-1}B gives θ’s action on the rational module; the integral polynomial ζ-actions preserve the lattice. Track bases and α to prove both composites. The Kummer exact sequence explains the M,t extension.

**Acceptance checks.**

- A product étale algebra and a noninvertible R_f-ideal remain allowed.
- The central quotient is not implemented as the naive quotient of integral SLₙ points.

<a id="st1-refinement-oriented-norm-pairs"></a>

### 1.74 Oriented norm pairs over a field

For a degree-n finite étale K-algebra L, n≥3 and f₀∈K×, define pairs (α,s)∈L××K× with N(α)=s²f₀^{n−3}. The SLₙ relation is (α,s)∼(c²α,N(c)s). For even n≥4 the central-quotient relation also allows t∈K× and sends the pair to (c²tα,N(c)t^{n/2}s). Both signs of s are retained until the relevant equivalence identifies them.

**Hypotheses.** Finite free étale algebra, not an arbitrarily large algebra on which a default norm has no intended meaning.

**Dependencies.** [Oriented ideal data for integral pencils](#st1-refinement-oriented-ideal-triples) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-oriented-ideal-triples`); `mathlib:Algebra.norm`; `mathlib:Module.finrank`; `mathlib:Algebra.IsSeparable`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Corollaries19–20, pp.8–9. The oriented pairs explain the possible two-to-one maps to ordinary squareclasses.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.NormPair` (constructor): Construct from n≥3, Module.finrank K L=n, Algebra.IsSeparable K L, α∈L× and s∈K× satisfying the norm equality, in a finite free K-algebra. The degree and étale conditions are part of the data.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.NormPair.rescale` (functoriality): Rescale by c∈L× as specified above.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.normPair_sign_iff` (characterisation): The pairs (α,s) and (α,−s) are SLₙ-equivalent exactly when some c∈L× satisfies c²=1 and N(c)=−1.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.NormPair.ext` (extensionality): Two norm pairs over the same degree-n algebra and f₀ are equal if their α and s fields are equal; proof fields add no data.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.normPair_unit` (computation): If f₀=1, the pair (1,1) satisfies the norm equation.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.normPair_negative_orientation` (non-example): In characteristic different from2 with f₀=1, (1,−1) satisfies the norm equation and its retained orientation differs from1; the constructor must not discard the sign.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.normPair_odd_split` (compatibility): In L=K³, c=(−1,1,1) has c²=1 and N(c)=−1, so the two unit orientations are SL₃-equivalent.
- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.normPair_wrong_degree` (non-example): NormPair with L=K, n=3 and f₀=1 is empty. The actual algebra degree must agree with n.

**Proof route.**

1. Specialize the triple classification to a field, where all full lattices are the whole algebra after choosing a generator. Use the determinant norm, and verify both rescaling formulas directly.

**Acceptance checks.**

- If f₀=1, the pair (1,1) satisfies the norm equation.
- If f₀=1, (1,−1) also satisfies it; the constructor must not discard the sign.
- In L=K³, c=(−1,1,1) has c²=1 and N(c)=−1, so the two unit orientations are SL₃-equivalent.
- L=K has K-dimension1 and must admit no NormPair with declared degree3, even when the displayed norm equation alone has a solution.

**Consumers.** BGW Corollaries19–20 pp.8–9, Theorem24 pp.14–16 and Theorem28 pp.18–19; field-pencil-stabilizers and pencil-existence — Passing to the fraction field replaces lattices by norm data; the retained sign of s controls the fibre over a squareclass and the norm-one two-torsion stabilizer.

<a id="st1-refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers"></a>

### 1.75 Field orbits and norm-one stabilizers

For n≥3 and f₀Δ≠0, field SLₙ-orbits with invariant f are the oriented norm-pair classes. Their stabilizer group scheme is ker(N:Res_{L/K}μ₂→μ₂). Forgetting s maps to squareclasses with norm f₀^{n−3} modulo K×² (norm f₀ in even degree) one-to-one if f has an odd degree K-factor and two-to-one otherwise. For even n≥4 use the central-quotient pair relation; the stabilizer scheme is ker(N)/μ₂, with the analogous fibre criterion involving odd factorizations, including quadratic-conjugate factors.

**Hypotheses.** Field characteristic not2.; Do not equate quotient-scheme K-points to the quotient of K-points.

**Dependencies.** [Oriented norm pairs over a field](#st1-refinement-oriented-norm-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-oriented-norm-pairs`); [Symmetric pencils and their invariant binary forms](#st1-refinement-symmetric-pencil) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-symmetric-pencil`)

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Corollaries19–20, pp.8–9; Proposition22, pp.11–12. The arithmetic stabilizer is a finite étale group scheme and includes nontrivial Galois descent.

**Proof route.**

1. Corollaries19–20 give the orbit correspondence. A square-one unit changes the orientation by its norm. The root-factor description of such units and the central quotient supply the fibre criteria and scheme stabilizers.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The split even degree n fibre has geometric stabilizer order 2^{n−2}.
- Counting squareclasses alone can undercount oriented orbits by a factor of two.

<a id="st1-refinement-pencil-existence"></a>

### 1.76 Existence of a rational pencil

For n=2g+2≥4, char K≠2 and f₀Δ≠0, the following eight conditions are equivalent: (a) a generic pencil with invariant f exists; (b) a regular augmented pencil with invariant fy² exists; (c) f₀∈K×²N(L×); (d) the degree-one generalized Picard torsor J_m¹ is 2-divisible in H¹(K,J_m); (e) the generalized Weierstrass class W_m[2] lifts under doubling from H¹(K,J_m[4]); (f) a two-cover F_m→J_m¹ of homogeneous spaces exists; (g) the maximal unramified abelian exponent-two cover of C minus its two points at infinity descends from Kˢ to K; (h) the maximal abelian exponent-two cover of C, ramified only at those two points, descends from Kˢ to K. Both covers have degree 2^{2g+1}. The smooth J¹ being 2-divisible alone does not replace these conditions. Theorem25 identifies their common obstruction in H²(K,J_m[2]), obtained from the connecting image of f₀ in K×/(K×²N(L×)).

**Hypotheses.** m is the two-point divisor above infinity, with its quadratic splitting field; generalized Jacobian data is retained.

**Dependencies.** [Field orbits and norm-one stabilizers](#st1-refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers`); [Common isotropic subspaces of a pencil](#st1-refinement-common-isotropic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-common-isotropic`); `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/JacobianChallenge#layer-d-the-relative-picard-functor-and-the-jacobian-scheme`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Theorems24–25, pp.14–16. The eight equivalent criteria have the generalized Jacobian and an explicit common obstruction.

**Proof route.**

1. The norm criterion follows from oriented norm pairs. On V⊕K² augment A by the block diag(1,0), and B by the block with entries B₁₂=B₂₁=1 and zero diagonal. The signed determinant becomes f·y². Use the regular augmented-pencil Fano torsor and generalized Picard doubling obstruction; BGW Theorem25 identifies the common H² obstruction. These geometric inputs remain explicit gaps.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For a negative definite real even-degree f, L is a product of C and the negative leading coefficient is not a norm times a square; there is no rational pencil.

<a id="st1-refinement-pencil-fano-torsor"></a>

### 1.77 Fano torsors and soluble rational orbits

For an even generic pencil n=2g+2≥4, the Fano scheme of common g-dimensional vector subspaces is a torsor F under the smooth hyperelliptic Jacobian J. The four-component group J⊔F⊔J¹⊔F satisfies 2[F]=[J¹]. For SLₙ, solubility uses the augmented regular-pencil Fano variety F_m and gives J_m¹(K)/2J_m(K); for SLₙ/μ₂ it uses F and gives J¹(K)/2J(K). In both cases soluble orbits exist exactly when C has a K-rational divisor of odd degree. These are torsor coset sets unless a basepoint is chosen.

**Hypotheses.** f₀Δ≠0, characteristic not2; rational divisor, not merely a rational geometric divisor class.

**Dependencies.** [Common isotropic subspaces of a pencil](#st1-refinement-common-isotropic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-common-isotropic`); [Existence of a rational pencil](#st1-refinement-pencil-existence) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-pencil-existence`); `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/JacobianChallenge#layer-d-the-relative-picard-functor-and-the-jacobian-scheme`; `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/JacobianChallenge#layer-a-line-bundles-divisors-picard-group-degree`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Theorem23, pp.12–13; Theorems28–29, pp.18–20; Proposition21, pp.10–11. Solubility and the group action determine which Picard torsor is parametrized.

**Proof route.**

1. Use Theorem23’s Fano group law. The regular augmentation realizes generalized doubling. The x−T Kummer map associates oriented norm pairs to actual divisors; the Brauer obstruction must vanish to pass from a rational Picard class to a divisor. The two group actions give the two distinct coset sets.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Vector dimension g is not g+1.
- For the negative definite real genus-two example, J¹(R) can be nonempty while no odd rational divisor exists, so no soluble pencil exists.

<a id="st1-refinement-locally-soluble-pencil-orbits"></a>

### 1.78 Locally soluble pencils and the 2-Selmer set

Over a global field K of characteristic not2, n=2g+2≥4 and f₀Δ≠0, assume Div¹(C) has a point at every completion. Locally soluble SLₙ/μ₂(K)-orbits of invariant f correspond to Sel₂(J¹), the set of locally soluble two-covers of J¹. This set is nonempty exactly when W[2] lifts under doubling from Sel₄(J). When nonempty it is a finite torsor under Sel₂(J), not canonically the group Sel₂(J).

**Hypotheses.** Local solubility includes every archimedean and nonarchimedean place.; F(K_v)≠∅ is the pencil’s local solubility condition.

**Dependencies.** [Fano torsors and soluble rational orbits](#st1-refinement-pencil-fano-torsor) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-pencil-fano-torsor`); [Field orbits and norm-one stabilizers](#st1-refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers`); `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/JacobianChallenge#layer-d-the-relative-picard-functor-and-the-jacobian-scheme`; `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4`

**Sources.** [S1/bgw](#source-s1-bgw), Theorems14,30–31, pp.5,21–24. The local condition yields a Selmer set and an action, rather than a canonical identification with an abstract group.

**Proof route.**

1. The norm/generalized-Picard existence criterion gives a rational orbit after the Selmer lift. Twisting by H¹(K,J[2]) changes its Fano torsor class. The obstruction is cup product with W[2]; local Kummer classes and the Hasse principle put Sel₂(J) in its kernel. Thus twisting gives the simply transitive Selmer action and identifies the two-cover set.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Choosing a soluble orbit identifies the torsor with Sel₂(J); changing that choice translates the identification.
- A rational orbit need not be locally soluble.

<a id="st1-refinement-integral-soluble-pencils"></a>

### 1.79 Integral representatives of locally soluble pencils
