### 4.19 The change of measure weighted by 1/m_p (Corollary 3.8)

Let p be a prime and φ: V_{Z_p} → R_{≥0} measurable and PGL_2(Q_p)-invariant (φ(γ·f) = φ(f) whenever f, γ·f ∈ V_{Z_p}), such that every f in the support of φ has Δ(f) ≠ 0, is Q_p-soluble, and satisfies 2⁴·3 | I(f), 2⁶·3³ | J(f). Then ∫_{V_{Z_p}} φ(f)/m_p(f) df = |1/27|_p (1 − p^{-2}) ∫_{(I,J) ∈ D_p} (1/#E^{I,J}(Q_p)[2]) Σ_{σ ∈ E^{I,J}(Q_p)/2E^{I,J}(Q_p)} φ(f_σ) dIdJ, where f_σ ∈ V_{Z_p} is any integral form in the PGL_2(Q_p)-class corresponding to σ under Theorem 3.2 (ST.1).

**Hypotheses.** D_p = {(I,J) ∈ Z_p² : Δ(I,J) ≠ 0, 2⁴·3 | I, 2⁶·3³ | J}. The outer integral is restricted to D_p; outside it integral representatives f_σ need not exist, so an unrestricted sum over such representatives is not defined.; The divisibility conditions guarantee (local form of Lemma 3.4, ST.1) that every soluble PGL_2(Q_p)-class with these invariants meets V_{Z_p}, so f_σ exists.; m_p is PGL_2(Z_p)-invariant and PGL_2(Q_p)-invariant on V_{Z_p} (rational-orbit-weight).

**Dependencies.** [The p-adic change-of-measure formula for binary quartic forms (Proposition 3.7)](#st4-p-adic-change-of-measure-for-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/p-adic-change-of-measure-for-binary-quartic-forms`); [The orbit weight as a sum of stabilizer ratios](#st4-orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum`); [The orbit weights m(f) and m_p(f)](#st4-rational-orbit-weight) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rational-orbit-weight`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E(K)[2]](#st1-stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion`); [Every Q_p-soluble quartic with invariants (-48A, -1728B) has a Z_p-integral representative](#st1-local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/local-integral-representatives-of-soluble-quartics`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Corollary 3.8, (51), p. 25. Exact hypotheses (continuity relaxed to measurability, as allowed by Proposition 3.12). [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Corollary 3.8, p. 26. The two ST.1 inputs.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply p-adic-change-of-measure-for-binary-quartic-forms to the PGL_2(Z_p)-invariant function φ/m_p.
2. Group the PGL_2(Z_p)-orbits f_1, …, f_k in V_{Z_p}(I, J) by PGL_2(Q_p)-class; by orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum, Σ_i φ(f_i)/(m_p(f_i)#Aut_{Z_p}(f_i)) = φ(f)/#Aut_{Q_p}(f).
3. By ST.1 (Theorem 3.2 over Q_p and the local Lemma 3.4) the soluble PGL_2(Q_p)-classes in V_{Z_p}(I, J) correspond to E^{I,J}(Q_p)/2E^{I,J}(Q_p), and Aut_{Q_p}(f) ≅ E^{I,J}(Q_p)[2].

**Acceptance checks.**

- With φ the indicator of the soluble forms with invariants in a small ball around (I_0, J_0), the right side is |1/27|_p(1 − p^{-2}) times the ball's volume times #(E(Q_p)/2E(Q_p))/#E(Q_p)[2].
- An implementation that forgets 1/m_p double-counts the PGL_2(Z_p)-orbits inside one PGL_2(Q_p)-class.

<a id="st4-local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms"></a>

### 4.20 The local mass formula (Proposition 3.9)

For every family F defined by congruence conditions and every prime p, ∫_{S_p(F)} m_p(f)^{-1} df = |2^{10}/27|_p (1 − p^{-2}) M_p(V, F).

**Hypotheses.** S_p(F) is the local set of locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family; Inv_p(F) ⊆ 3Z_p × 27Z_p because I(E) = −3A and J(E) = −27B.

**Dependencies.** [The change of measure weighted by 1/m_p (Corollary 3.8)](#st4-weighted-p-adic-change-of-measure) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/weighted-p-adic-change-of-measure`); [The weighted sets S(F), S_p(F) and S_∞(F) of locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st4-locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family`); [The Selmer-weighted local masses M_p(V, F), M_∞(V, F; X) and the archimedean mass M_∞(F; X)](#st4-local-masses-of-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-masses-of-a-family`); [Families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions, Inv_p, and large families](#st0-elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proposition 3.9, p. 26. Exact statement, with Vol(PGL_2(Z_p)) = 1 − p^{-2}.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply weighted-p-adic-change-of-measure to φ = 1_{S_p(F)}: every f ∈ S_p(F) has Δ(f) ≠ 0, is Q_p-soluble, and has invariants (2⁴I, 2⁶J) with 3 | I, 27 | J, so 2⁴·3 | I(f) and 2⁶·3³ | J(f); φ is PGL_2(Q_p)-invariant.
2. For (I, J) = (2⁴I', 2⁶J') the curves E^{I,J} and E^{I',J'} are isomorphic over Q_p ((x, y) ↦ (4x, 8y)), so the Selmer ratio is unchanged, and every soluble class is counted exactly when (I', J') ∈ Inv_p(F).
3. The substitution (I, J) = (2⁴I', 2⁶J') has Jacobian |2^{10}|_p, giving |2^{10}|_p·|1/27|_p(1 − p^{-2}) M_p(V, F).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For p ≥ 5 the factor |2^{10}/27|_p is 1; for p = 2 it is 2^{-10}; for p = 3 it is 27.
- The product over all p of |2^{10}/27|_p is 27/2^{10}, which cancels the archimedean factor 2^{10}/27 in selmer-average-as-product-of-local-masses.

<a id="st4-two-division-quotient-of-a-group-with-a-finite-index-zp-subgroup"></a>

### 4.21 #(G/2G) = |2|_p^{-1}·#G[2] for an abelian group with a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to Z_p

Let G be an abelian group and U ≤ G a subgroup of finite index with U ≅ (Z_p, +) as abstract groups, p prime. Then G[2] and G/2G are finite and #(G/2G) = |2|_p^{-1}·#G[2]: #(G/2G) = #G[2] for p odd and #(G/2G) = 2·#G[2] for p = 2.

**Hypotheses.** Only the abstract group structure is used; G is written additively and 2G is the image of multiplication by 2.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Subgroup.index_ker`; `mathlib:Subgroup.card_mul_index`; `mathlib:PadicInt`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Lemma 3.20, p. 34. The group-theoretic core of the lemma the source quotes from Brumer–Kramer [12, Lemma 3.1] (not read).

**Proof route.**

1. For an abelian group M with M[2] and M/2M finite put q(M) = #(M/2M)/#M[2]. For finite M, q(M) = 1: #M = #M[2]·#2M by the first isomorphism theorem (mathlib:Subgroup.index_ker, mathlib:Subgroup.card_mul_index).
2. Multiplication by 2 on 0 → U → G → G/U → 0 gives the exact sequence 0 → U[2] → G[2] → (G/U)[2] → U/2U → G/2G → (G/U)/2(G/U) → 0 (snake lemma), so G[2], G/2G are finite and q(G) = q(U)·q(G/U) = q(U).
3. q(Z_p) = #(Z_p/2Z_p)/#Z_p[2] = |2|_p^{-1}/1.

**Acceptance checks.**

- G = Z_2 × Z/2: #(G/2G) = 4 = 2·#G[2].
- G = Z_3 × Z/2 × Z/2: #(G/2G) = 4 = #G[2].

<a id="st4-local-two-descent-index"></a>

### 4.22 The local 2-descent index (Lemma 3.20)

Let p be a prime and E an elliptic curve over Q_p. Then #(E(Q_p)/2E(Q_p)) = #E(Q_p)[2] if p ≠ 2 and #(E(Q_p)/2E(Q_p)) = 2·#E(Q_p)[2] if p = 2.

**Hypotheses.** E elliptic over Q_p, given by any Weierstrass equation (the statement is invariant under isomorphism).

**Dependencies.** [#(G/2G) = |2|_p^{-1}·#G[2] for an abelian group with a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to Z_p](#st4-two-division-quotient-of-a-group-with-a-finite-index-zp-subgroup) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/two-division-quotient-of-a-group-with-a-finite-index-zp-subgroup`); `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-4-elliptic-curves-over-local-fields--reduction-tates-algorithm-the-tate-curve-aec-vii-ataec-ivv

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Lemma 3.20, p. 34. Exact statement.

**Proof route.**

1. E(Q_p) contains a subgroup of finite index isomorphic to (Z_p, +): for a minimal model, E_1(Q_p) ≅ Ê(pZ_p), Ê(p^rZ_p) ≅ (p^rZ_p, +) via the formal logarithm for r > 1/(p − 1), E_0(Q_p)/E_1(Q_p) ≅ Ẽ_ns(F_p) is finite and [E(Q_p) : E_0(Q_p)] is finite (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layers 1 and 4; request).
2. Apply two-division-quotient-of-a-group-with-a-finite-index-zp-subgroup.

**Acceptance checks.**

- E: y² = x³ − x over Q_3 has E(Q_3)[2] of order 4, so #(E(Q_3)/2E(Q_3)) = 4; over Q_2 it is 8.
- Over Q_5, y² = x³ + 1 = (x + 1)(x² − x + 1) has exactly one 2-torsion point besides O (−3 is not a square mod 5), so #(E(Q_5)/2E(Q_5)) = 2.

<a id="st4-archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half"></a>

### 4.23 The archimedean ratio #(E(R)/2E(R))/#E(R)[2] = 1/2

For (I, J) ∈ R² with Δ(I, J) ≠ 0 and E = E^{I,J}: #E(R)[2] = 4 and #(E(R)/2E(R)) = 2 if Δ(I, J) > 0, and #E(R)[2] = 2 and #(E(R)/2E(R)) = 1 if Δ(I, J) < 0; in both cases the ratio is 1/2. Moreover for f ∈ V_R^{(i)} with invariants (I, J), #Stab_{PGL_2(R)}(f) = #E(R)[2], i.e. n_0 = n_{2±} = 4 and n_1 = 2.

**Hypotheses.** Δ(I, J) = (4I³ − J²)/27 is the discriminant of the cubic x³ − (I/3)x − J/27 (polynomial identity).

**Dependencies.** [Averaging over the fundamental domain and cutting off the cusp: N(V_ℤ^(i); X) = Vol(R_X(L^(i)))/n_i + O(X^{3/4+ε})](#st2-averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp`); [Real solubility of binary quartic forms](#st4-real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms`); `mathlib:Cubic.discr_eq_prod_three_roots`; [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: E(K)/2E(K) and PGL2(K)-orbits of soluble quartics](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2: Stab_{PGL2(K)}(f) is isomorphic to E(K)[2]](#st1-stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.6, p. 33. Exact statement. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Lemma 2.2, pp. 20–21. The stabilizer orders n_i.

**Proof route.**

1. E(R)[2] = {O} ∪ {(r, 0) : r a real root of x³ − (I/3)x − J/27}; the cubic has three real roots iff its discriminant is positive and one iff negative (discriminant as the product of squared root differences, mathlib:Cubic.discr_eq_prod_three_roots over C: a complex-conjugate pair contributes a negative square).
2. By ST.1 (Theorem 3.2 over K = R), #(E(R)/2E(R)) is the number of R-soluble PGL_2(R)-orbits with invariants (I, J), and stabilizers are ≅ E(R)[2].
3. By the real orbit structure (ST.2, §2.1 of the source) the forms with invariants (I, J) form one SL_2^±(R)-orbit (in V^{(1)}) if Δ < 0 and three (in V^{(0)}, V^{(2+)}, V^{(2−)}) if Δ > 0; PGL_2(R)-orbits coincide with SL_2^±(R)-orbits for the twisted action.
4. By real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms the soluble ones are V^{(1)} (Δ < 0) and V^{(0)}, V^{(2+)} (Δ > 0), giving 1 and 2.

**Acceptance checks.**

- y² = x³ − x (Δ > 0): E(R) has two components, E(R)[2] has 4 points, E(R)/2E(R) has 2.
- y² = x³ + 1 (Δ < 0): E(R) is connected, E(R)[2] = {O,(−1,0)}, and E(R)/2E(R) is the trivial group (cardinality 1).

<a id="st4-local-selmer-mass-ratios"></a>

### 4.24 The local mass ratios (74)

For every family F defined by congruence conditions: M_p(V, F) = M_p(F) for every odd prime p, M_2(V, F) = 2·M_2(F), and M_∞(V, F; X) = M_∞(F; X)/2 for every X.

**Hypotheses.** M_p(F) is the local density of ST.0; the ratios hold whether or not M_p(F) is positive.

**Dependencies.** [The Selmer-weighted local masses M_p(V, F), M_∞(V, F; X) and the archimedean mass M_∞(F; X)](#st4-local-masses-of-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-masses-of-a-family`); [The local 2-descent index (Lemma 3.20)](#st4-local-two-descent-index) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-two-descent-index`); [The archimedean ratio #(E(R)/2E(R))/#E(R)[2] = 1/2](#st4-archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half`); [Families defined by local conditions, local densities and largeness](#st0-family-defined-by-local-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), (74), p. 34. Exact statement, in multiplied-out form (no division by M_p(F)).

**Proof route.**

1. The integrand of M_p(V, F) is identically 1 (p odd) or 2 (p = 2) on {Δ ≠ 0} by local-two-descent-index; integrate over Inv_p(F).
2. The integrand of M_∞(V, F; X) is identically 1/2 by archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half.

**Acceptance checks.**

- When all finite local masses are positive, the product of local mass ratios over all places is (1/2)·2 = 1. The multiplied-out identities remain true when a mass is zero; the quotient at that place is then not used.
- An implementation that uses the odd-prime value at p = 2 obtains the average 2 instead of 3.

<a id="st4-locally-soluble-set-is-cut-out-by-local-conditions"></a>

### 4.25 S(F) is cut out by the local sets S_p(F) and S_∞(F)

Let F = F_Σ be a family of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions (ST.0). For f ∈ V_Z: f ∈ S(F) if and only if f ∈ S_∞(F) and f ∈ S_p(F) for every prime p (regarding V_Z inside V_{Z_p} and V_R). Consequently, for f ∈ V_Z with Δ(f) ≠ 0 and φ_p := 1_{S_p(F)}/m_p: 1_{S_∞(F)}(f)·Π_p φ_p(f) = 1_{S(F)}(f)/m(f).

**Hypotheses.** F is presented as F_Σ: E^{I,J} ∈ F iff (I, J) ∈ Σ_p for every p, with Inv(F) ⊆ Inv_p(F) ⊆ Σ_p, and (I, J) = (−3A, −27B) for a minimal pair (A, B), a condition that is local at every prime.

**Dependencies.** [The weighted sets S(F), S_p(F) and S_∞(F) of locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st4-locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family`); [Global weights are products of local weights (Proposition 3.6)](#st4-global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights`); [Families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions, Inv_p, and large families](#st0-elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions`); [Families defined by local conditions, local densities and largeness](#st0-family-defined-by-local-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.5: 2-Selmer elements are PGL2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral quartics with invariants 2^4 I, 2^6 J](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.2, p. 25. The local description of S(F) and of its weights. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3, p. 22. The presentation of F used in the third step.

**Proof route.**

1. Locally soluble means R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for all p (ST.1).
2. (I(f), J(f)) = (2⁴I, 2⁶J) with (I, J) ∈ Z² iff 2⁴ | I(f) and 2⁶ | J(f), a condition at p = 2 only.
3. (I, J) ∈ Z² lies in Inv(F) iff it lies in Inv_p(F) for every p and in Inv_∞(F): one direction because Inv(F) ⊆ Inv_p(F); the other because (I, J) ∈ Inv_p(F) ⊆ Σ_p for all p puts E^{I,J} in F_Σ = F (ST.0).
4. Multiply the local weights: Π_p m_p(f)^{-1} = m(f)^{-1} by global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For F the family of all curves and f = x³y − 16xy³, f lies in every S_p(F) and in S_∞(F).
- For F = {E : A ≡ 1 (mod 5)} the condition at p = 5 alone excludes forms whose invariants have A ≢ 1 (mod 5).

<a id="st4-selmer-count-as-weighted-orbit-count"></a>

### 4.26 Nonidentity 2-Selmer elements as a weighted count of integral orbits

Let F be a family of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions. For every ε > 0 and X ≥ 1, Σ_{E ∈ F, H'(E) < X} (#S_2(E) − 1) = Σ_{PGL_2(Z)·f ⊆ S(F), f irreducible over Q, H(f) < 2^{12}X} 1/m(f) + O_ε(X^{3/4+ε}), where S_2(E) is the (finite) 2-Selmer group and the implied constant is independent of F.

**Hypotheses.** S_2(E) is finite (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 7) and is identified with the locally soluble 2-coverings of ST.1.; The weights 1/m(f) and 1/n(f) lie in (0, 1]; the error comes only from orbits with a nontrivial stabilizer in PGL_2(Q) and from forms that are products of two irreducible quadratic forms.

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.5: 2-Selmer elements are PGL2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral quartics with invariants 2^4 I, 2^6 J](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer`); [The orbit weights m(f) and m_p(f)](#st4-rational-orbit-weight) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rational-orbit-weight`); [The orbit weight as a sum of stabilizer ratios](#st4-orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum`); [The weighted sets S(F), S_p(F) and S_∞(F) of locally soluble binary quartic forms](#st4-locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family`); [Averaging over the fundamental domain and cutting off the cusp: N(V_ℤ^(i); X) = Vol(R_X(L^(i)))/n_i + O(X^{3/4+ε})](#st2-averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp`); [The normalisation 27·H(E) = 4·H′(E) between the naive height of a curve and the quartic height of its invariants](#st0-quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation`); [The height H(I, J) = max{|I|³, J²/4} on pairs of invariants and on integral binary quartic forms](#st0-binary-quartic-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-height`)

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.2, pp. 23–24. Exact statement (the height of the forms is 2^{12} times that of the curves, as in the proof of Theorem 3.19). [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Theorem 3.19, p. 33. The use in Theorem 3.19.

**Proof route.**

1. By ST.1 (Theorem 3.5), the nonidentity elements of S_2(E^{I,J}) correspond bijectively to the PGL_2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral forms with invariants (2⁴I, 2⁶J) and no rational linear factor; distinct curves have distinct invariants, and H(2⁴I, 2⁶J) = 2^{12}H(I, J) (ST.0).
2. Each such class C meets V_Z in n(f) PGL_2(Z)-orbits, and Σ_{orbits in C} 1/n(f) = 1.
3. By orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum, m(f) = n(f) unless some orbit in C has a nontrivial stabilizer in PGL_2(Q); by ST.2 (Lemma 2.4) the PGL_2(Z)-orbits of height < Y with nontrivial PGL_2(Q)-stabilizer number O_ε(Y^{3/4+ε}), and each weight is at most 1.
4. Forms with no rational linear factor are irreducible or products of two irreducible quadratic forms; the latter have a ≠ 0 and are reducible, so by ST.2 (Lemma 2.3 and Proposition 2.7: the cusp contains only forms with a = 0) they number O_ε(Y^{2/3+ε}).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For E: y² = x³ − x (A = −1, B = 0), S_2(E) has order 4 (E(Q) = E(Q)[2] and Ш[2] = 0), so E contributes 3 to the left side; since E(Q)[2] ≠ 0 its forms have nontrivial PGL_2(Q)-stabilizers and may be weighted differently on the right, which is why the error term is needed.
- The identity class (forms with a rational linear factor, e.g. x³y − 16xy³ for y² = x³ − x) is excluded from the right side.

<a id="st4-bad-forms-have-square-discriminant"></a>

### 4.27 Forms bad at an odd prime have discriminant divisible by p² (Proposition 3.18)

Call f ∈ V_{Z_p} bad at p if f is not Q_p-soluble or m_p(f) ≠ 1. If f ∈ V_Z (or V_{Z_p}) with Δ(f) ≠ 0 is bad at a prime p > 2, then p² | Δ(f). The half concerning m_p holds for every prime p.

**Hypotheses.** p > 2 for the solubility half; Δ(f) ≠ 0.

**Dependencies.** [A non-integral translate of an integral form forces p² | Δ](#st4-nonintegral-local-translates-force-square-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/nonintegral-local-translates-force-square-discriminant`); [An insoluble form at an odd prime has discriminant divisible by p²](#st4-local-solubility-away-from-square-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-solubility-away-from-square-discriminant`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proposition 3.18, p. 32. Exact statement.

**Proof route.**

1. If m_p(f) ≠ 1: nonintegral-local-translates-force-square-discriminant.
2. If f is not Q_p-soluble: local-solubility-away-from-square-discriminant.

**Acceptance checks.**

- f_0 = 2x⁴ + 4x²y² + 3xy³ + 2y⁴ is bad at 3 and 3² | Δ(f_0) = 28116.
- For p ≥ 5 every f with p² ∤ Δ(f) is good at p: this is what makes 1_{S_p(F)}/m_p acceptable.

<a id="st4-count-of-real-soluble-integral-orbits"></a>

### 4.28 The number of R-soluble integral orbits of bounded height

For a family F defined by congruence conditions and every ε > 0, N(V_Z ∩ S_∞(F); X) = (1/27)·Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))·M_∞(V, F; X) + O_ε(X^{3/4+ε}).

**Hypotheses.** Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R)) is taken with respect to |ω|_∞ for the ω of jacobian-of-the-orbit-map; its value 2ζ(2) is supplied by ST.2.

**Dependencies.** [Averaging over the fundamental domain and cutting off the cusp: N(V_ℤ^(i); X) = Vol(R_X(L^(i)))/n_i + O(X^{3/4+ε})](#st2-averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp`); [Real solubility of binary quartic forms](#st4-real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms`); [The archimedean ratio #(E(R)/2E(R))/#E(R)[2] = 1/2](#st4-archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half`); [The Selmer-weighted local masses M_p(V, F), M_∞(V, F; X) and the archimedean mass M_∞(F; X)](#st4-local-masses-of-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-masses-of-a-family`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.6, p. 33. Exact statement.

**Proof route.**

1. By ST.2 (Theorem 2.1 in the form (20), with the volumes (23)–(26)), N(V_Z^{(i)} ∩ {Inv_∞}; X) = Vol(R_X(L^{(i)}))/n_i + O_ε(X^{3/4+ε}) with Vol(R_X(L^{(i)})) = (1/27)·Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))·∫_{R^{(i)}(X)} dIdJ.
2. By real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms the R-soluble components over Inv_∞(F) are i ∈ {0, 2+} above Δ > 0 and i = 1 above Δ < 0.
3. By archimedean-selmer-ratio-is-one-half, n_i = #E(R)[2] and the number of soluble components above (I, J) is #(E(R)/2E(R)); summing, Σ_{soluble i} 1/n_i = #(E(R)/2E(R))/#E(R)[2], whose integral over {(I, J) ∈ Inv_∞(F), H < X} is M_∞(V, F; X).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For Inv_∞ = {Δ > 0}: 2·(1/27)·2ζ(2)·(8/5)X^{5/6}/4 = (8/135)ζ(2)X^{5/6}, which is (1/27)·2ζ(2)·(4/5)X^{5/6}.
- For Inv_∞ = {Δ < 0}: (1/27)·2ζ(2)·(32/5)X^{5/6}/2 = (32/135)ζ(2)X^{5/6}.

<a id="st4-lattice-points-of-bounded-invariant-height"></a>

### 4.29 Lattice points (I, J) of bounded height in residue classes

Let L ⊆ Z² be a union of k cosets of mZ² (m ≥ 1). Then, uniformly in X ≥ 1, #{(I, J) ∈ L : H(I, J) < X, 4I³ − J² > 0} = (k/m²)·(8/5)X^{5/6} + O_m(X^{1/2}) and #{(I, J) ∈ L : H(I, J) < X, 4I³ − J² < 0} = (k/m²)·(32/5)X^{5/6} + O_m(X^{1/2}).

**Hypotheses.** H(I, J) = max{|I|³, J²/4}; the regions R^±(X) have areas (8/5)X^{5/6} and (32/5)X^{5/6} (source (24), (25)).

**Dependencies.** [The height H(I, J) = max{|I|³, J²/4} on pairs of invariants and on integral binary quartic forms](#st0-binary-quartic-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-height`); `mathlib:MeasureTheory.Measure.haarMeasure`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.5, p. 31. Exact statement for L = Z², extended to congruence classes; proved here by column counting instead of Davenport's lemma. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Proposition 2.10, p. 14. The source's error term.

**Proof route.**

1. Count by columns: for fixed I with |I| < X^{1/3}, the admissible J form at most two intervals of total length ℓ_±(I) (|J| < 2X^{1/2} and J² < 4I³, resp. J² > 4I³), so each column contains ℓ_±(I)/m + O(1) points of each coset.
2. Summing over the O(X^{1/3}/m + 1) admissible I in each residue class gives (1/m)Σ_I ℓ_±(I) + O(X^{1/3}), and Σ_{I ≡ i_0 (m)} ℓ_±(I) = (1/m)∫ℓ_±(I) dI + O(max ℓ) = area/m + O(X^{1/2}), since ℓ_± is piecewise monotone with a bounded number of pieces.

**Acceptance checks.**

- L = Z² (k = m = 1): #{H < X, Δ > 0} = (8/5)X^{5/6} + O(X^{1/2}).
- L = 3Z × 27Z, the pairs (−3A, −27B), is the union of k = 9 cosets of 27Z², of density 9/27² = 1/81: the factor 3^{-4} in M_3 for the family of all curves before minimality.

<a id="st4-tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant"></a>

### 4.30 Uniform tail estimate: curves whose discriminant is divisible by p² for some large p

There is an absolute constant C such that for all M ≥ 5 and X ≥ 2, #{(A, B) ∈ Z² : 4|A|³ < X, 27B² < X, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0, p² | 4A³ + 27B² for some prime p > M} ≤ C(X^{5/6}/M + X^{5/6}/log X). In particular limsup_{X→∞} X^{-5/6}·#{E : H(E) < X, p² | Δ(E) for some p > M} = O(1/M).

**Hypotheses.** Pairs (A, B), not only minimal pairs, are counted; H(E_{A,B}) = max{4|A|³, 27B²}.; Δ(E_{A,B}) = −16(4A³ + 27B²); for p ≥ 5 the conditions p² | Δ and p² | 4A³ + 27B² agree.

**Dependencies.** [Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)](#st0-elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height`); [The height H(I, J) = max{|I|³, J²/4} on pairs of invariants and on integral binary quartic forms](#st0-binary-quartic-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/binary-quartic-height`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Proposition 3.16, p. 32. The two elementary counts of the source's proof, summed over p. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.5, p. 32. The consumer: the tail estimate is exactly the input of Theorem 3.17.

**Proof route.**

1. If p² | D := 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0 then p² ≤ |D| ≪ X, so only primes p ≪ X^{1/2} occur.
2. Multiplicative case p ∤ A (p ≥ 5): then p ∤ B, and for fixed A the congruence B² ≡ −4A³/27 (mod p²) has at most 2 solutions modulo p², so the number of pairs is ≪ (X^{1/3} + 1)(X^{1/2}/p² + 1) ≪ X^{5/6}/p² + X^{1/3}.
3. Additive case p | A: then p | B, and the number of pairs is ≪ (X^{1/3}/p + 1)(X^{1/2}/p + 1) ≪ X^{5/6}/p² + X^{1/2}/p + 1.
4. Sum over M < p ≪ X^{1/2}: Σ X^{5/6}/p² ≪ X^{5/6}/M, Σ X^{1/3} ≪ X^{1/3}·X^{1/2}/log X, Σ X^{1/2}/p ≪ X^{1/2} log log X, Σ 1 ≪ X^{1/2}.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Pairs with p | A and p | B satisfy p² | 4A³ + 27B² and have density p^{-2}, so the tail is ≫ X^{5/6}/(M log M): the bound O(X^{5/6}/M) is sharp up to the logarithm.
- The per-prime bound O(X^{5/6}/p² + X^{1/3}) is uniform, but its X^{1/3} remainder has no p-decay. Summing only over p ≪ X^{1/2} and using the elementary prime-counting bound is what gives the required o(X^{5/6}) remainder.

<a id="st4-uniformity-estimate-for-elliptic-curves"></a>

### 4.31 The number of curves with p² | Δ is O(X^{5/6}/p^{3/2}) (Proposition 3.16)

The number of elliptic curves E/Q with H'(E) < X and p² | Δ(E) is O(X^{5/6}/p^{3/2}), with the implied constant independent of p and X.

**Hypotheses.** The count is over Q-isomorphism classes, i.e. minimal pairs (A, B) (ST.0 / Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 8).; For p ≤ X^{1/3} the elementary counts of tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant suffice; for larger p the proof needs the Davenport–Heilbronn bound O(X/p²) for GL_2(Z)-classes of integral binary cubic forms with p² | disc, together with a uniform bound on the number of preimages.

**Dependencies.** [Uniform tail estimate: curves whose discriminant is divisible by p² for some large p](#st4-tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant`); [Proposition 29 (non-maximal part), for forms: the classes in W_p^DH have O(X/p^2) elements of discriminant < X, uniformly in p](#st2-uniformity-estimate-for-nonmaximal-binary-cubic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/uniformity-estimate-for-nonmaximal-binary-cubic-forms`); [Uniformity for totally ramified primes: the cubic fields with |Disc| < X totally ramified at p number O(X/p²), uniformly in p](#st3-cubic-fields-totally-ramified-at-large-primes-are-sparse) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3/cubic-fields-totally-ramified-at-large-primes-are-sparse`); [Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)](#st0-elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proposition 3.16 and proof, pp. 31–32. Exact statement. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Proposition 3.16, p. 32. The two imported inputs.

**Proof route.**

1. Embed x³ + Ax + B ↦ the binary cubic form x³ + Axy² + By³; a GL_2(Z)-class has at most 12 preimages, since each preimage gives a distinct integral solution of v(a, b) = 1 and a cubic Thue equation of nonzero discriminant has at most 12 solutions (Delone, Evertse; gap).
2. By Davenport–Heilbronn's Proposition 1 (equivalently Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman's Proposition 29 for Z_p = W_p ∪ Y_p) the GL_2(Z)-classes of integral binary cubic forms with |disc| < CX and p² | disc number O(X/p²): the forms nonmaximal at p are ST.2's uniformity estimate, the maximal forms totally ramified at p are ST.3's cubic-fields-totally-ramified-at-large-primes-are-sparse (stated there for forms maximal at every prime; gap). Hence the curves with p² | Δ number O(X/p²).
3. Additive reduction (p | A, p | B): O(X^{5/6}/p² + X^{1/2}/p + 1), combined with O(X/p²) gives O(X^{5/6}/p^{5/3}).
4. Multiplicative reduction with p² | Δ: O(X^{1/3}(X^{1/2}/p² + 1)), combined with O(X/p²) gives O(X^{5/6}/p^{3/2}).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For p > X^{1/2} the count is 0: H'(E) < X gives |4A³ + 27B²| ≤ 8X/27, and p² | Δ ≠ 0 forces p² ≤ 8X/27.
- Summing the bound over p > M gives O(X^{5/6}/M^{1/2}), a weaker tail than the elementary tail estimate but uniform in X.

<a id="st4-count-of-curves-in-a-large-family"></a>

### 4.32 The number of elliptic curves of bounded height in a large family (Theorem 3.17)

Let F be a large family of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions and N(F; X) := #{E ∈ F : H'(E) < X}. Then N(F; X) = M_∞(F; X)·Π_p M_p(F) + o(X^{5/6}), and the product converges: 1 − M_p(F) = O(p^{-2}) for all but finitely many p.

**Hypotheses.** Curves are counted up to Q-isomorphism, through their invariants (I, J) = (−3A, −27B) for the unique minimal pair (A, B) (ST.0, from Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 8).; The main term may vanish (if some M_p(F) = 0); the statement is still true, and theorems dividing by N(F; X) assume Π_p M_p(F) > 0.

**Dependencies.** [Lattice points (I, J) of bounded height in residue classes](#st4-lattice-points-of-bounded-invariant-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/lattice-points-of-bounded-invariant-height`); [Uniform tail estimate: curves whose discriminant is divisible by p² for some large p](#st4-tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant`); [The Selmer-weighted local masses M_p(V, F), M_∞(V, F; X) and the archimedean mass M_∞(F; X)](#st4-local-masses-of-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-masses-of-a-family`); [Families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions, Inv_p, and large families](#st0-elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions`); [Families defined by local conditions, local densities and largeness](#st0-family-defined-by-local-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions`); [Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)](#st0-elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height`)

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-8-selected-ℚ-specific-database-adapters

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.17, (70), p. 32. Exact statement; the source gives no proof beyond the analogy with Theorem 2.21 (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E506), supplied here.

**Proof route.**

1. First incorporate the local minimal-pair conditions and I ∈ 3Z_p, J ∈ 27Z_p into Σ_p, obtaining T_p. They are clopen off Δ = 0; hence T_p is relatively closed there and has null boundary. Inv_p(F) ⊆ T_p. For all sufficiently large p, largeness implies {p² ∤ Δ} ⊆ Inv_p(F) ⊆ T_p, so 1−μ_p(T_p)=O(p^{-2}).
2. If μ_q(T_q)=0 for some q, then μ_q(Inv_q(F))=0. Compact clopen outer neighbourhoods of the closure of T_q have arbitrarily small mass (adding Δ=0 costs zero mass). The finite-congruence lattice count bounds N(F;X)/X^{5/6} by an arbitrarily small constant, proving the claimed zero main term without any regularity assertion about Inv_p(F) at other primes.
3. Otherwise every μ_p(T_p)>0. Fix a prime q and a nonempty clopen ball B contained in the interior of T_q. CRT counts with finitely many inner clopen approximations to the other T_p have positive normalized main term: the infinite product of their masses is positive since 1−μ_p(T_p)=O(p^{-2}). Choose the approximation errors summably small and the prime cutoff Y large enough that the discriminant-tail bound O(1/Y) is smaller than this main term. Count first as X→∞ with all finite data fixed. At least one resulting global minimal pair lies in B, meets all T_p and satisfies the chosen real sign. Repeating inside every subball proves interior(T_q) ⊆ Inv_q(F).
4. Thus, in this positive-mass case, interior(T_p) ⊆ Inv_p(F) ⊆ T_p for every p. The difference is supported on ∂T_p, so μ_p(Inv_p(F))=μ_p(T_p)>0 and ∂Inv_p(F) is null. This supplies the boundary assertion; it is not inherited merely by taking a closed subset.
5. Finite approximation: for a finite set of primes P and closed-open sets U_p ⊆ Z_p² that are finite unions of cosets of p^kZ_p², lattice-points-of-bounded-invariant-height gives #{(I, J) ∈ Z² : (I, J) ∈ U_p ∀p ∈ P, (I, J) ∈ Inv_∞(F), H < X} = M_∞(F; X)Π_{p∈P} μ_p(U_p) + O_P(X^{1/2}).
6. Upper bound: in the positive-mass case, since ∂Inv_p(F) is null by the preceding CRT/tail argument, choose U_p ⊇ Inv_p(F) with μ_p(U_p \ Inv_p(F)) small; letting P grow gives limsup N(F; X)/X^{5/6} ≤ M_∞(F; 1)Π_p M_p(F).
7. Lower bound: choose U_p ⊆ Inv_p(F) for p ≤ Y; a pair in all U_p (p ≤ Y) but outside Inv(F) fails Inv_p(F) at some p > Y, and for Y beyond the exceptional primes of largeness this forces p² | Δ(I, J); by tail-estimate-for-square-divisors-of-the-discriminant these number O(X^{5/6}/Y + X^{5/6}/log X).
8. Convergence: for p ≥ 5 outside the exceptional set, Inv_p(F) ⊇ {p² ∤ Δ}, and μ_p{p² | Δ(I, J)} ≤ 3p^{-2} (at most 2 residues of J modulo p² for each unit I, and p² classes with p | I, p | J).
9. Let Y → ∞.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Family of all curves: N(F; X) ~ 8X^{5/6}/(81ζ(10)); in terms of H(E) < T this is (2^{4/3}/(3^{3/2}ζ(10)))T^{5/6}.
- For the large family of example E501 (a measure-zero Cantor-type condition at 5) the main term is 0 and N(F; X) = o(X^{5/6}).

<a id="st4-count-of-locally-soluble-orbits-in-a-large-family"></a>

### 4.33 The weighted count of locally soluble orbits is a product of local densities

Let F be a large family of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions. Then, as Y → ∞, Σ_{PGL_2(Z)·f ⊆ S(F), f irreducible, H(f) < Y} 1/m(f) = N(V_Z ∩ S_∞(F); Y)·Π_p ∫_{S_p(F)} m_p(f)^{-1} df + o(Y^{5/6}), where N(V_Z ∩ S_∞(F); Y) is the number of irreducible GL_2(Z)-orbits of integral forms that are R-soluble with invariants in Inv_∞(F) and height < Y, and the Euler product converges absolutely.

**Hypotheses.** F large: for all but finitely many p, Inv_p(F) contains every (I, J) ∈ Z_p² with p² ∤ Δ(I, J) (ST.0).; The sieve of ST.2 (Theorem 2.21) is applied separately to each component V^{(i)}, i ∈ {0, 1, 2+, 2−}; only the R-soluble components with invariants in Inv_∞(F) contribute.

**Dependencies.** [Theorem 2.13: a uniform tail estimate for binary quartic forms whose discriminant is divisible by p^2 for some p > M](#st2-uniformity-estimate-for-infinitely-many-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/uniformity-estimate-for-infinitely-many-congruence-conditions`); [Weights defined by congruence conditions and acceptable weights](#st0-acceptable-weight-function) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/acceptable-weight-function`); [The local weight m_p and Q_p-solubility are locally constant off Δ = 0](#st4-local-weights-and-solubility-are-locally-constant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-weights-and-solubility-are-locally-constant`); [S(F) is cut out by the local sets S_p(F) and S_∞(F)](#st4-locally-soluble-set-is-cut-out-by-local-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/locally-soluble-set-is-cut-out-by-local-conditions`); [Global weights are products of local weights (Proposition 3.6)](#st4-global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights`); [Forms bad at an odd prime have discriminant divisible by p² (Proposition 3.18)](#st4-bad-forms-have-square-discriminant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/bad-forms-have-square-discriminant`); [Real solubility of binary quartic forms](#st4-real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/real-solubility-of-binary-quartic-forms`); [Families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions, Inv_p, and large families](#st0-elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions`); [The number of elliptic curves of bounded height in a large family (Theorem 3.17)](#st4-count-of-curves-in-a-large-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/count-of-curves-in-a-large-family`); [The local mass formula (Proposition 3.9)](#st4-local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Proof of Theorem 3.19, (72), p. 33. The first line of (72), with the hypotheses of Theorem 2.21 verified. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §2.7, p. 19. The acceptability condition checked in the third step.

**Proof route.**

1. Use the regularity dichotomy proved in count-of-curves-in-a-large-family. When every local specification has positive mass, each actual Inv_p(F) has null boundary and the following acceptable-weight argument applies. If a specification has zero mass at q, then M_q(F)=0 and the local mass formula makes the Euler product zero. Bound 1_{S(F)}/m ≤ 1_{S_q(F)}; clopen outer approximations to the null inverse image of Inv_q(F), followed by the one-prime ST.2 lattice count, give a global o(Y^{5/6}) upper bound. No boundary assertion at the other primes is needed in that case.
2. Local weights: φ_p := 1_{S_p(F)}/m_p: V_{Z_p} → [0, 1] is locally constant outside a closed null set (local-weights-and-solubility-are-locally-constant).
3. Product: for f ∈ V_Z with Δ(f) ≠ 0 in an R-soluble component with invariants in Inv_∞(F), Π_p φ_p(f) = 1_{S(F)}(f)/m(f) (locally-soluble-set-is-cut-out-by-local-conditions, global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights); the product converges because φ_p(f) = 1 for p ∤ 6Δ(f) outside the exceptional primes of largeness.
4. Acceptability (ST.0/acceptable-weight-function): for p ≥ 5 outside the finite exceptional set, if p² ∤ Δ(f) then f is Q_p-soluble and m_p(f) = 1 (bad-forms-have-square-discriminant), and (2^{-4}I(f), 2^{-6}J(f)) ∈ Inv_p(F) by largeness since Δ(2^{-4}I, 2^{-6}J) = 2^{-12}Δ(f); so φ_p(f) = 1.
5. Apply Theorem 2.21 (ST.2) on each R-soluble component and add; the Euler product converges because 1 − ∫φ_p ≤ μ_p{p² | Δ} = O(p^{-2}) for large p.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For the family of all curves the local factor at p ≥ 5 is ∫_{S_p} m_p^{-1} = (1 − p^{-2})(1 − p^{-10}) (local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms and (74)).
- Replacing the weight 1/m by 1 would count PGL_2(Z)-orbits rather than Selmer elements and change every local factor at the primes dividing the discriminants.

<a id="st4-selmer-average-as-product-of-local-masses"></a>

### 4.34 The Selmer average as a product of local masses (Theorem 3.19)

Let F be a large family of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions with M_p(F) > 0 for every prime p. Then lim_{X→∞} (Σ_{E ∈ F, H'(E) < X} (#S_2(E) − 1)) / N(F; X) = Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))·(M_∞(V, F; X)/M_∞(F; X))·Π_p ((1 − p^{-2})·M_p(V, F)/M_p(F)), where the archimedean ratio M_∞(V, F; X)/M_∞(F; X) does not depend on X.

**Hypotheses.** The positivity hypothesis M_p(F) > 0 for all p is not in the source's statement; without it the main terms may vanish and the argument gives no limit (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E501).; Heights: forms of height < 2^{12}X correspond to curves of height H' < X.

**Dependencies.** [Nonidentity 2-Selmer elements as a weighted count of integral orbits](#st4-selmer-count-as-weighted-orbit-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/selmer-count-as-weighted-orbit-count`); [The weighted count of locally soluble orbits is a product of local densities](#st4-count-of-locally-soluble-orbits-in-a-large-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/count-of-locally-soluble-orbits-in-a-large-family`); [The number of R-soluble integral orbits of bounded height](#st4-count-of-real-soluble-integral-orbits) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/count-of-real-soluble-integral-orbits`); [The local mass formula (Proposition 3.9)](#st4-local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms`); [The number of elliptic curves of bounded height in a large family (Theorem 3.17)](#st4-count-of-curves-in-a-large-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/count-of-curves-in-a-large-family`); [The Selmer-weighted local masses M_p(V, F), M_∞(V, F; X) and the archimedean mass M_∞(F; X)](#st4-local-masses-of-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-masses-of-a-family`); [Averages of arithmetic functions over a height-ordered family](#st4-average-over-a-height-ordered-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-over-a-height-ordered-family`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.19, (71)–(73), p. 33. Exact statement, with the positivity hypothesis added.

**Proof route.**

1. Fix 0 < ε < 1/12 so that X^{3/4+ε}=o(X^{5/6}). Numerator: by selmer-count-as-weighted-orbit-count and count-of-locally-soluble-orbits-in-a-large-family, Σ(#S_2(E) − 1) = N(V_Z ∩ S_∞(F); 2^{12}X)·Π_p ∫_{S_p(F)} m_p^{-1} + o(X^{5/6}).
2. By count-of-real-soluble-integral-orbits and homogeneity (M_∞(V, F; 2^{12}X) = 2^{10}M_∞(V, F; X)), N(V_Z ∩ S_∞(F); 2^{12}X) = (2^{10}/27)Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))M_∞(V, F; X) + O(X^{3/4+ε}).
3. By local-mass-formula-for-locally-soluble-forms, ∫_{S_p(F)} m_p^{-1} = |2^{10}/27|_p(1 − p^{-2})M_p(V, F); the product formula gives (2^{10}/27)·Π_p |2^{10}/27|_p = 1.
4. Denominator: count-of-curves-in-a-large-family, with M_∞(F; X)Π_p M_p(F) ≍ X^{5/6} by the positivity hypothesis.
5. Take the ratio; M_∞(V, F; X)/M_∞(F; X) is constant by homogeneity (local-masses-of-a-family).

**Acceptance checks.**

- The Euler factors (1 − p^{-2})M_p(V, F)/M_p(F) are 1 − p^{-2} for odd p and 2(1 − 1/4) = 3/2 at p = 2.
- The limit is a product over all places, with the archimedean factor 2ζ(2)·(1/2).

<a id="st4-tamagawa-number-of-pgl2-is-two"></a>

### 4.35 The Tamagawa number of PGL_2 over Q is 2

With the measures |ω|_ν attached to the Z-generator ω of jacobian-of-the-orbit-map, Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))·Π_p vol(PGL_2(Z_p)) = 2ζ(2)·Π_p (1 − p^{-2}) = 2.

**Hypotheses.** The archimedean volume Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R)) = 2ζ(2) is supplied by ST.2 (the source cites Langlands [33]).

**Dependencies.** [Averaging over the fundamental domain and cutting off the cusp: N(V_ℤ^(i); X) = Vol(R_X(L^(i)))/n_i + O(X^{3/4+ε})](#st2-averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/averaging-over-the-fundamental-domain-and-cutting-the-cusp`); [The volume of PGL_2(Z_p) for the measure |ω|_p](#st4-volume-of-pgl2-zp) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/volume-of-pgl2-zp`); `mathlib:riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod`; `mathlib:riemannZeta_two`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.6, p. 34. Exact statement. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §2.4, (23), p. 13. The archimedean volume.

**Proof route.**

1. Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R)) = 2ζ(2) (ST.2).
2. vol(PGL_2(Z_p)) = 1 − p^{-2} (volume-of-pgl2-zp).
3. Π_p (1 − p^{-2})^{-1} = ζ(2) (Euler product, mathlib:riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod at s = 2), and ζ(2) = π²/6 ≠ 0 (mathlib:riemannZeta_two).

**Acceptance checks.**

- 2ζ(2)Π_p(1 − p^{-2}) = 2ζ(2)/ζ(2) = 2: check the cancellation explicitly.
- Truncating the product at p ≤ 3 gives 2·(π²/6)·(3/4)(8/9) ≈ 2.19, and the partial products decrease to 2.

<a id="st4-average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three"></a>

### 4.36 Theorem 3.1: the average size of S_2(E) over a large family is 3

Let F be a large family of elliptic curves over Q defined by congruence conditions (ST.0) with M_p(F) > 0 for every prime p. When the curves in F are ordered by height H (equivalently H'), the average size of the 2-Selmer group is 3: lim_{X→∞} Σ_{E ∈ F, H(E) < X} #S_2(E) / #{E ∈ F : H(E) < X} = 3. The average of #S_2(E) − 1 equals Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))·Π_p vol(PGL_2(Z_p)) = 2, the Tamagawa number of PGL_2.

**Hypotheses.** F must be large, not merely defined by congruence conditions: largeness allows infinitely many conditions but requires that at all but finitely many p nothing is excluded away from p² | Δ.; M_p(F) > 0 for every p: an added hypothesis without which the source's proof does not apply (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E501).; The ordering is by the naive height; a different ordering (by conductor or discriminant) is a different theorem.; S_2(E) is the 2-Selmer group Sel_2(E/Q) of Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 7, identified by ST.1 with the locally soluble 2-coverings; it is finite.

**Dependencies.** [The Selmer average as a product of local masses (Theorem 3.19)](#st4-selmer-average-as-product-of-local-masses) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/selmer-average-as-product-of-local-masses`); [The local mass ratios (74)](#st4-local-selmer-mass-ratios) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-selmer-mass-ratios`); [The Tamagawa number of PGL_2 over Q is 2](#st4-tamagawa-number-of-pgl2-is-two) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/tamagawa-number-of-pgl2-is-two`); [Averages of arithmetic functions over a height-ordered family](#st4-average-over-a-height-ordered-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-over-a-height-ordered-family`); [The normalisation 27·H(E) = 4·H′(E) between the naive height of a curve and the quartic height of its invariants](#st0-quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation`); [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.5: 2-Selmer elements are PGL2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral quartics with invariants 2^4 I, 2^6 J](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Definition of a large family, p. 22. The largeness hypothesis. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorem 3.1, p. 22. Exact statement, with the positivity hypothesis added. [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3.6, p. 34. The final evaluation.

**Proof route.**

1. By selmer-average-as-product-of-local-masses the average of #S_2(E) − 1 is Vol(PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(R))·(M_∞(V, F; X)/M_∞(F; X))·Π_p (1 − p^{-2})M_p(V, F)/M_p(F).
2. By local-selmer-mass-ratios the ratios are 1/2 at ∞, 2 at p = 2 and 1 at odd p.
3. By tamagawa-number-of-pgl2-is-two the value is 2ζ(2)·(1/2)·2·Π_p(1 − p^{-2}) = 2.
4. Add the constant 1 (average-over-a-height-ordered-family: averages add) and pass from H' to H (27H = 4H').

**Acceptance checks.**

- Largeness check: the families of all curves, of finitely many congruence conditions, and of semistable curves are large (ST.0); the semistable family excludes a positive-density set at every p (the additive pairs, all with p² | Δ) and is still large. What largeness forbids is excluding, at infinitely many p, pairs with p² ∤ Δ(I, J).
- Local-mass check: the ratio is 2 at p = 2 and 1 at the other primes; an implementation that treats p = 2 like the others obtains the average 2.
- Tamagawa check: 2ζ(2)Π_p(1 − p^{-2}) = 2ζ(2)/ζ(2) = 2; verify the cancellation explicitly.
- Averaging check: the theorem computes the average of #S_2(E), a size, not of the 2-Selmer rank; the passage to ranks costs the inequality 2k ≤ 2^k of rank-bound-from-the-selmer-average.
- Consistency: the value 3 agrees with the heuristic predictions of Poonen–Rains and of Delaunay combined with Goldfeld–Katz–Sarnak (source p. 2); those models are statements of ST.5, not inputs here.

<a id="st4-families-of-theorems-1-1-and-1-3-have-positive-local-masses"></a>

### 4.37 All curves, individual congruence classes and semistable curves have positive local masses

The family of all elliptic curves and the family of semistable elliptic curves are large families F_Σ with positive local masses. Every nonempty family of minimal pairs in a single residue class modulo m ≥ 1, with an optional discriminant sign condition, has the same properties. A general nonempty union of residue classes is a finite disjoint union of these families after empty classes are discarded. It is itself large and has positive local projection masses, but need not equal the intersection of those projections.

**Hypotheses.** Nonemptiness in (b): a union of residue classes containing no minimal pair with Δ ≠ 0 (e.g. p⁴ | A and p⁶ | B) defines the empty family.; In (c) semistability at 2 and 3 is a condition on the minimal model, not on the short model (A, B), which is never minimal at 2 when it has good reduction.

**Dependencies.** [The family of all elliptic curves over ℚ is large](#st0-all-elliptic-curves-form-a-large-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/all-elliptic-curves-form-a-large-family`); [Families of elliptic curves defined by congruence conditions, Inv_p, and large families](#st0-elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-families-defined-by-congruence-conditions`); [Families defined by local conditions, local densities and largeness](#st0-family-defined-by-local-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions`); [The Selmer-weighted local masses M_p(V, F), M_∞(V, F; X) and the archimedean mass M_∞(F; X)](#st4-local-masses-of-a-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/local-masses-of-a-family`); `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.HasGoodReduction`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.HasMultiplicativeReduction`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.IsMinimal`

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-4-elliptic-curves-over-local-fields--reduction-tates-algorithm-the-tate-curve-aec-vii-ataec-ivv

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §3, p. 22. Exact statement of largeness; positivity of the local masses is added.

**Proof route.**

1. For one residue class, CRT factors its condition into independent prime-power conditions. Intersect these with local minimality and the permitted real sign. For all curves use the trivial residue condition. For semistability use the good-or-multiplicative locus, relatively clopen off Δ=0 by the layer-4 reduction-type input; at 2 and 3 this is a condition on a minimal model, not the original short equation.
2. To show density in a specified admissible ball at one prime, choose a nonzero integer B satisfying that ball and all the finitely many prescribed congruences. For each additional prime dividing B, impose A≡1 there by CRT; at specified primes retain the existing local minimality conditions. For semistability impose the open good-or-multiplicative conditions at 2 and 3 first and require gcd(A,B) prime to every other prime. The resulting progression of A has arbitrarily large positive and negative members, providing either discriminant sign and avoiding the finitely many singular choices. This proves the needed actual local closures and largeness.
3. Each nonempty local condition has interior containing a ball around a member of the family. For semistability use y²+y=x³−x as a simultaneous witness of good reduction at 2 and 3; local constancy supplies the balls. Haar measure of a nonempty ball is positive.
4. For a general allowed set modulo m, partition it into its individual residue classes. Apply the preceding assertions separately; do not replace the allowed set by the product of its projections, which can add classes.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For (a): M_p = 1 − p^{-10} (p ≥ 5), M_3 = 3^{-4}(1 − 3^{-10}), M_2 = 1 − 2^{-10}.
- The family {B = 0} (j = 1728) is not large (ST.0), and the Cantor-type family of E501 is large with M_5(F) = 0: both fail the hypotheses.
- A∈{0,1} mod 6 is not equivalent to its separate projections at 2 and 3: their intersection also permits A≡3,4 mod 6. Use the two disjoint classes A≡0 and A≡1, each with its own product of local conditions.

### 4.38 Theorems 1.1 and 1.3: average size 3 over all curves, congruence families and semistable curves

When all elliptic curves over Q are ordered by height (Theorem 1.1), or those in any nonempty family E: y² = x³ + Ax + B defined by finitely many congruence conditions on A and B (Theorem 1.3), or all semistable elliptic curves, the average size of the 2-Selmer group S_2(E) is 3.

**Hypotheses.** Ordering by the naive height H(E_{A,B}) = max{4|A|³, 27B²} of the minimal pair.

**Dependencies.** [Theorem 3.1: the average size of S_2(E) over a large family is 3](#st4-average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three`); [All curves, individual congruence classes and semistable curves have positive local masses](#st4-families-of-theorems-1-1-and-1-3-have-positive-local-masses) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/families-of-theorems-1-1-and-1-3-have-positive-local-masses`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3, pp. 1–2. Exact statements.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three to all curves, to each nonempty individual residue class, and to the semistable family. For a finite disjoint union F=⊔F_i, the deviations Σ_{E∈F_i,H<X}(#S₂(E)−3) are o(N(F_i;X)); for any ε>0 choose a common threshold for all finitely many i, add the bounds, and divide by Σ_i N(F_i;X). The union also has average 3, without any assertion that it is one independent product of local conditions.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Restricting to A ≡ 1 (mod 5) does not change the average: it is still 3.
- Restricting to Δ > 0 or Δ < 0 (a condition at ∞) does not change the average either.

<a id="st4-two-selmer-rank-identity"></a>

### 4.39 The 2-Selmer rank identity (2)

For every elliptic curve E over Q: r_2(S_2(E)) = r(E) + r_2(E(Q)[2]) + r_2(Ш_E[2]), where r(E) is the rank of E(Q) and r_2(G) = dim_{F_2} G for an elementary abelian 2-group G. In particular r(E) ≤ r_2(S_2(E)) and 2^{r(E)}·#E(Q)[2] ≤ #S_2(E).

**Hypotheses.** E(Q) is finitely generated (Mordell–Weil), so E(Q)/2E(Q) ≅ F_2^{r(E) + r_2(E(Q)[2])}.; S_2(E) is finite (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 7); Ш_E[2] is its quotient by the image of E(Q)/2E(Q), finite as well. Nothing here controls Ш_E.

**Dependencies.** `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.card_range_μ`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.fg_point_of_numberField`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.pow_rank_le_card_of_range_μ_le`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.selmerGroup₂`; [Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.5: 2-Selmer elements are PGL2(Q)-classes of locally soluble integral quartics with invariants 2^4 I, 2^6 J](#st1-binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/binary-quartic-parametrization-of-two-selmer`)

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii; tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Equations (1)–(2), pp. 1–2. Exact statement.

**Proof route.**

1. The exact sequence 0 → E(Q)/2E(Q) → S_2(E) → Ш_E[2] → 0 of F_2-vector spaces (Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 7).
2. #(E(Q)/2E(Q)) = 2^{r(E)}·#E(Q)[2] (tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.card_range_μ, with E(Q) finitely generated by tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.fg_point_of_numberField), transported to the cohomological carrier by the comparison of explicit and cohomological 2-Selmer groups (layer 7 milestone, used through ST.1).
3. Take F_2-dimensions. The inequality 2^{r}·#E(Q)[2] ≤ #S_2(E) is also tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.pow_rank_le_card_of_range_μ_le for the explicit 2-Selmer group tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.selmerGroup₂.

**Acceptance checks.**

- y² = x³ − x: r = 0, r_2(E(Q)[2]) = 2, Ш[2] = 0, r_2(S_2) = 2.
- The identity is between dimensions; equality of r_2(S_2) with the rank r(E) holds only when E(Q)[2] and Ш_E[2] vanish.

<a id="st4-rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero"></a>

### 4.40 0% of elliptic curves have rational 2-torsion

#{(A, B) ∈ Z² : max{4|A|³, 27B²} < X, x³ + Ax + B has a rational root} = O(X^{1/2}). Consequently, for every large family F with M_p(F) > 0 for all p, the proportion of E ∈ F with E(Q)[2] ≠ 0 tends to 0 and the average of r_2(E(Q)[2]) over F is 0.

**Hypotheses.** E_{A,B}(Q)[2] ≠ 0 iff x³ + Ax + B has a rational root; r_2(E(Q)[2]) ≤ 2.

**Dependencies.** [The number of elliptic curves of bounded height in a large family (Theorem 3.17)](#st4-count-of-curves-in-a-large-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/count-of-curves-in-a-large-family`); [Averages of arithmetic functions over a height-ordered family](#st4-average-over-a-height-ordered-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-over-a-height-ordered-family`); [Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)](#st0-elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height`); `mathlib:isInteger_of_is_root_of_monic`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), §1.1, p. 2. Exact statement; the source gives no proof.

**Proof route.**

1. A rational root of the monic integral cubic is an integer r (mathlib:isInteger_of_is_root_of_monic), and then B = −r³ − Ar.
2. With |A| ≤ α := (X/4)^{1/3}: if r² ≥ 4α then |r³ + Ar| ≥ (3/4)|r|³ ≥ 6α^{3/2} > (X/27)^{1/2}, so |r| < 2α^{1/2} ≪ X^{1/6}; each pair (A, r) determines B, giving O(X^{1/3}·X^{1/6}) = O(X^{1/2}) pairs.
3. By count-of-curves-in-a-large-family, N(F; X) ≫ X^{5/6} when Π_p M_p(F) > 0; divide.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The family y² = x³ + Ax (B = 0, r = 0) has rational 2-torsion and O(X^{1/3}) members of height < X.
- The bound is a density statement, not an inequality between ranks.

<a id="st4-rank-bound-from-the-selmer-average"></a>

### 4.41 Corollary 1.2: average 2-Selmer rank and average rank at most 1.5

Let F be a large family with M_p(F) > 0 for every prime p (for Corollary 1.2 itself, the family of all elliptic curves), ordered by height. Then limsup_{X→∞} Avg_F(r_2(S_2(E)); X) ≤ 3/2 and limsup_{X→∞} Avg_F(r(E); X) ≤ 3/2: the average 2-Selmer rank, and hence the average rank, of elliptic curves in F is bounded by 1.5. This bounds the Mordell–Weil rank; it does not compute it, since r(E) and r_2(S_2(E)) differ by r_2(E(Q)[2]) + r_2(Ш_E[2]), which is not controlled.

**Hypotheses.** The conclusion is about the upper average (limsup); no lower bound and no limit is asserted.; The inequality 2k ≤ 2^k for k ∈ N, an equality exactly at k = 1, 2, is where the loss from average size 3 to average rank 1.5 occurs.; The rank bound needs E(Q) finitely generated and S_2(E) finite (two-selmer-rank-identity).

**Dependencies.** [Theorem 3.1: the average size of S_2(E) over a large family is 3](#st4-average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three`); [The 2-Selmer rank identity (2)](#st4-two-selmer-rank-identity) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/two-selmer-rank-identity`); [Averages of arithmetic functions over a height-ordered family](#st4-average-over-a-height-ordered-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-over-a-height-ordered-family`); `mathlib:Nat.mul_le_pow`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-shankar-2013](#source-p-bhargava-shankar-2013), Corollary 1.2 with the identity (2) and the surrounding argument, p. 2. Exact statement, read as a bound on the upper average (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E510), for every family satisfying Theorem 3.1.

**Proof route.**

1. Pointwise, 2·r_2(S_2(E)) ≤ 2^{r_2(S_2(E))} = #S_2(E) (mathlib:Nat.mul_le_pow with a = 2: 2k ≤ 2^k).
2. Average: Avg_F(r_2(S_2); X) ≤ Avg_F(#S_2; X)/2 → 3/2 by average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three, so the upper average is at most 3/2.
3. r(E) ≤ r_2(S_2(E)) (two-selmer-rank-identity), so the upper average of r(E) is at most 3/2 (upperFamilyAverage_mono).

**Acceptance checks.**

- ST.4's acceptance condition is met here: the Selmer average bounds the rank through the proved inequality 2k ≤ 2^k, and the Selmer rank is not equated with the Mordell–Weil rank; the difference r_2(E(Q)[2]) + r_2(Ш_E[2]) is not controlled.
- Check the loss: #S_2(E) is always a power of 2, and 2k ≤ 2^k is an equality only at k = 1, 2. Mean size 3 gives mean 2-Selmer rank ≤ 3/2 through this inequality (Jensen's inequality would give only log₂3 ≈ 1.585). The conjectured average rank 1/2 (Goldfeld, Katz–Sarnak, p. 1) is a separate statement about Mordell–Weil ranks.
- Check the direction: Theorem 1.1 is an equality (average exactly 3); Corollary 1.2 is only an upper bound for ranks.
- Check that the 2-torsion term is handled by a density statement (rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero), not by an inequality.

### 4.42 The average of r_2(Ш_E[2]) is at most 1.5 and the average of r_2(E(Q)[2]) is 0

For every large family F with M_p(F) > 0 for all p: limsup_{X→∞} Avg_F(r_2(Ш_E[2]); X) ≤ 3/2 and Avg_F(r_2(E(Q)[2]); X) → 0.

**Hypotheses.** Ш_E[2] is the 2-torsion of the Shafarevich–Tate group of Tau Ceti EllipticCurves layer 7; no finiteness of Ш_E is assumed.

**Proof route.**

1. The three summands in two-selmer-rank-identity are nonnegative, so r_2(Ш_E[2]) ≤ r_2(S_2(E)); apply rank-bound-from-the-selmer-average.
2. The 2-torsion average is rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero.

<a id="st4-refinement-admissibility"></a>

### 4.43 Admissible hyperelliptic congruence families

For n=2g+2 with g≥1 and a congruence family F of integral binary forms, let L_p be its actual p-adic coefficient closure. The added admissibility predicate says that there is P such that, for every prime p>P, L_p contains every coefficient tuple a for which z²=Σ_i a_i x^(n−i)y^i has a Q_p-point with (x,y)≠(0,0). Smooth nonzero-discriminant models suffice: for closed L_p, point-bearing singular equations lie in their closure by point-preserving smooth perturbation. This predicate supplements the imported congruence-family definition; it does not assert positive density, local Div¹-solubility at small places or admissibility of an arbitrary collection of local sets.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Functions and sets defined by congruence conditions; acceptable functions](#st2-functions-defined-by-congruence-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/functions-defined-by-congruence-conditions`); [Hyperelliptic equation models](#st0-hyperelliptic-model-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/hyperelliptic-model-family`); `mathlib:PadicInt`

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Definition 43 p.34. For n=2g+2 with g≥1 and a congruence family F of integral binary forms, let L_p be its actual p-adic coefficient closure. The added admissibility predicate says that there is P such that, for every prime p>P, L_p contains every coefficient tuple a for which z²=Σ_i a_i x^(n−i)y^i has a Q_p-point with (x,y)≠(0,0). Smooth nonzero-discriminant models suffice: for closed L_p, point-bearing singular equations lie in their closure by point-preserving smooth perturbation. This predicate supplements the imported congruence-family definition; it does not assert positive density, local Div¹-solubility at small places or admissibility of an arbitrary collection of local sets.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_threshold` (characterisation): Admissibility is equivalent to a single integer threshold beyond which all local point-bearing tuples are allowed.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_mono` (functoriality): If L_p⊆M_p for every prime and L is admissible, M is admissible.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_finite_change` (compatibility): If L is admissible and L_p=M_p beyond a fixed threshold, M is admissible.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_of_local_points` (constructor): Containing the local point locus at every prime implies admissibility.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_univ` (computation): All local coefficient sets equal to the whole space satisfy the predicate.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_finite_exclusion` (degenerate): Taking the empty set for p≤P and the whole space for p>P passes the local threshold predicate. A family application must separately verify that its local inputs are actual closures; this test only checks finite-place insensitivity.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_empty_nonexample` (non-example): Taking every local coefficient set empty is not admissible: a₀=1 and a_i=0 for i>0 has the local point (x,y,z)=(1,0,1) for every prime, including the generic n=0 interface.

**Proof route.**

1. Use ST.0 coefficient models and the actual local closures from ST.2.
2. At each sufficiently large prime impose inclusion of the point-bearing locus. Closedness permits smooth perturbation; changing finitely many local conditions preserves the predicate.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Check all local places and the exact height denominator; retain every displayed hypothesis.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorem 5 and Theorem A.2 — The parity construction changes finitely many primes and uses local points to retain all four twists outside them.

<a id="st4-refinement-degree-one-arithmetic-comparison"></a>

### 4.44 Degree-one torsors and odd-degree points

For a smooth hyperelliptic C/Q of genus g≥1 with a Q-rational degree-two hyperelliptic divisor class d represented by a divisor, and actual degree-one divisors over every completion, every rational Picard-scheme point descends to an actual line bundle/divisor. Thus J¹(Q)≠∅ iff C has a point over some finite odd-degree extension iff index(C)=1; otherwise index(C)=2. Here index is the positive generator of the degree subgroup of rational divisors, not the minimum degree of a closed point.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** `JacobianChallengePartII:JC0/picard-torsors`; `JacobianChallengePartII:JC4/actual-to-relative-obstruction`; `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ClassFieldTheory#layer-10-global-carriers-the-brauer-sequence-and-the-sum-of-local-invariants`

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Introduction pp.1–4, Theorems 1,2,12. For a smooth hyperelliptic C/Q of genus g≥1 with a Q-rational degree-two hyperelliptic divisor class d represented by a divisor, and actual degree-one divisors over every completion, every rational Picard-scheme point descends to an actual line bundle/divisor. Thus J¹(Q)≠∅ iff C has a point over some finite odd-degree extension iff index(C)=1; otherwise index(C)=2. Here index is the positive generator of the degree subgroup of rational divisors, not the minimum degree of a closed point.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.degree_one_arithmetic_comparison`.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply the Picard/Brauer obstruction sequence and global-to-local injectivity of Br(Q); local actual Div¹ kills the obstruction.
2. Trace an odd-degree point, then subtract ((k−1)/2)d. Conversely an odd-degree rational divisor must involve an odd-degree closed point. The rational degree-two divisor forces the index to divide two.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Check all local places and the exact height denominator; retain every displayed hypothesis.

<a id="st4-refinement-generic-weierstrass-class"></a>

### 4.45 Generic nontrivial Weierstrass class

In the coefficient-height genus-g model family, outside a density-zero exceptional set, the finite J[2]-torsor W[2]={P∈J¹:2P=d}, the fibre of the canonical map J¹→J² over the hyperelliptic class d, defines a nonzero class in H¹(Q,J[2]), and J(Q)[2]=0. On the subfamily with everywhere locally soluble actual Div¹, W[2] belongs to Sel₂(J). These conclusions hold relatively in every such sieve-controlled congruence subfamily of positive lower density.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Field orbits and norm-one stabilizers](#st1-refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-field-pencil-stabilizers`); [Locally soluble pencils and the 2-Selmer set](#st1-refinement-locally-soluble-pencil-orbits) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-locally-soluble-pencil-orbits`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.2`; [A density-one subset stays of density one in every subfamily of positive lower density](#st0-density-one-restricts-to-subfamilies-of-positive-lower-density) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/density-one-restricts-to-subfamilies-of-positive-lower-density`)

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Introduction p.2, Theorem 5 proof pp.3–4, and §8 pp.21–22.. The full S_n specialization argument gives a nonzero cohomology class of the Weierstrass fibre and no rational two-torsion. Membership in the Selmer group additionally uses everywhere local degree-one divisors, as in §8 pp.21–22.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.generic_weierstrass_class`.

**Proof route.**

1. Identify W[2]-points with odd factorisations and nonzero rational two-torsion with even factorisations, including quadratically conjugate factors.
2. Hilbert irreducibility gives full symmetric Galois group away from a density-zero set. Restrict using positive-density denominator comparison.
3. Use a local degree-one divisor to identify J¹(Q_v) with a J(Q_v)-torsor with a point. The class of W[2] is then a local Kummer class. This step is conditional on local Div¹, whereas full S_n gives nonvanishing without that condition.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For n=4, S4 has no invariant odd partition and no nontrivial even partition modulo complement; no claim is made about each exceptional polynomial.
- Distinguish a nonzero H¹(Q,J[2]) class in all models from its Selmer membership in the locally actual-Div¹-soluble subfamily.

<a id="st4-refinement-pencil-local-global-weight"></a>

### 4.46 Global weights for soluble pencils

For G=SL_(2g+2)/μ₂ acting on pairs of symmetric matrices, define w(v) as the reciprocal of the imported finite rational-orbit weight when v is locally soluble and its invariant belongs to F, and zero otherwise. The global weight is the product of its integral-local counterparts, is locally constant off the discriminant locus, and equals one at sufficiently large odd primes with p²∤Disc(f). The group is the central quotient as an algebraic group; rational points cannot be replaced by SL_n(Q)/{±1}.

### 4.47 Selmer sets as weighted rational pencil counts

For F with locally soluble actual Div¹ and coefficients in 16Z, the sum of #Sel₂(J¹_f) over H(f)<X is at most the sum of the weighted integral-orbit counts N_w over the real soluble components, plus o(X^(n+1)), after generic rational stabilizers are separated. The left side itself equals the unweighted rational locally soluble orbit count represented integrally. An individual rational class with integral representatives v_i satisfies Σ_i w(v_i)/#Stab_Z(v_i)=1/#Stab_Q(v). One may use Σ_i w(v_i)=1 only when the rational stabilizer is trivial.

<a id="st4-refinement-hyperelliptic-local-mass-ratio"></a>

### 4.48 Local two-cover mass ratios

For an abelian variety J/Q_v of dimension g and a nonempty J-torsor T(Q_v), the finite torsor quotient T(Q_v)/2J(Q_v) has the same cardinality as J(Q_v)/2J(Q_v). For the hyperelliptic Jacobian this gives ρ_v=#(J¹(Q_v)/2J(Q_v))/#J[2](Q_v): ρ_∞=2^(−g), ρ_2=2^g and ρ_p=1 for odd p. Thus Π_vρ_v=1. The quotient numerator is not the number of rational points, and an empty local torsor is excluded.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

### 4.50 Tamagawa number of the even special-linear central quotient

For every even n≥4, the split Q-group G=SL_n/μ₂ has Tamagawa number two, for the adelic measure attached to an integral invariant top differential and the matching convergence convention. G(Q) is the group-scheme quotient’s rational points, not the naive quotient of SL_n(Q) by its rational centre. The rational Jacobian constant in the orbit integral changes no Tamagawa value.

### 4.51 Weighted hyperelliptic numerator bound

Let n=2g+2, g≥1, and F be a positive-mass sieve-controlled congruence family contained in the everywhere actual-Div¹-soluble locus, with all coefficients in 16Z. For each non-negative-definite real root stratum I(m), let its allowed part be F_∞∩I(m); use the full strata when no extra real restriction is imposed. Assuming the corresponding real-region count, the Selmer numerator is at most 2 Σ_m μ_∞({f∈F_∞∩I(m):H(f)<X}) Π_p μ_p(F_p)+o_F(X^(n+1)). Here F_∞ is a union of these strata; more general real restrictions require the matching counting extension. The same allowed real mass occurs in the coefficient denominator. The value τ(SL_n/μ₂)=2 has the explicit general-formula supplier gap. The infinite-weight count gives an upper bound without a matching lower bound.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_mem` (characterisation): Membership requires membership in S and every local condition.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_subset` (relation): The restricted set is contained in S.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_finite` (structure): If S is finite, its restricted set is finite.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_mono` (functoriality): Enlarging every I_v enlarges the restricted set. Applying this to I_k⊆I_(k+2) gives the order inclusion.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_card_le` (compatibility): For finite S, the natural cardinal of its restriction is at most S.ncard.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_transport` (equivalence): For an equivalence e:A≃B, transporting S and precomposing loc with e⁻¹ transports the restricted set by e.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_one_place` (computation): For S=Fin 3, identity localisation at one place and image {0,2}, the restriction is {0,2}.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_all_places` (non-example): For two identity localisations with images {0,1} and {1,2}, the answer is {1}, not their union.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_no_places` (degenerate): With no places the restriction is S.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.restricted_empty_image` (degenerate): An empty image at one place makes the restriction empty.

**Proof route.**

1. Intersect the pullbacks of the effective-divisor images with the finite Selmer set.
2. The construction is independent of the presentation of candidates. Translate torsor identifications and divisor images together; adding d proves the geometric order-k to order-(k+2) inclusion.
3. Import Sym^k C→Pic^k, D↦O(D), from JacobianChallenge Layer D and the section-free Pic¹ convention from JC2. Translate by the actual degree-two hyperelliptic divisor. The remaining ST.1 request concerns compatibility with covering localisation, not a second construction of the Abel map.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Check all local places and the exact height denominator; retain every displayed hypothesis.

**Consumers.** BGW Theorem 7 — Local effective-divisor images restrict the full two-Selmer set before the archimedean sieve.; BGW Corollary 8 — An effective global odd-degree divisor yields a member of the corresponding restricted set.

### 4.53 Odd subsets of real components

Define S_m(k)=Σ_(0≤j≤k,j odd) binomial(m,j), with binomial(m,j)=0 for j>m; the empty sum is zero. For m≥1 the normalized component bound is S_m(k)/2^(m−1). This numerical construction records the image bound from degree-k real divisors; it is not asserted to equal the geometric image cardinal in every real model.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Nat.choose`

For m≥1 the normalized component bound is S_m(k)/2^(m−1). **API.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_bound_mono` (functoriality): S_m(k)≤S_m(l) for k≤l.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_bound_le` (relation): For m>0, S_m(k)≤2^(m−1).
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_bound_saturated` (characterisation): For m>0 and k≥m, S_m(k)=2^(m−1).
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_bound_strict` (relation): For m>0, k odd and k<m−1, S_m(k)<2^(m−1).
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_bound_ratio_tendsto` (compatibility): For each fixed k, S_m(k)/2^(m−1) tends to zero as m→∞.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_three_one` (computation): S_3(1)=3, distinguishing the missing third-degree contribution.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_five_three` (computation): S_5(3)=15, strictly smaller than 16.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_zero` (degenerate): S_m(0)=0 for every m.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_saturation` (computation): S_3(9)=4: terms above m vanish and even terms stay excluded.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.component_single` (computation): S_1(k)=1 for k>0.

**Proof route.**

1. Count odd subsets of connected components. Each real point contributes its component mod two; a conjugate pair contributes zero.
2. Use finite binomial sums and the exponential denominator to obtain the stated API.

Let A/K be principally polarized, F/K finite Galois with group G, p prime, and Θ=Σ_i n_i H_i a Brauer relation (Σ_i n_i Ind_(H_i)^G 1=0). Here c̃=Π_(finite v)c_v|ω/ω_v^Néron|_v for a fixed global invariant top differential; Sha^[p] is the finite p-primary part of Sha modulo its maximal divisible subgroup. No finiteness of all Sha is assumed and the p=2 factor may not be dropped.
