Then Σ_(ρ∈S_Θ)m_ρ≡ord_p Π_i( c̃_(A/F^Hi)·#Sha_(A/F^Hi)^[p])^(n_i) mod 2. Here c̃=Π_(finite v)c_v|ω/ω_v^Néron|_v for a fixed global invariant top differential; Sha^[p] is the finite p-primary part of Sha modulo its maximal divisible subgroup. **Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.selmer_regulator_parity`.

**Proof route.**

1. Import self-duality and the isogeny-quotient formula for Selmer duals; retain the finite Sha quotient from that formula.
2. Use regulator-constant multiplicativity on the self-dual decomposition. Non-self-dual dual pairs have square regulator constant. At odd p the finite Sha contribution is a square; at p=2 use the formula before removing the polarization obstruction.

**Acceptance checks.**

<a id="st4-refinement-biquadratic-parity-formula"></a>

### 4.56 Biquadratic parity with the finite Sha quotient

For every principally polarized A/K and biquadratic F=K(√α,√β), the sum of the four 2∞-Selmer coranks of A,A^α,A^β,A^(αβ) over K is congruent modulo two to ord₂[c̃_(K√α)c̃_(K√β)c̃_(K√αβ)/(c̃_F c̃_K²)] plus ord₂[#Sha^[2]_(K√α)#Sha^[2]_(K√β)#Sha^[2]_(K√αβ)/(#Sha^[2]_F (#Sha^[2]_K)²)]. All A subscripts in the local products refer to the same base-changed A. The coranks of twists come from the four character multiplicities, not from a presumed equality with Mordell–Weil ranks.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Selmer parity from Brauer regulator constants](#st4-refinement-selmer-regulator-parity) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-selmer-regulator-parity`); `SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2`

**Proof route.**

1. Use Θ={1}−H_α−H_β−H_(αβ)+2G. Each of the four one-dimensional characters has regulator constant square class two.
2. Identify each character multiplicity by quadratic descent. Reversing the quotient in the integer valuation leaves its parity unchanged.

<a id="st4-refinement-four-twist-local-parity"></a>

### 4.57 Four-twist parity from a single split node

Let F=K(√α,√β) be biquadratic and let p₀ have a unique prime above it. Let C/K be a smooth curve with Jacobian J. Require C(K_p₀)≠∅ and split semistable reduction of J of toric rank one at p₀. At every other finite prime with a unique prime above it, require C(K_p)≠∅ and good reduction of J. The sum of the four 2∞-Selmer coranks is odd. If all four twists of C also have local points at every prime with a unique prime above it, the sum of the four finite 2-Selmer dimensions is odd. At other places decomposition groups are cyclic and their Brauer local products cancel.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Biquadratic parity with the finite Sha quotient](#st4-refinement-biquadratic-parity-formula) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-biquadratic-parity-formula`); `SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L1`; `NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties:R11.4/graph-monodromy`; `NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties:R11.3`; `tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/InductionRestriction#layer-0-the-functorial-core----transitivity-and-the-projection-formula`

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Theorem A.3 p.36 and proof p.39. Let F=K(√α,√β) be biquadratic and let p₀ have a unique prime above it. Let C/K be a smooth curve with Jacobian J. Require C(K_p₀)≠∅ and split semistable reduction of J of toric rank one at p₀. At every other finite prime with a unique prime above it, require C(K_p)≠∅ and good reduction of J. The sum of the four 2∞-Selmer coranks is odd. If all four twists of C also have local points at every prime with a unique prime above it, the sum of the four finite 2-Selmer dimensions is odd. At other places decomposition groups are cyclic and their Brauer local products cancel.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.four_twist_local_parity`.

**Proof route.**

1. Group modified Tamagawa and deficiency contributions by places of K. Use cyclic decomposition cancellation at places with more than one prime above them.
2. Actual local points kill deficiency; good reduction kills all remaining terms except p₀. The split toric-rank-one monodromy factor gives square class two there.
3. Compare finite Selmer dimension with 2∞ corank, rational two-torsion and the finite Sha quotient. The four twists have the same two-torsion and their deficiency contributions cancel under the additional point hypothesis.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The extra four-twist local-point hypothesis is required for finite Selmer dimensions. Never say every odd prime splits completely in Q(i,√2).

### 4.58 A congruence family with both corank parities

For squarefree f(x)=Σ_(i=0)^n a_ix^i over Q, n≥3 and n∈{2g+1,2g+2}, suppose a₂≡1 mod8, a_(2g+1)≡4 mod8 and all other a_i≡0 mod8. Among the four curves y²=f,−f,2f,−2f, at least one Jacobian has even and at least one has odd 2∞-Selmer corank. This proposition alone is not a finite-2-Selmer parity assertion.

<a id="st4-refinement-odd-residue-field-models"></a>

### 4.59 Local models for good and split nodal reduction

Let K/Q_p be finite with p odd, residue field F_q, and let C:y²=f(x) be a smooth hyperelliptic curve with integral coefficients and degree n≥3, hence genus ⌊(n−1)/2⌋. Reduction may drop degree in (iii), but (i) and (ii) retain degree n. (i) If f̄ is squarefree of degree n and has an F_q-root, J has good reduction and every quadratic twist of C has a K-point. (ii) If f̄=(x−a)²h, h squarefree of degree n−2, h(a) a nonzero square, and h has an F_q-root, J is split semistable of toric rank one and every quadratic twist has a K-point. (iii) If f̄ is not a scalar multiple of a square and q>4n², then C(K)≠∅. In (ii) the root of h is automatically different from a and simple. In (iii) the factorisation f̄=l h² does not require l,h coprime.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** `NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties:R11.4/normalization-exact-sequence`; `NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties:R11.4/picard-neron-identity`; `NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties:R11.4/graph-monodromy`; [Hyperelliptic equation models](#st0-hyperelliptic-model-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/hyperelliptic-model-family`); `WeilConjectures:WC.5`

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Lemma A.5 p.37. The three local reduction/point statements are Lemma A.5 with n the degree of the characteristic-zero polynomial. Part (iii) permits degree drop and common factors between its odd-multiplicity part and square part; the repaired Hasse–Weil estimate is recorded in E-ST4-4.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.odd_residue_field_models`.

**Proof route.**

1. For (i),(ii), lift the simple residue root of f by Hensel; the point (b,0) survives all twists. Compute the split-node graph and Néron identity component.
2. For (iii), factor the odd-multiplicity squarefree part and use the finite-field curve point bound, excluding the finitely many roots and points at infinity, to get a smooth affine point. Hensel lifts it.

**Acceptance checks.**

- A node with h(a) nonsquare is not split; a repeated root does not replace the simple root used for twist points.

<a id="st4-refinement-hyperelliptic-average-two"></a>

### 4.60 Average size of the degree-one two-Selmer set

For each g≥1, coefficient-height ordering of all smooth integral degree-(2g+2) binary models whose actual Div¹ is soluble over every completion has limsup average #Sel₂(J¹)≤2. The same holds in positive-mass congruence families for which excluded p-adic coefficients, at every sufficiently large p, reduce into a fixed codimension-at-least-two coefficient subscheme. In particular it holds for the full locally C-soluble and locally Div¹-soluble families and admissible positive-mass families restricted to local Div¹. Existence of an average equal to two is not asserted. The full printed reduction-only Definition 39 extension requires the saturation repair recorded as a gap.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

### 4.61 Strict average bound for fixed small odd degree

For k>0 odd and k<g, the limsup average cardinality of the order-k two-Selmer set over the full coefficient-height family of locally soluble genus-g hyperelliptic models is strictly below two. The same conclusion applies to positive-mass sieve-controlled finite-prime congruence subfamilies that retain positive measure of the fully split real stratum. No conclusion is made for a family whose real restrictions delete that stratum.

<a id="st4-refinement-order-k-vanishing-average"></a>

### 4.62 Vanishing restricted Selmer averages as genus grows

For fixed k>0 odd, let A_(g,k) be the limsup coefficient-height average of the order-k two-Selmer set over either the full locally C-soluble or the full locally actual-Div¹-soluble genus-g model family. Then A_(g,k)→0 as g→∞. Height tends to infinity first, separately for each g. The statement is not a uniform joint estimate in height and genus and does not apply to arbitrary genus-dependent real subfamilies.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Average size of the degree-one two-Selmer set](#st4-refinement-hyperelliptic-average-two) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-hyperelliptic-average-two`); [Real Picard images of effective odd-degree divisors](#st4-refinement-real-effective-divisor-image) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-real-effective-divisor-image`); [Odd subsets of real components](#st4-refinement-odd-component-bound) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-odd-component-bound`); `ProbabilisticAndMetricNumberTheory:PM.1`; [Hyperelliptic equation models](#st0-hyperelliptic-model-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/hyperelliptic-model-family`); [Integral coefficient boxes](#st0-coefficient-box) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/coefficient-box`)

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Theorem 7 and (23) p.34. Theorem 7 gives the locally C-soluble version. The same real-image and upper-bound argument extends to the locally actual-Div¹-soluble family, whose denominator is at least the C-soluble denominator; the genus-uniform denominator and few-root proof remain the stated supplier obligations.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.order_k_vanishing_average`.

**Proof route.**

1. For a fixed component cutoff M, control the many-component real strata by sup_(m≥M) S_m(k)/2^(m−1).
2. Uniform independent coefficients on [−1,1] satisfy the fixed-few-root probability theorem; a finite sum over each bounded real-root count tends to zero. Handle zero-root/no-point strata and compare the locally soluble denominator with the full coefficient denominator, using a genus-uniform positive lower bound (e.g. the cited >75% local-solubility bound).
3. Take genus→∞, then M→∞. No log n/log log n endpoint estimate is needed.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Supply the genus-uniform local-solubility denominator comparison, not merely a different positive constant for each genus.

<a id="st4-refinement-small-odd-degree-points-disappear"></a>

### 4.63 Absence of bounded odd-degree points in large genus

For every fixed positive integer m, the lower density, among all smooth genus-g coefficient-height hyperelliptic models, of curves with no point over any odd-degree extension of degree≤m tends to one as g→∞. Height tends to infinity first. All extensions are included, not only Galois extensions or rational points.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Selmer sets with local effective-divisor restrictions](#st4-refinement-restricted-selmer-set) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-restricted-selmer-set`); [Vanishing restricted Selmer averages as genus grows](#st4-refinement-order-k-vanishing-average) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-order-k-vanishing-average`); [Hyperelliptic equation models](#st0-hyperelliptic-model-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/hyperelliptic-model-family`); [Source-specific density denominators](#st0-density-denominator-comparisons) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/density-denominator-comparisons`)

**Sources.** [S4/bgw](#source-s4-bgw), Corollary 8 p.3. For every fixed positive integer m, the lower density, among all smooth genus-g coefficient-height hyperelliptic models, of curves with no point over any odd-degree extension of degree≤m tends to one as g→∞. Height tends to infinity first. All extensions are included, not only Galois extensions or rational points.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.small_odd_degree_points_disappear`.

**Proof route.**

1. Choose the largest odd k≤m. Trace a point of any smaller odd degree to an effective rational divisor and add effective degree-two hyperelliptic fibres to reach k.
2. An odd-degree global divisor together with the degree-two divisor gives an actual degree-one divisor over each completion. Hence a curve outside the locally actual-Div¹-soluble family has no odd-degree point. Inside that family, the effective degree-k divisor gives a member of the restricted Selmer set; Markov’s inequality bounds the proportion with such a point by its average cardinal. Multiply by the family’s proportion, which is at most one. Use the ordered-limit Div¹ version and its uniform denominator bound; no local C-point implication is used.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Do not assume an odd-degree global point implies C(Q_v)≠∅. It gives actual Div¹(Q_v), which is the required family for the extended order-k argument.

### 4.64 Positive densities of both Selmer corank parities

For every degree n≥3, in the full coefficient-height family of smooth hyperelliptic equations y²=f(x) of degree n over Q, both even and odd 2∞-Selmer corank occur with lower density at least 2^(−4n−4). Assuming finiteness of the Jacobians’ 2-primary Sha groups, the same bound holds for Mordell–Weil rank parity. Without that assumption this remains a Selmer-corank statement.

**Proof route.**

1. The prescribed coefficient residue class modulo eight, inside H<X/2, has density 8^(−n−1)2^(−n−1)=2^(−4n−4) relative to H<X. Its four twists stay in H<X.
2. The blocks are disjoint: their x² coefficients have residues 1,7,2,6 modulo eight, so each block determines its original member. Select one member of each parity. Singular equations have density zero. Sha finiteness identifies corank with Mordell–Weil rank only in the conditional clause.

### 4.69 Degree-one torsor points are generically empty or infinite

For density one of locally actual-Div¹-soluble genus-g coefficient-height models, J¹(Q) is either empty or infinite. If it is nonempty, the nonzero W[2] lies in J(Q)/2J(Q), while J(Q)[2]=0; the finitely generated group J(Q) consequently has positive Mordell–Weil rank.

### 4.71 Rank-one criterion over Q from a p-Selmer line

Let E/Q have squarefree conductor with at least two odd prime factors, p≥5 a prime of good ordinary reduction, and irreducible E[p]. If Sel_p(E)≅F_p and its restriction to E(Q_p)/pE(Q_p) is not contained in the image of E(Q_p)[p], then both algebraic and analytic rank of E are one. ### 4.72 Rank-one criterion for an imaginary quadratic twist

### 4.73 The Bhargava–Skinner sieve family

RankOneFamily is the set of integral short pairs (A,B) with v₂(A)=3, v₂(B)=4, Δ₀=−4A³−27B²=256d, d positive odd squarefree, gcd(Δ₀,195)=1, Δ₀ a square modulo 39, 7|d, 864B a nonsquare in F_7, and #E_(A,B)(F_5) not congruent to one modulo five. **API.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_delta` (projection): A pair in F has Δ₀=256d with d>0, odd and squarefree.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_good_discriminant` (structure): A pair in F is nonsingular and gcd(Δ₀,195)=1.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_ordinary_test` (characterisation): Its actual finite-field point count satisfies #E(F_5) mod5≠1.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_twist_disjoint` (relation): For (A,B)∈F the raw −39 twist pair (39²A,(−39)³B) is not in F, since its discriminant is divisible by 39.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_twist_height` (compatibility): For every raw short pair H(39²A,(−39)³B)=39⁶H(A,B). The family-properties theorem supplies that the twist pair is already minimal-short, so this equals isomorphism-class height.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_example` (computation): (−136,16) belongs to F: d=39277=7·31·181, Δ₀ mod39=10=7² mod39, 864B mod7=6, and #E(F_5)=8.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_wrong_seven` (non-example): (−136,−16) fails the nonsplit-seven test: 864B mod7=1 is a square, although Δ₀ and the two-adic valuations are unchanged.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_wrong_sign` (non-example): (136,16) has negative d and is excluded.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_wrong_two` (non-example): (−16,16) violates v₂(A)=3 and is excluded.
- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.rankOne_wrong_ordinary` (non-example): The pair (−1000,1136) satisfies the other coefficient conditions but has #E(F₅)=6, so it is excluded by the ordinary test.

**Proof route.**

1. Replace the local reduction conditions by their discriminant/c₆ and finite-field trace tests; the gcd and squarefree conditions make the models smooth and the seven-valuation exactly one.
2. Take the subset of the existing short-pair carrier, not a new quotient of arbitrary Weierstrass equations.

### 4.74 Arithmetic and density properties of the sieve family

F has asymptotic count c_F X^(5/6)+o(X^(5/6)), c_F>0, in the minimal-short-pair height. Every E∈F is semistable of odd squarefree conductor d, with at least two odd factors; E[5] is irreducible and ramified at every factor of d. For D=−39, 2 and 5 split in Q(√D), seven is inert, and E,E^D have opposite root numbers. The twist short pair is minimal and H(E^D)=39⁶H(E); the original and twisted families are disjoint as isomorphism classes.

2. The local quotient modulo the torsion image has size p. A finite F_p-space of dimension≥2 has at least p−1 nonzero kernel elements; dimension≥3 has at least p²−1. Dimension-one trapped lines contribute p−1. Divide the total inequality by p−1.
3. Repeat for the twisted family. Opposite root numbers and p-Selmer parity interchange N_even,N_odd.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The source proof’s odd-rank≥3 case requires Sel_p not isomorphic to F_p, not merely nonzero. At p=5 the trapped-line leading bound is N/4.

### 4.78 At least half the sieve family satisfies a rank-one criterion

Let N_sat count E∈F_(H<X) satisfying the Q criterion and N_sat^D those satisfying the imaginary-twist criterion. These are disjoint subsets of the original F, because the first has odd finite five-Selmer dimension and the second has dimension zero. Then N_sat+N_sat^D≥(1−2/(p−1))N+o(X^(5/6)) with p=5, so their sum is at least N/2+o(X^(5/6)). This does not count every twist by its own height at this step.

### 4.80 Many generic rational three-Selmer elements

Among height-ordered elliptic curves, the number of pairs (E,s) with s a nonidentity Kummer image in Sel₃(E), H(E)<X, is at least cX^(5/6) for some c>0. Each rank-one E supplies at least two such classes of exact order three; their associated smooth plane cubics have a rational projective point and no rational flex. The positive proportion relative to all nonidentity Sel₃ elements also follows from average #Sel₃=4.

### 4.81 Integral ternary representatives of soluble descent classes

For integral ternary cubics use G=PGL₃ acting by (γ·f)(x)=det(γ)^(−1)f(xγ); scalar matrices act trivially. A(v),B(v) are normalized so the Jacobian is y²=x³+Ax+B and H_AB=max(|A|³,B²), homogeneous of degree twelve in v. Over Q, soluble rational G-orbits at fixed invariants correspond to E(Q)/3E(Q) and have stabilizer E(Q)[3]. Every everywhere locally soluble Sel₃ class at integral invariants admits an integral representative, and one can choose distinct G(Z)-orbits for distinct classes. Generic means nonsingular with no Q-flex. SL₃(Z)-orbits give the same integral action image; PGL₃(Q)-orbits must not be replaced by SL₃(Q)-orbits.

### 4.82 Globally soluble forms in a homogeneous fundamental region

For the integral ternary-cubic representation and H_AB invariant height, take a finite-volume real fundamental region F₁ with compatible orbit and stabilizer multiplicities. Require a fixed finite bound M≥1 on the multiplicity of each coefficient vector, with M=1 for a set of representatives; boundary choices must satisfy the same convention. Its dilate F_t=tF₁ corresponds to H_AB<t^12. Weighted generic integral points satisfy N_gen(F_t)=c₁t^10+o(t^10), c₁>0, and weighted generic points with a rational projective zero have count at least c₃t^10+o(t^10), c₃>0. The total, soluble and bounded-intersection counts use this one convention. Passing from a multiset count to distinct coefficient vectors divides a lower bound by at most M.

### 4.83 Positive proportion of rationally soluble integral plane cubics

Let c run over all integral ten-tuples, the coefficients of x³,x²y,x²z,xy²,xyz,xz²,y³,y²z,yz²,z³. For the cube |c_i|≤T, let N_sol(T) count tuples whose homogeneous cubic has a nonzero rational zero. Then liminf_(T→∞) N_sol(T)/(2⌊T⌋+1)^10>0. Restricting the numerator and denominator to smooth plane cubics preserves this conclusion because the discriminant-zero coefficient locus has density zero. The denominator counts equation models without GL₃, scalar or isomorphism quotients.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions, family conventions and local hypotheses stated above are part of this target.

**Dependencies.** [Globally soluble forms in a homogeneous fundamental region](#st4-refinement-soluble-ternary-fundamental-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/refinement-soluble-ternary-fundamental-count`); [Integral coefficient boxes](#st0-coefficient-box) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/coefficient-box`); `GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4/davenport-semialgebraic-count`; `mathlib:Set.ncard`; `mathlib:Filter.limsup`

Then liminf_(T→∞) N_sol(T)/(2⌊T⌋+1)^10>0. Restricting the numerator and denominator to smooth plane cubics preserves this conclusion because the discriminant-zero coefficient locus has density zero. **Proof route.**

1. Choose r so the bounded intersection F₁∩r[−1,1]^10 captures all but less than c₃/2 of the generic total weighted mass. Use the total asymptotic minus the bounded-intersection lattice asymptotic to control the omitted cusp count. Volume smallness alone is insufficient.
2. At least (c₃/2)t^10 weighted soluble generic points remain in rt[−1,1]^10. The fixed multiplicity bound M gives at least (c₃/(2M))t^10 distinct integral coefficient vectors. Put T=rt and divide by the actual ten-dimensional lattice-box count, giving lower bound c₃/(2M(2r)^10)>0.
3. Remove singular forms only using their codimension-one lattice estimate; the all-form and smooth denominators are asymptotic. The same bound holds along integer coefficient cutoffs by monotonicity and adjacent-cutoff comparison.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Check all local places and the exact height denominator; retain every displayed hypothesis.

**Open interface P/9: The p-adic change-of-variables formula for polynomial maps has no owner in the atlas.** Needed statement: let U ⊆ Z_p^n be compact open and ψ: U → Q_p^n a map given by polynomials with coefficients in Q_p whose Jacobian determinant does not vanish on U. Then ψ is a local homeomorphism onto an open set, and for every nonnegative measurable φ on Q_p^n, ∫_{Q_p^n} φ(y)·#(ψ^{-1}(y) ∩ U) dy = ∫_U φ(ψ(x))·|det Dψ(x)|_p dx (Haar measure); together with the multivariable Hensel lemma (p-adic inverse function theorem) it rests on (Igusa, An introduction to the theory of local zeta functions, §7.4; Serre, Lie algebras and Lie groups, Part II). Mathlib has only the one-variable hensels_lemma over ℤ_[p] and no Haar-measure theory specific to Q_p^n (no MeasurableSpace instance on ℤ_[p] at the pin). Searched all atlas stages for 'change of variables', 'Igusa', 'p-adic integration', 'Jacobian', 'inverse function', 'Hensel': LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory:LD.2 (definable integration, rationality of Igusa series) and TropicalAndBerkovichArithmetic:TB.7 mention p-adic integration but do not plan this formula. The source uses it implicitly in the proof of Proposition 3.12 (sourceIssue ArithmeticStatistics/E505). Recommendation: plan it once in a foundational p-adic analysis owner and import it here and in AnalyticNumberTheory:AN.8 (local zeta integrals).

Its positive constant for a fixed g is insufficient. The locally actual-Div¹ family has at least that denominator. Fixed-few-root probability is requested from PM.1 with exact coefficient hypotheses.

<a id="layer-5"></a>

## Layer 5: Higher moments and distribution laws

The first strand constructs finite-group probability laws and proves their mass and moment formulas. Arithmetic Cohen–Lenstra and Selmer identifications remain conjectural unless an arithmetic moment theorem is supplied. Poonen–Rains and BKLPR use quadratic or alternating models; finite quadratic-module and generic product-probability theory are imported. The locally compact refinement keeps a homeomorphic polar adjoint and finite-flat/fppf theta input, including the dyadic case.

The second strand derives higher Selmer and rank bounds from genuine finite-height averages. Local equidistribution is stronger than a global mean, and separate limsups cannot be summed as though they shared a common exceptional sequence. Wood's multivariate grid theorem uses its stated finite exponential moments and growth bound; the bounded-exponent result leaves a full-group tail obligation.

The remaining strands treat local hypersurface statistics, finite-field polarization and bundle comparisons, and function-field Hurwitz moments. The last uses exact discriminant slices, specified infinity types, marked surjections and rational-component profiles. A liminf lower bound for bad types does not prove an ordinary limit without eventual component-profile constancy.

**Worked checks.** Two selected prime factors in the joint Selmer model share one parity, giving weight `2w₁(d₁)w₂(d₂)` on equal parities and zero on mixed ones; the empty selection has mass one. The polar diagonal equals `2q(x)` without dividing by 2. The rank-zero and low-rank rational bounds retain `16503/80000` and `100501/120000`, respectively. An endomorphism rank bound requires the explicit positive index-growth hypothesis; it is not true for an arbitrary endomorphism order. Wood's lexicographic induction is on a fixed finite power of N, where it is well-founded.

<a id="st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family"></a>

### 5.1 Higher height moments in an arithmetic family

Let F be an arithmetic family ordered by a height (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/arithmetic-family): a set F with h : F → ℝ such that F(X) := {x ∈ F : h(x) < X} is finite for every X, and N_F(X) := #F(X) → ∞. For f : F → [0, ∞] and an integer m ≥ 1 put S_m(f; X) := Σ_{x ∈ F(X)} f(x)^m. The upper and lower m-th height moments of f are M⁺_m(f) := limsup_{X→∞} S_m(f;X)/N_F(X) and M⁻_m(f) := liminf_{X→∞} S_m(f;X)/N_F(X), both in [0, ∞]; the m-th moment exists when they agree. For m = 1 these give extended nonnegative upper and lower averages. For real-valued f ≥ 0 with eventually bounded averages, the upper moment is ENNReal.ofReal of the real upper average of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-over-a-height-ordered-family; when the averages converge, both moments equal that average. Without boundedness the extended upper moment can be ∞ while real limsup takes a junk value. For an indicator 1_A they are the upper and lower relative densities of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/relative-density; ST.5 writes μ^±(A) for those densities and does not redefine them. The family, its height and its counting function are imported unchanged from ST.0; this node adds the higher moments and the [0, ∞]-valued upper and lower versions. Limits are taken over real X → ∞; no weighting other than the one fixed by ST.0 (counting each member once) is used.

**Hypotheses.** F(X) finite for every real X and N_F(X) → ∞; f takes values in [0, ∞]; m ≥ 1; The suggested existing compatibility theorem takes limsup after ENNReal.ofReal; it does not move ENNReal.ofReal outside a real limsup. The additional real-limsup comparison carries an eventual upper-bound hypothesis.

**Dependencies.** [Arithmetic families: objects up to equivalence, ordered by a Northcott height, with weighted and unweighted counting functions](#st0-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/arithmetic-family`); [Upper, lower and limiting relative densities of a subfamily in a height-ordered family](#st0-relative-density) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/relative-density`); [Averages of arithmetic functions over a height-ordered family](#st4-average-over-a-height-ordered-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-over-a-height-ordered-family`); `mathlib:Filter.limsup`

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), §1.2, Conjecture 1.1(a), parenthetical definition, p. 2. Probabilities (densities) are limits over the finitely many curves of bounded height; this node pins the limsup/liminf form of that convention. [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §5.5, Remark 5.12, p. 20. Moments are limsup averages; a density-zero subset can carry positive mass unless a higher moment is bounded.

**API.**

- `familyUpperMoment` (constructor): M⁺_m(f) := limsup_{X→∞} (Σ_{x∈F(X)} f(x)^m)/#F(X) in [0,∞].
- `familyLowerMoment` (data): M⁻_m(f) := liminf_{X→∞} (Σ_{x∈F(X)} f(x)^m)/#F(X) in [0,∞].
- `familyUpperDensity` (compatibility): familyUpperMoment of the indicator of A with m = 1 equals ST.0's upper relative density d̄(A | F) (the Lean prototype declares it locally until ST.0's declaration is imported).
- `familyLowerDensity` (compatibility): familyLowerMoment of the indicator of A with m = 1 equals ST.0's lower relative density d̲(A | F).
- `familyUpperMoment_one_eq_upperFamilyAverage` (compatibility): For real f ≥ 0, the extended upper moment equals limsup in ENNReal of ENNReal.ofReal of the finite-cutoff averages. Identifying this with ENNReal.ofReal of ST.4 real limsup additionally requires eventual boundedness above of those averages.
- `familyLowerMoment_le_familyUpperMoment` (relation): M⁻_m(f) ≤ M⁺_m(f) once #F(X) → ∞.
- `familyUpperMoment_mono` (relation): f ≤ g pointwise implies M⁺_m(f) ≤ M⁺_m(g) and M⁻_m(f) ≤ M⁻_m(g).
- `familyUpperMoment_add_le` (relation): M⁺_1(f + g) ≤ M⁺_1(f) + M⁺_1(g) (subadditivity of limsup).
- `familyLowerDensity_compl` (characterisation): μ⁻(F \ A) = 1 − μ⁺(A).
- `familyUpperDensity_le_upperMoment_div` (other): Markov: for t > 0, μ⁺({x : t ≤ f(x)}) ≤ M⁺_1(f)/t.
- `familyUpperMoment_const` (simp): For the constant function c, M⁺_m(c) = M⁻_m(c) = c^m.
- `familyUpperMoment_one_eq_ofReal_limsup` (compatibility): For real f ≥ 0 with eventually bounded finite-cutoff averages, the extended upper first moment equals ENNReal.ofReal of the real limsup. The eventual boundedness premise is essential.

**Checks.**

- `familyUpperDensity.test_even_integers` (computation): For F = positive integers ordered by h(n) = n and A = even integers, familyUpperDensity A = familyLowerDensity A = 1/2.
- `familyUpperDensity.test_finite_set` (degenerate): If #F(X) → ∞ and A is finite then familyUpperDensity A = 0.
- `familyUpperMoment.test_not_additive` (non-example): There is A ⊆ ℤ_{≥1} (the integers n with ⌊log₂ n⌋ even) with familyUpperDensity A + familyUpperDensity (F \ A) > 1, so upper density is not additive and cannot be replaced by a limit without proof.
- `familyUpperMoment.test_indicator_square` (characterisation): For an indicator function, familyUpperMoment (1_A) m = familyUpperDensity A for every m ≥ 1.

**Proof route.**

1. Define S_m(f;X) as a finite sum over F(X) (finiteness from ST.0/arithmetic-family) and the ratio S_m(f;X)/N_F(X) in [0, ∞] for X large enough that F(X) is nonempty.
2. Define M⁺_m, M⁻_m as limsup and liminf along X → ∞ in [0, ∞] (Filter.limsup / Filter.liminf on ENNReal, which always exist), and the densities as the first moments of indicator functions.
3. Relative density: the ratio of the two counting functions of B and A, defined when #(A ∩ F(X)) → ∞.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For F = ℤ_{≥1} with height h(n) = n and A the even integers, μ⁺(A) = μ⁻(A) = 1/2.
- M⁻_m(f) ≤ M⁺_m(f) always; equality for f constant.
- Markov inequality: μ⁺({f ≥ t}) ≤ M⁺_1(f)/t for every t > 0, the step used to pass from average Selmer sizes to proportions of Selmer ranks.

**Consumers.** Bhargava–Shankar, 3-Selmer Theorem 1; 4-Selmer Theorem 1; 5-Selmer Theorem 1 — the averages of #Sel_n over curves ordered by height are first moments M_1; Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan, Theorem 1.1 — the second moment M⁺_2(#Sel_2) ≤ 15; Poonen–Rains, Conjecture 1.1(c) — the m-th moments of #Sel_p are predicted to be ∏(p^i + 1); BKLOS §9.2; Burungale–Tian Theorems 3.3, 3.5 — lower densities of twists with Selmer corank zero

<a id="st5-gaussian-binomial-coefficient"></a>

### 5.2 The Gaussian binomial coefficient and the count of subspaces of 𝔽_q^n

For an element t of a field (or t = q a prime power) and integers 0 ≤ k ≤ n, the Gaussian binomial coefficient is [n k]_t := ∏_{i=1}^{k} (1 − t^{n−k+i})/(1 − t^{i}) when t is not a root of unity of order ≤ n, extended as the polynomial in ℤ[t] defined by the recursion [n 0]_t = [n n]_t = 1, [n+1 k]_t = [n k−1]_t + t^{k}[n k]_t, and [n k]_t := 0 for k > n. For a finite field 𝔽_q, [n k]_q equals the number of k-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽_q^n.

**Hypotheses.** 0 ≤ k; for the subspace count: q = #𝔽_q a prime power

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:card_linearIndependent`; `mathlib:Matrix.card_GL_field`; `mathlib:Polynomial.coeff`

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proof of Proposition 2.6(e), p. 7. The closed formula for a_{d,n} is derived from Cauchy's q-binomial theorem, whose coefficients are Gaussian binomials. [P/smith-selmer2-2022](#source-p-smith-selmer2-2022), §2, Case 2.12, p. 9 (arXiv v2). Kernel-dimension laws of random matrices over 𝔽_ℓ are products of Gaussian-binomial type factors.

**API.**

- `gaussBinom` (constructor): [n k]_t as an element of a field, via the recursion (0 for k > n).
- `gaussBinom_zero_right` (simp): [n 0]_t = 1.
- `gaussBinom_self` (simp): [n n]_t = 1.
- `gaussBinom_succ_succ` (simp): [n+1 k+1]_t = [n k]_t + t^{k+1}[n k+1]_t.
- `gaussBinom_eq_prod` (characterisation): When no t^i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) equals 1: [n k]_t = ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − t^{n−k+i})/(1 − t^i).
- `gaussBinom_symm` (relation): [n k]_t = [n n−k]_t for k ≤ n.
- `gaussBinom_one` (compatibility): [n k]_1 = Nat.choose n k.
- `card_submodules_finrank_eq_gaussBinom` (equivalence): For a finite field K with q elements, #{W ≤ K^n : dim W = k} = [n k]_q.

**Checks.**

- `gaussBinom.test_four_two` (computation): gaussBinom 2 4 2 = 35.
- `gaussBinom.test_zero_rows` (degenerate): gaussBinom t n 0 = 1 and gaussBinom t 0 k = 0 for k ≥ 1.
- `gaussBinom.test_classical` (compatibility): gaussBinom 1 5 2 = 10 = Nat.choose 5 2.
- `gaussBinom.test_not_binomial` (non-example): gaussBinom 2 3 1 = 7 ≠ 3 = Nat.choose 3 1: the q-analogue is not the ordinary binomial.

**Proof route.**

1. Define [n k]_t by the recursion in ℤ[t] (a polynomial), and evaluate at t.
2. Product formula: induct on n; the recursion [n+1 k]_t = [n k−1]_t + t^k[n k]_t is the identity (1 − t^{n+1})/(1 − t^{k}) · P = P' + t^k P'' between the products, checked by clearing denominators (routine algebra in the fraction field).
3. Subspace count: the k-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽_q^n are the orbits of GL_k(𝔽_q) acting freely on linearly independent k-tuples; divide mathlib:card_linearIndependent (#independent k-tuples = ∏_{i<k}(q^n − q^i)) by mathlib:Matrix.card_GL_field (#GL_k(𝔽_q) = ∏_{i<k}(q^k − q^i)) and compare with the product formula.

**Acceptance checks.**

- [n k]_1 = binomial(n, k) (specialisation t = 1 of the polynomial).
- [4 2]_2 = 35 = number of 2-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽_2^4.
- [n k]_t = [n n−k]_t.

**Consumers.** Poonen–Rains, Proposition 2.6(e) — closed formula for the intersection law a_{d,n}; Smith II, §2 (Cases 2.12–2.13) — kernel laws P(j | n) of random matrices over 𝔽_ℓ; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-matrix-kernel-law — number of j-dimensional kernels of alternating matrices; Koymans–Pagano §7.3 (MacWilliams' count) — counts of symmetric matrices over 𝔽_2 by rank

<a id="st5-cauchy-q-binomial-theorem"></a>

### 5.3 Cauchy's q-binomial theorem

For an element t of a commutative ring and n ≥ 0, in the polynomial ring in z: ∏_{i=0}^{n−1} (1 + t^{i} z) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} t^{k(k−1)/2} [n k]_t z^{k}.

**Hypotheses.** n ≥ 0; t arbitrary

**Dependencies.** [The Gaussian binomial coefficient and the count of subspaces of 𝔽_q^n](#st5-gaussian-binomial-coefficient) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient`); `mathlib:Polynomial.coeff`

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proof of Proposition 2.6(e), p. 7. PR derive (e) from Cauchy's q-binomial theorem (formula (18) of Cauchy 1843) with t = 1/p.

**Proof route.**

1. Induct on n: multiply the identity for n by (1 + t^{n} z) and compare coefficients of z^{k} using the recursion [n+1 k]_t = t^{k}[n k]_t + [n k−1]_t (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient, API gaussBinom_succ_succ and gaussBinom_symm).
2. Coefficient comparison is routine algebra in ℤ[t][z] (mathlib:Polynomial.coeff).

**Acceptance checks.**

- n = 1: 1 + z = 1 + z.
- n = 2: (1 + z)(1 + tz) = 1 + (1 + t)z + t z².

<a id="st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>

### 5.4 Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions

The carrier L of isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups is the type of pairs (n, λ) with n ∈ ℕ and λ a partition of n (Mathlib Nat.Partition n). For a prime p the class (n, λ) is realised by the standard representative A_λ = ⊕_i ℤ/p^{λ_i} (parts in decreasing order), a group of order p^n. Attached data: the conjugate partition λ'_i = #{j : λ_j ≥ i} (so λ'_1 is the p-rank and p^{λ'_1} = |A_λ[p]|), the multiplicity m_i(λ) = #{j : λ_j = i}, the automorphism count |Aut A_λ|, and the trivial class (0, ∅). Every finite abelian p-group is isomorphic to A_λ for exactly one λ.

**Hypotheses.** p prime (for the realisation and the classification)

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Nat.Partition`; `mathlib:AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite`; `mathlib:ZMod.card`; `mathlib:Multiset.sort`

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771. The carrier L of EVW §8.1, realised by partitions. [P/majumder-weighted-2014](#source-p-majumder-weighted-2014), arXiv 1407.3066v1, §2, p. 3–4. The partition parametrisation and the order |G_λ| = p^{|λ|}.

**API.**

- `FinAbPGroupClass.toGroup` (constructor): The standard representative ⊕_i ℤ/p^{λ_i} of a class, an additive commutative group.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.card_toGroup` (characterisation): For p prime, |toGroup p (n, λ)| = p^n.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.exists_addEquiv_toGroup` (equivalence): Every finite abelian group G in which every element is killed by a power of p is isomorphic to toGroup p A for some class A (compatibility with Mathlib's structure theorem AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite).
- `FinAbPGroupClass.eq_of_addEquiv` (extensionality): If toGroup p A ≅ toGroup p B then A = B.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.conjPart` (projection): The conjugate partition λ'_i = #{j : λ_j ≥ i}.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.partMult` (projection): The multiplicity m_i(λ) of the part i.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.card_torsion_eq_pow_conjPart` (characterisation): |{x ∈ A_λ : p x = 0}| = p^{λ'_1} (the p-rank).
- `FinAbPGroupClass.autCard` (data): |Aut(A_λ)|, the number of additive automorphisms of the representative.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.autCard_pos` (other): |Aut A_λ| > 0.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.trivial` (constructor): The trivial class (0, ∅).
- `FinAbPGroupClass.subsingleton_toGroup_trivial` (simp): The representative of the trivial class is the zero group.

**Checks.**

- `FinAbPGroupClass.test_autCard_cyclic` (computation): |Aut(ℤ/p)| = p − 1 for the class (1, (1)).
- `FinAbPGroupClass.test_autCard_trivial` (degenerate): The trivial class has exactly one automorphism.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.test_card_elementary` (compatibility): Nat.card of the representative of (2, (1,1)) is p².
- `FinAbPGroupClass.test_cyclic_ne_elementary` (non-example): The representatives of (2, (2)) and (2, (1,1)) are not isomorphic although they have the same order, so a carrier indexed by the order alone is wrong.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the carrier as the dependent pair type Σ n, Nat.Partition n; sort the parts decreasingly and take the product of ZMod (p^{λ_i}) as representative, with its AddCommGroup structure from the Pi instance.
2. Order: |A_λ| = ∏ p^{λ_i} = p^{Σλ_i} = p^n (ZMod.card and Fintype.card of a Pi type).
3. Existence of a class for a finite abelian p-group G: apply AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite to get G ≅ ⊕ ℤ/q_i^{e_i}; since G is p-primary every q_i = p (or e_i = 0), so the exponents form a partition of log_p|G|.
4. Uniqueness: the conjugate partition is recovered from the invariants |p^{i-1}G/p^iG| = p^{λ'_i}, which are isomorphism invariants, and a partition is determined by its conjugate.
5. The p-torsion count |A_λ[p]| = p^{λ'_1}: each cyclic factor ℤ/p^{λ_j} with λ_j ≥ 1 contributes a factor p.

**Acceptance checks.**

- |A_{(1)}| = p, |Aut A_{(1)}| = p − 1; the trivial class has one automorphism.
- ℤ/p² and (ℤ/p)² both have order p² and are different classes (conjugate partitions (1,1) and (2)).

**Consumers.** EVW §8.1–8.4; Wood 2019 Lemma 3.2 — the probability space on which the Cohen–Lenstra measure and the surjection moments are defined; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-measure — the measure is a function on this carrier; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5 function-field part (EVW Theorem 1.2) and Lipnowski–Tsimerman §5.7 — class-group and point-group laws are measures on this carrier

<a id="st5-automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>

### 5.5 The order of the automorphism group of a finite abelian p-group

For p prime and a partition λ with conjugate partition λ' and part multiplicities m_i, |Aut(A_λ)| = p^{Σ_i (λ'_i)²} · ∏_i ∏_{s=1}^{m_i} (1 − p^{−s}). Equivalently (Hillar–Rhea, Theorem 4.1), for A = ⊕_{k=1}^{n} ℤ/p^{e_k} with e_1 ≤ … ≤ e_n, d_k = max{l : e_l = e_k}, c_k = min{l : e_l = e_k}: |Aut A| = ∏_k (p^{d_k} − p^{k−1}) ∏_j (p^{e_j})^{n−d_j} ∏_i (p^{e_i−1})^{n−c_i+1}.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; λ a partition

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); `mathlib:Matrix.card_GL_field`

**Sources.** [P/hillar-automorphisms-2007](#source-p-hillar-automorphisms-2007), Amer. Math. Monthly 114 (2007); arXiv math/0605185v1, Theorem 4.1, PDF/printed p. 6 (matrix description and invertibility criterion pp. 3–5). The general automorphism count (displayed formula follows the excerpt). [P/majumder-weighted-2014](#source-p-majumder-weighted-2014), arXiv 1407.3066v1, Lemma 3 and p. 4. The conjugate-partition form p^{Σ(λ'_i)²} ∏_i ∏_{s=1}^{λ'_i−λ'_{i+1}} (1 − p^{−s}).

**Proof route.**

1. Describe End(A) as the ring of n×n matrices (a_{ij}) with a_{ij} ∈ ℤ/p^{e_i} and p^{e_i−e_j} | a_{ij} when e_i > e_j (Hillar–Rhea Theorem 3.3).
2. An endomorphism is an automorphism iff its reduction modulo p is invertible on each block of equal exponents (Hillar–Rhea Theorem 3.6): count the block-triangular matrices over F_p with invertible diagonal blocks and multiply by the number of lifts of each entry.
3. Collect the powers of p into p^{Σ(λ'_i)²} using Σ_{i,j} min(λ_i, λ_j) = Σ_i (λ'_i)² and the diagonal-block orders |GL_{m_i}(F_p)| = p^{m_i²} ∏_{s=1}^{m_i}(1 − p^{−s}) (Mathlib Matrix.card_GL_field).

**Acceptance checks.**

- |Aut(ℤ/p^k)| = p^k − p^{k−1}; |Aut((ℤ/p)^m)| = |GL_m(F_p)|.
- |Aut(ℤ/p² × ℤ/p)| = p³(p − 1)²; for p = 3: 108 = |Aut(ℤ/9 × ℤ/3)|, the value used in EVW item 125.

<a id="st5-surjection-count"></a>

### 5.6 The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups

For additive abelian groups X and A, Sur(X, A) is the set of surjective group homomorphisms X → A and |Sur(X, A)| its cardinality (Nat.card; it is finite when X is finitely generated and A finite).

**Hypotheses.** X, A abelian groups

**Dependencies.** Only the coefficient and elementary algebra conventions fixed above.

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771. Definition of Sur used in the moments. [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, §1, p. 3. The surjection count whose expectation is the moment.

**API.**

- `surjCard` (constructor): |Sur(X, A)| as a natural number.
- `surjCard_congr` (functoriality): Isomorphisms X ≅ X', A ≅ A' give |Sur(X, A)| = |Sur(X', A')|.
- `surjCard_toGroup_self` (characterisation): |Sur(A_λ, A_λ)| = |Aut(A_λ)|.
- `surjCard_le_card_hom` (relation): |Sur(X, A)| ≤ |Hom(X, A)| for finite X, A.
- `surjCard_punit` (simp): |Sur(X, 0)| = 1.
- `surjCard_eq_zero_of_card_lt` (relation): If |X| < |A| (finite) then |Sur(X, A)| = 0.

**Checks.**

- `surjCard.test_cyclic_square_to_prime` (computation): |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p)| = p − 1.
- `surjCard.test_elementary_to_prime` (computation): |Sur(ℤ/p × ℤ/p, ℤ/p)| = p² − 1.
- `surjCard.test_to_trivial` (degenerate): |Sur(ℤ/5, 0)| = 1.
- `surjCard.test_prime_to_cyclic_square` (non-example): |Sur(ℤ/p, ℤ/p²)| = 0 although |Hom(ℤ/p, ℤ/p²)| = p: a definition counting homomorphisms fails.

**Proof route.**

1. Define |Sur(X, A)| as Nat.card of the subtype {f : X →+ A // f surjective}.
2. Invariance: composing with isomorphisms X ≅ X', A ≅ A' is a bijection on surjections.
3. For finite X, A: a surjection from a group of smaller order does not exist; surjective endomorphisms of a finite group are automorphisms.

**Acceptance checks.**

- |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p)| = p − 1 and |Sur((ℤ/p)², ℤ/p)| = p² − 1.
- |Sur(X, 0)| = 1 for every X.

**Consumers.** EVW Lemma 8.2 and Proposition 8.3 — the moment of a measure is the expectation of |Sur(−, A)|; Wood 2019 Theorem 2.9 and Lemma 3.2 — the moments of cokernels of random matrices and of the Cohen–Lenstra measure; LOWW Proposition 7.1 — Cohen–Lenstra–Martinet predictions are stated for equivariant surjection counts

<a id="st5-exact-surjection-count-formula"></a>

### 5.7 Exact count of surjections between finite abelian p-groups

Let p be prime, X = A_ξ and A = A_α finite abelian p-groups with conjugate partitions x_i = ξ'_i and a_i = α'_i. If x_i < a_i for some i then |Sur(X, A)| = 0. Otherwise |Sur(X, A)| = ∏_{i ≥ 1} p^{x_i a_{i+1}} ∏_{j = a_{i+1}}^{a_i − 1} (p^{x_i} − p^j).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; X, A finite abelian p-groups

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`)

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.4, p. 772 (formula supplied by the extraction PAPER-ELLENBERG-VENKATESH-WESTERLAND-16, item 77, to repair E6). The claim whose repaired proof uses the exact surjection count.

**Proof route.**

1. Use the coordinate perfect pairings A_λ × A_λ → Q/Z, with each Z/p^e factor paired by xy/p^e mod Z. Dualizing a homomorphism gives a bijection Sur(X,A) ≃ Inj(A,X); these pairings explicitly identify each finite group with its character dual.
2. Let V_i = p^{i−1}X[p^i] ⊆ X[p]. These form a decreasing flag of F_p-spaces of dimensions x_i. Write A as a direct sum with m_i=a_i−a_{i+1} cyclic generators of order p^i, and choose their images from the largest i downwards. An additive map A→X is injective iff it is injective on A[p]: every nonzero subgroup of a finite p-group meets A[p].
3. The order-p images already chosen from longer cyclic factors span a_{i+1} independent vectors in V_i. Choosing the m_i new order-p images therefore gives ∏_{j=a_{i+1}}^{a_i−1}(p^{x_i}−p^j). If x_i<a_i for some i, this cannot be done.
4. Each chosen order-p vector in V_i lifts to X[p^i] under p^{i−1} in exactly |X[p^{i−1}]| = p^{Σ_{k<i}x_k} ways. For all m_i generators the total lift exponent is Σ_i m_i Σ_{k<i}x_k = Σ_k x_k a_{k+1}. Multiplying gives the stated formula.

**Acceptance checks.**

- |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p)| = p − 1, |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p²)| = p(p − 1) = |Aut(ℤ/p²)|, |Sur(ℤ/p × ℤ/p², ℤ/p²)| = p²(p − 1).
- Exhaustive check for p = 2 and all pairs with |X| ≤ 16: the formula agrees with direct enumeration of homomorphisms (carried out in this blueprint's preparation).

**Interface qualification.** Formula stated by the extraction PAPER-ELLENBERG-VENKATESH-WESTERLAND-16 (item 77) and re-checked here by enumeration; not printed in EVW.

<a id="st5-partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part"></a>

### 5.8 Partitions with parts at least u+1 versus partitions by largest part

For u, m ≥ 0 let a_m be the number of partitions of m with every part ≥ u + 1 and b_{i,j} the number of partitions of i with largest part exactly j. Then a_m = Σ_{i + uj = m} b_{i,j}; equivalently, as formal power series, ∏_{j ≥ u+1} (1 − q^j)^{−1} = Σ_{n ≥ 0} f_n(q) q^{nu} with f_n(q) = Σ_N b_{N,n} q^N.

**Hypotheses.** u ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Nat.Partition.hasProd_powerSeriesMk_card_restricted`; `mathlib:Nat.Partition.restricted`

**Sources.** [P/majumder-weighted-2014](#source-p-majumder-weighted-2014), arXiv 1407.3066v1, Lemmas 1–2, p. 2. The bijection of Lemma 1; Lemma 2 is its generating-function form.

**Proof route.**

1. Adding u copies of the row of length j to the Young diagram of a partition of i with largest part j gives a partition of i + uj whose largest part occurs at least u + 1 times, and this is a bijection.
2. Conjugation exchanges 'largest part occurs at least u + 1 times' with 'every part is at least u + 1'.
3. The generating function of partitions with all parts ≥ u + 1 is ∏_{j≥u+1}(1 − q^j)^{−1} (Mathlib Nat.Partition.hasProd_powerSeriesMk_card_restricted with the predicate u + 1 ≤ ·); regroup the right side by n.

**Acceptance checks.**

- u = 0: a_m = p(m) = Σ_j b_{m,j}.
- m = 2, u = 1: a_2 = 1 (the partition (2)) and b_{2,0} + b_{1,1} = 0 + 1 = 1.

<a id="st5-hall-partition-identity"></a>

### 5.9 Hall's partition identity

For every n ≥ 0 and a prime p, with q = p^{−1}: f_n(q) := Σ_{N≥0} b_{N,n} q^N = Σ_{λ ⊢ n} 1/|Aut A_λ|, where b_{N,n} counts partitions of N with largest part exactly n. Equivalently f_n(q) = Σ_{μ ⊢ n} q^{Σ μ_i²} ∏_i ψ_{μ_i, μ_{i−1} − μ_i}(q) with ψ_{a,b}(q) = ∏_{i=1}^{a+b}(1 − q^i)/(∏_{i=1}^{a}(1 − q^i) ∏_{i=1}^{b}(1 − q^i)), ψ_{a,∞}(q) = 1/∏_{i=1}^{a}(1 − q^i) and μ_0 = ∞.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; n ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** [The order of the automorphism group of a finite abelian p-group](#st5-automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); `mathlib:Nat.Partition`; [The Gaussian binomial coefficient and the count of subspaces of 𝔽_q^n](#st5-gaussian-binomial-coefficient) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient`)

**Sources.** [P/majumder-weighted-2014](#source-p-majumder-weighted-2014), arXiv 1407.3066v1, pp. 5–6 (following Hall 1938). Hall's bijection proving the identity.

**Proof route.**

1. Given a partition ν of N with largest part n, take the Young diagram D of ν' (height n) and cut out the Durfee-type squares μ_1 × μ_1, μ_2 × μ_2, … stacked vertically down the left edge (μ_1 largest with (μ_1, μ_1) ∈ D, μ_i largest with (μ_1+…+μ_i, μ_i) ∈ D); then |μ| = n.
2. The cells to the right of the i-th square form a partition of height ≤ μ_i and width ≤ μ_{i−1} − μ_i, counted by ψ_{μ_i, μ_{i−1}−μ_i}(q); the construction is reversible. The rows of the i-th strip are μ₁+⋯+μ_{i−1} < x ≤ μ₁+⋯+μ_i; the source incorrectly prints a strict upper inequality. The rectangle generating function ψ is the Gaussian binomial, obtained by splitting partitions at the last row/column and applying its recursion.
3. Substitute the automorphism count (ST.5/automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups): 1/|Aut A_λ| = q^{Σ(λ'_i)²}∏_i 1/(q)_{λ'_i−λ'_{i+1}}, and the product ∏_i ψ_{μ_i, μ_{i−1}−μ_i}(q) telescopes to ∏_i 1/(q)_{μ_i−μ_{i+1}}; with μ = λ' the right side is Σ_{λ⊢n} 1/|Aut A_λ|.

**Acceptance checks.**

- n = 1: Σ_N b_{N,1} q^N = q/(1 − q) = 1/(p − 1) = 1/|Aut ℤ/p|.
- n = 0: both sides are 1.

<a id="st5-weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum"></a>

### 5.10 The weighted sum of inverse automorphism counts

For a prime p and u ≥ 0: Σ_{A ∈ L} 1/(|A|^u |Aut A|) = ∏_{j ≥ u+1} (1 − p^{−j})^{−1}, the sum converging in ℝ.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; u ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** [Hall's partition identity](#st5-hall-partition-identity) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/hall-partition-identity`); [Partitions with parts at least u+1 versus partitions by largest part](#st5-partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part`); [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`)

**Sources.** [P/majumder-weighted-2014](#source-p-majumder-weighted-2014), arXiv 1407.3066v1, Theorem, p. 1. The statement proved (the published form of Cohen–Lenstra, Cor. 3.7(i)). [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, proof of Lemma 3.2, p. 10. The same identity as used for the Cohen–Lenstra measure.

**Proof route.**

1. Group the sum by n = log_p|A|: Σ_A |A|^{−u}|Aut A|^{−1} = Σ_n q^{nu} Σ_{λ⊢n} |Aut A_λ|^{−1} with q = 1/p.
2. By Hall's identity Σ_{λ⊢n}|Aut A_λ|^{−1} = f_n(q) (ST.5/hall-partition-identity).
3. By ST.5/partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part, Σ_n f_n(q) q^{nu} = ∏_{j≥u+1}(1 − q^j)^{−1}; the power series converge absolutely at q = 1/p < 1, so the formal identity specialises (nonnegative coefficients, monotone convergence). To justify analytic evaluation independently of the formal-series topology, expand finite products as nonnegative series and apply monotone convergence as the allowed part sizes grow. Their values are bounded by the positive convergent inverse Euler product, since Σ_j q^j < ∞. Thus the full series is finite; evaluation at q is not asserted to be continuous for the formal-series topology.

**Acceptance checks.**

- u = 0: Σ_A 1/|Aut A| = ∏_{j≥1}(1 − p^{−j})^{−1} (Hall's 'strange formula').
- p = 2, u = 0: the truncation to |A| ≤ 2 gives 1 + 1 = 2 ≤ ∏(1 − 2^{−j})^{−1} ≈ 3.46.

<a id="st5-cohen-lenstra-mass-formula"></a>

### 5.11 The Cohen–Lenstra mass formula

For a prime p and u ≥ 0, Σ_{A ∈ L} c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|) = 1, i.e. the Cohen–Lenstra weights have total mass one.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; u ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** [The weighted sum of inverse automorphism counts](#st5-weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum`); [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, Lemma 3.2, p. 9. Mass one of μ_{p,u}. [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771. Mass one for u = 0.

**Proof route.**

1. Multiply ST.5/weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum by c_{p,u} = ∏_{j≥u+1}(1 − p^{−j}); the product is multipliable and nonzero, so c_{p,u}·c_{p,u}^{−1} = 1.
2. Transport the real series to ℝ≥0∞ (ENNReal.ofReal of nonnegative terms) to get the HasSum statement used by the PMF.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For u = 0, p = 3: the masses of 0, ℤ/3, ℤ/9, (ℤ/3)² are ≈ 0.5601, 0.2801, 0.0934, 0.0117.
- The statement fails for the weights 1/|A|^u alone (they do not sum to a finite value for u = 0).

<a id="st5-cohen-lenstra-measure"></a>

### 5.12 The Cohen–Lenstra measure μ_{p,u}

For a prime p and an integer u ≥ 0 put c_{p,u} = ∏_{i ≥ u+1} (1 − p^{−i}). The Cohen–Lenstra measure μ_{p,u} is the probability measure on the isomorphism classes L of finite abelian p-groups with μ_{p,u}(A) = c_{p,u} / (|A|^u · |Aut A|). The case u = 0 is the Cohen–Lenstra distribution of EVW §8.1 (imaginary quadratic fields); u = 1 is the real-quadratic distribution. Total mass one is the mass formula (ST.5/cohen-lenstra-mass-formula), which the construction takes as input.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; u ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [The order of the automorphism group of a finite abelian p-group](#st5-automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [The Cohen–Lenstra mass formula](#st5-cohen-lenstra-mass-formula) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-mass-formula`)

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771. Definition of μ = μ_{ℓ,0} (the displayed mass is ∏_{i≥1}(1 − ℓ^{−i})|Aut A|^{−1}). [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, Theorem 1.3, p. 3. The u-weighted measure μ_{p,u}(B) = ∏_{k≥1}(1 − p^{−k−u})/(|B|^u|Aut B|). [P/lipnowski-ag-2018](#source-p-lipnowski-ag-2018), arXiv 1511.02212v1, §5.7.1, p. 35. LT's CL_ℓ is μ_{ℓ,0} (merged item PAPER-LIPNOWSKI-TSIMERMAN-18/cl-measure).

**API.**

- `cohenLenstraConstant` (data): c_{p,u} = ∏_{i≥u+1} (1 − p^{−i}).
- `cohenLenstraWeight` (data): The weight c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|) ∈ [0, ∞].
- `cohenLenstraMeasure` (constructor): μ_{p,u} as a probability mass function on the carrier (built from the mass formula).
- `cohenLenstraMeasure_apply` (simp): μ_{p,u}(A) = c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|).
- `cohenLenstraConstant_pos` (other): 0 < c_{p,u}.
- `cohenLenstraConstant_lt_one` (other): c_{p,u} < 1.
- `cohenLenstraConstant_eq_mul_succ` (relation): c_{p,u} = (1 − p^{−(u+1)}) c_{p,u+1}.
- `cohenLenstraWeight_trivial` (simp): μ_{p,u}(0) = c_{p,u}.
- `cohenLenstraWeight_mul_card_autCard` (characterisation): μ_{p,u}(A) · |A|^u |Aut A| = c_{p,u}: the measure is proportional to 1/(|A|^u |Aut A|).
- `cohenLenstraMeasure_rank_eq` (relation): The p-rank law: μ_{p,u}(p-rank = k) = p^{−k(k+u)} ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − p^{−i})^{−1} ∏_{i=1}^{k+u}(1 − p^{−i})^{−1} ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{−i}) (Wood, Corollary 3.5).

**Checks.**

- `cohenLenstraMeasure.test_trivial` (degenerate): μ_{p,0}(0) = c_{p,0}.
- `cohenLenstraMeasure.test_cyclic` (computation): μ_{p,0}(ℤ/p) = c_{p,0}/(p − 1).
- `cohenLenstraMeasure.test_cyclic_u_one` (computation): μ_{p,1}(ℤ/p) = c_{p,1}/(p(p − 1)) (the real-quadratic weight carries the extra 1/|A|).
- `cohenLenstraMeasure.test_not_uniform_in_order` (non-example): μ_{p,0}(ℤ/p²) = (p² − 1) μ_{p,0}((ℤ/p)²): a measure depending only on |A| is wrong.
- `cohenLenstraMeasure.test_three_indivisible` (computation): 0.56 < c_{3,0} < 0.561.

**Proof route.**

1. Define c_{p,u} as the convergent infinite product ∏_{i≥0} (1 − p^{−(i+u+1)}) (tprod), positive and < 1 because Σ p^{−i} < ∞.
2. Define the weight w(A) = c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|) in [0, ∞] using the carrier's order p^{A.1} and autCard.
3. By the mass formula the weights sum to 1, so they define a probability mass function (Mathlib PMF).

**Acceptance checks.**

- μ_{p,0}(0) = c_{p,0}; c_{3,0} ≈ 0.5601 is the predicted proportion of imaginary quadratic fields with 3 ∤ h (EVW §1.1 prints this as the indivisibility probability 1 − c_3 ≈ 0.440, a misprint recorded as ArithmeticStatistics/E624).
- μ_{p,0}(ℤ/p²) = (p² − 1) μ_{p,0}((ℤ/p)²).

**Consumers.** EVW §8.1, Lemma 8.2, Theorem 1.2 — the limiting law of ℓ-parts of class groups over F_q(t) and the target of the moment method; Wood 2019 Theorems 1.2–1.3 — the limit law of cokernels of random p-adic matrices; Lipnowski–Tsimerman §5.7 — the model CL_ℓ for point groups A(F_p)_ℓ of abelian varieties; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-heuristic-for-quadratic-fields — the conjectured law of class groups of quadratic fields; ArithmeticStatisticsPartIIRandomGammaGroups (LWZB §7.1) — the abelianization of the random Γ-group model recovers these measures

<a id="st5-surjection-moment"></a>

### 5.13 Surjection moments of a measure on finite abelian p-groups

For a nonnegative measure ν on L (a function L → [0, ∞]) and a class A, the A-moment of ν is ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν = Σ_{X ∈ L} ν(X) |Sur(X, A)| ∈ [0, ∞]. The trivial-target moment is the total mass; all rearrangements are of nonnegative series.

**Hypotheses.** p prime (to realise classes as groups)

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`); `mathlib:ENNReal.tsum_add`; `mathlib:PMF.tsum_coe`

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), §8.2, p. 771. Definition of the A-moment.

**API.**

- `surjectionMoment` (constructor): ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν = Σ_X ν(X)|Sur(X, A)|.
- `surjectionMoment_trivial` (characterisation): The moment at the trivial class is the total mass Σ_X ν(X).
- `surjectionMoment_add` (simp): The moment is additive in ν.
- `surjectionMoment_const_mul` (simp): The moment is homogeneous in ν.
- `surjectionMoment_mono` (relation): ν ≤ ν' pointwise implies ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν ≤ ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν'.
- `surjectionMoment_single` (example): The moment of the Dirac mass at X is |Sur(X, A)|.

**Checks.**

- `surjectionMoment.test_zero` (degenerate): The zero measure has all moments 0.
- `surjectionMoment.test_dirac_cyclic` (computation): The Dirac mass at ℤ/p has ℤ/p-moment p − 1.
- `surjectionMoment.test_probability_trivial_target` (characterisation): A probability mass function has trivial-target moment 1.
- `surjectionMoment.test_dirac_not_hom_count` (non-example): The moment counts surjections, not homomorphisms: the Dirac mass at (ℤ/p)² has ℤ/p-moment p² − 1, not |Hom((ℤ/p)², ℤ/p)| = p².

**Proof route.**

1. Define the moment as the ℝ≥0∞-valued tsum of ν(X)·|Sur(X_p, A_p)| over the carrier.
2. Linearity and monotonicity in ν follow from ENNReal.tsum_add and monotonicity of tsum.
3. For A trivial, |Sur(X, 0)| = 1, so the moment is Σ ν(X).

**Acceptance checks.**

- The Dirac mass at ℤ/p has ℤ/p-moment p − 1.
- Every probability measure has trivial-target moment 1.

**Consumers.** EVW Lemma 8.2, Proposition 8.3, (8.5.1) and Theorem 8.8 — moments of class-group laws are computed by point counts on Hurwitz spaces and determine the law; Wood 2019 Theorem 2.9 — the moments of cokernels of random matrices; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-moments — the moments of μ_{p,u} are |A|^{−u}

<a id="st5-extension-groupoid-of-finite-abelian-groups"></a>

### 5.14 The groupoid of extensions of finite abelian groups has cardinality one

For finite abelian groups G and K, consider exact sequences 0 → K →ι B →f G → 0 with B abelian, and isomorphisms of such sequences that are the identity on K and on G. Then Σ over isomorphism classes of sequences of 1/|Aut(sequence)| = 1. Equivalently, Σ_{[B]} #{f ∈ Sur(B, G) : ker f ≅ K}/|Aut B| = 1/|Aut K|.

**Hypotheses.** G, K finite abelian groups

**Dependencies.** [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`); `mathlib:AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite`

**Sources.** [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, proof of Lemma 3.2, p. 10. The identity this lemma proves (Cohen–Lenstra's proof is not public).

**Proof route.**

1. Write G = ⊕_i ℤ/n_i (Mathlib AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite, after splitting into cyclic factors). An extension is determined up to isomorphism by choosing lifts b_i ∈ B of the generators: n_i b_i lies in ι(K), and its class in K/n_iK does not depend on the lift; conversely every tuple (k_i) ∈ ∏_i K/n_iK arises (B = (K ⊕ ℤ^r)/⟨n_i e_i − k_i⟩). So the isomorphism classes are in bijection with ∏_i K/n_iK.
2. The automorphisms of a sequence are φ = id + ι∘h∘f with h ∈ Hom(G, K) ≅ ∏_i K[n_i].
3. |K/n_iK| = |K[n_i]| (kernel and cokernel of multiplication by n_i on the finite group K have the same order), so the groupoid cardinality is ∏|K/n_iK| / ∏|K[n_i]| = 1.
4. For the second form: a fixed B contributes #{(ι, f)}/|Aut B| by orbit counting, and #{(ι, f)} = #{f ∈ Sur(B, G) : ker f ≅ K}·|Aut K|.

**Acceptance checks.**

- G = K = ℤ/p: B = ℤ/p² contributes (p − 1)/(p(p − 1)) = 1/p and B = (ℤ/p)² contributes (p² − 1)/((p² − 1)(p² − p)) = 1/(p(p − 1)); the sum is 1/(p − 1) = 1/|Aut ℤ/p|.
- G = 0: only B ≅ K contributes, with 1/|Aut K|.

<a id="st5-surjection-weighted-class-count"></a>

### 5.15 Surjection-weighted class counts

For a prime p, a finite abelian p-group G of order p^g and i ≥ g: Σ_{|B| = p^i} |Sur(B, G)|/|Aut B| = Σ_{|K| = p^{i−g}} 1/|Aut K|, the sums over isomorphism classes.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; G a finite abelian p-group of order p^g; i ≥ g

**Dependencies.** [The groupoid of extensions of finite abelian groups has cardinality one](#st5-extension-groupoid-of-finite-abelian-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/extension-groupoid-of-finite-abelian-groups`); [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`); [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, proof of Lemma 3.2, p. 10. The identity, quoted from Cohen–Lenstra Prop. 4.1(ii) (not public); the groupoid proof is supplied here.

**Proof route.**

1. The left side is the groupoid cardinality of pairs (B, f : B ↠ G) with |B| = p^i, isomorphisms of B commuting with f: Σ_B |Sur(B, G)|/|Aut B|.
2. Sort the surjections by the isomorphism class K of the kernel (|K| = p^{i−g}): by ST.5/extension-groupoid-of-finite-abelian-groups the kernel-K part contributes exactly 1/|Aut K|.
3. Sum over the classes K of order p^{i−g}.

**Acceptance checks.**

- G = 0: both sides equal Σ_{|B|=p^i} 1/|Aut B|.
- i = g = 1, G = ℤ/p: left (p − 1)/(p − 1) = 1, right 1/|Aut 0| = 1.

<a id="st5-cohen-lenstra-moments"></a>

### 5.16 The moments of the Cohen–Lenstra measure

For a prime p, u ≥ 0 and every finite abelian p-group A: ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_{μ_{p,u}} = Σ_X μ_{p,u}(X)|Sur(X, A)| = |A|^{−u}. In particular every moment of μ_{p,0} equals 1.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; u ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** [Surjection-weighted class counts](#st5-surjection-weighted-class-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-weighted-class-count`); [The weighted sum of inverse automorphism counts](#st5-weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum`); [The Cohen–Lenstra measure μ_{p,u}](#st5-cohen-lenstra-measure) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-measure`); [Surjection moments of a measure on finite abelian p-groups](#st5-surjection-moment) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-moment`); [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-matrices-2019](#source-p-wood-matrices-2019), arXiv 1504.04391v1, Lemma 3.2, p. 9. The moment identity for μ_{p,u} (Y distributed as the product of μ_{p,u}). [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771. The case u = 0 (EVW item 72).

**Proof route.**

1. Write the moment as c_{p,u} Σ_i p^{−iu} Σ_{|X|=p^i} |Sur(X, A)|/|Aut X|.
2. Apply ST.5/surjection-weighted-class-count to each i ≥ log_p|A| (terms with i < log_p|A| vanish by surjCard_eq_zero_of_card_lt): the inner sum is Σ_{|K|=p^{i}/|A|} 1/|Aut K|.
3. Reindex by K: Σ_i p^{−iu} Σ_{|K| = p^i/|A|} 1/|Aut K| = |A|^{−u} Σ_K 1/(|K|^u|Aut K|) = |A|^{−u} c_{p,u}^{−1} (ST.5/weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum); multiply by c_{p,u}.

**Acceptance checks.**

- u = 0, A = ℤ/p: Σ_X μ(X)(p^{rk X} − 1) = 1, so E[p^{rank}] = 2 under μ_{p,0}.
- A = 0 gives total mass 1 (the mass formula).

<a id="st5-cohen-lenstra-contraction-constant"></a>

### 5.17 The Cohen–Lenstra constant exceeds one half for odd primes

For an odd prime ℓ, c_ℓ = ∏_{i≥1}(1 − ℓ^{−i}) > 1/2; hence β = c_ℓ^{−1} − 1 < 1. For ℓ = 2, c_2 ≈ 0.2888 < 1/2 and β > 1.

**Hypotheses.** ℓ an odd prime

**Dependencies.** [The Cohen–Lenstra measure μ_{p,u}](#st5-cohen-lenstra-measure) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-measure`); `mathlib:tsum_geometric_of_lt_one`

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.2, p. 771. The alternating series converges only if β < 1 (EVW item 113).

**Proof route.**

1. c_ℓ is increasing in ℓ (each factor increases), so c_ℓ ≥ c_3.
2. Bound c_3 from below: ∏_{i≥1}(1 − 3^{−i}) ≥ (1 − 1/3)(1 − 1/9)(1 − Σ_{i≥3} 3^{−i}) = (2/3)(8/9)(1 − 1/18) = 0.5597… > 1/2 (using ∏(1 − x_i) ≥ 1 − Σ x_i for the tail, Mathlib geometric series).
3. For ℓ = 2: (1 − 1/2)(1 − 1/4) = 3/8 < 1/2 already bounds c_2 above.

**Acceptance checks.**

- c_3 ≈ 0.5601, so β ≈ 0.785 for ℓ = 3.
- Non-example ℓ = 2: β ≈ 2.46, so the alternating iteration in EVW Lemma 8.2 does not converge.

<a id="st5-moments-determine-the-cohen-lenstra-measure"></a>

### 5.18 A probability measure with all surjection moments 1 is the Cohen–Lenstra measure

Let ℓ be an odd prime and ν a probability measure on L with ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν = 1 for every A ∈ L. Then ν = μ_{ℓ,0}.

**Hypotheses.** ℓ an odd prime; ν a probability measure on L; all surjection moments of ν equal 1

**Dependencies.** [The moments of the Cohen–Lenstra measure](#st5-cohen-lenstra-moments) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-moments`); [The Cohen–Lenstra constant exceeds one half for odd primes](#st5-cohen-lenstra-contraction-constant) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-contraction-constant`); [Surjection moments of a measure on finite abelian p-groups](#st5-surjection-moment) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-moment`); [The Cohen–Lenstra measure μ_{p,u}](#st5-cohen-lenstra-measure) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cohen-lenstra-measure`); `mathlib:PMF.ext`

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), Lemma 8.2, p. 771. Statement (EVW item 74).

**Proof route.**

1. Put u_A = |Aut A|·ν(A) ≥ 0. The moment identity reads u_A + Σ_{B ≠ A} (|Sur(B, A)|/|Aut B|) u_B = 1 (EVW (8.2.1)).
2. By ST.5/cohen-lenstra-moments with u = 0 the same identity holds for u_B = c_ℓ, so β_A := Σ_{B≠A}|Sur(B, A)|/|Aut B| = c_ℓ^{−1} − 1 =: β for every A.
3. If L ≤ u_B ≤ U for all B then 1 − βU ≤ u_A ≤ 1 − βL; starting from 0 ≤ u ≤ 1 the bounds are alternating partial sums of Σ(−β)^k.
4. Since β < 1 (ST.5/cohen-lenstra-contraction-constant) both bounds converge to 1/(1 + β) = c_ℓ, so ν(A) = c_ℓ/|Aut A| = μ_{ℓ,0}(A).

**Acceptance checks.**

- ν = μ_{ℓ,0} satisfies the hypothesis (ST.5/cohen-lenstra-moments).
- For ℓ = 2 the argument fails (β > 1); uniqueness at ℓ = 2 is ST.5/moments-determine-cohen-lenstra-limits-for-all-p-and-u.

<a id="st5-enlargement-of-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>

### 5.19 Enlargements of a finite abelian ℓ-group

For finite abelian ℓ-groups A, A' and s ≥ 0, A' is an s-enlargement of A if some surjection A' ↠ A has kernel of order ℓ^s (a 1-enlargement is an enlargement). Equivalently |A'| = ℓ^s|A| and the Young diagram of A is contained in that of A' (a_i ≤ a'_i for the conjugate partitions). The set E_s(A) of isomorphism classes of s-enlargements is finite, with at most p(s + m) elements where ℓ^m = |A|. The surjection is data separate from the isomorphism class.

**Hypotheses.** ℓ prime

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`); [Exact count of surjections between finite abelian p-groups](#st5-exact-surjection-count-formula) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/exact-surjection-count-formula`)

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.4, p. 772. Definition of enlargement (EVW item 76). [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.4, p. 772–773. Definition of s-enlargement.

**API.**

- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement` (constructor): A' is an s-enlargement of A: ∃ surjection A' ↠ A with kernel of order ℓ^s.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.enlargements` (data): The finite set E_s(A) of classes of order ℓ^{s}|A| whose diagram contains that of A.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.isEnlargement_iff_conjPart` (characterisation): IsEnlargement ℓ s A' A ↔ |A'| = ℓ^s|A| and a_i ≤ a'_i for all i.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.mem_enlargements` (characterisation): B ∈ E_s(A) ↔ B is an s-enlargement of A.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.card_enlargements_le` (relation): |E_s(A)| ≤ p(m + s), the number of partitions of m + s.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement.trans` (functoriality): An s-enlargement of a t-enlargement is an (s + t)-enlargement.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.isEnlargement_zero_iff` (extensionality): The 0-enlargements of A are A itself.

**Checks.**

- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement.test_cyclic_of_trivial` (degenerate): ℤ/ℓ is a 1-enlargement of the trivial group.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement.test_split_and_nonsplit` (computation): Both (ℤ/ℓ)² (split) and ℤ/ℓ² (non-split) are 1-enlargements of ℤ/ℓ.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement.test_not_enlargement` (non-example): ℤ/ℓ³ is not a 1-enlargement of (ℤ/ℓ)²: the order is right but (ℤ/ℓ)² is not a quotient.
- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement.test_pointwise_lift_fails` (non-example): For π(x, y) = (x mod 3, y) : ℤ/9 × ℤ/3 ↠ (ℤ/3)² and f(x, y) = (y, x mod 3) there is no homomorphism g with π ∘ g = f (EVW item 114).

**Proof route.**

1. Define IsEnlargement ℓ s A' A by the existence of a surjective homomorphism of the representatives with kernel of cardinality ℓ^s.
2. Characterisation: by exact-surjection-count-formula, a surjection A′↠A exists precisely when every conjugate-partition coordinate of A is bounded by the corresponding coordinate of A′. The order condition then fixes the kernel cardinality and s.
3. Hence E_s(A) is the image of the partitions of m + s containing α, a finite set of size ≤ p(m + s).
4. Composition: an s-enlargement of a t-enlargement is an (s+t)-enlargement (compose the surjections, orders multiply).

**Acceptance checks.**

- (ℤ/ℓ)² and ℤ/ℓ² are the two 1-enlargements of ℤ/ℓ.
- EVW item 114: X = A' = ℤ/9 × ℤ/3, A = (ℤ/3)², π(x, y) = (x mod 3, y); the surjection f(x, y) = (y, x mod 3) has no lift X → A' through π, so the pointwise lifting claim in EVW's proof of (8.4.1) is false (ArithmeticStatistics/E620); item 125: of the 48 surjections X → (ℤ/3)², 36 have no lift and 12 have 9 lifts each, while |Aut(ℤ/9 × ℤ/3)| = 108 ≥ 2·48.

**Consumers.** EVW proof of Lemma 8.4 — iterating enlargements dominates |Sur(X, A)| for large X by an average over E_s(A); ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/aggregate-enlargement-inequality — the least-column enlargement gives the factor ℓ − 1; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/finite-enlargement-domination-of-tails — M = E_s(A) is the finite set of Lemma 8.4

<a id="st5-aggregate-enlargement-inequality"></a>

### 5.20 The aggregate enlargement inequality (EVW (8.4.1), corrected proof)

Let ℓ be prime and X, A finite abelian ℓ-groups with Sur(X, A) ≠ ∅ and |X| > |A|. Then there is a 1-enlargement A' of A with |Sur(X, A')| ≥ (ℓ − 1)|Sur(X, A)|. One may take A' with conjugate partition a'_j = a_j + 1 at the least j with x_j > a_j, and a'_i = a_i otherwise.

**Hypotheses.** ℓ prime; Sur(X, A) ≠ ∅; |X| > |A|

**Dependencies.** [Exact count of surjections between finite abelian p-groups](#st5-exact-surjection-count-formula) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/exact-surjection-count-formula`); [Enlargements of a finite abelian ℓ-group](#st5-enlargement-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/enlargement-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`)

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.4, (8.4.1), p. 772. The statement (EVW item 78); the proof is replaced.

**Proof route.**

1. Since X ↠ A, x_i ≥ a_i for all i (ST.5/exact-surjection-count-formula), and |X| > |A| gives some i with x_i > a_i; let j be the least.
2. For j>1, minimality of j gives a_{j−1}=x_{j−1}≥x_j≥a_j+1, so increasing a_j preserves the partition inequalities. For j=1 there is no preceding coordinate to check. In both cases a′ contains a and has total size one greater, hence defines a 1-enlargement.
3. Compare the products of the exact formula for (X, A') and (X, A): the factor at index j − 1 changes by ℓ^{x_{j−1}}/(ℓ^{x_{j−1}} − ℓ^{a_j}) ≥ 1, and index j gains the factor ℓ^{x_j} − ℓ^{a_j} ≥ ℓ^{a_j}(ℓ − 1) ≥ ℓ − 1; all other factors agree. When j=1 omit the j−1 factor; there is no index-zero factor in the formula.
4. EVW's argument that every f ∈ Sur(X, A) lifts through a fixed A' ↠ A is false (EVW item 114, ArithmeticStatistics/E620); only the aggregate count is used.

**Acceptance checks.**

- X = ℤ/ℓ², A = ℤ/ℓ: A' = ℤ/ℓ², ratio ℓ ≥ ℓ − 1.
- EVW item 125 (X = ℤ/9 × ℤ/3, A = (ℤ/3)², A' = X): |Sur(X, A')| = 108 ≥ 2 · 48 = (ℓ − 1)|Sur(X, A)| although 36 of the 48 surjections do not lift.

<a id="st5-partition-tail-domination"></a>

### 5.21 Partition numbers are dominated by (ℓ − 1)^s

For an integer ℓ ≥ 3 and fixed m ≥ 0, p(s + m)(ℓ − 1)^{−s} → 0 as s → ∞, where p(n) is the number of partitions of n.

**Hypotheses.** ℓ ≥ 3; m ∈ ℕ

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Nat.Partition.hasProd_powerSeriesMk_card_restricted`; `mathlib:tsum_geometric_of_lt_one`

**Sources.** [P/ellenberg-hurwitz-2016](#source-p-ellenberg-hurwitz-2016), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.4, printed p. 772 (PDF p. 44). The asymptotic used without proof (EVW item 79).

**Proof route.**

1. Choose r with (ℓ − 1)^{−1} < r < 1 (possible since ℓ − 1 ≥ 2).
2. Expand finite Euler products with nonnegative coefficients and use monotone convergence to obtain Σ_n p(n)r^n=∏_{j≥1}(1−r^j)⁻¹<∞. Positivity and nonvanishing of the product follow from Σ_j r^j<∞. The formal partition identity identifies the coefficients, but its formal topology alone does not justify evaluation at nonzero r. Hence p(n)r^n→0.
3. p(s + m)(ℓ − 1)^{−s} = p(s + m) r^{s+m} · r^{−m} · (r(ℓ − 1))^{−s} → 0.

**Acceptance checks.**

- ℓ = 3, m = 0: p(s)/2^s → 0 (p(20) = 627 < 2^{20}).
- ℓ = 2 is excluded: p(s)·1^{−s} → ∞.

<a id="st5-finite-enlargement-domination-of-tails"></a>

### 5.22 Tails of surjection counts are dominated by enlargements (EVW Lemma 8.4)
