**Dependencies.** [Reduction of maximal isotropic subspaces to X^⊥/X](#st5-isotropic-reduction-map) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map`); [Maximal isotropic subspaces of a quadratic space over 𝔽_p](#st5-maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space`); [The Gaussian binomial coefficient and the count of subspaces of 𝔽_q^n](#st5-gaussian-binomial-coefficient) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(a) and its proof, pp. 5–6. Statement of the fibre count. [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proof of Proposition 2.6(a), p. 6. Reduction to dim X = 1 and the bijection with hyperplanes of W.

**Proof route.**

1. Reduce to dim X = 1 by choosing a full flag 0 = X_0 ⊂ X_1 ⊂ … ⊂ X_k = X and factoring π_X as the composite of the reductions π_{X_{i}/X_{i−1}} (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map, API isotropicReduction_comp); the space at stage i has dimension 2(n − i + 1).
2. Case X = 𝔽_p v: fix W̄ ∈ I_{X^⊥/X} and its preimage W ⊇ X in I_V. The map Z ↦ Z ∩ W from the fibre over W̄ to {hyperplanes of W not containing v} ∪ {W} is a bijection: if v ∈ Z then Z = W; if v ∉ Z then Z ∩ W is a hyperplane W_1 of W.
3. Conversely, for a hyperplane W_1 ⊂ W not containing v, the Z ∈ I_V containing W_1 correspond to maximal isotropic lines of the 2-dimensional weakly metabolic space W_1^⊥/W_1 ≅ (𝔽_p², xy), of which there are exactly two (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space, API maxIsotropicSubspaces_hyperbolicPlane): one is W, the other Z has Z ∩ W = W_1 and reduces to W̄. Since v∉W₁, the other Z cannot contain v (otherwise it contains W₁+F_pv=W and equals W). The printed source omits this necessary hyperplane restriction.
4. Count: the hyperplanes of the n-dimensional W not containing v number (p^n − 1)/(p − 1) − (p^{n−1} − 1)/(p − 1) = p^{n−1}; adding Z = W gives p^{n−1} + 1 elements in each fibre when dim X = 1; the product over the flag gives ∏_{i=1}^{dim X}(p^{n−i} + 1).

**Acceptance checks.**

- dim X = 0: fibres are singletons (empty product).
- n = 1, X a line: the fibre over the single point of I_0 is all of I_V, of size p^0 + 1 = 2.

<a id="st5-number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces"></a>

### 5.53 Number of maximal isotropic subspaces of a weakly metabolic 𝔽_p-space

If (V, Q) is a weakly metabolic quadratic space of dimension 2n over 𝔽_p, then #I_V = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1} (p^{j} + 1).

**Hypotheses.** (V, Q) weakly metabolic over 𝔽_p, dim V = 2n

**Dependencies.** [Every fibre of the isotropic reduction map has ∏(p^{n−i} + 1) elements](#st5-fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(b) and proof, pp. 5–6. Statement; the proof applies (a) with X maximal isotropic.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map with X a maximal isotropic subspace (dim X = n): X^⊥/X = 0 has exactly one maximal isotropic subspace, so #I_V = ∏_{i=1}^{n}(p^{n−i} + 1) = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(p^j + 1).

**Acceptance checks.**

- n = 1: #I_V = 2 (the hyperbolic plane).
- p = 2, n = 2: #I_V = (1 + 1)(2 + 1) = 6.

<a id="st5-intersection-dimension-generating-function"></a>

### 5.54 Generating function of dim(Z ∩ W) for a uniformly random maximal isotropic Z

Let (V, Q) be weakly metabolic of dimension 2n over 𝔽_p and fix W ∈ I_V. For Z uniform on I_V let X_n := dim(Z ∩ W) and a_{d,n} := Prob(X_n = d). Then X_n is distributed as a sum of independent Bernoulli variables B_1, …, B_n with Prob(B_i = 1) = 1/(p^{i−1} + 1); equivalently Σ_{d≥0} a_{d,n} z^{d} = ∏_{i=0}^{n−1} (z + p^{i})/(1 + p^{i}), i.e. Σ_{Z ∈ I_V} z^{dim(Z ∩ W)} = ∏_{i=0}^{n−1} (z + p^{i}) as polynomials in z.

**Hypotheses.** (V, Q) weakly metabolic over 𝔽_p, dim V = 2n; W ∈ I_V fixed; Z uniformly distributed on the finite set I_V

**Dependencies.** [Reduction of maximal isotropic subspaces to X^⊥/X](#st5-isotropic-reduction-map) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map`); [Every fibre of the isotropic reduction map has ∏(p^{n−i} + 1) elements](#st5-fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map`); [Number of maximal isotropic subspaces of a weakly metabolic 𝔽_p-space](#st5-number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(c),(d), pp. 6–7. The Bernoulli decomposition of X_n. [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(d), p. 6. Generating functions of a_{d,n} and of the limit a_d.

**Proof route.**

1. Induction on n; n = 0 is trivial. For n > 0 fix 0 ≠ v ∈ W and X = 𝔽_p v, and write Z̄ := π_X(Z) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map).
2. dim(Z ∩ W) = dim(Z̄ ∩ W̄) + [v ∈ Z], where W̄ = W/X ∈ I_{X^⊥/X} (dim 2n − 2).
3. Z̄ is uniform on I_{X^⊥/X} because every fibre of π_X has the same size p^{n−1} + 1 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map); so dim(Z̄ ∩ W̄) has the law of X_{n−1}.
4. Conditionally on Z̄, exactly one of the p^{n−1} + 1 elements of the fibre contains v (the preimage of Z̄ in X^⊥), so [v ∈ Z] is Bernoulli with parameter 1/(p^{n−1} + 1), independent of Z̄.
5. Multiply generating functions: (z + p^{n−1})/(1 + p^{n−1}) times the generating function of X_{n−1}; the count form follows from ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces.

**Acceptance checks.**

- n = 1: X_1 is 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each.
- z = 1 gives total mass 1; z = −1 gives Prob(X_n even) − Prob(X_n odd) = 0 for n ≥ 1 (the i = 0 factor vanishes).

<a id="st5-intersection-dimension-law-closed-form"></a>

### 5.55 Closed formula for the finite intersection law a_{d,n}

In the setting of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-generating-function, for 0 ≤ d ≤ n: a_{d,n} = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1} (1 + p^{−j})^{−1} · ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^{j} − 1) · ∏_{j=0}^{d−1} (1 − p^{j−n}).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; 0 ≤ d ≤ n

**Dependencies.** [Generating function of dim(Z ∩ W) for a uniformly random maximal isotropic Z](#st5-intersection-dimension-generating-function) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-generating-function`); [Cauchy's q-binomial theorem](#st5-cauchy-q-binomial-theorem) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cauchy-q-binomial-theorem`); [The Gaussian binomial coefficient and the count of subspaces of 𝔽_q^n](#st5-gaussian-binomial-coefficient) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(e) and proof, pp. 6–7. The closed formula.

**Proof route.**

1. Rewrite the generating function as ∏_{i=0}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−i}z) / ∏_{i=0}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−i}).
2. Apply ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/cauchy-q-binomial-theorem with t = 1/p: the coefficient of z^d in ∏_{i=0}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−i} z) is p^{−d(d−1)/2}[n d]_{1/p}.
3. Simplify p^{−d(d−1)/2}[n d]_{1/p} = ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^j − 1) · ∏_{j=0}^{d−1}(1 − p^{j−n}) using the product formula gaussBinom_eq_prod (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient); routine algebra.

**Acceptance checks.**

- n = 1, d = 0, 1: a_{0,1} = a_{1,1} = 1/2.
- d = n: a_{n,n} = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(1 + p^{j})^{−1} = 1/#I_V (Z = W).

<a id="st5-poonen-rains-distribution"></a>

### 5.56 The Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_p}

For a prime p, the Poonen–Rains distribution is the probability measure on ℤ_{≥0} with Prob(X_{Sel_p} = d) = a_d := c_p ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^{j} − 1), where c_p := ∏_{j≥0} (1 + p^{−j})^{−1} = (1/2) ∏_{i≥0} (1 − p^{−(2i+1)}). (The j = 0 factor is 1/2.) That the a_d sum to 1 is the theorem ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains, which is used to package the weights as a probability mass function.

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [Closed formula for the finite intersection law a_{d,n}](#st5-intersection-dimension-law-closed-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-law-closed-form`); `mathlib:tprod`; `mathlib:Multipliable`

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(f), p. 6. The limit law a_d and the two expressions for c. [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Definition 2.9, p. 7. X_{Sel_p} is the random variable with Prob(X_{Sel_p} = d) = a_d.

**API.**

- `poonenRainsConstant` (constructor): c_p := ∏'_{j≥0} (1 + p^{−j})^{−1}.
- `poonenRainsWeight` (data): a_d := c_p ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^{j} − 1).
- `poonenRainsDistribution` (data): The probability mass function on ℕ with weights a_d.
- `poonenRainsConstant_eq_half_prod` (characterisation): c_p = (1/2) ∏'_{i≥0} (1 − p^{−(2i+1)}).
- `poonenRainsWeight_succ` (simp): a_{d+1} = a_d · p/(p^{d+1} − 1).
- `poonenRainsWeight_pos` (other): a_d > 0 for every d.
- `poonenRainsDistribution_apply` (simp): poonenRainsDistribution p d = a_d.
- `poonenRainsDistribution_even` (relation): The total mass on even d is 1/2 (parity equidistribution).
- `poonenRainsDistribution_eq_alternatingKernelLimit` (compatibility): a_d equals the parity-averaged limit law of dim ker of a random alternating n×n matrix over 𝔽_p (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains).

**Checks.**

- `poonenRainsWeight.test_zero` (computation): poonenRainsWeight p 0 = poonenRainsConstant p.
- `poonenRainsWeight.test_ratio` (characterisation): poonenRainsWeight 2 1 = 2 · poonenRainsWeight 2 0.
- `poonenRainsDistribution.test_not_cohen_lenstra` (non-example): poonenRainsWeight 2 0 ≠ ∏'_{i≥1}(1 − 2^{−i}) (the Cohen–Lenstra probability that the 2-rank is 0), since c_2 < 1/4 < 0.28.
- `poonenRainsWeight.test_positive` (degenerate): poonenRainsWeight p d > 0 for all d, so no dimension is excluded.

**Proof route.**

1. Define c_p as the convergent infinite product ∏_{j≥0}(1 + p^{−j})^{−1} (convergent since Σ p^{−j} < ∞; mathlib:tprod, mathlib:Multipliable).
2. Define the weights a_d by the finite products and the measure from the summation theorem.
3. The second expression for c_p: substitute 1 + p^{−j} = (1 − p^{−2j})/(1 − p^{−j}) for j ≥ 1 and cancel (telescoping of even exponents).

**Acceptance checks.**

- p = 2: c_2 = (1/2)∏_{i≥0}(1 − 2^{−(2i+1)}) ≈ 0.2097, a_0 ≈ 0.2097, a_1 ≈ 0.4194, a_2 ≈ 0.2796.
- a_{d+1}/a_d = p/(p^{d+1} − 1).

**Consumers.** Poonen–Rains, Conjecture 1.1(a) — predicted law of dim Sel_p E over all E ordered by height; Kane, Theorem 3 and Corollaries 4–5; Heath-Brown; Swinnerton-Dyer — the proved law of dim Sel_2(E^b) − 2 in twist families; Smith I, Definition 1.4 and Theorem 1.5 — P^Alt(j | ∞), the starting law of Smith's Markov chain, equals a_j at p = 2; BKLPR, §5.5 — the model Sel_p law recovered from the p-adic model

<a id="st5-intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains"></a>

### 5.57 The finite intersection laws converge to the Poonen–Rains distribution, which has total mass one

For every d ≥ 0, a_{d,n} → a_d as n → ∞; Σ_{d≥0} a_d = 1; Σ_d a_d z^d = ∏_{i≥0}(1 + p^{−i}z)/(1 + p^{−i}) for every complex z (both sides converge absolutely); and the laws of X_n converge in total variation to the Poonen–Rains distribution.

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [Closed formula for the finite intersection law a_{d,n}](#st5-intersection-dimension-law-closed-form) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-law-closed-form`); [The Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_p}](#st5-poonen-rains-distribution) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution`); `mathlib:tprod`; `mathlib:ENNReal.tsum_mul_left`

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.6(d),(f), p. 6; proof of (f), p. 7. The limit law is the limit of (e).

**Proof route.**

1. Termwise limit: in the closed formula (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-law-closed-form) the factor ∏_{j=0}^{d−1}(1 − p^{j−n}) → 1 and ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−j})^{−1} → c_p (mathlib:tprod of a multipliable family).
2. Total mass: a_{d,n} ≤ C·∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^j − 1) with C independent of n, and Σ_d ∏_{j=1}^d p/(p^j−1) < ∞ (ratio test: consecutive ratio p/(p^{d+1} − 1) → 0); dominated convergence for sums (mathlib:ENNReal.tsum_mul_left for the rearrangement) gives Σ_d a_d = lim_n Σ_d a_{d,n} = 1.
3. For each fixed complex z the same majorant with an extra |z|^d is summable by the ratio test. Dominated convergence therefore passes the finite generating polynomial to Σ_d a_d z^d. The finite products converge absolutely because Σ_i |z−1|p^{−i}/(1+p^{−i})<∞. This also proves both convergence assertions in the complex generating-function statement.
4. Total variation: pointwise convergence of probability mass functions with limit of total mass 1 (Scheffé's lemma for counting measure) implies convergence in total variation.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Σ_d a_d = 1 for p = 2 and p = 3 numerically to 10 digits.
- a_{d,n} = 0 for d > n, while a_d > 0: the convergence is not uniform in d in ratio.

<a id="st5-poonen-rains-moments"></a>

### 5.58 Moments of p^{X}: the Poonen–Rains moment formula

For m ≥ 0: E[p^{m X_n}] = ∏_{i=1}^{m} (p^{i} + 1)/(1 + p^{−(n−i)}) for n ≥ m, and E[p^{m X_{Sel_p}}] = ∏_{i=1}^{m} (p^{i} + 1). In particular E[p^{X_{Sel_p}}] = p + 1 and E[p^{2X_{Sel_p}}] = (p + 1)(p² + 1) (= 15 for p = 2).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; m ≥ 0

**Dependencies.** [Generating function of dim(Z ∩ W) for a uniformly random maximal isotropic Z](#st5-intersection-dimension-generating-function) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-generating-function`); [The finite intersection laws converge to the Poonen–Rains distribution, which has total mass one](#st5-intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.22(a) and proof, p. 12. The moment formulas.

**Proof route.**

1. Substitute z = p^m in the generating function of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-generating-function: ∏_{i=0}^{n−1}(p^m + p^i)/(1 + p^i); the factors with i ≥ m telescope against the denominators, leaving the stated product.
2. Substitute z=p^m in the entire generating-function identity proved in intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains and cancel the finite shifted factors, obtaining ∏_{i=1}^m(p^i+1). Alternatively couple X_n=Σ_{i≤n}B_i with independent Bernoulli B_i: then p^{mX_n} increases almost surely, so monotone convergence applies to these random variables. The individual masses a_{d,n} are not monotone in n (a_{0,n} decreases), so monotone convergence cannot be applied to those masses.

**Acceptance checks.**

- m = 1, p = 2: E[2^{X}] = 3, the Bhargava–Shankar average of #Sel_2.
- m = 2, p = 2: 15, the bound of Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan Theorem 1.1.

<a id="st5-poonen-rains-parity"></a>

### 5.59 Parity equidistribution and parity-conditioned moments of the Poonen–Rains law

Prob(X_n even) = 1/2 for every n > 0 and Prob(X_{Sel_p} even) = 1/2. Conditioning on either parity leaves the moments E[p^{m X_{Sel_p}}] unchanged, and the same holds for E[p^{m X_n}] when m < n.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; n > 0

**Dependencies.** [Generating function of dim(Z ∩ W) for a uniformly random maximal isotropic Z](#st5-intersection-dimension-generating-function) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-generating-function`); [Moments of p^{X}: the Poonen–Rains moment formula](#st5-poonen-rains-moments) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-moments`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), Proposition 2.22(b),(c), p. 12. Parity and parity-conditioned moments.

**Proof route.**

1. Substitute z = −1 in the generating function (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-dimension-generating-function): the i = 0 factor (z + 1)/2 vanishes, so Σ_d (−1)^d a_{d,n} = 0.
2. Substitute z = −p^m: the factor with i = m vanishes when m < n, so Σ_d (−1)^d a_{d,n} p^{md} = 0, i.e. even and odd parts contribute equally; pass to the limit as in ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-moments.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Σ_{d even} a_d = Σ_{d odd} a_d = 1/2.

<a id="st5-delaunay-sha-p-rank-law"></a>

### 5.60 Delaunay's law for dim_{𝔽_p} Ш[p] in rank r

For a prime p and r ∈ ℤ_{≥0}, X_{Ш[p],r} is the probability measure on 2ℤ_{≥0} with Prob(X_{Ш[p],r} = 2n) = p^{−n(2r+2n−1)} ∏_{i=n+1}^{∞} (1 − p^{−(2r+2i−1)}) / ∏_{i=1}^{n} (1 − p^{−2i}). It is Delaunay's heuristic law with Poonen–Rains' correction (u/2 replaced by u = r).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; r ≥ 0

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:tprod`

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), §5, p. 21. The displayed law of X_{Ш[p],r}.

**API.**

- `delaunayWeight` (constructor): delaunayWeight p r n = Prob(X_{Ш[p],r} = 2n).
- `delaunayWeight_zero` (simp): delaunayWeight p r 0 = ∏'_{i≥1}(1 − p^{−(2r+2i−1)}).
- `delaunayWeight_pos` (other): All weights are positive.
- `hasSum_delaunayWeight` (characterisation): Σ_n delaunayWeight p r n = 1.
- `delaunayWeight_eq_alternatingCokernel` (compatibility): delaunayWeight p 0 n is the limit, over even sizes 2m → ∞, of the probability that a random alternating 2m × 2m matrix over 𝔽_p has kernel of dimension 2n (the p-rank marginal of A_0).

**Checks.**

- `delaunayWeight.test_rank_zero_trivial` (computation): delaunayWeight p 0 0 = ∏'_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}).
- `delaunayWeight.test_rank_decreases_mass` (characterisation): delaunayWeight p 1 0 > delaunayWeight p 0 0 (higher rank makes Ш[p] smaller).
- `delaunayWeight.test_odd_excluded` (non-example): The law is indexed by n with dimension 2n and already has total mass Σ_n delaunayWeight p 0 n = 1, so odd dimensions get mass 0: dim Ш[p] is even (alternating pairing).
- `delaunayWeight.test_poonen_rains_identity` (compatibility): poonenRainsWeight p (2n) = delaunayWeight p 0 n / 2 and poonenRainsWeight p (2n+1) = delaunayWeight p 1 n / 2.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the weights by the convergent product (mathlib:tprod); total mass one is part of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-compatibility-of-the-selmer-model for r ∈ {0, 1} and follows in general from ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit (the law of dim G[p] under A_r).

**Acceptance checks.**

- Prob(X_{Ш[p],0} = 0) = ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}).
- Supported on even integers only.

**Consumers.** Poonen–Rains, Theorem 5.2 — compatibility of the Selmer model with Delaunay's Ш heuristics forces rank 0 or 1 with probability 1/2; BKLPR, Theorem 1.6(c) and Theorem 5.15 — the Ш part of the p-adic model agrees with Delaunay's law

<a id="st5-delaunay-compatibility-of-the-selmer-model"></a>

### 5.61 The only rank law compatible with the Selmer and Ш models is 50% rank 0, 50% rank 1

For each prime p, the unique ℤ_{≥0}-valued random variable R such that X_{Sel_p} and R + X_{Ш[p],R} have the same distribution is the variable taking the values 0 and 1 with probability 1/2 each. (Here X_{Ш[p],R} is drawn from Delaunay's law with parameter r = R.)

**Hypotheses.** p prime; R is a nonnegative-integer-valued prior; conditionally on R=r, draw the Sha-dimension from the Delaunay law with that parameter. No unconditional independence of R and the resulting dimension is assumed.

**Dependencies.** [The Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_p}](#st5-poonen-rains-distribution) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution`); [Delaunay's law for dim_{𝔽_p} Ш[p] in rank r](#st5-delaunay-sha-p-rank-law) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-sha-p-rank-law`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), §5, Theorem 5.2 and proof, pp. 21–22. Statement; the proof follows on p. 22.

**Proof route.**

1. Existence: the identities Prob(X_{Sel_p} = 2n) = (1/2)Prob(X_{Ш[p],0} = 2n) and Prob(X_{Sel_p} = 2n + 1) = (1/2)Prob(X_{Ш[p],1} = 2n), obtained by rewriting c_p ∏_{j=1}^{2n} p/(p^j − 1) with c_p = (1/2)∏(1 − p^{−(2i+1)}) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution, API poonenRainsConstant_eq_half_prod) and splitting even and odd factors; routine product manipulation.
2. Uniqueness: with f_r(s) := Prob(X_{Ш[p],r} = s − r), the hypothesis gives Σ_r Prob(R = r) f_r = Σ_r Prob(R' = r) f_r for the conjectured R'; the f_r are linearly independent in the ℓ¹ sense because f_r(s) = 0 for s < r and f_r(r) > 0 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-sha-p-rank-law, API delaunayWeight_pos); induct on r.

**Acceptance checks.**

- p = 2: a_0 = (1/2)Prob(X_{Ш[2],0} = 0) = (1/2)∏_{i≥1}(1 − 2^{1−2i}) ≈ 0.2097.

<a id="st5-count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices"></a>

### 5.62 Proportion of invertible alternating matrices over 𝔽_p

Let M_m(𝔽_p)^alt be the set of alternating m × m matrices over 𝔽_p (zero diagonal, Aᵗ = −A), of cardinality p^{m(m−1)/2}, and GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt its subset of invertible ones. If m is odd, GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt = ∅. If m is even, #GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt / #M_m(𝔽_p)^alt = ∏_{i=1}^{m/2} (1 − p^{1−2i}).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; m ≥ 0

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Matrix.card_GL_field`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §3.6, Lemma 3.6 and proof, p. 8. Statement and the first step of the counting proof.

**Proof route.**

1. #M_m(𝔽_p)^alt = p^{m(m−1)/2}: an alternating matrix is determined freely by its strictly upper triangular entries.
2. Odd m: det A = det Aᵗ = det(−A) = −det A in odd dimension, and for p = 2 an alternating (zero-diagonal symmetric) form of odd rank does not exist; in all characteristics the rank of an alternating form is even (symplectic basis), so A is singular.
3. The m=0 case is the unique empty matrix and gives the empty product 1. For even m≥2, Even m, induction on m: the first column of an invertible alternating A is any of the p^{m−1} − 1 nonzero vectors with zero first entry; the number of completions does not depend on it (a change of basis in GL_m(𝔽_p) fixing e_1 moves any admissible column to any other), and splitting off the hyperbolic plane spanned by e_1 and a partner leaves p^{m−2} free coupling entries times an invertible alternating (m − 2)-matrix: #GL_m^alt = (p^{m−1} − 1) p^{m−2} #GL_{m−2}^alt.
4. Divide by p^{m(m−1)/2} = p^{2m−3} p^{(m−2)(m−3)/2}: the factor is (p^{m−1} − 1)/p^{m−1} = 1 − p^{1−m}; with m = 2i this is 1 − p^{1−2i}.

**Acceptance checks.**

- m = 2: the invertible alternating 2 × 2 matrices are [[0, a], [−a, 0]] with a ≠ 0: ratio (p − 1)/p = 1 − p^{−1}.
- p = 2, m = 4: 28 of the 64 alternating matrices are invertible, and (1 − 2^{−1})(1 − 2^{−3}) = 7/16 = 28/64.

<a id="st5-alternating-matrix-kernel-law"></a>

### 5.63 Kernel law of a uniformly random alternating matrix over 𝔽_p (Smith's P^Alt)

For a prime p and integers n ≥ j ≥ 0, P_p(j | n) is the probability that a uniformly random alternating n × n matrix over 𝔽_p has kernel of dimension exactly j: P_p(j | n) := #{A ∈ M_n(𝔽_p)^alt : dim ker A = j} / p^{n(n−1)/2}. It vanishes unless j ≡ n (mod 2). The parity-averaged limit law is P_p(j | ∞) := lim_{n→∞} (1/2)(P_p(j | 2n) + P_p(j | 2n+1)). For p = 2 these are Smith's P^Alt(j | n) and P^Alt(j | ∞) (Smith I, Definition 1.4); (P_2(j' | j))_{j,j'} are the transition probabilities of the Markov chain r_2 ≥ r_4 ≥ … of 2^k-Selmer ranks in Smith's theorem, which is owned by ArithmeticStatisticsPartIISmithMethod.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; 0 ≤ j ≤ n

**Dependencies.** [Proportion of invertible alternating matrices over 𝔽_p](#st5-count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices`); `mathlib:Module.finrank`

**Sources.** [P/smith-selmer-2026](#source-p-smith-selmer-2026), §1.1, Definition 1.4, pp. 3–4 (arXiv v2). Smith's P^Alt(j | n), continued: the probability that a uniformly selected alternating n × n matrix over 𝔽_2 has kernel of dimension exactly j. [P/smith-selmer2-2022](#source-p-smith-selmer2-2022), §2, Case 2.13, p. 9 (arXiv v2). Definition of P(j | n) for alternating matrices over 𝔽_2 and its parity vanishing.

**API.**

- `alternatingKernelLaw` (constructor): P_p(j | n) as a rational number (finite count divided by p^{n(n−1)/2}).
- `alternatingKernelLaw_eq_zero_of_parity` (simp): j ≢ n (mod 2) ⇒ P_p(j | n) = 0.
- `alternatingKernelLaw_self` (simp): P_p(n | n) = p^{−n(n−1)/2}.
- `sum_alternatingKernelLaw` (characterisation): Σ_{j=0}^{n} P_p(j | n) = 1.
- `alternatingKernelLaw_eq_formula` (characterisation): Closed formula (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-formula).
- `alternatingKernelLimit` (data): P_p(j | ∞) := lim (1/2)(P_p(j | 2n) + P_p(j | 2n+1)).
- `alternatingKernelLimit_eq_poonenRains` (compatibility): P_p(j | ∞) = poonenRainsWeight p j.

**Checks.**

- `alternatingKernelLaw.test_two_by_two` (computation): alternatingKernelLaw 2 0 2 = 1/2 and alternatingKernelLaw 2 2 2 = 1/2.
- `alternatingKernelLaw.test_four` (computation): alternatingKernelLaw 2 2 4 = 35/64 and alternatingKernelLaw 2 0 4 = 28/64.
- `alternatingKernelLaw.test_parity` (non-example): alternatingKernelLaw p 1 2 = 0: an alternating 2 × 2 matrix never has a 1-dimensional kernel.
- `alternatingKernelLaw.test_zero_size` (degenerate): alternatingKernelLaw p 0 0 = 1.
- `alternatingKernelLaw.test_not_all_matrices` (non-example): alternatingKernelLaw 2 1 3 = 7/8, whereas a uniformly random 3 × 3 matrix over 𝔽_2 has a 1-dimensional kernel with probability 294/512 = 147/256: the alternating constraint changes the law.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the finite count over the finite set of alternating matrices (Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) (ZMod p) with zero diagonal and transpose equal to the negative) and the kernel dimension via Module.finrank of LinearMap.ker of mulVecLin.
2. Define the parity-averaged limit as a limit of real sequences; its existence and value are ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains.

**Acceptance checks.**

- P_p(n | n) = p^{−n(n−1)/2} (only the zero matrix).
- P_2(0 | 2) = P_2(2 | 2) = 1/2; P_2(2 | 4) = 35/64.
- P_p(j | n) = 0 when j ≢ n (mod 2).

**Consumers.** Smith I, Theorem 1.5 — transition probabilities P^Alt(r_{2^k} | r_{2^{k−1}}) of the Markov chain of 2^k-Selmer ranks; Smith II, Theorem 1.4 and Case 2.13 — the same law in the potentially favored/alternating case; BKLPR, Lemma 3.7 and proof of Theorem 1.10 — kernels of random alternating maps control the size of the reduced matrix; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-sha-p-rank-law — the p-rank law of Ш in the rank-0 model is the even-n kernel law

<a id="st5-alternating-kernel-law-formula"></a>

### 5.64 Closed formula for the kernel law of random alternating matrices over 𝔽_p

For n ≥ j ≥ 0 with n ≡ j (mod 2): P_p(j | n) = [n j]_p · p^{(n−j)(n−j−1)/2} ∏_{i=1}^{(n−j)/2}(1 − p^{1−2i}) / p^{n(n−1)/2} = p^{−j(j−1)/2} ∏_{k=1}^{j} (1 − p^{−(n−j)−k})/(1 − p^{−k}) · ∏_{k=1}^{(n−j)/2} (1 − p^{1−2k}). For p = 2 this corrects the display in Smith II, Case 2.13, whose factor 1 − 2^{−n−j+k} must read 1 − 2^{−n+j−k} (ArithmeticStatistics/E601).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; n ≥ j ≥ 0; n ≡ j (mod 2)

**Dependencies.** [Kernel law of a uniformly random alternating matrix over 𝔽_p (Smith's P^Alt)](#st5-alternating-matrix-kernel-law) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-matrix-kernel-law`); [The Gaussian binomial coefficient and the count of subspaces of 𝔽_q^n](#st5-gaussian-binomial-coefficient) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient`); [Proportion of invertible alternating matrices over 𝔽_p](#st5-count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices`)

**Sources.** [P/smith-selmer2-2022](#source-p-smith-selmer2-2022), §2, Case 2.13, displayed formula for P(j | n), p. 9 (arXiv v2). Smith's formula for p = 2, corrected in the exponent (see sourceIssues E601). [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §3.6, Lemma 3.6, p. 8. The count of nondegenerate alternating matrices used in the kernel count.

**Proof route.**

1. Count by kernels: for each j-dimensional subspace K ⊆ 𝔽_p^n, the alternating A with ker A = K correspond bijectively to nondegenerate alternating forms on 𝔽_p^n / K (an alternating form vanishing on K descends; ker A = K exactly when the descended form is nondegenerate).
2. There are [n j]_p subspaces K (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/gaussian-binomial-coefficient) and, for each, #GL_{n−j}(𝔽_p)^alt = p^{(n−j)(n−j−1)/2}∏_{i=1}^{(n−j)/2}(1 − p^{1−2i}) forms (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices).
3. Divide by p^{n(n−1)/2} and rewrite [n j]_p = p^{j(n−j)} ∏_{k=1}^{j}(1 − p^{−(n−j)−k})/(1 − p^{−k}); the exponent j(n−j) + (n−j)(n−j−1)/2 − n(n−1)/2 equals −j(j−1)/2 (routine).

**Acceptance checks.**

- P_2(2 | 2) = 1/2 (the printed Smith II display gives 7/8).
- P_2(3 | 3) = 1/8 (only the zero matrix; printed display ≈ 0.303).
- P_2(2 | 4) = 35/64 (printed display gives 155/256).

<a id="st5-alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains"></a>

### 5.65 Random alternating kernels have the Poonen–Rains law in the parity-averaged limit

For every j ≥ 0: lim_{n→∞, n ≡ j (mod 2)} P_p(j | n) = 2 a_j, where a_j = c_p ∏_{i=1}^{j} p/(p^{i} − 1) is the Poonen–Rains weight. Consequently P_p(j | ∞) = a_j, and for p = 2 Smith's starting law P^Alt(j | ∞) is the Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_2}; the laws (1/2)(P_p(· | 2n) + P_p(· | 2n+1)) converge to it in total variation.

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [Closed formula for the kernel law of random alternating matrices over 𝔽_p](#st5-alternating-kernel-law-formula) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-formula`); [The Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_p}](#st5-poonen-rains-distribution) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution`); [The finite intersection laws converge to the Poonen–Rains distribution, which has total mass one](#st5-intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains`)

**Sources.** [P/smith-selmer-2026](#source-p-smith-selmer-2026), §1.1, after Definition 1.4, p. 4 (arXiv v2). The parity-averaged limit P^Alt(j | ∞). [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), §1.1, p. 1. The same law arises as the stationary distribution of the Swinnerton-Dyer/Kane Markov process.

**Proof route.**

1. From ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-formula, as n → ∞ with n ≡ j: ∏_{k=1}^{j}(1 − p^{−(n−j)−k}) → 1 and ∏_{k=1}^{(n−j)/2}(1 − p^{1−2k}) → ∏_{k≥1}(1 − p^{1−2k}) = 2c_p (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution, API poonenRainsConstant_eq_half_prod).
2. p^{−j(j−1)/2}∏_{k=1}^{j}(1 − p^{−k})^{−1} = ∏_{k=1}^{j} p^{−(k−1)}/(1 − p^{−k}) = ∏_{k=1}^{j} p/(p^{k} − 1); so the limit is 2a_j. For fixed j only one of P_p(j | 2n), P_p(j | 2n+1) is nonzero, giving P_p(j | ∞) = a_j.
3. Total variation: pointwise convergence and total mass Σ a_j = 1 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains) give convergence in total variation (Scheffé).

**Acceptance checks.**

- j = 0, p = 2: lim_{n even} P_2(0 | n) = ∏_{k≥1}(1 − 2^{1−2k}) ≈ 0.4194 = 2 a_0.
- Smith I, Figure 1.1: the Markov chain starts at an even state with probability 1/2 and an odd state with probability 1/2.

<a id="st5-symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>

### 5.66 Symplectic finite abelian p-groups and their symplectic automorphism groups

A symplectic p-group is a finite abelian p-group G with a nondegenerate alternating bilinear pairing [ , ] : G × G → ℚ_p/ℤ_p; Sp(G) is the group of automorphisms preserving [ , ]. G admits such a pairing if and only if G ≅ H × H for a finite abelian p-group H, and any two symplectic structures on the same group are isomorphic; hence isomorphism classes of symplectic p-groups are the classes of groups H × H, indexed by partitions all of whose parts occur with even multiplicity (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), and #Sp(G) depends only on the class of G.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; G finite abelian p-group

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); `mathlib:LinearMap.IsAlt`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §3.2, p. 6. Definition of symplectic abelian groups and Sp(G).

**API.**

- `IsSymplecticClass` (constructor): A class ⟨n, λ⟩ is symplectic iff every part of λ has even multiplicity (G ≅ H × H).
- `symplecticAutCard` (data): #Sp(G) for the standard symplectic structure on the representative of a symplectic class.
- `isSymplecticClass_iff_exists_pairing` (characterisation): A finite abelian p-group admits a nondegenerate alternating ℚ_p/ℤ_p-valued pairing iff its class is symplectic.
- `symplectic_pairing_unique` (extensionality): Two nondegenerate alternating pairings on the same group are isomorphic.
- `symplecticAutCard_pos` (other): #Sp(G) ≥ 1.
- `symplecticAutCard_elementary` (example): #Sp((ℤ/p)^{2k}) = p^{k²}∏_{i=1}^{k}(p^{2i} − 1).

**Checks.**

- `symplecticAutCard.test_rank_two` (computation): symplecticAutCard p (the class of (ℤ/p)²) = p(p² − 1).
- `IsSymplecticClass.test_cyclic` (non-example): The class of ℤ/p is not symplectic.
- `IsSymplecticClass.test_trivial` (degenerate): The trivial class is symplectic and symplecticAutCard p trivial = 1.
- `IsSymplecticClass.test_mixed` (non-example): ℤ/p² × ℤ/p × ℤ/p is not symplectic although its order p⁴ is a square.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the pairing condition (bilinear into ℚ_p/ℤ_p, alternating [x, x] = 0, nondegenerate: the adjoint G → Hom(G, ℚ_p/ℤ_p) is bijective).
2. Normal form: a nondegenerate alternating pairing on a finite abelian p-group has a symplectic basis {e_i, f_i} with ⟨e_i⟩ ≅ ⟨f_i⟩ ≅ ℤ/p^{a_i} and [e_i, f_i] = p^{−a_i}; induct on the exponent by splitting off a hyperbolic pair generated by an element of maximal order and a partner of equal order (routine).
3. Existence on H × H: the standard pairing [(h, χ), (h', χ')] := χ'(h) − χ(h') on H × H^∨ with H^∨ ≅ H; uniqueness follows from the normal form.

**Acceptance checks.**

- G = (ℤ/p)²: Sp(G) = SL_2(𝔽_p), of order p(p² − 1).
- G = ℤ/p has no symplectic structure.
- G = 0: Sp(G) is trivial.

**Consumers.** BKLPR, Theorems 3.9 and 3.11 — the limiting cokernel law A_r(G) = (#G)^{1−r}/#Sp(G) ∏(1 − p^{1−2i}); BKLPR, Proposition 5.5 — T carries a canonical nondegenerate alternating pairing, as Ш[p^∞] does (Cassels–Tate); Delaunay's heuristics (via BKLPR Theorem 1.6(c)) — Ш[p^∞] is modelled as a random symplectic p-group

<a id="st5-alternating-cokernel-law"></a>

### 5.67 Cokernel law of a Haar-random alternating matrix over ℤ_p

For n even and a finite abelian p-group class G, π_n(G) is the probability that coker(A) ≅ G for A Haar-random in M_n(ℤ_p)^alt. It is computed at finite level: for any e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0, π_n(G) = #{Ā ∈ M_n(ℤ/p^e)^alt : coker(Ā) ≅ G} / p^{e·n(n−1)/2}, and this is independent of such e. (A cokernel coker(A) ≅ ℤ_p^s ⊕ F is isomorphic to G iff s = 0 and F ≅ G, which is detected mod p^e.)

**Hypotheses.** p prime; n even; e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0

**Dependencies.** [Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups, indexed by partitions](#st5-isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [Proportion of invertible alternating matrices over 𝔽_p](#st5-count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices`); `mathlib:ZMod`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §1.4 and §3.7, pp. 4, 9. The cokernel law of a Haar-random alternating matrix.

**API.**

- `alternatingCokernelLaw` (constructor): π_n(G) via the finite-level count modulo p^e with e one greater than the largest exponent a among the cyclic factors Z/p^a of G (take e=1 for G=0).
- `alternatingCokernelLaw_eq_of_le` (characterisation): The finite-level count is the same for every e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0.
- `alternatingCokernelLaw_trivial` (simp): π_n(0) = ∏_{i=1}^{n/2}(1 − p^{1−2i}).
- `alternatingCokernelLaw_eq_zero_of_not_symplectic` (simp): π_n(G) = 0 if G is not symplectic.
- `sum_alternatingCokernelLaw` (other): Σ_G π_n(G) = 1 (the singular locus has measure zero).
- `alternatingCokernelLaw_tendsto` (relation): π_n(G) → A_0(G) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit).

**Checks.**

- `alternatingCokernelLaw.test_trivial_two` (computation): alternatingCokernelLaw p 2 trivial = 1 − p^{−1}.
- `alternatingCokernelLaw.test_cyclic_zero` (non-example): alternatingCokernelLaw p n (class of ℤ/p) = 0: cokernels of alternating matrices are symplectic.
- `alternatingCokernelLaw.test_n_zero` (degenerate): For n = 0, alternatingCokernelLaw p 0 G = 1 if G is trivial and 0 otherwise.
- `alternatingCokernelLaw.test_level_independent` (characterisation): For G = (ℤ/p)², the counts with e = 2 and e = 3 give the same value.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the finite count over alternating matrices with entries in ZMod (p^e) and the cokernel as the quotient of (ℤ/p^e)^n by the image of Ā, compared with the standard representative of G.
2. Independence of e: reduction M_n(ℤ/p^{e+1})^alt → M_n(ℤ/p^e)^alt is surjective with fibres of size p^{n(n−1)/2}, and for p^{e−1}G = 0 the condition coker ≅ G is detected mod p^e (a cyclic summand ℤ/p^f, f ≥ e, or a free summand would give an element of order p^e in the reduction).

**Acceptance checks.**

- π_n(0) = #GL_n(𝔽_p)^alt / #M_n(𝔽_p)^alt (e = 1).
- π_n(G) = 0 unless G is symplectic.

**Consumers.** BKLPR, Theorem 3.9 — the limit A_0(G) = #G/#Sp(G) ∏(1 − p^{1−2i}); BKLPR, §1.4 — model for Ш[p^∞] of rank-0 curves; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model — the r = 0 part of the model

<a id="st5-bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit"></a>

### 5.68 BKLPR: limiting cokernel law of random alternating matrices

(a) For each symplectic p-group G, lim_{n→∞, n even} π_n(G) = A_0(G) := #G/#Sp(G) · ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}), and Σ_G A_0(G) = 1. (b) For r ≥ 0, define A_r(G) := (#G)^{1−r}/#Sp(G) · ∏_{i≥r+1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) for symplectic G; then Σ_G A_r(G) = 1, and A_r is the limit as n → ∞ (n − r even) of the laws of (coker A)_tors for A drawn from the natural probability measure on alternating n × n matrices over ℤ_p of rank n − r (BKLPR Theorem 3.11).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; G a symplectic p-group

**Dependencies.** [Cokernel law of a Haar-random alternating matrix over ℤ_p](#st5-alternating-cokernel-law) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-cokernel-law`); [Symplectic finite abelian p-groups and their symplectic automorphism groups](#st5-symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups`); [Proportion of invertible alternating matrices over 𝔽_p](#st5-count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices`); [The number of surjective homomorphisms between abelian groups](#st5-surjection-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §3.7, Theorem 3.9 and proof, pp. 9–10. Statement (a). [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §3.8, Theorem 3.11, p. 11. Statement (b).

**Proof route.**

1. (a) Fix G and m = n − dim_{𝔽_p} G[p]. Surjections ℤ_p^n → G pull back the pairing of G to alternating pairings on ℤ_p^n inducing G; Sp(G) acts freely on Sur(ℤ_p^n, G) with these pairings as orbits, so there are #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/#Sp(G) of them (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups, ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjection-count).
2. The probability that the pairing of A equals a fixed one is #GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt/#M_m(𝔽_p)^alt · (#G)^{1−n} (BKLPR Corollaries 3.4–3.5: A ∈ D + D M_n(ℤ_p) D with rank condition), so π_n(G) = #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/#Sp(G) · #GL_m^alt/#M_m^alt · (#G)^{1−n}; as n → ∞, #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/(#G)^n → 1 and ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices gives the limit.
3. Total mass: Σ_G π_n(G)=1 because the determinant polynomial is not identically zero on even alternating matrices, so its zero set has Haar measure zero. Let c=∏_{i≥1}(1−p^{1−2i})>0. Fatou and the established pointwise limit c·#G/#Sp(G) give Σ_G #G/#Sp(G)≤1/c<∞. The bound π_n(G)≤#G/#Sp(G) is now a summable domination, so dominated convergence yields Σ_G A_0(G)=1.
4. (b) For r ≥ 1 the measure on rank-(n − r) alternating matrices is the normalised canonical measure on the ℤ_p-points of that scheme (BKLPR Proposition 2.1, Lemma 3.13); its existence and the pushforward identity are the gap 'Canonical measure on ℤ_p-points (Oesterlé–Serre)'. Given it, the proof integrates |det|^r (BKLPR Lemma 3.12) and repeats (a).

**Acceptance checks.**

- A_0(0) = ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) ≈ 0.4194 for p = 2.
- A_1(0) = ∏_{i≥2}(1 − p^{1−2i}).
- The p-rank marginal of A_0 is the even-n limit of the kernel law P_p(· | n) (reduce A mod p).

<a id="st5-bklpr-model"></a>

### 5.69 The BKLPR model for the p^∞-Selmer sequence

For a prime p, the BKLPR distribution Q is the probability measure on pairs (r, T), r ∈ ℤ_{≥0} and T a symplectic p-group class, given by Q(r, T) := (1/2) A_r(T) for r ∈ {0, 1} and Q(r, T) := 0 for r ≥ 2 (A_r from ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit). A pair (r, T) stands for the split short exact sequence 0 → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r ⊕ T → T → 0 of co-finite type ℤ_p-modules, which models 0 → E(k) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p → Sel_{p^∞}(E) → Ш(E)[p^∞] → 0; every isomorphism class of such split sequences with finite cokernel arises from exactly one pair. BKLPR define Q as the limit of the laws Q_{2n} of intersections of random maximal isotropic ℤ_p-submodules; their proof of Theorem 1.2 identifies Q_{2n} with this mixture (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-random-isotropic-intersection-law).

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [BKLPR: limiting cokernel law of random alternating matrices](#st5-bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit`); [Symplectic finite abelian p-groups and their symplectic automorphism groups](#st5-symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §5.4, proof of Theorem 1.2, p. 19. Q_{2n} equals the mixture over r ∈ {0,1} of T_{2n,r}; in the limit, of A_r. [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §1.3, Conjecture 1.3, p. 2. R, S, T model the rank part, Sel_{p^∞} and Ш[p^∞].

**API.**

- `bklprModel` (constructor): The probability mass function on ℕ × FinAbPGroupClass with weights (1/2)A_r(T) for r ≤ 1.
- `bklprModel_apply` (simp): bklprModel p (r, T) = (1/2)·bklprShaLaw p r T if r ≤ 1, else 0.
- `bklprModel_rank_marginal` (characterisation): The marginal law of r is uniform on {0, 1}.
- `bklprModel_sha_conditional` (projection): Conditionally on r ∈ {0, 1}, T has law A_r.
- `bklprModel_selmer_p_rank` (compatibility): The law of r + dim T[p] under bklprModel is poonenRainsDistribution p.
- `bklprShaLaw` (data): A_r(T) = (#T)^{1−r}/#Sp(T) ∏_{i≥r+1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) on symplectic classes, 0 otherwise.

**Checks.**

- `bklprModel.test_rank_two` (non-example): bklprModel p (2, T) = 0 for every T: the model gives rank ≥ 2 probability zero.
- `bklprModel.test_trivial_rank_zero` (computation): bklprModel p (0, trivial) = (1/2)∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}).
- `bklprModel.test_symplectic_support` (non-example): bklprModel p (0, class of ℤ/p) = 0 since ℤ/p is not symplectic.
- `bklprModel.test_total_mass` (characterisation): Σ_{(r,T)} bklprModel p (r, T) = 1.

**Proof route.**

1. Define Q on ℕ × (symplectic classes) by the displayed weights; total mass (1/2)(Σ A_0 + Σ A_1) = 1 by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit.
2. Derived laws: the modelled Selmer group S = (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r ⊕ T, its p-torsion rank r + dim T[p], and S[p^e].

**Acceptance checks.**

- Q(r = 0) = Q(r = 1) = 1/2 and Q(r ≥ 2) = 0.
- The law of dim_{𝔽_p} S[p] = r + dim T[p] under Q is the Poonen–Rains distribution (BKLPR §5.5, PR Theorem 5.2 identities).

**Consumers.** BKLPR, Conjecture 1.3 — the density of curves with Selmer sequence of type (r, T) is Q(r, T); BKLPR, §5.3 — prediction: 50% rank 0, 50% rank 1; Smith I, §1.1 after Theorem 1.5 — Sel_{2^∞} of twists has the distribution predicted by BKLPR Conjecture 1.3

<a id="st5-bklpr-random-isotropic-intersection-law"></a>

### 5.70 BKLPR: intersections of random maximal isotropic ℤ_p-submodules realise the model

Let n≥1 and V = ℤ_p^{2n} with the hyperbolic form Q(x, y) = Σ x_i y_i, OGr_n(ℤ_p) its maximal isotropic direct summands with the canonical probability measure, and Z, W ∈ OGr_n(ℤ_p) independent random. Put R := (Z ∩ W) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p, S := (Z ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p) ∩ (W ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p) and T := S/R. Then: (i) R ≅ (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r with r = rk(Z ∩ W) ∈ {0, 1}, each with probability 1/2 (Proposition 5.6); (ii) T is finite and the sequence splits (Corollaries 5.2–5.3); (iii) the law Q_{2n} of (r, T) converges as n → ∞ to the BKLPR model Q, and the law T_{2n,r} of T given r converges to A_r (Theorems 1.2, 1.6(a)–(b), 1.10(b)); (iv) S[q] ≅ Z/qZ ∩ W/qW for q a power of p (Proposition 5.4).

**Hypotheses.** p prime; Z, W independent and distributed by the canonical measure on OGr_n(ℤ_p); n ≥ 1; when n=0 the only pair is Z=W=0 and the rank law is concentrated at 0.

**Dependencies.** [The BKLPR model for the p^∞-Selmer sequence](#st5-bklpr-model) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model`); [BKLPR: limiting cokernel law of random alternating matrices](#st5-bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit`); [Kernel law of a uniformly random alternating matrix over 𝔽_p (Smith's P^Alt)](#st5-alternating-matrix-kernel-law) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-matrix-kernel-law`); [Maximal isotropic subspaces of a quadratic space over 𝔽_p](#st5-maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §1.2, Theorem 1.2, p. 2. Existence and convergence of Q_{2n}. [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §5.3, Proposition 5.6, p. 17. Rank 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each.

**Proof route.**

1. Canonical measure: OGr_n is a smooth projective ℤ-scheme of relative dimension n(n − 1)/2 with two isomorphic components distinguished by parity (BKLPR Propositions 4.4–4.5); the measure on OGr_n(ℤ_p) is the normalised limit of counts mod p^e (Proposition 2.1). This input is the gap 'Canonical measure on ℤ_p-points (Oesterlé–Serre) and the orthogonal Grassmannian'.
2. (i): the Schubert loci S_{n,r} with r ≥ 2 have smaller dimension (Proposition 4.9) hence measure zero; the parity of rk(Z ∩ W) is equidistributed by the isomorphism of the two components.
3. (ii),(iv): divisibility and co-finite type arguments (BKLPR Proposition 5.1, Corollaries 5.2–5.3, Proposition 5.4); routine module theory over ℤ_p.
4. (iii): represent Z = W_1ᵀ ⊕ graph(A) for a random decomposition and a random alternating A of corank r, so T ≅ (coker A)_tors; the size n − m of A tends to ∞ in probability (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-matrix-kernel-law and BKLPR Lemma 3.7), so T_{2n,r} → A_r by ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit; combine with (i).

**Acceptance checks.**

- Q_{2n}(r ≥ 2) = 0 for every n.
- For q = p, (iv) and PR's Proposition 2.6 recover the Poonen–Rains Selmer model.

<a id="st5-maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers"></a>

### 5.71 Number of maximal isotropic direct summands of (ℤ/p^e)^{2n}

For q = p^e (e ≥ 1), the hyperbolic quadratic ℤ/qℤ-module (ℤ/q)^{2n} has #OGr_n(ℤ/qℤ) = q^{n(n−1)/2} ∏_{i=1}^{n} (1 + p^{i−n}) maximal isotropic direct summands.

**Hypotheses.** p prime; e ≥ 1

**Dependencies.** [Number of maximal isotropic subspaces of a weakly metabolic 𝔽_p-space](#st5-number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces`); [Proportion of invertible alternating matrices over 𝔽_p](#st5-count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §4.3, Lemma 4.8, p. 14. Statement and the smoothness argument.

**Proof route.**

1. e = 1: #OGr_n(𝔽_p) = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(p^j + 1) = p^{n(n−1)/2}∏_{i=1}^{n}(1 + p^{i−n}) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces).
2. Lifting: every maximal isotropic direct summand mod p^e lifts to mod p^{e+1} in exactly p^{n(n−1)/2} ways (smoothness of OGr_n of relative dimension n(n − 1)/2, BKLPR Proposition 4.4; concretely, lifts of Z̄ = graph(Ā) over a complement correspond to alternating corrections p^e B with B ∈ M_n(𝔽_p)^alt). The chart description gives the count directly: near a point, maximal isotropic summands transverse to a fixed complement are graphs of alternating maps.

**Acceptance checks.**

- n = 1: #OGr_1(ℤ/q) = 2 for every q (the two coordinate lines).

<a id="st5-bklpr-injection-moments"></a>

### 5.72 BKLPR: moments of injection counts in the mod-q model

For q = p^e and m ≥ 0, let I_m(G) be the number of injective homomorphisms (ℤ/qℤ)^m → G. As Z, W range over OGr_n(ℤ/qℤ) (uniformly and independently), the average of I_m(Z ∩ W), for m≤n, equals q^{m(m+1)/2} ∏_{i=0}^{m−1}(1 − p^{i−n}) ∏_{i=n−m}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−i})^{−1}, which tends to q^{m(m+1)/2} as n → ∞. If m>n the injection count is zero. The reciprocal on the last product corrects the displayed simplification in the cited preprint.

**Hypotheses.** q = p^e, e ≥ 1; m ≥ 0

**Dependencies.** [Number of maximal isotropic direct summands of (ℤ/p^e)^{2n}](#st5-maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers`); [Reduction of maximal isotropic subspaces to X^⊥/X](#st5-isotropic-reduction-map) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §5.5, Theorem 5.10 and proof, p. 20. Statement and proof.

**Proof route.**

1. For m>n there are no injections. For m≤n fix W using orthogonal transitivity. A map h:(Z/p^e)^m→W≅(Z/p^e)^n is injective iff its reduction modulo p has full column rank; the Smith normal form proves this criterion. Consequently im(h) is a direct summand, and the number of injections is q^{nm}∏_{i=0}^{m−1}(1−p^{i−n}), involving p rather than q in the factors.
2. The Z ⊇ im(h) correspond to maximal isotropic direct summands of im(h)^⊥/im(h), a hyperbolic module of rank 2n − 2m (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map, over ℤ/q); their number is #OGr_{n−m}(ℤ/q) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers).
3. The ratio of the two Grassmannian counts is q^{−nm+m(m+1)/2}/∏_{i=n−m}^{n−1}(1+p^{−i}). Multiply by the injection count to obtain the displayed corrected formula. For fixed m, both finite products tend to 1 as n→∞. The finite-field isotropic-reduction node supplies motivation; over Z/p^e use the direct-summand orthogonal quotient and a hyperbolic basis, as in the lifting charts of maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers.

**Acceptance checks.**

- q = p, m = 1: limit p, i.e. the average of #(Z ∩ W) − 1 is p, so the average of #Sel_p is p + 1 (PR Proposition 2.22).
- q = p, general m: equivalent to PR Proposition 2.22(a) (BKLPR Remark 5.13).
- n=m=1: for fixed W, half the two isotropic lines equal W, so the average is φ(p^e)/2 = p^e(1−1/p)/2. This rules out multiplying by the final factor 2. For e>1, injections from (Z/p^e)^m into an arbitrary finite module are not determined by its cardinality; no such polynomial claim is used.

<a id="st5-poonen-rains-selmer-conjecture"></a>

### 5.73 The Poonen–Rains conjecture for p-Selmer groups over ℚ (as a stated proposition)

For a prime p, the Poonen–Rains conjecture over ℚ is the proposition PR(p): over the family of elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B (A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0, no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B) ordered by the naive height H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (the family and height of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0), (a) for every d ≥ 0 the set {E : dim_{𝔽_p} Sel_p(E) = d} has density a_d (the Poonen–Rains weight), and (c) for every m ≥ 1 the m-th moment of #Sel_p(E) exists and equals ∏_{i=1}^{m}(p^{i} + 1) (moments as in ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family); (b) is (c) with m = 1, average p + 1. It is a conjecture: this node defines the proposition so that theorems can take it as a hypothesis and proved cases can be compared with it. Sel_p(E) is the p-Selmer group of Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 7. Poonen–Rains state it over any global field with an unspecified height on the coefficients; the definition is pinned over ℚ with the height above.

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)](#st0-invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs`); [Arithmetic families: objects up to equivalence, ordered by a Northcott height, with weighted and unweighted counting functions](#st0-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/arithmetic-family`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`); [The Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_p}](#st5-poonen-rains-distribution) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution`); [Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)](#st0-elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), §1.2, Conjecture 1.1, p. 2. The conjecture (a)–(c).

**API.**

- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture` (constructor): The proposition PR(p) = (∀ d, density of dim Sel_p = d is a_d) ∧ (∀ m ≥ 1, m-th moment of #Sel_p is ∏(p^i + 1)).
- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.density` (projection): PR(p) ⇒ for each d, density{E : dim Sel_p E = d} = a_d.
- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.moment` (projection): PR(p) ⇒ for each m ≥ 1, M_m(#Sel_p) = ∏_{i=1}^{m}(p^i + 1).
- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.average` (projection): PR(p) ⇒ the average of #Sel_p is p + 1.
- `poonenRainsSelmerConjecture_of_bklpr` (relation): The BKLPR conjecture for p implies clause (a) of PR(p) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-conjecture-implies-rank-and-selmer-laws).

**Checks.**

- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.test_average_two` (compatibility): PR(2) implies that the average of #Sel_2 is 3, the value proved by Bhargava–Shankar (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three).
- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.test_second_moment` (computation): PR(2) predicts the second moment 15 = (2 + 1)(4 + 1).
- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.test_not_rank` (non-example): PR(p) is a statement about dim Sel_p, not about rank E(ℚ): it gives positive density to dim Sel_p = 2, which is not a rank prediction.
- `PoonenRainsSelmerConjecture.test_zero_moment` (degenerate): The m=0 moment is 1 for every eventually nonempty finite-cutoff family, including the full elliptic-curve family, so the moment clause starts at m=1.

**Proof route.**

1. Compose: the family carrier and height (ST.0, EC Layer 8 minimal short models), Sel_p(E) and its 𝔽_p-dimension (EC Layer 7), the densities and moments (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family), and the weights (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution).
2. The proposition is the conjunction of the density statement for each d and the moment statement for each m.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Proved instances of clause (c) with m = 1: p = 2, 3, 5 (Bhargava–Shankar); with m = 2, p = 2 the upper bound 15 (Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan) but not the equality.
- Clause (a) is left conjectural for the full family in the cited sources; this blueprint provides no proof of it.

**Consumers.** Bhargava–Shankar 3-, 4-, 5-Selmer papers — proved cases of clause (b) (p = 3, 5) and of the σ(n) conjecture; Bhargava–Shankar–Swaminathan, Conjecture 1.3 and Theorem 1.1 — the m = 2, p = 2 case as an upper bound; BKLPR, §5.5 — Conjecture 1.3 implies PR Conjecture 1.1(a)

<a id="st5-bhargava-shankar-selmer-average-conjecture"></a>

### 5.74 The σ(n) conjecture for average Selmer sizes (as a stated proposition)

For an integer n ≥ 1, BS(n) is the proposition: over the family of elliptic curves E_{A,B}/ℚ ordered by naive height (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0), the average of #Sel_n(E) exists and equals σ(n) = Σ_{d | n} d. It is Bhargava–Shankar's Conjecture 4, the n-analogue of Poonen–Rains Conjecture 1.4(b); proved for n ≤ 5.

**Hypotheses.** n ≥ 1

**Dependencies.** [The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)](#st0-invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`); [Elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height, on EllipticCurves Layer 8's minimal-pair carrier, with the invariant map (I, J) = (−3A, −27B)](#st0-elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-4selmer-2013](#source-p-bhargava-4selmer-2013), §1, Conjecture 4, p. 2 (arXiv v1). Statement of the conjecture.

**API.**

- `SelmerAverageConjecture` (constructor): BS(n): the average of #Sel_n over E_{A,B} ordered by height exists and equals σ(n).
- `SelmerAverageConjecture.average` (projection): BS(n) ⇒ M_1(#Sel_n) = σ(n).
- `selmerAverageConjecture_one` (example): BS(1) holds.
- `selmerAverageConjecture_prime_iff` (compatibility): For n = p prime, BS(p) is clause (b) of the Poonen–Rains conjecture (p + 1 = σ(p)).

**Checks.**

- `SelmerAverageConjecture.test_sigma_four` (computation): BS(4) predicts the average 7 = 1 + 2 + 4 (proved by Bhargava–Shankar).
- `SelmerAverageConjecture.test_sigma_six` (computation): BS(6) predicts the average 12 = σ(6).
- `SelmerAverageConjecture.test_one` (degenerate): BS(1) is true since Sel_1(E) = 0 has one element.
- `SelmerAverageConjecture.test_not_multiplicative_moment` (non-example): BS(4) is not implied by BS(2): the average of #Sel_4 is not the second moment of #Sel_2 (7 ≠ 15).

**Proof route.**

1. Compose the family and height (ST.0), Sel_n(E) (EC Layer 7) and the first moment (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family).

**Acceptance checks.**

- BS(1) holds trivially (Sel_1 = 0, σ(1) = 1).
- BS(2), BS(3), BS(4), BS(5) are theorems (ST.4 and ST.5 nodes).

**Consumers.** Bhargava–Shankar 4-Selmer, Proposition 5 — BS(n) for infinitely many n implies 100% of curves have rank ≤ 1; Bhargava–Shankar 5-Selmer, Theorem 1 — proved case n = 5

<a id="st5-selmer-average-conjecture-implies-rank-at-most-one"></a>

### 5.75 If the σ(n) conjecture holds for infinitely many n, then 100% of curves have rank at most 1

Assume BS(n) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bhargava-shankar-selmer-average-conjecture) for every n in an infinite set N of positive integers. Then the set of E_{A,B}/ℚ with rank E(ℚ) ≥ 2 has density zero.

**Hypotheses.** BS(n) for all n in an infinite set N

**Dependencies.** [The σ(n) conjecture for average Selmer sizes (as a stated proposition)](#st5-bhargava-shankar-selmer-average-conjecture) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bhargava-shankar-selmer-average-conjecture`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`)

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4; tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-6-the-mordellweil-theorem-aec-viii

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-4selmer-2013](#source-p-bhargava-4selmer-2013), §1, Proposition 5, p. 2 (arXiv v1). Statement.

**Proof route.**

1. If rank E(ℚ) ≥ 2 then (ℤ/n)² ↪ E(ℚ)/nE(ℚ) ↪ Sel_n(E), so #Sel_n(E) ≥ n² (Kummer injection of EC Layer 7 and Mordell–Weil structure, EC Layer 6).
2. Markov (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family, API familyUpperDensity_le_upperMoment_div): μ⁺(rank ≥ 2) ≤ σ(n)/n².
3. σ(n)/n² → 0 along N since σ(n) = O(n log log n) (routine: σ(n)/n ≤ Σ_{d|n} 1/d ≤ 1 + log n suffices).

**Acceptance checks.**

- With N = {2, 3, 4, 5} alone one only gets μ⁺(rank ≥ 2) ≤ min(3/4, 4/9, 7/16, 6/25) = 6/25.

<a id="st5-bklpr-selmer-conjecture"></a>

### 5.76 The BKLPR conjecture for p^∞-Selmer sequences over ℚ (as a stated proposition)

For a prime p, BKLPR(p) is the proposition: over the family E_{A,B}/ℚ ordered by naive height (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0), for every r ≥ 0 and every finite abelian p-group class G, the set {E : rank E(ℚ) = r and Ш(E)[p^∞] ≅ G} has density Q(r, G) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model). Since E(ℚ) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p is divisible the sequence 0 → E(ℚ) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p → Sel_{p^∞}(E) → Ш(E)[p^∞] → 0 splits, and its isomorphism class is determined by (r, Ш[p^∞]) when Ш[p^∞] is finite; so this is BKLPR Conjecture 1.3 for k = ℚ. It is a conjecture, defined as a proposition.

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [The BKLPR model for the p^∞-Selmer sequence](#st5-bklpr-model) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`); [Arithmetic families: objects up to equivalence, ordered by a Northcott height, with weighted and unweighted counting functions](#st0-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/arithmetic-family`); `SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2`

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §1.3, Conjecture 1.3, p. 2. The conjecture.

**API.**

- `BKLPRSelmerConjecture` (constructor): BKLPR(p): ∀ r G, density{E : rank E(ℚ) = r ∧ Ш(E)[p^∞] ≅ G} = Q(r, G).
- `BKLPRSelmerConjecture.density` (projection): The density statement for a given (r, G).
- `BKLPRShaConjecture` (data): BKLPR Conjecture 1.7 over ℚ: for r with infinitely many rank-r curves, the density of Ш[p^∞] ≅ G among rank-r curves is A_r(G).
- `bklprSelmerConjecture_rank` (relation): BKLPR(p) ⇒ density{rank 0} = density{rank 1} = 1/2 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-conjecture-implies-rank-and-selmer-laws).

**Checks.**

- `BKLPRSelmerConjecture.test_rank_two_density` (characterisation): BKLPR(p) implies density{E : rank E(ℚ) ≥ 2} = 0.
- `BKLPRSelmerConjecture.test_cyclic_sha` (non-example): BKLPR(p) gives density 0 to Ш[p^∞] ≅ ℤ/p (not symplectic), consistent with Cassels–Tate.
- `BKLPRSelmerConjecture.test_independent_of_p_rank` (compatibility): BKLPR(p) for two primes p, p' predicts the same rank densities 1/2, 1/2.
- `BKLPRSelmerConjecture.test_trivial` (computation): BKLPR(p) predicts density{rank 0, Ш[p^∞] = 0} = (1/2)∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}).

**Proof route.**

1. Compose the family (ST.0), rank E(ℚ) (EC Layer 6), Ш(E)[p^∞] and Sel_{p^∞} (EC Layer 7 and SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2), densities (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) and Q.
2. Equivalence with the sequence formulation: a split sequence 0 → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r → S → T → 0 with T finite is determined up to isomorphism by (r, T) (routine).

**Acceptance checks.**

- BKLPR(p) predicts density 1/2 · ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) for rank 0 with Ш[p^∞] = 0.

**Consumers.** BKLPR, §5.3 and §5.5 — consequences: 50% rank 0/1, Ш[p^∞] finite for 100%, PR Conjecture 1.1(a); Smith I, §1.1 — the 2^∞-Selmer distribution of twists is consistent with BKLPR Conjecture 1.3

<a id="st5-rational-p-torsion-has-density-zero"></a>

### 5.77 For each prime p, 100% of curves E_{A,B}/ℚ have no rational p-torsion

For every prime p, the set of E_{A,B} with E(ℚ)[p] ≠ 0 has density 0 in the family of elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by naive height.

**Hypotheses.** p prime

**Dependencies.** [The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)](#st0-invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs`); [Arithmetic families: objects up to equivalence, ordered by a Northcott height, with weighted and unweighted counting functions](#st0-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/arithmetic-family`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.2`; [0% of elliptic curves have rational 2-torsion](#st4-rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero`)

**Sources.** [P/poonen-isotropic-2012](#source-p-poonen-isotropic-2012), §5, first paragraph, p. 21. The statement and its route. [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §5.5, Lemma 5.7 and proof, p. 19. All-torsion version; only one prime p is needed here, so no uniform torsion bound is used.

**Proof route.**

1. p = 2: this is ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rational-two-torsion-has-density-zero (an integer root t of x³ + Ax + B gives B = −t³ − At with |t| ≪ X^{1/6}, so O(X^{1/2}) pairs against ≍ X^{5/6} curves).
2. p odd: E(ℚ)[p] ≠ 0 forces a rational root of the p-division polynomial of E_{A,B}. The generic curve over ℚ(A, B) has no rational p-torsion (its mod-p image is GL_2(𝔽_p); gap 'Generic mod-p image'), so the set is contained in a thin set of (A, B) ∈ ℤ², which by the counting form of Hilbert irreducibility has o(X^{5/6}) points in the box |A| ≪ X^{1/3}, |B| ≪ X^{1/2} (request InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.2).

**Acceptance checks.**

- The Tate normal forms show infinitely many curves with rational 3-, 5- and 7-torsion, so the set is infinite; it has density zero only.

<a id="st5-bklpr-conjecture-implies-rank-and-selmer-laws"></a>

### 5.78 Consequences of the BKLPR conjecture: rank law, finiteness of Ш[p^∞] and the Poonen–Rains law

Assume BKLPR(p) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-selmer-conjecture) for a prime p. Then over E_{A,B}/ℚ ordered by height: (i) the sets of curves of rank 0 and of rank 1 each have density 1/2, and rank ≥ 2 has density 0; (ii) Ш(E)[p^∞] is finite for a density-one set of E; (iii) for every d, the set {E : dim_{𝔽_p} Sel_p(E) = d} has density a_d, i.e. clause (a) of PR(p) holds.

**Hypotheses.** BKLPR(p)

**Dependencies.** [The BKLPR conjecture for p^∞-Selmer sequences over ℚ (as a stated proposition)](#st5-bklpr-selmer-conjecture) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-selmer-conjecture`); [The BKLPR model for the p^∞-Selmer sequence](#st5-bklpr-model) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model`); [For each prime p, 100% of curves E_{A,B}/ℚ have no rational p-torsion](#st5-rational-p-torsion-has-density-zero) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/rational-p-torsion-has-density-zero`); [Random alternating kernels have the Poonen–Rains law in the parity-averaged limit](#st5-alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains`); [The only rank law compatible with the Selmer and Ш models is 50% rank 0, 50% rank 1](#st5-delaunay-compatibility-of-the-selmer-model) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-compatibility-of-the-selmer-model`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`); [The Poonen–Rains conjecture for p-Selmer groups over ℚ (as a stated proposition)](#st5-poonen-rains-selmer-conjecture) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-selmer-conjecture`)

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §1.3, list after Remark 1.5, p. 3. The three consequences. [P/bhargava-modeling-2015](#source-p-bhargava-modeling-2015), §5.5, Proposition 5.9, p. 19. Sel_{p^e} ≅ Sel_{p^∞}[p^e] for torsion-free E.

**Proof route.**

1. (i),(ii): sum the densities Q(r, G) over G (countably many classes; Σ_G Q(r, G) = 1/2 for r ≤ 1, 0 for r ≥ 2) — the density of a countable union needs a tightness step: the densities of the finitely many-G events are lower densities, and 1 − Σ_{r ≤ 1, G} Q(r, G) = 0 bounds the upper density of the complement (routine with ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family, API familyLowerDensity_compl).
2. (iii): off the density-zero set of curves with E(ℚ)[p] ≠ 0 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/rational-p-torsion-has-density-zero), Sel_p(E) ≅ Sel_{p^∞}(E)[p] (BKLPR Proposition 5.9(c); Kummer sequences of EC Layer 7), so dim Sel_p(E) = r + dim Ш[p^∞][p].
3. Under Q, r + dim T[p] has the Poonen–Rains law (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bklpr-model, API bklprModel_selmer_p_rank; for r = 0 from the kernel law of alternating matrices, ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains, and for r = 1 from the identity a_{2n+1} = (1/2)Prob(X_{Ш[p],1} = 2n) of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/delaunay-compatibility-of-the-selmer-model together with the equality of the p-rank marginal of A_1 with Delaunay's X_{Ш[p],1} (gap 'p-rank marginal of A_1')).
4. Sum the densities over the classes with given r + dim G[p], as in the first step.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The conclusion (i) is Goldfeld–Katz–Sarnak's minimalist prediction; it follows from BKLPR(p) for a single p.

<a id="st5-average-size-of-the-3-selmer-group"></a>

### 5.79 Bhargava–Shankar: the average size of the 3-Selmer group is 4

When the curves of any nonempty subfamily of E_{A,B}/ℚ defined by finitely many congruence conditions are ordered by height, the average of #Sel_3(E) exists and equals 4. In particular (the whole family) the average size of Sel_3(E) is 4. Family: elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B with A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0 and no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B (one representative of each ℚ-isomorphism class), ordered by H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0 and Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 8); a subfamily defined by finitely many congruence conditions is the set of E_{A,B} with (A, B) in a finite union of residue classes modulo some N (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions). Averages are first moments in the sense of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family; Sel_n(E) is the n-Selmer group of EllipticCurves Layer 7.

**Hypotheses.** F a family of E_{A,B}/ℚ defined by finitely many congruence conditions on (A, B); F is nonempty and its height counting function tends to infinity; finite congruence conditions must admit minimal nonsingular models. Empty congruence families are excluded.

**Dependencies.** [Families defined by local conditions, local densities and largeness](#st0-family-defined-by-local-conditions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions`); [The eligible invariant pairs ordered by H(I, J), with the curve normalisation 27·H_E = 4·H′ (the binary-quartic invariant and height interface)](#st0-invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`); [Ternary cubic forms and their invariants c_4, c_6](#st1-ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants`); [c_4 and c_6 are SL3-invariants of weights 4 and 6](#st1-invariance-of-ternary-cubic-invariants) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/invariance-of-ternary-cubic-invariants`); [Genus-one model stabilizer schemes in degrees2–5](#st1-refinement-genus-one-stabilizer-schemes) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/refinement-genus-one-stabilizer-schemes`); [Ternary-cubic acceptable-weight count](#st2-refinement-ternary-cubic-acceptable-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2/refinement-ternary-cubic-acceptable-count`); [Theorem 3.1: the average size of S_2(E) over a large family is 3](#st4-average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/average-size-of-the-2-selmer-group-is-three`)

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-ternary-2015](#source-p-bhargava-ternary-2015), §1, Theorem 1, p. 1 (arXiv v2). The theorem for the whole family. [P/bhargava-ternary-2015](#source-p-bhargava-ternary-2015), §1, Theorem 3, p. 1 (arXiv v2). The congruence-family version. [P/bhargava-ternary-2015](#source-p-bhargava-ternary-2015), §1, p. 2 (arXiv v2). Method: ternary cubic forms and SL_3.

**Proof route.**

1. Parametrisation (source §3): 3-Selmer elements of E_{A,B} correspond to PGL_3(ℚ)-classes for the determinant-twisted action γ·f(x)=det(γ)⁻¹f(xγ) of locally soluble ternary cubic forms with invariants (I, J) matching (A, B) (up to fixed scalars), with integral representatives and stabiliser E[3]; this is a genus-one orbit parametrisation in the scope of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1 (gap 'Orbit parametrisations of 3-, 4- and 5-Selmer elements').
2. Counting (source §2): the number of SL_3(ℤ)-classes of strongly irreducible integral ternary cubic forms (no rational flex) of height < X, via averaging over a fundamental domain for SL_3(ℤ) acting on SL_3(ℝ) and cutting off the cusp, is (vol) · X^{5/6} + o(X^{5/6}); this is the geometry-of-numbers step of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.2 for the representation Sym³(3) of SL_3, with Davenport's lemma imported from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4.
3. Sieve to locally soluble forms and to F (source §3): multiply by local masses; the uniformity estimate for infinitely many congruence conditions is the ST.2 tail estimate.
4. Mass computation: the product of local masses and the Tamagawa number τ(PGL_3) = 3 give 3 nontrivial elements on average; add the identity element: 1 + 3 = 4 = σ(3). The smooth finite-field ternary-cubic count in source Lemma 33 must use stack weights: the claim of exactly one F_p-isomorphism class per j is false because of twists. For each elliptic curve, degree-3 line bundles modulo translations carry mass #E(F_p)/3E(F_p) divided by #E[3](F_p), which is 1; summing 1/#Aut(E) over elliptic curves gives p. Equation scalings then give p(p−1)#PGL₃(F_p). This repairs the stated finite-field count without the false j-class assertion.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The value 4 = 3 + 1 is the Poonen–Rains prediction p + 1 at p = 3 and BS(3) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bhargava-shankar-selmer-average-conjecture).
- Independent of the congruence family: the average is 4 for every such F (contrast: twist families, BKLOS).

<a id="st5-average-rank-bound-from-the-3-selmer-average"></a>

### 5.80 The average 3-Selmer rank, hence the average rank, is at most 7/6

Over E_{A,B}/ℚ ordered by height, the upper average of the 3-Selmer rank r_3(E) := dim_{𝔽_3} Sel_3(E) is at most 7/6; hence the upper average of rank E(ℚ) is at most 7/6 < 1.17. Family: elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B with A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0 and no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B (one representative of each ℚ-isomorphism class), ordered by H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0 and Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 8); a subfamily defined by finitely many congruence conditions is the set of E_{A,B} with (A, B) in a finite union of residue classes modulo some N (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/family-defined-by-local-conditions). Averages are first moments in the sense of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family; Sel_n(E) is the n-Selmer group of EllipticCurves Layer 7.

**Hypotheses.** the average of #Sel_3 is 4 (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/average-size-of-the-3-selmer-group)

**Dependencies.** [Bhargava–Shankar: the average size of the 3-Selmer group is 4](#st5-average-size-of-the-3-selmer-group) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/average-size-of-the-3-selmer-group`); [Higher height moments in an arithmetic family](#st5-height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family`); [Corollary 1.2: average 2-Selmer rank and average rank at most 1.5](#st4-rank-bound-from-the-selmer-average) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rank-bound-from-the-selmer-average`)

**Upstream contracts.** tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves#layer-7-selmer-groups-and-sha-aec-x4

**Sources.** [P/bhargava-ternary-2015](#source-p-bhargava-ternary-2015), §1, Corollary 2, p. 1 (arXiv v2). Statement with the inequality 6r − 3 ≤ 3^r.

**Proof route.**

1. For every integer r ≥ 0, 6r − 3 ≤ 3^r (equality at r = 1, 2; convexity).
2. At each nonempty height cutoff, the pointwise inequality gives 6·Avg(r₃)≤Avg(3^{r₃})+3. Take limsup and use Avg(3^{r₃})→4 to obtain M⁺₁(r₃)≤7/6. This is an affine inequality at finite cutoffs; an upper moment is not generally linear under sums.
3. rank E(ℚ) ≤ r_3(E) since E(ℚ)/3E(ℚ) ↪ Sel_3(E) (EllipticCurves Layer 7), the step of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.4/rank-bound-from-the-selmer-average.

**Acceptance checks.**

- With 2r ≤ 2^r and the 2-Selmer average 3 the same argument gives the ST.4 bound 3/2.
