**Dependencies.** [Real discriminant slices over F_q(t) are monic squarefree polynomials of even degree](#st5-real-exact-slice-parametrization) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/real-exact-slice-parametrization`); [The convergence mode 'fixed large degree, q → ∞'](#st5-eventual-degree-large-q-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.4`; `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; [Rigid finite-height and exact-slice averages](#st0-wood-average-normalizations) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-average-normalizations`); [Marked global extensions and infinity conventions](#st0-wood-infinity-and-type-adapter) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-infinity-and-type-adapter`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, real case, p.25 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The real case of Theorem 4.8.

**Proof route.**

1. Proposition 4.4, second bijection (IG.4; PAPER-WOOD-19 /74, /75): triples (K, ρ, y) ↔ marked (G′, c)-extensions of trivial infinity type; the quadratic discriminant has norm q^{Σ n_i} (∞ unramified; the printed Σ n_i + 1 is sourceIssues ArithmeticStatistics/E671).
2. Theorem 4.5(2)–(3) and Theorem 4.7 (IG.5) for CHur^{c,1}_{G′,2n}: one Frobenius-fixed component with q^{2n} + O_n(q^{2n−1/2}) points.
3. #RQ_{=q^{2n}} = q^{2n} − q^{2n−1} (ST.5/real-exact-slice-parametrization).

**Acceptance checks.**

- This is the rigid pair count; dividing by |c|·|Aut_{G′}(G)| (ST.3's conversion) gives E^+.
- The printed discriminant sentence is corrected (E671).

<a id="st5-imaginary-normalized-nonabelian-moment"></a>

### 5.168 Wood Theorem 1.2, good imaginary case

Let G be finite and G′ ≤ G ≀ S₂ admissible, good and centre-free, c its outside involutions. For n sufficiently large, E⁻_{F_q(t), q^{2n}}(G, G′)/|H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| → 1/|Aut_{G′}(G)| as q → ∞ with (q, |G′|) = 1, where E⁻ is the average number of unramified G-extensions L/K split at ∞ with Gal(L̃/F_q(t)) of type G′, over K ∈ IQ_{=q^{2n}}, and H₂(G′, c) is the reduced Schur multiplier. The torsion count |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| varies with q and is divided out inside the limit.

**Hypotheses.** G′ admissible, good, Z(G′) = 1; q coprime to |G′|; n ≥ n₀(G, G′)

**Dependencies.** [Wood Theorem 4.8, imaginary good case: unit moment per component invariant](#st5-imaginary-per-component-unit-moment) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/imaginary-per-component-unit-moment`); [The convergence mode 'fixed large degree, q → ∞'](#st5-eventual-degree-large-q-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit`); [Nonabelian quadratic-field moments and predictions](#st3-nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3/nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; `InductionRestrictionPartII:RS.4`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Theorem 1.2, p.2 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.379). Statement of Theorem 1.2. [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 1.2, p.23 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.407). Deduction from Theorem 4.8. [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), §8.2, table p.34 (arXiv v2). The row for C₃² lists reduced Schur multiplier C₃, refuting the packet’s claim that this multiplier correction always vanishes for odd abelian G.

**Proof route.**

1. The Frobenius-fixed component invariants of the imaginary slice number exactly |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| (Wood Theorem 4.5(3) with Proposition 4.1; gap 'Reduced Schur multiplier inputs': PAPER-WOOD-19 /68–/70, owner InductionRestrictionPartIIReducedSchur).
2. Sum ST.5/imaginary-per-component-unit-moment over them: along q with |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| = d fixed, Ẽ⁻ → d; since d takes finitely many values the normalised ratio Ẽ⁻/|H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| → 1 along all allowed q. Use the component-uniform constant K_{2n−1} of Theorem 4.7, so summing over invariants that vary with q preserves a uniform O_n(q⁻¹ᐟ²) estimate.
3. Convert rigid to unrigid: E⁻ = Ẽ⁻/|Aut_{G′}(G)| (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3, PAPER-WOOD-19 /13).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For nontrivial odd abelian G, the generalised dihedral G′ is good, but its reduced multiplier need not be trivial. Wood §8.2 lists G=C₃² with H₂(G′,c)=C₃: the normaliser is 3 for q≡1 mod 3 and 1 for q≡2 mod 3. The raw Cohen–Lenstra unit surjection moment follows when gcd(q−1,|G|)=1; the displayed normalised theorem includes the roots-of-unity correction.
- Not the fixed-q large-discriminant statement (ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit).

<a id="st5-real-normalized-nonabelian-moment"></a>

### 5.169 Wood Theorem 1.2, good real case

With G, G′, c as in ST.5/imaginary-normalized-nonabelian-moment (G′ good), for n sufficiently large, E⁺_{F_q(t), q^{2n}}(G, G′)/|H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| → 1/(|c|·|Aut_{G′}(G)|) as q → ∞ with (q, |G′|) = 1.

**Hypotheses.** G′ admissible, good, Z(G′) = 1; q coprime to |G′|; n ≥ n₀(G, G′)

**Dependencies.** [Wood Theorem 4.8, real good case: unit moment per component invariant](#st5-real-per-component-unit-moment) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/real-per-component-unit-moment`); [The convergence mode 'fixed large degree, q → ∞'](#st5-eventual-degree-large-q-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit`); [Nonabelian quadratic-field moments and predictions](#st3-nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3/nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; `InductionRestrictionPartII:RS.4`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Theorem 1.2, p.2 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.379). The torsion normalisation and N_{G′}.

**Proof route.**

1. Sum ST.5/real-per-component-unit-moment over the |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| Frobenius-fixed invariants of the real slice (Proposition 4.1; gap 'Reduced Schur multiplier inputs').
2. Convert rigid to unrigid with the good real multiplicity A(G, G′) = |c|·|Aut_{G′}(G)| (Wood Lemma 2.1; ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3, PAPER-WOOD-19 /17).

**Acceptance checks.**

- For nontrivial odd abelian G, |c|=|G| and the normalised value is 1/(|G|·|Aut G|). The raw real Cohen–Lenstra moment requires trivial (q−1)-torsion in the reduced multiplier, for example gcd(q−1,|G|)=1.
- For bad G′ the multiplicity A(G, G′) is not |c||Aut_{G′}(G)|.

<a id="st5-stable-parity-multidegree-count"></a>

### 5.170 Exact count of stable parity multidegrees (stars and bars)

Let N ≥ 1, N₀ ≥ 0, d ≥ 0 and ε ∈ {0, 1}^N. Let a_i be the least integer ≥ N₀ with a_i ≡ ε_i (mod 2). The number of m ∈ Z_{≥0}^N with m_i ≥ N₀, m_i ≡ ε_i (mod 2) and Σ m_i = d is the binomial coefficient C(L + N − 1, N − 1) if L := (d − Σ a_i)/2 is a nonnegative integer, and 0 otherwise.

**Hypotheses.** N ≥ 1, N₀ ≥ 0, d ≥ 0, ε ∈ {0,1}^N

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Nat.choose`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The parity-vector count, made exact.

**Proof route.**

1. The map m_i = a_i + 2z_i is a bijection between such m and z ∈ Z_{≥0}^N with Σ z_i = L.
2. Weak compositions of L into N parts number C(L + N − 1, N − 1) (Mathlib Nat.choose and the stars-and-bars count); when d − Σ a_i is odd or negative the set is empty.

**Acceptance checks.**

- N = 1: the count is 1 if d ≥ N₀ and d ≡ ε₁ (mod 2), else 0.
- N = 2, N₀ = 0, ε = (0, 0), d = 4: L = 2, count C(3, 1) = 3 ({(0,4), (2,2), (4,0)}).

<a id="st5-many-large-parity-vectors"></a>

### 5.171 Many large parity vectors

For N ≥ 2, N₀ ≥ 0 and ε ∈ {0,1}^N there is v > 0 (depending only on N, N₀) such that for all sufficiently large d with d ≡ Σ ε_i (mod 2), the number of m ∈ Z^N with m_i ≥ N₀, m_i ≡ ε_i (mod 2) and Σ m_i = d is at least v·d^{N−1}.

**Hypotheses.** N ≥ 2; d ≡ Σ ε_i (mod 2), d large

**Dependencies.** [Exact count of stable parity multidegrees (stars and bars)](#st5-stable-parity-multidegree-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count`); `mathlib:Nat.choose`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The lower bound on the number of good parity vectors.

**Proof route.**

1. By ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count the number is C(L + N − 1, N − 1) with L = (d − Σ a_i)/2 ≥ d/2 − N(N₀ + 1).
2. C(L + N − 1, N − 1) ≥ L^{N−1}/(N − 1)!, which is ≥ v d^{N−1} for d large.

**Acceptance checks.**

- N = 2: the count grows linearly in d.
- The constant does not depend on q.

<a id="st5-bad-type-lower-bound"></a>

### 5.172 Wood Theorem 4.8, bad types: a liminf lower bound

Let G′ ≤ G ≀ S₂ be admissible and centre-free but not good, with N_{G′} ≥ 2 classes of outside involutions. There is w > 0 depending only on G, G′ such that for n sufficiently large, liminf_{q→∞, (q,|G′|)=1} Ẽ^±_{F_q(t), q^{2n}}(G, G′)/|H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| ≥ w·n^{N_{G′}−1}. The printed statement asserts a limit; only this liminf bound is proved (sourceIssues ArithmeticStatistics/E668).

**Hypotheses.** G′ admissible, centre-free, not good; q coprime to |G′|; n large

**Dependencies.** [Many large parity vectors](#st5-many-large-parity-vectors) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/many-large-parity-vectors`); [Imaginary discriminant slices over F_q(t) are monic squarefree polynomials of odd degree](#st5-imaginary-exact-slice-parametrization) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/imaginary-exact-slice-parametrization`); [Real discriminant slices over F_q(t) are monic squarefree polynomials of even degree](#st5-real-exact-slice-parametrization) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/real-exact-slice-parametrization`); [The convergence mode 'fixed large degree, q → ∞'](#st5-eventual-degree-large-q-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.4`; `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; [Rigid finite-height and exact-slice averages](#st0-wood-average-normalizations) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-average-normalizations`); [Marked global extensions and infinity conventions](#st0-wood-infinity-and-type-adapter) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-infinity-and-type-adapter`); `InductionRestrictionPartII:RS.4`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.24–25 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The bad-type conclusion, which the argument proves as a liminf bound.

**Proof route.**

1. Keep only multidegrees m with Σ m_i = 2n − 1 (imaginary; 2n real), every m_i ≥ N₀ and the parities of Wood Proposition 4.1 (m_1 odd, others even, imaginary; all even, real): at least v n^{N−1} of them (ST.5/many-large-parity-vectors).
2. For each such m the Frobenius-fixed components number exactly |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| (Theorem 4.5(3) (IG.5) and Proposition 4.1; gap 'Reduced Schur multiplier inputs'), each with q^{Σ m_i} + O_n(q^{Σ m_i − 1/2}) points (Theorem 4.7, IG.5).
3. All other components contribute nonnegatively; divide by #IQ_{=q^{2n}} (or #RQ) and |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]|, then take liminf in q.

**Acceptance checks.**

- N_{G′} = 1 (good) is excluded; there the limit exists (ST.5/imaginary-normalized-nonabelian-moment).
- No upper bound and no existence of the limit is claimed (ST.5/printed-bad-type-ordinary-limit-assertion).

<a id="st5-bad-type-normalization-transfer"></a>

### 5.173 Transfer of the bad-type bound to unrigid averages

In ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound, the same liminf lower bound (with a smaller positive constant) holds for the unrigid averages E^±_{F_q(t), q^{2n}}(G, G′)/|H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]|: E⁻ = Ẽ⁻/|Aut_{G′}(G)| and E⁺ = Ẽ⁺/A(G, G′), where A(G, G′) is the real rigidification multiplicity (not |c||Aut_{G′}(G)| for bad G′).

**Hypotheses.** as in ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound

**Dependencies.** [Wood Theorem 4.8, bad types: a liminf lower bound](#st5-bad-type-lower-bound) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound`); [Nonabelian quadratic-field moments and predictions](#st3-nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3/nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface`); [Rigid finite-height and exact-slice averages](#st0-wood-average-normalizations) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-average-normalizations`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Theorem 1.2, p.2 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.379). The printed bad-type clause of Theorem 1.2 (text layer of the displayed cases).

**Proof route.**

1. The rigidification multiplicities |Aut_{G′}(G)| and A(G, G′) are positive and depend only on G, G′ (ArithmeticStatistics:ST.3, PAPER-WOOD-19 /13; ST.0 for A(G, G′), /16).
2. Divide the bound of ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound by them.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For bad G′ the good-only formula A = |c||Aut_{G′}(G)| is not used.
- This does not prove existence of a limit.

<a id="st5-printed-bad-type-ordinary-limit-assertion"></a>

### 5.174 The printed bad-type limit assertion, as an unproved proposition

For G′ admissible, centre-free and bad, with N = N_{G′}, the proposition PBL(G, G′): there are w > 0 and n₀ such that for every n ≥ n₀ the limit L_n := lim_{q→∞, (q,|G′|)=1} Ẽ^±_{F_q(t), q^{2n}}(G, G′)/|H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| exists and L_n ≥ w·n^{N−1}. This is a precise statement not proved by the argument audited in this packet; its proved replacement is ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound (liminf), and by ST.5/ordinary-limit-iff-eventual-profile-constancy its existence clause is equivalent to eventual constancy in q of the whole component profile.

**Hypotheses.** G′ admissible, centre-free, not good; the limit is in the mode of ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit

**Dependencies.** [The convergence mode 'fixed large degree, q → ∞'](#st5-eventual-degree-large-q-limit) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/eventual-degree-large-q-limit`); [Rigid finite-height and exact-slice averages](#st0-wood-average-normalizations) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-average-normalizations`); [Marked global extensions and infinity conventions](#st0-wood-infinity-and-type-adapter) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.0/wood-infinity-and-type-adapter`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.23 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.406). The printed bad-type limit. [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The proof discards all multidegrees outside C, which only bounds the liminf.

**API.**

- `PrintedBadTypeLimitAssertion` (constructor): The proposition ∃ w > 0, ∃ n₀, ∀ n ≥ n₀, ∃ L, E(·, n)/M → L along A_m and w n^{N−1} ≤ L.
- `PrintedBadTypeLimitAssertion.liminf_bound` (relation): PBL implies the eventual liminf bound liminf_q E(q, n)/M(q) ≥ w n^{N−1}.
- `PrintedBadTypeLimitAssertion.of_eventually_const` (constructor): If, for all large n, E(q, n)/M(q) is eventually constant in q with value ≥ w n^{N−1}, then PBL holds.

**Checks.**

- `PrintedBadTypeLimitAssertion.test_const` (computation): For E(q, n) = n^{N−1} and M ≡ 1, PBL holds with w = 1.
- `PrintedBadTypeLimitAssertion.test_zero` (degenerate): For E ≡ 0 and N = 1, PBL fails (w > 0).
- `PrintedBadTypeLimitAssertion.test_oscillating` (non-example): For E(q, n) = n^{N−1}·c(q) with c(q) = 3 if q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and c(q) = 1 otherwise, and M ≡ 1, the liminf bound holds with w = 1 but PBL fails (both residues occur for infinitely many allowed prime powers, so there is no limit in q).

**Proof route.**

1. Define PBL for an arbitrary function E(q, n) with normaliser M(q) ≥ 1 and exponent N: ∃ w > 0, ∃ n₀, ∀ n ≥ n₀, ∃ L, (E(·, n)/M → L along A_{|G′|}) ∧ w n^{N−1} ≤ L; specialise E = Ẽ^±, M(q) = |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]|.
2. PBL implies the liminf bound; the converse fails for oscillating functions.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The packet supplies neither a proof of this ordinary-limit assertion nor a counterexample for an admissible bad type; this is not a claim about the current global state of the literature.
- The source records the limit as proved (sourceIssues ArithmeticStatistics/E668).

**Consumers.** Wood 2019 Theorems 1.2 and 4.8, bad case (ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound) — the printed conclusion, kept as a hypothesis-free proposition to be proved or refuted; ST.5/ordinary-limit-iff-eventual-profile-constancy — reduces the existence clause of PBL to eventual constancy of the component profile

<a id="st5-whole-fixed-degree-component-profile"></a>

### 5.175 The whole fixed-degree component profile

Fix a centre-free admissible F = G′ with outside involution classes c_1, …, c_N, a sign ± and n ≥ 2; put d = 2n − 1 and g = (1, 1, σ) in the imaginary case, d = 2n and g = 1 in the real case. For q coprime to |F| let C_n^±(q) be the total number of Frobenius-fixed geometric components of ⊔_m CHur^{c,g}_{F,m} over all multidegrees m ∈ Z_{≥0}^N with Σ m_i = d, and M(q) := |H₂(F, c)[q − 1]| ≥ 1. The profile is P_n^±(q) := C_n^±(q)/M(q) ∈ Q_{≥0}. It includes every multidegree, not only the stable range m_i ≥ N₀. In the suggested formalisation the geometric counts are carried as data: a function m ↦ C_m(q) and the normaliser M.

**Hypotheses.** F centre-free admissible; q coprime to |F|; n ≥ 2; all multidegrees of total degree d are included

**Dependencies.** `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; `mathlib:Nat.choose`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Theorem 4.5(3), p.21 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.404). Component counts, classified only in the stable range; the profile sums all ranges.

**API.**

- `FixedDegreeComponentData` (structure): Data (N, d, counts C_m(q) for m of total degree d, normaliser M(q) ≥ 1) abstracting the Hurwitz component counts.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile` (constructor): P(q) := (Σ_{Σ m_i = d} C_m(q))/M(q) ∈ Q.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile_nonneg` (other): P(q) ≥ 0.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile_mem_finite` (characterisation): If Σ_m C_m(q) ≤ B and M(q) ≤ K for all q, then P takes values in the finite set {a/b : 0 ≤ a ≤ B, 1 ≤ b ≤ K}.

**Checks.**

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.test_profile_zero` (degenerate): If every count C_m(q) is 0 then the profile is 0.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.test_profile_single` (computation): For N = 1, d = 3, C_{(3)}(q) = 2 and M(q) = 1, the profile is 2.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.test_profile_counts_boundary` (non-example): For N = 2, d = 2, N₀ = 1 and counts C_{(2,0)} = 1, C_{(1,1)} = 0, C_{(0,2)} = 0, M = 1, the profile is 1 although the stable-range sum (all m_i ≥ 1) is 0.

**Proof route.**

1. The set of multidegrees of total degree d is finite (the antidiagonal tuples).
2. Geometric components are open and closed (the schemes are smooth, finite étale over Conf_d: IG.5), and Frobenius permutes them; C_m(q) counts the fixed ones.
3. P_n^±(q) := (Σ_m C_m(q))/M(q).

**Acceptance checks.**

- If every C_m(q) = 0 the profile is 0.
- N = 1: a single multidegree (d).

**Consumers.** ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes — the rigid moment divided by M(q) differs from the profile by O_n(q^{−1/2}); ST.5/ordinary-limit-iff-eventual-profile-constancy — the existence of the ordinary limit is decided by the profile

<a id="st5-boundary-component-remainder"></a>

### 5.176 Stable and boundary parts of the component profile

In ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile fix the stable threshold N₀ of Wood Theorem 4.5(3). Split the multidegrees of total degree d into the stable ones (every m_i ≥ N₀) and the boundary ones (some m_i < N₀), and C_n(q) = C_{stable,n}(q) + C_{boundary,n}(q) accordingly. The boundary remainder is R_{boundary,n}(q) := C_{boundary,n}(q)/M(q) ≥ 0. No formula for it is assumed: the stable lifting-invariant classification does not describe braid components in the boundary.

**Hypotheses.** as in ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile; N₀ a stable threshold for F

**Dependencies.** [The whole fixed-degree component profile](#st5-whole-fixed-degree-component-profile) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile`)

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The stable range; the remaining multidegrees form the boundary.

**API.**

- `stableMultidegrees` (constructor): The multidegrees m with Σ m_i = d and every m_i ≥ N₀.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.stableCount` (projection): C_stable(q) = Σ over stable multidegrees.
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.boundaryRemainder` (projection): R_boundary(q) = (Σ over non-stable multidegrees)/M(q).
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile_eq_stable_add_boundary` (relation): P(q) = C_stable(q)/M(q) + R_boundary(q).
- `FixedDegreeComponentData.boundaryRemainder_nonneg` (other): R_boundary(q) ≥ 0.

**Checks.**

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.test_boundary_threshold_zero` (degenerate): With N₀ = 0 the boundary remainder is 0 for every q.
- `stableMultidegrees.test_card` (computation): For N = 2, d = 4, N₀ = 1 the stable multidegrees are (1,3), (2,2), (3,1): three of them.
- `stableMultidegrees.test_excludes_small` (non-example): (0, 4) is a multidegree of total degree 4 but not a stable one for N₀ = 1.

**Proof route.**

1. The stable and boundary sets partition the finite set of multidegrees of total degree d.
2. Sum the counts over each part; divide by M(q).

**Acceptance checks.**

- N₀ = 0: every multidegree is stable and the remainder is 0.
- The remainder is nonnegative, which is all the bad-type argument uses.

**Consumers.** ST.5/complete-stable-range-component-sum — computes the stable part exactly; ST.5/printed-bad-type-ordinary-limit-assertion — the uncontrolled boundary part is why only a liminf is proved

<a id="st5-complete-stable-range-component-sum"></a>

### 5.177 The complete stable-range component sum

Let F = G′, c = ⊔_{i ≤ N} c_i its outside involution classes, A = H₂(F, c), g ∈ c ∪ {1}, q odd coprime to |F| and N₀ a stable threshold. For a set S ⊆ {0,1}^N of surviving parity vectors (those compatible with [g] in F^ab and with v₂(q − 1) ≥ t_A(b(g, ε)) + 1, Wood Proposition 4.1/Remark 4.2 as refined in PAPER-WOOD-19 /301, /304), define Σ_stable(d) := Σ_{ε ∈ S} #{m : m_i ≥ N₀, m_i ≡ ε_i (mod 2), Σ m_i = d}. Then C_{stable,d}^g(q)/|A[q − 1]| = Σ_stable(d): each surviving parity class of stable multidegrees contributes exactly |A[q − 1]| Frobenius-fixed components per multidegree, the others none. The boundary remainder is not included.

**Hypotheses.** F centre-free admissible, q odd coprime to |F|; N₀ a stable threshold; S the surviving parity vectors determined by the reduced-Schur-multiplier criterion

**Dependencies.** [Exact count of stable parity multidegrees (stars and bars)](#st5-stable-parity-multidegree-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count`); [Stable and boundary parts of the component profile](#st5-boundary-component-remainder) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/boundary-component-remainder`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; `InductionRestrictionPartII:RS.4`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Remark 4.2, p.19 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.401). The parity criterion and the fibre size.

**API.**

- `parityMultidegreeCount` (data): #{m ∈ N^N : m_i ≥ N₀, m_i ≡ ε_i mod 2, Σ m_i = d}.
- `stableRangeComponentSum` (constructor): Σ_stable(d) = Σ_{ε ∈ S} parityMultidegreeCount N N₀ d ε.
- `stableRangeComponentSum_empty` (simp): Σ_stable = 0 for S = ∅.
- `stableRangeComponentSum_union` (relation): Additivity over disjoint unions of parity sets.
- `parityMultidegreeCount_eq` (characterisation): The stars-and-bars formula of ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count.

**Checks.**

- `stableRangeComponentSum.test_empty` (degenerate): stableRangeComponentSum N N₀ d ∅ = 0.
- `stableRangeComponentSum.test_one_part` (computation): For N = 1, N₀ = 0, d = 4 and S = {0}: the sum is 1.
- `stableRangeComponentSum.test_parity_mismatch` (non-example): For N = 1, N₀ = 0, d = 4 and S = {1}: the sum is 0 (an odd part cannot have even total).

**Proof route.**

1. Define the parity-class count (ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count) and sum it over S.
2. For each stable m, the Frobenius-fixed components are the q^{−1}-fixed lifting invariants over (g, m) (Theorem 4.5(3), IG.5); their number is |A[q − 1]| if the parity vector of m survives and 0 otherwise (PAPER-WOOD-19 /301, /304; gap 'Reduced Schur multiplier inputs').
3. The survival criterion depends only on m mod 2, so the stable count is |A[q − 1]| times Σ_stable(d).

**Acceptance checks.**

- S = ∅ gives 0.
- N = 1, N₀ = 0, S = {0}, d = 4: Σ_stable(4) = 1.

**Consumers.** ST.5/weight-polynomial-formula-for-the-stable-orthant — its generating function is computed in closed form; ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound — a single surviving parity class already gives the liminf bound

<a id="st5-moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes"></a>

### 5.178 The normalised rigid moment differs from the component profile by O(q^{−1/2})

In ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile, let B_n bound the total number of geometric components (uniformly in q) and K_d be the uniform component error of Wood Theorem 4.7. Then |Ẽ_n^±(q)/M(q) − P_n^±(q)| ≤ B_n(K_d q^{−1/2} + q^{−1})/(1 − q^{−1}); in particular the difference is O_n(q^{−1/2}). One may take B_n = D_d, the degree of the finite étale map CHur_{F,d} → Conf_d.

**Hypotheses.** as in ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile; B_n a q-uniform bound on the number of geometric components

**Dependencies.** [The whole fixed-degree component profile](#st5-whole-fixed-degree-component-profile) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile`); [Imaginary discriminant slices over F_q(t) are monic squarefree polynomials of odd degree](#st5-imaginary-exact-slice-parametrization) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/imaginary-exact-slice-parametrization`); [Real discriminant slices over F_q(t) are monic squarefree polynomials of even degree](#st5-real-exact-slice-parametrization) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/real-exact-slice-parametrization`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.4`; `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Theorem 4.7, p.21 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.404–405). The uniform component estimate summed here.

**Proof route.**

1. A rational point lies on a Frobenius-fixed component; non-fixed open and closed components contribute no F_q-points.
2. Each fixed component C has |#C(F_q) − q^d| ≤ K_d q^{d−1/2} (Theorem 4.7, IG.5; PAPER-WOOD-19 /88); the rigid moment numerator is Σ_C #C(F_q) (Proposition 4.4, IG.4).
3. The denominator is q^d(1 − q^{−1}) (ST.5/imaginary-exact-slice-parametrization, ST.5/real-exact-slice-parametrization); divide by it and by M(q) ≥ 1, using C_n(q) ≤ B_n.
4. B_n = D_d is q-independent because the degree of CHur_{F,d} → Conf_d is constant over the connected base (IG.5; PAPER-WOOD-19 /314).

**Acceptance checks.**

- If no component is fixed, the moment is O_n(q^{−1/2}).
- The bound is uniform in q at fixed n only.

<a id="st5-ordinary-limit-iff-eventual-profile-constancy"></a>

### 5.179 The ordinary q-limit exists iff the component profile is eventually constant

Under ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes (with M(q) ≤ K uniformly, as M(q) divides |H₂(F, c)|), the limit of Ẽ_n^±(q)/M(q) as q → ∞ along allowed prime powers exists iff P_n^±(q) is eventually equal to a single rational value, and then that value is the limit. This is a criterion, not a proof that every bad type satisfies it.

**Hypotheses.** as in ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes; M(q) ≤ K := |H₂(F, c)| for all q

**Dependencies.** [The normalised rigid moment differs from the component profile by O(q^{−1/2})](#st5-moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes`); [The whole fixed-degree component profile](#st5-whole-fixed-degree-component-profile) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile`); `mathlib:Finite.instDiscreteTopology`; `mathlib:Filter.tendsto_pure`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 1.2, p.23 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.407). The normalisation by |H₂(G′, c)[q − 1]| whose finitely many values make the criterion work.

**Proof route.**

1. The profile takes values in the finite set {a/b : 0 ≤ a ≤ B_n, 1 ≤ b ≤ K} (API profile_mem_finite).
2. By ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes the moment converges iff the profile converges, to the same limit.
3. A convergent function with values in a finite subset of R is eventually constant: a finite subset of a T1 space is discrete (Mathlib Finite.instDiscreteTopology) and convergence to a point of a discrete subtype is eventual equality (Mathlib Filter.tendsto_pure).

**Acceptance checks.**

- Constant profile: the limit exists.
- Profile alternating between two values: no limit, even though the liminf bound may hold.

<a id="st5-liminf-limsup-from-recurrent-profile-values"></a>

### 5.180 Liminf and limsup of the moment are the extreme recurrent profile values

Under ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes, let R_n^± be the set of profile values attained for arbitrarily large allowed q. It is a nonempty finite set, and liminf_q Ẽ_n^±(q)/M(q) = min R_n^±, limsup_q Ẽ_n^±(q)/M(q) = max R_n^±. In particular the bad-type bound of ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound bounds every recurrent value from below.

**Hypotheses.** as in ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes

**Dependencies.** [The normalised rigid moment differs from the component profile by O(q^{−1/2})](#st5-moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/moment-minus-component-profile-vanishes`); [The whole fixed-degree component profile](#st5-whole-fixed-degree-component-profile) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/whole-fixed-degree-component-profile`); [Wood Theorem 4.8, bad types: a liminf lower bound](#st5-bad-type-lower-bound) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/bad-type-lower-bound`); `mathlib:Filter.limsup`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proof of Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409). The component counts that the recurrent values refine.

**Proof route.**

1. Finitely many profile values occur (API profile_mem_finite); discard those taken only for boundedly many q; the remaining set is nonempty.
2. Along an unbounded sequence of q with profile value r, the moment tends to r (error O(q^{−1/2})); conversely every limit point of the moment is a limit point of the profile, hence in R_n^±.

**Acceptance checks.**

- If R_n^± is a singleton, the limit exists (ST.5/ordinary-limit-iff-eventual-profile-constancy).
- The printed assertion needs |R_n^±| = 1.

<a id="st5-weight-polynomial-formula-for-the-stable-orthant"></a>

### 5.181 Generating function of the stable-range component sums

In ST.5/complete-stable-range-component-sum, let δ ≡ N₀ (mod 2), 1 = (1, …, 1), and W(X) := Σ_{ε ∈ S} X^{wt(ε + δ·1)} (the weight enumerator of the surviving parities shifted by N₀). Then, as formal power series, Σ_{d ≥ 0} Σ_stable(d) X^d = X^{N·N₀} W(X)/(1 − X²)^N, equivalently (1 − X²)^N · Σ_d Σ_stable(d) X^d = X^{N N₀} W(X).

**Hypotheses.** as in ST.5/complete-stable-range-component-sum

**Dependencies.** [The complete stable-range component sum](#st5-complete-stable-range-component-sum) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/complete-stable-range-component-sum`); [Exact count of stable parity multidegrees (stars and bars)](#st5-stable-parity-multidegree-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count`); `mathlib:PowerSeries`

**Sources.** [P/wood-nonabelian-2019](#source-p-wood-nonabelian-2019), Proposition 4.1, p.18 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.400). The parity dependence summed into the generating function.

**Proof route.**

1. For a fixed ε the least allowed coordinate is N₀ + ((ε_i − N₀) mod 2), and the other allowed values add 2z_i, z_i ≥ 0: the generating series of the parity class is X^{N N₀ + wt(ε + δ·1)}/(1 − X²)^N.
2. Sum over ε ∈ S; the coefficient identity is ST.5/stable-parity-multidegree-count (stars and bars). No analytic convergence is used.

**Acceptance checks.**

- N = 1, N₀ = 0, S = {0}: Σ_d Σ_stable(d) X^d = 1/(1 − X²).
- The formula covers only the stable orthant; the boundary remainder is separate.

<a id="st5-surjections-onto-a-semidirect-product"></a>

### 5.182 Surjections onto H ⋊ Γ as tuples (ρ, N, s, φ)

Let Γ be a finite group, H a finite Γ-group and G a profinite group. There is a bijection between Sur(G, H ⋊ Γ) (continuous surjections) and tuples (ρ, N, s, φ) with ρ ∈ Sur(G, Γ), N ⊆ ker ρ a closed normal subgroup of G, s : Γ → G/N a homomorphic section of the induced map ρ : G/N → Γ, and φ : ker ρ/N → H a Γ-isomorphism, where Γ acts on ker ρ/N through s and conjugation. The bijection sends ψ to (projection of ψ to Γ, ker ψ, ψ^{−1} restricted to Γ, ψ|_{ker ρ/N}).

**Hypotheses.** Γ and H are finite, with discrete topologies; H carries the specified Γ-action.; G profinite; homomorphisms continuous, N closed

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:SemidirectProduct`; `mathlib:SemidirectProduct.rightHom`; `mathlib:SemidirectProduct.inr`

**Sources.** [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Lemma 9.1, p.37 (arXiv v2). Statement of Lemma 9.1 (the tuple set (9.2) follows).

**Proof route.**

1. Forward map as stated; ψ^{−1}(Γ) makes sense on G/N ≅ H ⋊ Γ.
2. Inverse: from 1 → ker ρ/N → G/N → Γ → 1 and the section s get G/N ≅ ker ρ/N ⋊ Γ; extend φ to ker ρ/N ⋊ Γ ≅ H ⋊ Γ (Mathlib SemidirectProduct and its universal properties) and compose with G → G/N. Since N is closed and G/N is compact and finite, it is discrete. Thus the resulting algebraic isomorphisms and section are continuous, as required.
3. The two constructions are mutually inverse (direct check).

**Acceptance checks.**

- H = 1: surjections G → Γ correspond to (ρ, ker ρ, the unique section, the unique map).
- Γ = 1: Sur(G, H) ↔ (N, φ) with φ : G/N ≅ H.

<a id="st5-complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate"></a>

### 5.183 Complements of a coprime abelian normal subgroup are conjugate

Let E be a finite group and H ⊴ E an abelian normal subgroup with gcd(|H|, [E : H]) = 1. Then H has a complement in E and any two complements are conjugate by an element of H. Consequently, for Γ finite and H a finite abelian Γ-group with gcd(|H|, |Γ|) = 1, the sections of H ⋊ Γ → Γ form one H-conjugacy orbit, and there are exactly [H : H^Γ] of them.

**Hypotheses.** E finite; H abelian normal; |H| and [E : H] coprime

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Subgroup.exists_right_complement'_of_coprime`; `mathlib:SemidirectProduct`

**Sources.** [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Proof of Lemma 9.3, p.39 (arXiv v2). The section count, proved here for abelian ker ρ/N.

**Proof route.**

1. Existence is Mathlib's Schur–Zassenhaus theorem (Subgroup.exists_right_complement'_of_coprime).
2. Two complements K, K' ≅ Γ := E/H give a 1-cocycle c : Γ → H with k' = c(γ)k; H¹(Γ, H) is killed by |Γ| (corestriction–restriction) and by |H|, hence is 0 when they are coprime, so c is a coboundary c(γ) = hγ(h)^{−1} and K' = h K h^{−1}.
3. Sections of H ⋊ Γ → Γ correspond to complements; H acts on them by conjugation transitively, with stabiliser of the standard section Γ equal to H^Γ.

**Acceptance checks.**

- H = 1: one section.
- Γ = Z/2 acting by −1 on H = Z/3: [H : H^Γ] = 3 sections, the three involutions' subgroups of S_3.

**Interface qualification.** Conjugacy of complements for nonabelian coprime H (Schur–Zassenhaus in general, which needs Feit–Thompson or a solvability hypothesis) is planned by the accepted Part II ArithmeticStatisticsPartIIRandomGammaGroups, which imports ST.5; ST.5 therefore states LWZB Lemma 9.3 and Theorem 1.4 with an explicit section-conjugacy hypothesis and proves that hypothesis here only in the abelian case needed by Corollary 1.5.

<a id="st5-counting-unramified-h-extensions-via-semidirect-extensions"></a>

### 5.184 LWZB Lemma 9.3: moments of unramified H-extensions as counts of H ⋊ Γ-extensions

Let Γ be finite, Q = Q or F_q(t), and H a finite Γ-group with gcd(|H|, |Γ|) = 1 such that (SZ) all sections of H ⋊ Γ → Γ are H-conjugate (true when H is abelian: ST.5/complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate). Let N(H, Γ, D, Q) be the number of surjections Gal(Q̄/Q) → H ⋊ Γ whose H ⋊ Γ-extension K has rDisc K = D, whose H-extension K/K^H is unramified everywhere and split completely above ∞, and whose Γ-extension K^H/Q is split completely at ∞. Then Σ_ρ |Sur_Γ(Gal(K_ρ^{un,∞}/K_ρ)^{(|Γ|′)}, H)| = [H : H^Γ]^{−1} N(H, Γ, D, Q), where ρ runs over surjections Gal(Q̄/Q) → Γ split completely at ∞ with rDisc = D (Γ-extensions with their identification, not isomorphism classes) and the Γ-action is that of the chosen section on the maximal pro-|Γ|′ quotient. Summing instead over isomorphism classes E_Γ(D, Q), the right side acquires the factor |Z(Γ)|/|Γ|.

**Hypotheses.** Γ finite; H finite Γ-group with gcd(|H|, |Γ|) = 1; (SZ): sections of H ⋊ Γ → Γ are H-conjugate; left side summed over surjections ρ (see the correction for isomorphism classes)

**Dependencies.** [Surjections onto H ⋊ Γ as tuples (ρ, N, s, φ)](#st5-surjections-onto-a-semidirect-product) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/surjections-onto-a-semidirect-product`); [Complements of a coprime abelian normal subgroup are conjugate](#st5-complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.4`

**Sources.** [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Lemma 9.3, p.38 (arXiv v2). Statement of Lemma 9.3. [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Introduction, p.3 (arXiv v2). The isomorphism-class normalisation corrected by |Z(Γ)|/|Γ|.

**Proof route.**

1. Apply ST.5/surjections-onto-a-semidirect-product with G = Gal(Q̄/Q).
2. For each ρ, the maximal pro-|Γ|′ quotient ker ρ/M carries a distinguished section s_ρ (LWZB Definition 2.1); tuples with s = s_ρ correspond to Γ-surjections ker ρ/M → H; the local conditions and rDisc = D match on both sides.
3. By (SZ), all sections of G/N → Γ are ker ρ/N-conjugate with stabiliser (ker ρ/N)^Γ, so there are [H : H^Γ] sections, each with the same number of φ's.
4. Isomorphism classes of Γ-extensions are orbits of Inn(Γ) of size [Γ : Z(Γ)] on surjections, and |Sur_Γ(…, H)| is constant on orbits; this gives the factor |Z(Γ)|/|Γ| (sourceIssues ArithmeticStatistics/E673).

**Acceptance checks.**

- H = 1: each isomorphism class of S_3-extensions with its Γ-action gives exactly |Inn(S_3)| = 6 surjections, so N(1,S_3,D,Q) = 6·#E_{S_3}(D,Q). There is at least one totally real example at D = 229: the splitting field of x³ − 4x + 1, an irreducible cubic with positive nonsquare discriminant 229. No uniqueness of that field is needed.
- The moment ratios of Theorem 1.4 are unchanged by the normalisation.

**Interface qualification.** The distinguished section and the Γ-action on Gal(K^#/K) (LWZB Definition 2.1) are planned at InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.4 (PAPER-LIU-WOOD-ZUREICKBROWN-24 route 1).

<a id="st5-liu-wood-zureick-brown-function-field-moments"></a>

### 5.185 LWZB Theorem 1.4: moments of Gal(K^#/K) over F_q(t) as q → ∞

Let Γ be finite and H a finite admissible Γ-group satisfying (SZ). For prime powers q with gcd(q, |Γ||H|) = 1 and gcd(q − 1, |H|) = 1 put R_b(q) := Σ_{n ≤ b} Σ_{K ∈ E_Γ(q^n, F_q(t))} |Sur_Γ(Gal(K^#/K), H)| / Σ_{n ≤ b} |E_Γ(q^n, F_q(t))|, where E_Γ(D, F_q(t)) is the set of Γ-extensions of F_q(t) split completely at ∞ with radical discriminant norm D and K^# is the maximal unramified extension of K split completely above ∞ with all finite subextensions of degree prime to q(q − 1)|Γ|. Then lim_{b→∞} limsup_{q→∞} R_b(q) = lim_{b→∞} liminf_{q→∞} R_b(q) = [H : H^Γ]^{−1}. For every sufficiently large b, every limit point of R_b(q) in q lies within O_G(1/b) of [H : H^Γ]^{−1}; the existence of lim_{q→∞} R_b(q) is not proved.

**Hypotheses.** Γ finite; H finite admissible Γ-group; (SZ); q prime power, gcd(q, |Γ||H|) = 1, gcd(q − 1, |H|) = 1 (these force |H| odd)

**Dependencies.** [LWZB Lemma 9.3: moments of unramified H-extensions as counts of H ⋊ Γ-extensions](#st5-counting-unramified-h-extensions-via-semidirect-extensions) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/counting-unramified-h-extensions-via-semidirect-extensions`); [Top compactly supported cohomology counts Frobenius-fixed components](#st5-top-cohomology-counts-rational-components) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/top-cohomology-counts-rational-components`); `InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5`; `SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2`; `DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.7`

**Sources.** [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Theorem 1.4, p.3 (arXiv v2). Statement (displayed double limit follows). [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Proof of Theorem 1.4, p.41 (arXiv v2). Conclusion of the proof; the inner limit is only bounded.

**Proof route.**

1. Write a_Γ=|Z(Γ)|/|Γ|. The numerator over isomorphism classes is a_Γ[H:H^Γ]⁻¹ Σ_{n≤b}N(H,Γ,q^n,F_q(t)), while the denominator is a_Γ Σ_{n≤b}N(1,Γ,q^n,F_q(t)). Thus a_Γ cancels in the ratio. The Γ-surjections to H factor through Gal(K^#/K), since |H| is prime to q(q−1)|Γ|.
2. N(H, Γ, q^n, F_q(t)) = #Hur^n_{G,c}(F_q) with G = H ⋊ Γ and c the nonidentity elements of the order of their image in Γ; after cancellation, the denominator is Σ_n #Hur^n_{Γ,Γ∖1}(F_q) (LWZB Lemma 10.2, IG.5).
3. If Γ=1, admissibility forces H=1 and the ratio is identically 1, using the unique trivial extension of radical discriminant 1. Otherwise fix an allowed residue a of q modulo |G|² and replace b by b_a, the largest integer ≤b whose residue lies in E_a modulo M_a from Theorem 10.4. The omitted slices have no rational points. Since E_a is nonempty, 0≤b−b_a<M_a; for sufficiently large b this gives b_a≍b, uniformly over the finitely many a. Apply all following top-degree and error estimates at b_a, not at an empty degree-b slice.
4. Grothendieck–Lefschetz (SF.2), Deligne's bound (DWP.7) and the Betti comparison (LWZB Lemma 10.3, IG.5) give |#Hur^b(F_q) − π(q, b) q^b| ≤ B(b) Σ_{j<2b} q^{j/2}, with the top-degree trace counting Frobenius-fixed components (ST.5/top-cohomology-counts-rational-components); lower n contribute O_b(q^{b−1/2}).
5. LWZB Theorem 10.4 (IG.5): π_{G,c}(q, b) = π_Γ(q, b) + O_G(b^{d_Γ(q)−2}) and π_Γ(q, b) ≥ C_G b^{d_Γ(q)−1} on the residues where it is nonzero; so R_b(q) = [H : H^Γ]^{−1}(1 + O_G(b^{−1}) + O_b(q^{−1/2})) along each residue class of q mod |G|², hence every limit point in q lies in [H : H^Γ]^{−1}(1 + O_G(1/b)).
6. Let b → ∞. The printed lim_q is replaced by limsup/liminf (sourceIssues ArithmeticStatistics/E672); the value is the μ_Γ-moment of the random-group model, whose identification (LWZB Theorem 6.2) belongs to ArithmeticStatisticsPartIIRandomGammaGroups and is not used here.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Γ = Z/2, H = Z/3 with inversion: [H : H^Γ]^{−1} = 1/3, the real-quadratic Cohen–Lenstra 3-moment, in the q → ∞ mode.
- Even |H| is excluded by the hypotheses (q or q − 1 is even).

**Interface qualification.** Admissible Γ-groups and Property E (LWZB Definition 2.3, Proposition 2.2) are items of the RandomGammaGroups Part II and of IG.4; here admissibility is used only through LWZB Lemma 10.2 and Theorem 10.4 (IG.5).

<a id="st5-cohen-lenstra-martinet-moments-over-function-fields"></a>

### 5.186 LWZB Corollary 1.5: Cohen–Lenstra–Martinet moments over F_q(t)

Let Γ be finite and H a finite abelian Γ-group with gcd(|H|, |Γ|) = 1 and H^Γ = 1. Then with q running over prime powers with gcd(q, |Γ||H|) = 1 and gcd(q − 1, |H|) = 1, lim_{b→∞} limsup_q and lim_{b→∞} liminf_q of Σ_{n ≤ b} Σ_{K ∈ E_Γ(q^n, F_q(t))} |Sur_Γ(Cl(O_K), H)| / Σ_{n ≤ b} |E_Γ(q^n, F_q(t))| both equal |H|^{−1}.

**Hypotheses.** Γ finite; H finite abelian Γ-group, gcd(|H|, |Γ|) = 1, H^Γ = 1; q as in ST.5/liu-wood-zureick-brown-function-field-moments

**Dependencies.** [LWZB Theorem 1.4: moments of Gal(K^#/K) over F_q(t) as q → ∞](#st5-liu-wood-zureick-brown-function-field-moments) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/liu-wood-zureick-brown-function-field-moments`); [Complements of a coprime abelian normal subgroup are conjugate](#st5-complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate`); `FunctionFieldArithmetic:FA.4`

**Sources.** [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), Corollary 1.5, p.4 (arXiv v2). Statement. [P/liu-unramified-2024](#source-p-liu-unramified-2024), §1, p.4 (arXiv v2). The class-field-theory identification.

**Proof route.**

1. An abelian Γ-group is admissible iff gcd(|H|, |Γ|) = 1 and H^Γ = 1 (LWZB §7.1); (SZ) holds by ST.5/complements-of-a-coprime-abelian-normal-subgroup-are-conjugate.
2. By class field theory for function fields (FunctionFieldArithmetic:FA.4), Gal(K^#/K)^{ab} is the prime-to-q(q − 1)|Γ| part of Cl(O_K), so Γ-surjections onto the abelian H coincide.
3. Apply ST.5/liu-wood-zureick-brown-function-field-moments: [H : H^Γ]^{−1} = |H|^{−1}.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Γ = Z/2 acting by −1 on H = Z/ℓ^k (ℓ odd): the real-quadratic Cohen–Lenstra moment |H|^{−1}.
- Fields are ordered by radical discriminant, not discriminant.

<a id="st5-symmetric-image-obstruction"></a>

### 5.187 The image obstruction for a symmetric border

For a field F, n ≥ 0, a symmetric matrix S in M_n(F), and v in F^n, v belongs to im S if and only if v·z = 0 for every z in ker S. The pairing is the ordinary bilinear coordinate dot product, without conjugation.

**Hypotheses.** F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:Matrix.IsSymm`; `mathlib:Matrix.mulVecLin`; `mathlib:Subspace.forall_mem_dualAnnihilator_apply_eq_zero_iff`; `mathlib:Pi.basisFun`; `mathlib:Pi.basisFun_repr`; `mathlib:Module.Basis.sum_repr`

**Sources.** [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), printed p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). Spells out the image-versus-kernel step behind the first proof’s three border-rank fibers using the pinned dual-annihilator API.

**Proof route.**

1. If v=Sx and Sz=0, symmetry gives v·z=x·Sz=0.
2. For the converse use the native dual-annihilator criterion for W=im S. Every functional φ vanishing on W is a dot product z·(−): take z_i=φ(e_i) and expand with the coordinate basis and its finite reconstruction theorem. Vanishing on each S e_i says Sᵀz=0, hence Sz=0 by symmetry.
3. The assumed annihilation gives φ(v)=z·v=0. The dual-annihilator criterion implies v∈W. This argument does not identify bilinear forms with quadratic forms and uses no division by two.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For S=0, the criterion gives v=0.
- For the alternating plane S=[[0,1],[1,0]] over F₂, every column lies in the image.

<a id="st5-symmetric-border-rank-in-image"></a>

### 5.188 The corner obstruction inside the image

For a field F and symmetric S in M_n(F), let x∈F^n, v=Sx, a∈F, and B=[[S,v],[vᵀ,a]] on F^n⊕F. Then rank B = rank S if a=x·Sx, and rank B = rank S+1 otherwise, equivalently rank S plus the indicator of a≠x·Sx.

**Hypotheses.** F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.

**Dependencies.** [The image obstruction for a symmetric border](#st5-symmetric-image-obstruction) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-image-obstruction`); `mathlib:Matrix.fromBlocks`; `mathlib:Matrix.rank`; `mathlib:LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker`; `mathlib:LinearEquiv.finrank_eq`; `mathlib:Module.finrank_prod`; `mathlib:Module.finrank_fin_fun`

**Sources.** [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), printed p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). Expands the rank-preserving and rank-one-jump fibers; replaces generalized-inverse notation by an arbitrary preimage with a proved invariant corner value.

**Proof route.**

1. Put c=a−x·Sx. The invertible coordinate change (y,t)↦(y+tx,t) identifies ker B with ker S × {t∈F : ct=0}. Indeed B(y,t)=0 is equivalent to S(y+tx)=0 and ct=0, since vᵀy=xᵀSy.
2. When c=0 the second factor is F and adds one to the kernel dimension; when c≠0 it is zero-dimensional. Use native finrank invariance, the product-dimension identity and rank-nullity in dimension n+1.
3. The scalar x·Sx is independent of the chosen preimage of v: two preimages differ by an element of ker S and v annihilates that kernel.

**Acceptance checks.**

- S=0 and x=0 give rank B=0 for a=0 and rank B=1 for a≠0.
- For an alternating S over characteristic two, x·Sx=0; the same formula remains valid.

<a id="st5-symmetric-border-rank-outside-image"></a>

### 5.189 The rank-two jump outside the image

For a field F, a symmetric matrix S in M_n(F), v∈F^n outside im S, and every a∈F, the symmetric border B=[[S,v],[vᵀ,a]] has rank S+2.

**Hypotheses.** F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.

**Dependencies.** [The image obstruction for a symmetric border](#st5-symmetric-image-obstruction) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-image-obstruction`); `mathlib:Matrix.fromBlocks`; `mathlib:Matrix.rank`; `mathlib:Module.Dual.finrank_ker_add_one_of_ne_zero`; `mathlib:LinearMap.finrank_range_add_finrank_ker`; `mathlib:LinearEquiv.finrank_eq`; `mathlib:Module.finrank_fin_fun`

**Sources.** [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), printed p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). Supplies the kernel argument for the two-rank jump; it applies uniformly to alternating and nonalternating symmetric matrices.

**Proof route.**

1. The top block equation Sy+tv=0 forces t=0, since a nonzero t would put v in im S. Thus ker B is linearly isomorphic to {y∈ker S : v·y=0} via y↦(y,0).
2. The image-obstruction lemma says y↦v·y is a nonzero linear functional on ker S. Apply the native codimension-one kernel theorem to this restricted functional.
3. Rank-nullity for S and B now gives rank B=(n+1)−(dim ker S−1)=rank S+2. The nonzero restricted functional also ensures dim ker S≥1, so no negative dimension or truncated subtraction is used.

**Acceptance checks.**

- For n=1,S=0,v=1, the border [[0,1],[1,a]] has rank two for every a, including in characteristic two.
- An invertible S admits no column outside its image.

<a id="st5-symmetric-border-rank-fibers"></a>

### 5.190 The three symmetric-border rank fibers

Let F have q elements and S∈M_n(F) be symmetric of rank r. For every k≥0, the number of pairs (v,a)∈F^n×F for which [[S,v],[vᵀ,a]] has rank k is q^r if k=r; (q−1)q^r if k=r+1; q^(n+1)−q^(r+1) if k=r+2; and zero otherwise. The diagonal entry a is unrestricted.

**Hypotheses.** F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.

**Dependencies.** [The corner obstruction inside the image](#st5-symmetric-border-rank-in-image) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-border-rank-in-image`); [The rank-two jump outside the image](#st5-symmetric-border-rank-outside-image) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-border-rank-outside-image`); `mathlib:Matrix.rank`; `mathlib:Module.natCard_eq_pow_finrank`; `mathlib:Nat.card_congr`; `mathlib:Nat.card_sigma`; `mathlib:Matrix.rank_le_width`

**Sources.** [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), printed p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). Makes all four cases in Stanley’s border-count statement explicit, including the unrestricted corner and the vanishing outside ranks.

**Proof route.**

1. The image of S has q^r elements by the native finite-vector-space cardinality theorem and the definition of Matrix.rank.
2. For each column in the image the in-image rank lemma gives exactly one corner preserving rank and q−1 other corners increasing it by one. Count columns v, not preimages x; the invariant corner value was proved independent of the preimage.
3. There are q^n−q^r columns outside the image, and every one of their q corners increases rank by two. The outside-image rank lemma excludes all other ranks. The bound r≤n ensures each natural subtraction is exact. Sum the disjoint finite fibers.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The three counts sum to q^(n+1).
- For q=2,n=2,S=0 they are 1,1,6.
- For q=3,n=2,r=1 they are 3,6,18.
- If r=n the rank-two fiber is empty.

<a id="st5-symmetric-rank-count-recurrence"></a>

### 5.191 The symmetric rank-count recurrence

Let F have q elements, and let N_F(n,k) count symmetric matrices in M_n(F) of rank k, using the existing native finite subtype. Define the numerical coefficient c_q(n,r,k) to be q^r when k=r, (q−1)q^r when k=r+1, q^(n+1)−q^(r+1) when k=r+2, and zero otherwise. Then for every n,k≥0, N_F(n+1,k)=Σ_{r=0}^n N_F(n,r)c_q(n,r,k). This notation introduces no new carrier or separately defined library object.

**Hypotheses.** F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.

**Dependencies.** [The three symmetric-border rank fibers](#st5-symmetric-border-rank-fibers) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-border-rank-fibers`); `mathlib:Matrix.IsSymm`; `mathlib:Matrix.fromBlocks`; `mathlib:Nat.card_congr`; `mathlib:Nat.card_sigma`; `mathlib:Matrix.rank_reindex`; `mathlib:Matrix.rank_le_width`

**Sources.** [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), printed p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). A boundary-safe finite-sum form of equation (4.3), with a complete finite-fiber counting proof.

**Proof route.**

1. Reindex Fin(n+1) by Fin n plus a singleton. Reading the principal block, the extra column and the corner is a bijection from symmetric matrices to triples (S,v,a); writing the symmetric block matrix is its inverse.
2. Native reindexing preserves rank. Group the finite count first by the principal block S and then by its rank r, using the native dependent-sum cardinality theorem. Every rank lies in 0,…,n by the native width bound.
3. Substitute the border-fiber formula. The sum version states the boundary cases without negative rank indices or negative exponents; for 2≤k≤n+1 it becomes N_F(n+1,k)=q^kN_F(n,k)+(q−1)q^(k−1)N_F(n,k−1)+(q^(n+1)−q^(k−1))N_F(n,k−2).

**Acceptance checks.**

- N_F(0,0)=1 and N_F(0,k)=0 for k>0.
- At q=2 the first rows are (1), (1,1), (1,3,4), (1,7,28,28).
- At q=3,n=2 the row is (1,8,18).

<a id="st5-symmetric-rank-product-recurrence"></a>

### 5.192 The rational product recurrence

For natural q≥2 and s,t≥0, let P_q(s,t)=[∏_{i=1}^{⌊t/2⌋} q^(2i)/(q^(2i)−1)]·∏_{i=0}^{t−1}(q^(s−i)−1), interpreted in ℚ; natural s−i is truncated at zero. Thus P_q(s,0)=1 and P_q(s,t)=0 for t>s. With c_q(n,r,k) as in symmetric-rank-count-recurrence, P_q(n+1,k)=Σ_{r=0}^n P_q(n,r)c_q(n,r,k) for all n,k≥0. P is local mathematical notation for the displayed expression, not a new library definition.

**Hypotheses.** q,n,k are natural numbers with q ≥ 2.

**Dependencies.** Only the coefficient and elementary algebra conventions fixed above.

**Sources.** [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), printed p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). Writes out the parity algebra behind Stanley’s instruction to check that (4.2) solves (4.3), including every boundary case.

**Proof route.**

1. All denominators q^(2i)−1 are nonzero since i≥1 and q≥2. Empty products give the k=0 case. For k=1 use q(q^n−1)+(q−1)=q^(n+1)−1, with the empty-size boundary included.
2. For 2≤k≤n+1 put D=P_q(n,k−2), a=q^(k−1), t=q^(n−k+2). Cancel the common nonzero D. If k is even put C=qa/(qa−1). The ratios P_q(n,k)/D, P_q(n,k−1)/D and P_q(n+1,k)/D are respectively C(t−1)(t/q−1), t−1 and C(at−1)(t−1). The recurrence reduces to qa·C(t−1)(t/q−1)+(q−1)a(t−1)+a(t−1)=C(at−1)(t−1).
3. If k is odd, k≥3; put C=a/(a−1). The same three ratios are C(t−1)(t/q−1), C(t−1) and C(at−1)(t−1). The reduced identity is qa·C(t−1)(t/q−1)+(q−1)a·C(t−1)+a(t−1)=C(at−1)(t−1). Both identities follow after multiplying by their displayed nonzero denominators and ordinary polynomial algebra.
4. When k=n+2 the only possibly contributing term is r=n, whose coefficient q^(n+1)−q^(n+1) is zero. For k>n+2 there are no contributing terms. The factor with i=s makes every P_q(s,k) with k>s vanish, so these cases agree with the left side. Cast the natural coefficients to ℚ using r≤n before distributing subtraction.

**Acceptance checks.**

- The identity holds for all integer q≥2, independently of whether q is a prime power.
- The k=n+1 boundary has t=q and the P_q(n,k) factor vanishes; no division by q^0−1 occurs.
- At n=0, k=0,1 and k≥2 it yields 1,q−1 and 0.

<a id="st5-macwilliams-symmetric-rank-count"></a>

### 5.193 MacWilliams' count of symmetric matrices of given rank

For a finite field F with q elements and 0 ≤ k ≤ s, writing k = 2h or 2h + 1, the number of symmetric s × s matrices of rank k is N(s, k) = ∏_{i=1}^{h} q^{2i}/(q^{2i} − 1) · ∏_{i=0}^{k−1} (q^{s−i} − 1).

**Hypotheses.** F finite field with q elements; k ≤ s

**Dependencies.** [The symmetric rank-count recurrence](#st5-symmetric-rank-count-recurrence) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-rank-count-recurrence`); [The rational product recurrence](#st5-symmetric-rank-product-recurrence) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-rank-product-recurrence`); `mathlib:Matrix.rank_le_width`; `mathlib:Matrix.rank_zero`; `mathlib:Fintype.one_lt_card`

**Sources.** [P/safarji-rank-2025](#source-p-safarji-rank-2025), arXiv 2509.10332, §1, p. 3. Public restatement of MacWilliams (1969), Theorem 2 (the original is not publicly available). [P/koymans-stevenhagen-2022](#source-p-koymans-stevenhagen-2022), arXiv 2201.13424v1, proof of Theorem 7.13, p. 74. KP's use of MacWilliams (item /207). [P/stanley-kontsevich-1998](#source-p-stanley-kontsevich-1998), §4, First Proof (J. MacWilliams), p.355, equations (4.2)–(4.3). Public recurrence proof now decomposed into image obstruction, border ranks, fiber counting, and explicit product algebra.

**Proof route.**

1. Use the native subtype count N_F(n,k), with N_F(0,0)=1 and N_F(0,k)=0 for k>0: the empty matrix is unique and its image has dimension zero. For k>n the count is zero by the native rank-width bound.
2. The characteristic-free symmetric-rank-count-recurrence gives every next row from the preceding row; its finite sum also covers k=0,1 and k>n+1.
3. The rational product has the same initial row and satisfies symmetric-rank-product-recurrence. Induction on n, simultaneously for every k, equates the natural count cast to ℚ with the product.
4. Specialize to k≤s and write k=2h or 2h+1 to obtain the stated product. Characteristic two uses precisely the same border kernels; alternating matrices are included with their unrestricted symmetric-matrix companions.

**Acceptance checks.**

- q = 2, s = 2: N = 1, 3, 4 for k = 0, 1, 2.
- Exhaustive enumeration over F_2 for s ≤ 4 agrees with the formula (carried out in this blueprint's preparation).
- Exact enumeration agrees over F₂ through size 5, F₃ through size 4 and F₄,F₅,F₇,F₈ through size 3.
- The empty-size count is one at rank zero and zero at positive ranks; the characteristic-two alternating plane is included.

**Interface qualification.** The recurrence proof is supplied by six explicit lemma nodes, using the public Stanley 1998 account and native linear algebra. MacWilliams 1969 itself remains unread. The product theorem is a plan; no implementation is claimed.

<a id="st5-limit-of-the-symmetric-kernel-law"></a>

### 5.194 The limit of P_Sym(r, n) with an explicit rate

Over F_2, for every n ≥ 0: lim_{r→∞} P_Sym(r, n) = P_Sym(∞, n) := ∏_{j≥0}(1 − 2^{−(2j+1)}) / ∏_{i=1}^{n}(2^i − 1), and |P_Sym(r, n) − P_Sym(∞, n)| ≤ 2^{n+1−r} for all r ≥ 1. The limits sum to 1.

**Hypotheses.** n ∈ ℕ; r ≥ 1

**Dependencies.** [MacWilliams' count of symmetric matrices of given rank](#st5-macwilliams-symmetric-rank-count) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/macwilliams-symmetric-rank-count`); [The kernel law P_Sym(r, n) of uniformly random symmetric matrices](#st5-symmetric-matrix-kernel-law) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/symmetric-matrix-kernel-law`); `mathlib:tsum_geometric_of_lt_one`

**Sources.** [P/koymans-stevenhagen-2022](#source-p-koymans-stevenhagen-2022), arXiv 2201.13424v1, Theorem 7.13, p. 74. The limit lim_s P_Sym(s, n) whose existence and rate this node supplies (item /207; the displayed theorem is ST.3's).

**Proof route.**

1. If n>r, the finite kernel mass is zero and the target limit lies in [0,1], while 2^{n+1−r}≥1, so the stated bound is immediate. Assume henceforth n≤r. By ST.5/macwilliams-symmetric-rank-count with k = r − n = 2h or 2h + 1: P_Sym(r, n) = 2^{−n(n+1)/2} ∏_{i=1}^{h}(1 − 2^{−2i})^{−1} ∏_{j=n+1}^{r}(1 − 2^{−j}) (the exponent kr − k(k−1)/2 − r(r+1)/2 simplifies to −n(n+1)/2).
2. Letting r → ∞: P_Sym(∞, n) = 2^{−n(n+1)/2}∏_{i≥1}(1 − 2^{−2i})^{−1}∏_{j≥n+1}(1 − 2^{−j}) = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j})/∏_{i=1}^{n}(2^i − 1).
3. Rate: P_Sym(r, n) = P_Sym(∞, n)·R with R = ∏_{i>h}(1 − 2^{−2i})/∏_{j>r}(1 − 2^{−j}); since 2h + 2 ≥ r − n + 1, 1 − (2/3)2^{n−r} ≤ R ≤ 1 + 2^{1−r}, and P_Sym(∞, n) ≤ 1. Explicitly, the omitted even-factor tail is at most (4/3)2^{−2h−2}≤(2/3)2^{n−r}; the denominator tail is at least 1−2^{−r}, and (1−2^{−r})⁻¹≤1+2^{1−r} for r≥1.
4. Σ_n P_Sym(∞, n) = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j}) Σ_n 2^{−n(n+1)/2}/∏_{i≤n}(1 − 2^{−i}) = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j})∏_{i≥1}(1 + 2^{−i}) = 1 (Euler).

**Acceptance checks.**

- P_Sym(∞, 0) = α = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j}) ≈ 0.41942, the constant of Stevenhagen's conjecture.
- r = 2, n = 0: |1/2 − 0.4194| ≈ 0.081 ≤ 1/2; numerically the ratio of the error to 2^{n+1−r} stays below 0.17 for r ≤ 40.

<a id="st5-refinement-lc-quadratic"></a>

### 5.195 Nondegenerate locally compact quadratic module

For a locally compact Hausdorff topological abelian group V, a continuous QuadraticMap ℤ V (ℝ/ℤ) q has a polar adjoint V ≃ₜ+ Hom_cont(V,ℝ/ℤ), with compact-open topology; its value on (x,y) is q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y). Store this homeomorphic additive equivalence, not just injectivity. Second countability is imposed on the measure theorem, not on the carrier.

**Hypotheses.** V is locally compact, Hausdorff and a topological abelian group.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:QuadraticMap`; `mathlib:QuadraticMap.polar`; `mathlib:QuadraticMap.polarBilin`; `mathlib:ContinuousAddEquiv`; `mathlib:ContinuousAddMonoidHom`

**Sources.** [S5/pr](#source-s5-pr), Definition 2.13 and preceding nondegeneracy convention, pp. 8–9. For a locally compact Hausdorff topological abelian group V, a continuous QuadraticMap ℤ V (ℝ/ℤ) q has a polar adjoint V ≃ₜ+ Hom_cont(V,ℝ/ℤ), with compact-open topology; its value on (x,y) is q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y). Store this homeomorphic additive equivalence, not just injectivity. Second countability is imposed on the measure theorem, not on the carrier.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.orthogonal` (data): For an additive subgroup W, W⊥ consists of x with polar(q)(x,y)=0 for every y∈W.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.mem_orthogonal` (characterisation): Membership in W⊥ is exactly the displayed vanishing condition.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.polar_formula` (compatibility): The adjoint evaluates to q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y), agreeing with QuadraticMap.polar.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.polar_self` (simp): The value on (x,x) is 2q(x), including at p=2.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.adjoint_bijective` (equivalence): The adjoint is bijective onto all continuous characters.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.orthogonal_antitone` (functoriality): W≤U implies U⊥≤W⊥.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_zero` (degenerate): q(0)=0.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_diagonal` (compatibility): polar(q)(x,x)=2q(x).
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_zero_form` (non-example): If q is the zero quadratic map, V is a subsingleton.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_surjective_dual` (characterisation): Every continuous additive character is the polar character of some x.

**Proof route.**

1. Use the existing quadratic-map and continuous-homomorphism carriers.
2. Record the adjoint equation as a constraint on the actual topological additive equivalence.
3. Obtain orthogonal subgroups from the kernel equations of the polar bilinear map.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Retain every stated hypothesis and the exact normalization and convergence mode.
- All named API statements and all discriminating tests below must hold with these carriers and conventions.

**Consumers.** PR Theorem 2.19 — The self-dual topology controls the finite reductions and their inverse limit.; PR Theorem 4.13 — The adelic cup-product quadratic map is an instance.

<a id="st5-refinement-weak-metabolic"></a>

### 5.196 Weakly metabolic compact-open subgroup

Given locally compact quadratic data D and an additive subgroup W≤V, weak metabolicity means that W is compact and open, q vanishes on W, and W⊥=W. Vanishing of the polar form alone is insufficient, particularly at 2.

**Hypotheses.** D is as in the locally compact quadratic carrier.

**Dependencies.** [Nondegenerate locally compact quadratic module](#st5-refinement-lc-quadratic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/refinement-lc-quadratic`)

**Sources.** [S5/pr](#source-s5-pr), Definition 2.14, p. 9. Given locally compact quadratic data D and an additive subgroup W≤V, weak metabolicity means that W is compact and open, q vanishes on W, and W⊥=W. Vanishing of the polar form alone is insufficient, particularly at 2.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.weaklyMetabolic_iff` (characterisation): Equivalent to the four explicit conditions in the definition.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.weaklyMetabolic_isotropic` (projection): q(x)=0 for every x∈W.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.weaklyMetabolic_self_orthogonal` (projection): The computed orthogonal subgroup equals W.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.weaklyMetabolic_intersection_open` (structure): The intersection of two such distinguished subgroups is open.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_top` (degenerate): If the whole self-dual space is weakly metabolic, V is a subsingleton.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_nonsingular` (non-example): An element x∈W with q(x)≠0 precludes weak metabolicity.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.test_finite` (compatibility): For finite discrete V the predicate reduces exactly to quadratic vanishing and W⊥=W.

**Proof route.**

1. Define the predicate by compactness, openness, quadratic vanishing and computed self-annihilation.

### 5.197 Closed maximal isotropic subgroup space

I(V) consists of closed additive subgroups Z≤V on which q vanishes and with Z⊥=Z. It is the subtype of actual subgroups satisfying these equations. Its probability topology is supplied by finite quotient reductions; it is not the discrete topology on a countable list of subgroup names.

**Hypotheses.** D is locally compact quadratic data.

**Dependencies.** [Nondegenerate locally compact quadratic module](#st5-refinement-lc-quadratic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/refinement-lc-quadratic`); [Weakly metabolic compact-open subgroup](#st5-refinement-weak-metabolic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/refinement-weak-metabolic`)

**Sources.** [S5/pr](#source-s5-pr), Paragraph preceding Theorem 2.19 and Theorem 2.19(c), p. 9. I(V) consists of closed additive subgroups Z≤V on which q vanishes and with Z⊥=Z. It is the subtype of actual subgroups satisfying these equations. Its probability topology is supplied by finite quotient reductions; it is not the discrete topology on a countable list of subgroup names.

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.maximalIsotropics_isotropic` (projection): For a point Z and x in its underlying subgroup, q(x)=0.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.LCQuadraticData.maximalIsotropics_self_orthogonal` (projection): Each point equals its computed annihilator.

**Checks.**

2. Construct the inverse-limit topology only after the finite quotient comparison.

### 5.198 Parity-coupled product of prime Selmer laws

For k selected prime factors and weights w_i(d), define the joint weight on d∈ℕ^k to be 1 when k=0; for k>0 it is 2^(k−1)∏_i w_i(d_i) when all d_i have the same parity, and zero otherwise. Each marginal must have total even and total odd mass 1/2. The k=0 carrier is the singleton function space, corresponding to n=1.

**Hypotheses.** The prime laws are nonnegative and summable; each parity has mass 1/2.

**Dependencies.** [Parity equidistribution and parity-conditioned moments of the Poonen–Rains law](#st5-poonen-rains-parity) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-parity`); [The Poonen–Rains distribution X_{Sel_p}](#st5-poonen-rains-distribution) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/poonen-rains-distribution`)

**Sources.** [S5/pr](#source-s5-pr), Conjecture 1.4(a), p. 3, with the n=1 convention separated. Each marginal must have total even and total odd mass 1/2. The k=0 carrier is the singleton function space, corresponding to n=1.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight_empty` (simp): The weight on the unique empty rank vector is 1.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight_single` (compatibility): For k=1 the joint weight is precisely w₀(d₀).
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight_mixed` (characterisation): If two coordinates have different parity, the joint weight is zero.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight_nonneg` (structure): Nonnegative marginals give nonnegative joint weights.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight_total` (structure): Under nonnegativity, summability and half-mass of each parity, the joint weights are summable and sum to 1.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight.test_two_equal` (computation): For two factors and rank vector (0,0), the weight is 2w₀(0)w₁(0).
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight.test_two_mixed` (non-example): For two factors and rank vector (0,1), the weight is zero.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.parityCoupledWeight.test_empty` (degenerate): The empty rank vector has weight 1.

**Proof route.**

2. Mix the two common-parity conditional product laws with equal weight.
3. Treat the empty product directly, rather than applying the nonempty normalization.

### 5.199 Wood grid-separating product

For a prime p and an antitone nonnegative integer vector b of length m+1, set S_i(b)=∑_{j≤i}b_j. Define H_b(z)=∏_{j≥b₀+1}(1−z₀/p^j) · ∏_{i=1}^m ∏_{j=S_i(b)+1}^{S_{i−1}(b)+b_{i−1}}(1−z_i/p^j). Empty finite products are 1. H_b is entire, vanishes at z_i=p^{S_i(f)} for every antitone f lexicographically greater than b, and is nonzero at the grid point of b.

**Hypotheses.** p is prime; b is antitone; the coordinate length is positive.

**Dependencies.** `mathlib:tprod`; `mathlib:HasProd`

**Sources.** [S5/wood](#source-s5-wood), Lemma 8.1 and proof, pp. 28–29. For a prime p and an antitone nonnegative integer vector b of length m+1, set S_i(b)=∑_{j≤i}b_j. Define H_b(z)=∏_{j≥b₀+1}(1−z₀/p^j) · ∏_{i=1}^m ∏_{j=S_i(b)+1}^{S_{i−1}(b)+b_{i−1}}(1−z_i/p^j). Empty finite products are 1. H_b is entire, vanishes at z_i=p^{S_i(f)} for every antitone f lexicographically greater than b, and is nonzero at the grid point of b.

**API.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator_zero` (simp): At z=0 the value is 1.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator_one_variable` (compatibility): When m=0 only the one-variable infinite product remains.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator_upper` (characterisation): At the grid point of any antitone f lexicographically greater than b, the value is zero.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator_diagonal` (characterisation): At the grid point of the antitone b itself, the value is nonzero.

**Checks.**

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator.test_origin` (degenerate): For m=0,p=2,b=0,z=0 the value is 1.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator.test_upper` (computation): For m=0,p=2,b=0,z=2 the value is zero.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator.test_diagonal` (non-example): For m=0,p=2,b=0,z=1 the value is nonzero.
- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.woodGridSeparator.test_second_coordinate` (computation): For m=1,p=2,b=(2,0),z=(4,8) the finite second-coordinate factor vanishes.

**Proof route.**

1. Use the infinite product only in coordinate zero, and finite polynomials in the other coordinates.
2. At the first larger coordinate of f, identify a vanishing factor.
3. Use absolute convergence and nonvanishing of all factors at b to separate the diagonal.

<a id="st5-refinement-lc-finite-reductions"></a>

### 5.200 Finite reductions of a locally compact quadratic module

For second-countable nondegenerate locally compact quadratic (V,q) with a weakly metabolic W, compact-open q-isotropic subgroups X form a countable directed system ordered by reverse inclusion. X⊥/X is a finite nondegenerate quadratic module. The reduction of Z∈I(V) is ((Z∩X⊥)+X)/X, a maximal isotropic subgroup; reductions compose. If a cofinal decreasing sequence X_j has intersection zero, I(V) is bijective to the inverse limit of these finite isotropic spaces.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions in the statement are hypotheses.

**Dependencies.** [Nondegenerate locally compact quadratic module](#st5-refinement-lc-quadratic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/refinement-lc-quadratic`); [Weakly metabolic compact-open subgroup](#st5-refinement-weak-metabolic) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/refinement-weak-metabolic`); [Closed maximal isotropic subgroup space](#st5-refinement-maximal-isotropics) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/refinement-maximal-isotropics`); `tauceti:TauCeti.FiniteQuadraticModule`; [Reduction of maximal isotropic subspaces to X^⊥/X](#st5-isotropic-reduction-map) (`ArithmeticStatistics:ST.5/isotropic-reduction-map`); `ArithmeticGaloisDuality:D7`

**Sources.** [S5/pr](#source-s5-pr), Theorem 2.19(a)–(c) and proof, pp. 9–10. X⊥/X is a finite nondegenerate quadratic module. The reduction of Z∈I(V) is ((Z∩X⊥)+X)/X, a maximal isotropic subgroup; reductions compose. If a cofinal decreasing sequence X_j has intersection zero, I(V) is bijective to the inverse limit of these finite isotropic spaces.

**Intended theorem name.** `ArithmeticStatistics.ST5.lc_finite_reductions`.

**Proof route.**

1. Use compact-open annihilator duality to show finiteness and nondegeneracy of X⊥/X.
2. Reuse the finite quadratic carrier and finite isotropic reduction already owned by IntegralLattices and the parent.
3. Choose a countable cofinal system inside W; lift compatible subgroups and prove closure, isotropy and self-annihilation.

**Acceptance checks.**

- Retain every stated hypothesis and the exact normalization and convergence mode.
- In a finite discrete metabolic space, X=0 recovers the original finite maximal-isotropic set and the reduction map is the identity.

**Interface qualification.** Finite quadratic reductions, their transition maps, probability topology, or fppf/theta cohomology interfaces are not exported together at the pin; see G-lc-duality and G-fppf-theta.

### 5.201 Canonical probability on maximal isotropic subgroups

Assume additionally that p is prime and pV=0. The inverse-limit topology on I(V) carries a unique Borel probability whose pushforward to every finite quadratic reduction is the uniform maximal-isotropic law. This measure is invariant under every continuous quadratic isometry of V. Second countability and the inverse-limit Borel structure are part of the assertion.

### 5.202 Almost-sure discrete isotropic intersection

Under the preceding hypotheses a random Z∈I(V) is discrete almost surely and Z∩W is finite almost surely. If V has infinite F_p-dimension, dim_Fp(Z∩W) has exactly the parent Poonen–Rains law. A finite-dimensional V instead has the parent finite intersection law, not its infinite limit.

<a id="st5-refinement-sha-one-vanishing"></a>

### 5.204 Vanishing of the everywhere locally trivial finite-module group

For a global field k, Sha¹(k,M)=ker(H¹(k,M)→∏_v H¹(k_v,M)). It vanishes for constant cyclic Z/n modules, permutation modules and their direct summands. For a finite F_p-module M it also vanishes when every Sylow p-subgroup of Aut(M) is cyclic. In particular Sha¹(k,E[p])=0 for elliptic E and p≠char(k); for an odd-degree hyperelliptic Jacobian with char(k)≠2, Sha¹(k,J[2])=0.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions in the statement are hypotheses.

**Dependencies.** `SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L0`; `ArithmeticGaloisDuality:D7`

### 5.205 Selmer group as an adelic quadratic intersection

Let k be global, A/k abelian, and λ:A→Â a self-dual isogeny of odd degree or induced by a symmetric line bundle. The theta-group quadratic maps into local Brauer groups, followed by invariants in R/Z, have polarization equal to the negative Weil-cup pairing (without division by 2) and make V=∏′_v H¹(k_v,A[λ]) a second-countable weakly metabolic locally compact quadratic module. <a id="st5-refinement-joint-parity-moments"></a>

### 5.206 Moments of the common-parity product law

For k≥1 prime laws w_i with half even/odd mass, assume for every m≥1 each parity-restricted sum Σ_{d≡ε(2)}w_i(d)p_i^(md) equals (1/2)∏_{j=1}^m(p_i^j+1). The normalized common-parity law then has m-th cardinality moment ∏_i∏_{j=1}^m(p_i^j+1). Its first moment is ∏_i(p_i+1)=σ(∏p_i) for distinct primes. For k=0 the moment is 1.

**Hypotheses.** All parameter restrictions in the statement are hypotheses.

<a id="st5-refinement-squarefree-selmer-conjecture"></a>

### 5.207 Joint squarefree Selmer conjecture

Fix a global field k and a squarefree integer n>1. In the source’s coefficient-model family from Conjecture 1.1, use short Weierstrass coefficients a,b in k of height bounded by B when char(k) is not 2 or 3, and the source’s long Weierstrass equations in characteristics 2 and 3; discard singular models and let B tend to infinity. The joint dimensions dim_Fp Sel_p(E), p|n, are conjectured to have the common-parity product law. Separately, every positive m-th cardinality moment of Sel_n is conjectured to tend to ∏_{p|n}∏_{j=1}^m(p^j+1). Distribution convergence alone does not establish these unbounded moments. At n=1 the group is trivial. The denominator counts these coefficient models, not minimal integral Q-isomorphism classes ordered by invariant height.

**Hypotheses.** This is a stated conjectural proposition, not an established arithmetic limit.

### 5.211 Smooth split orthogonal Grassmannian over Z

For n≥0 the subfunctor of Gr(n,2n) consisting of rank-n locally direct-summand subbundles on which q(x,y)=Σ_i x_i y_i vanishes is represented by a smooth projective Z-scheme OGr_n of relative dimension n(n−1)/2. ### 5.212 Two components distinguished by intersection parity

For n>0, OGr_n is the disjoint union of two isomorphic Z-schemes with geometrically integral fibres, distinguished over every field by parity of dim(Z∩W) for the standard W. Two points Z,Z′ lie on the same component iff dim(Z∩Z′)≡n mod2. For n=0 there is one point, with an empty odd component.

### 5.214 Dimensions of fixed-parity intersection loci

For 0≤r≤n the locus S_(n,r)⊂OGr_n of points with dim(Z∩W)≥r and dim(Z∩W)≡r mod2 is closed and has relative dimension (n−r)(n+r−1)/2. Its exact-rank open stratum has this dimension. Fixed-rank random models use the intrinsic measure on S_(n,r); when r≥2 they cannot be defined by conditioning the ambient OGr law on a positive-probability rank-r event.
